heading: Dockingbird
summary: Dockingbird runs Claude Code and Codex side by side on your git repo, each in its own container.
text:
Dockingbird runs Claude Code and Codex side by side on your git repo, each in its own container.
Agents never overwrite each other and never touch your Mac.
Each agent works on its own copy of your branch, and its work comes back to you as commits through `dockingbird sync`.
Zeusfyi makes it, and it runs on an Apple silicon Mac or on arm64 Linux.

heading: Dockingbird > Prerequisites
summary: Dockingbird needs four tools and a license key.
text:
Dockingbird needs four tools and a license key. [Prerequisites](docs/getting-started/prerequisites.md) gives the check for each.

- An Apple silicon Mac or arm64 Linux. Intel Macs, x86 Linux and Windows are not supported.
- Docker Desktop, which includes the buildx plugin. Docker Engine on Linux needs Docker's `docker-buildx-plugin` package.
- [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). On a Mac, `brew install uv` installs it.
- git at `/usr/bin/git`.
- A license key from your purchase email, or no key and a trial.

heading: Dockingbird > Install
summary: On a Mac, copy the key from your purchase email, then run this line.
text:
On a Mac, copy the key from your purchase email, then run this line.
It hands the key to uv as the index's password, so the key never reaches your shell history or a command line.

```bash
UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_USERNAME=license UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD="$(pbpaste)" uv tool install dockingbird --index zeusfyi=https://license.zeus.fyi/simple/
```

On Linux, read the key with `read -rs`, which does not echo it, and clear it afterwards.

```bash
read -rs UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD
UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_USERNAME=license UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD="$UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD" uv tool install dockingbird --index zeusfyi=https://license.zeus.fyi/simple/
unset UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD
```

Check the install with `dockingbird --version`, then run `dockingbird license activate` to give this computer its seat.
Never run a bare `uv tool install dockingbird`. That name on PyPI is not this product.
The index serves an active license only, so a trial cannot install from it.
[Install](docs/getting-started/install.md) has the details and the failures.

heading: Dockingbird > Use it
summary: Every command explains itself with `dockingbird -h`, and `-h` after a command shows that command's help.
text:
| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `cd your-repo` then `dockingbird init` | Makes the repo ready: project file, rules, example swarm, skills |
| `dockingbird claude` | Starts Claude Code on the repo you are in, in its own container |
| `dockingbird codex` | Starts Codex on the same repo, in another terminal |
| `dockingbird status` | Shows who is working on what, and what needs you |
| `dockingbird sync` | Takes the agents' commits and sends them yours |
| `dockingbird login claude` | Signs in again; `dockingbird login claude --api-key` uses an API key instead |
| `dockingbird update` | Gets the latest Dockingbird, Claude Code and Codex |
| `dockingbird clean` | Frees disk space |
| `dockingbird stop` | Turns everything off; nothing is lost |
| `dockingbird egress` | Shows or sets what agents can reach |
| `dockingbird start "fix the flaky test"` | Hands an agent a task; it works without a terminal |
| `dockingbird wait claude-1` | Shows the agent's next message as it comes |
| `dockingbird inbox` | Lists what waits for you, numbered |
| `dockingbird read 1` | Shows one message and the files it names |
| `dockingbird send claude-1 "yes"` | Answers a question, or sends a new task |
| `dockingbird results claude-1` | Saves the files the agent attached |
| `dockingbird watch claude-1` | Shows the agent's browser, when its config asks for one |
| `dockingbird config add agents/triage.toml` | Adds a command of your own, usable in every repo |
| `dockingbird config list` | Lists your configs and this repo's |
| `dockingbird trust --off` | Keeps this repo's own settings, hooks and MCP servers off |
| `dockingbird license activate` | Asks for your key, hidden, and takes a seat for this computer |
| `dockingbird license trial` | Starts this computer's trial instead |
| `dockingbird license status` | Shows the plan, its seats and the day the term ends |
| `dockingbird clean --all` | Removes everything Dockingbird made |
| `uv tool uninstall dockingbird` | Removes the command; run it after `clean --all` |

Every command explains itself with `dockingbird -h`, and `-h` after a command shows that command's help.

heading: Dockingbird > How the first start works
summary: There is nothing to configure.
text:
There is nothing to configure.
The first `dockingbird claude` checks your branch, builds the image, starts Dockingbird and copies the branch for the agents.
A branch holding files the agents do not take is refused in seconds, with each file named and nothing set up.
Such files are a symlink leaving the repo, a submodule or a Git LFS file.
The build takes about 5 minutes and downloads about 1 GB, once.
Each tool then uses the login already on your Mac, or shows a sign-in link once, inside Docker.
Every agent works in its own container. Nothing on your Mac is mounted into an agent unless you connect a folder by name.
To leave an agent working, close its window.
Dockingbird turns itself off after 30 minutes with no agent, and the next command turns it back on.

heading: Dockingbird > Exit codes
summary: Exit codes are 0 for done, 1 for a problem with its next step printed, and 2 for a usage error.
text:
Exit codes are 0 for done, 1 for a problem with its next step printed, and 2 for a usage error.
`dockingbird claude` and `dockingbird codex` exit with the tool's own status.
[Exit codes](docs/reference/integration/exit-codes.md) lists every code.

heading: Dockingbird quickstart
summary: This page takes you from a fresh computer to a running agent, then through the daily loop and a clean uninstall.
text:
This page takes you from a fresh computer to a running agent, then through the daily loop and a clean uninstall.
Each step ends with the line Dockingbird prints when it worked, and each step links to its own page for detail.

Dockingbird runs Claude Code and Codex side by side on your git repo, each in its own container.
They never overwrite each other or touch your Mac, and their work comes back to you as commits.

heading: Dockingbird quickstart > Before you start
summary: You need all five of these.
text:
You need all five of these. [Prerequisites](getting-started/prerequisites.md) gives the check for each.

- An Apple silicon Mac or arm64 Linux. Intel Macs, x86 Linux and Windows are not supported.
- Docker Desktop, which includes the buildx plugin. Docker Engine on Linux needs the `docker-buildx-plugin` package.
- [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). On a Mac, `brew install uv` installs it.
- git at `/usr/bin/git`.
- A license key from your purchase email, or no key and a trial.

heading: Dockingbird quickstart > 1. Install
summary: Copy the key from your purchase email, then run this line on a Mac.
text:
Copy the key from your purchase email, then run this line on a Mac.
It hands the key to uv as the index's password, so the key never reaches your shell history or a command line.

```bash
UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_USERNAME=license UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD="$(pbpaste)" uv tool install dockingbird --index zeusfyi=https://license.zeus.fyi/simple/
dockingbird --version
dockingbird completion --install
```

On Linux, `read -rs UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD` reads the key without echo, and `unset` clears it afterwards.
[Install](getting-started/install.md) shows the whole Linux sequence.

Never run a bare `uv tool install dockingbird`. That name on PyPI is not this product, so the line above must carry `--index`.

Done when `dockingbird --version` prints a line that starts with `dockingbird` and a version.
`dockingbird completion --install` then prints "Open a new terminal." for tab completion.
If `dockingbird` is not found, run `uv tool update-shell` and open a new terminal.

heading: Dockingbird quickstart > 2. Activate
summary: Dockingbird asks for the key and does not show it.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license activate
```

Dockingbird asks for the key and does not show it. `pbpaste | dockingbird license activate` also works.
A key typed on the command line is refused with exit 2.
No key? `dockingbird license trial` starts this computer's trial, but a trial cannot install from the index or update.

One seat is one person, who may link up to three computers.
[Activate](getting-started/activate.md) explains seats, the trial and the refusals.

Done when Dockingbird prints these two lines.

```text
This computer is activated: {plan}, {seats}, {term}.
You use Dockingbird under its terms: {link}
```

If every computer of the license is linked, the message is `LICENSE_SEATS_FULL` and it names the command that frees one.

heading: Dockingbird quickstart > 3. Make a repository ready
summary: `dockingbird init` writes `.dockingbird/project.toml`, the rules file, an example swarm, and the skills and agent definitions of this release.
text:
```bash
cd your-repo
dockingbird init
git add .dockingbird .agents .claude && git commit
```

`dockingbird init` writes `.dockingbird/project.toml`, the rules file, an example swarm, and the skills and agent definitions of this release.
Agents start from your last commit, so commit these files before the first start.
Without an org login, `init` says the project is not in an organisation's store and still exits 0.
Add `--no-register` to skip that line.

Done when the first line reads "Set up {project} for Dockingbird {release}: the project file, its rules,". The next lines tell you to keep the files in git.
Run in a folder that is no git repo, it stops with `INIT_NOT_A_CHECKOUT`.
[First run](getting-started/first-run.md) lists what `init` writes.

heading: Dockingbird quickstart > 4. First run
summary: The first start checks your branch, builds the image, starts Dockingbird and copies the branch for the agents.
text:
```bash
dockingbird claude
```

The first start checks your branch, builds the image, starts Dockingbird and copies the branch for the agents.
The build takes about 5 minutes and downloads about 1 GB, once.
The first start of each tool also fetches that tool's latest release.
Dockingbird refuses a branch holding a symlink that leaves the repo, a submodule or a Git LFS file. It does so in seconds, names each file, and sets nothing up.
Then it starts `claude-1`.

Claude shows a sign-in link once. Open it on this Mac, sign in, and paste the code back.
Codex works the same way with `dockingbird codex`: open its link and enter the one-time code.
With no Claude or ChatGPT account, quit the sign-in. Then run `dockingbird login claude --api-key` or `dockingbird login codex --api-key`.

The repo's own settings, hooks and MCP servers load in the agent, and Claude does not ask whether to trust `/work/your-repo`.
For a repo you do not control, run `dockingbird trust --off` in it.
To leave the agent working, close the window. A bare `dockingbird claude` in that repo reconnects to it.
Dockingbird turns itself off after 30 minutes with no agent, and the next command turns it back on.

Done when the start prints these lines and Claude opens its sign-in.

```text
Copying your-repo (main) for the agents ({size}) ... done ({elapsed})
Starting claude-1 on your-repo (main). Claude will show a sign-in link:
open it on this Mac, sign in, then paste the code here. Only this once.
```

Run as many agents as you like, each in its own terminal, in as many repos as you like.

heading: Dockingbird quickstart > 5. Every day
summary: - `status` shows who is working on what and what needs you.
text:
```bash
dockingbird status
dockingbird sync
dockingbird stop
```

- `status` shows who is working on what and what needs you. Its first line reads "Dockingbird {version}, signed in to Claude and Codex".
- `sync` takes the agents' commits and sends yours. It prints "Updated your {branch} to {head}." for commits taken and "up to date." when nothing moved.
- `stop` turns everything off and prints "Dockingbird is off until you next use it." Nothing is lost.
- Agents start from your last commit, never from uncommitted edits, and their work reaches you only through `dockingbird sync`.
- `sync` never rewrites history. It keeps your uncommitted edits, and when both sides have new commits it offers to merge.
- To undo an agent's commit, make a commit of your own with `git revert COMMIT`, then run `dockingbird sync`.
- A one-shot works too: `dockingbird claude -p "Summarize the open TODOs"` prints only the answer.
- `dockingbird login claude` signs in again, `dockingbird update` gets the latest versions, and `dockingbird clean` frees disk space.
- A second computer joins with `dockingbird fleet hosts set NAME --ssh DEST`, or with `--gcloud VM --zone ZONE --project PROJECT`. [Choose a topology](getting-started/choose-a-topology.md) compares the options.
- The GUI (`dockingbird ui`) is not yet available to customers, so use the terminal commands on this page.

heading: Dockingbird quickstart > 6. Delegate
summary: `start` hands an agent a task without a terminal.
text:
```bash
dockingbird start "Fix the flaky test"
dockingbird wait claude-1
dockingbird inbox
dockingbird read 1
dockingbird search "closed issues"
dockingbird send claude-1 "The new one"
dockingbird results claude-1
dockingbird stop claude-1
```

`start` hands an agent a task without a terminal. `wait` shows its next message as it comes.
`inbox` lists what waits for you. `read` opens one message and the files it names. `search` finds a message by its words.
`send` answers a question or sends a new task. `results` saves the files it attached. `stop claude-1` stops it, and its messages and results stay.
A question the agent asks also leads `dockingbird status` until you answer it.

Done when `start` prints "claude-1 started on your-repo (main)." and a thread line that names `dockingbird wait claude-1`.
`dockingbird inbox` prints "Nothing is waiting in your inbox." when no message waits.
[Delegating tasks](guides/delegating-tasks.md) has the full loop.

heading: Dockingbird quickstart > 7. Uninstall
summary: `clean --all` lists what it removes, then asks you to type `delete`.
text:
```bash
dockingbird clean --all
uv tool uninstall dockingbird
```

`clean --all` lists what it removes, then asks you to type `delete`. It gives this computer's seat back first.
Uninstalling first would leave Dockingbird's containers, volumes and image behind.
`clean --all` keeps one empty folder, `logs`, in the Dockingbird home, so a later start works while Docker Desktop still shares it.
Docker keeps the build cache of Dockingbird's image, shared with every other project's, and `docker builder prune` frees all of it.

Done when `clean --all` prints these lines.

```text
Removed everything Dockingbird made ({freed}). Your code is untouched.
To remove the command too: uv tool uninstall dockingbird
```

heading: Dockingbird quickstart > When it fails
summary: - [`DOCKER_NOT_INSTALLED`](troubleshooting.md#docker_not_installed) appears when no `docker` command exists.
text:
- [`DOCKER_NOT_INSTALLED`](troubleshooting.md#docker_not_installed) appears when no `docker` command exists. Install Docker Desktop, or Docker on Linux.
- [`HOME_NOT_EMPTY`](troubleshooting.md#home_not_empty) appears when the folder Dockingbird would use holds files it did not make. Unset `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` or point it at an empty folder.
- [`COMPLETION_ALREADY`](troubleshooting.md#completion_already) appears when you install completion a second time. Nothing is wrong.
- [`LICENSE_KEY_IN_ARGV`](troubleshooting.md#license_key_in_argv) appears when you type the key on the command line. Nothing ran, so run `dockingbird license activate` and paste the key.
- [`LICENSE_TRIAL_USED`](troubleshooting.md#license_trial_used) appears when this computer already had its trial. Activate it with a key.
- [`INIT_NOT_A_CHECKOUT`](troubleshooting.md#init_not_a_checkout) appears when `init` runs outside a git repo. Run it in your repo.
- [`INIT_INSIDE_HOME`](troubleshooting.md#init_inside_home) appears when `init` runs inside the Dockingbird home. Run it in your repo.
- [`SIGNIN_NEEDED`](troubleshooting.md#signin_needed) appears when the tool has no sign-in. Run `dockingbird claude` again, or use an API key.

Every command explains itself with `dockingbird -h`.
All messages are in [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md), and the [operator guide](operator-guide.md) has the rest.

heading: Prerequisites
summary: This page lists what a computer needs before Dockingbird installs, and the command that checks each item.
text:
This page lists what a computer needs before Dockingbird installs, and the command that checks each item.
When all four checks pass, go on to [install](install.md).

heading: Prerequisites > Before you start
summary: You need a terminal on the computer that will run Dockingbird, and a license key or a decision to use a trial.
text:
You need a terminal on the computer that will run Dockingbird, and a license key or a decision to use a trial.
The key arrives in your purchase email. [Activate](activate.md) covers the trial.

heading: Prerequisites > Supported computers
summary: Dockingbird runs on an Apple silicon Mac or on arm64 Linux.
text:
Dockingbird runs on an Apple silicon Mac or on arm64 Linux.
Intel Macs, x86 Linux and Windows are not supported.
The first start checks the platform before it builds anything.

heading: Prerequisites > 1. Docker
summary: Dockingbird runs every agent in a container and builds its own image, so Docker must answer.
text:
Dockingbird runs every agent in a container and builds its own image, so Docker must answer.

- On a Mac, install Docker Desktop. It shares your home folder by default, which Dockingbird needs, and it includes the buildx plugin.
- On Linux, install Docker Engine and Docker's `docker-buildx-plugin` package.

```bash
docker version
docker buildx version
```

Done when `docker version` answers without an error and `docker buildx version` prints the plugin's version.
Dockingbird starts Docker Desktop itself when it is stopped, so a stopped Docker Desktop is not a failure on a Mac.

heading: Prerequisites > 2. uv
summary: uv installs the `dockingbird` command from Zeusfyi's release index.
text:
uv installs the `dockingbird` command from Zeusfyi's release index.
On a Mac, `brew install uv` installs it. Other platforms follow the [uv documentation](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/).

```bash
uv --version
```

Done when uv prints its version.

heading: Prerequisites > 3. git
summary: Dockingbird looks for git at `/usr/bin/git`.
text:
Dockingbird looks for git at `/usr/bin/git`.
It works on a git repository and copies your branch for the agents, so the repo needs a commit on a branch.

```bash
git --version
```

Done when git prints its version.

heading: Prerequisites > 4. Disk space and network
summary: The first start builds the image on your computer, with no image to pull from a registry.
text:
The first start builds the image on your computer, with no image to pull from a registry.
It takes about 5 minutes and downloads about 1 GB, once.
The build also fills a folder of Ubuntu packages, `apt-pool`, inside the Dockingbird home, 441 MB once per pinned snapshot.
The home is `~/.local/share/dockingbird` unless `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` names another folder.
Docker keeps the build cache of Dockingbird's image, shared with every other project's, and `docker builder prune` frees all of it.

The first start of each tool, Claude Code and Codex, then fetches that tool's latest release.
Both downloads need a working network.

heading: Prerequisites > 5. A way to sign in the agents
summary: Claude Code and Codex each need a sign-in or an API key.
text:
Claude Code and Codex each need a sign-in or an API key.
Dockingbird reads the login Claude Code or Codex already uses on this computer, and keeps a copy.
Without one, the tool shows a sign-in link once at the first start, or you use an API key.
[First run](first-run.md) shows both routes.

heading: Prerequisites > When it fails
summary: - If there is no `docker` command, Dockingbird prints [`DOCKER_NOT_INSTALLED`](../troubleshooting.md#docker_not_installed).
text:
- If there is no `docker` command, Dockingbird prints [`DOCKER_NOT_INSTALLED`](../troubleshooting.md#docker_not_installed). Install Docker Desktop on a Mac, or Docker on Linux.
- Docker that has not started in time ends in [`DOCKER_NOT_RUNNING`](../troubleshooting.md#docker_not_running). On Linux, start the service yourself and run the command again.
- The image build needs the buildx plugin, and its absence gives [`DOCKER_BUILDX_MISSING`](../troubleshooting.md#docker_buildx_missing). Update Docker Desktop, or add the `docker-buildx-plugin` package on Linux.
- A home folder with files Dockingbird did not make gives [`HOME_NOT_EMPTY`](../troubleshooting.md#home_not_empty). Point `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` at an empty or new folder, then retry.

heading: Install
summary: This page installs the `dockingbird` command from Zeusfyi's release index, checks that it runs, and adds tab completion.
text:
This page installs the `dockingbird` command from Zeusfyi's release index, checks that it runs, and adds tab completion.
Activation comes next, on the [activate](activate.md) page.

heading: Install > Before you start
summary: - The items on [prerequisites](prerequisites.md) pass their checks: `docker version`, `docker buildx version`, `uv --version` and `git --version`.
text:
- The items on [prerequisites](prerequisites.md) pass their checks: `docker version`, `docker buildx version`, `uv --version` and `git --version`.
- Your license key is copied from your purchase email. A trial cannot install from the index, because the index serves an active license only.

heading: Install > 1. Install on a Mac
summary: Copy your key from the purchase email, then run the line below.
text:
Copy your key from the purchase email, then run the line below.
uv gets the key through its environment, so your shell history never holds it.
The record of the install keeps the index address and leaves the key out.

```bash
UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_USERNAME=license UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD="$(pbpaste)" uv tool install dockingbird --index zeusfyi=https://license.zeus.fyi/simple/
```

The index is named `zeusfyi`, and that name decides the variable names `UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_USERNAME` and `UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD`.
The user name is the word `license`, and the password is the key you copied.

Done when uv exits 0 and `dockingbird --version` finds the command (step 3).

heading: Install > 2. Install on Linux
summary: Linux has no `pbpaste`, so the key goes into a shell variable instead.
text:
Linux has no `pbpaste`, so the key goes into a shell variable instead.
Run the first line, paste the key and press Enter. The terminal shows nothing while you paste.
The second line installs, and the third clears the variable.

```bash
read -rs UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD
UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_USERNAME=license UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD="$UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD" uv tool install dockingbird --index zeusfyi=https://license.zeus.fyi/simple/
unset UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD
```

Done when uv exits 0 and `unset` has run.

heading: Install > 3. Check the install
summary: The step is done when the command prints a line that starts with `dockingbird` and the version.
text:
```bash
dockingbird --version
```

The step is done when the command prints a line that starts with `dockingbird` and the version.

```text
dockingbird {version} (Claude Code {claude_code}, Codex {codex})
```

The two tool versions fill in after the first start, which downloads Claude Code and Codex.
[First run](first-run.md) covers that start.
If your shell reports that `dockingbird` is not found, run `uv tool update-shell` and open a new terminal.

heading: Install > 4. Add tab completion
summary: It writes the completion script for the shell that `$SHELL` names, or for the one you name (`zsh`, `bash` or `fish`).
text:
```bash
dockingbird completion --install
```

It writes the completion script for the shell that `$SHELL` names, or for the one you name (`zsh`, `bash` or `fish`).
The script goes into the `completion` folder of the Dockingbird home.
It also adds two lines to `~/.zshrc` or `~/.bashrc`, once however often you run it. One is a comment, and one loads the script.
For fish, the file `~/.config/fish/conf.d/dockingbird.fish` holds them.
`dockingbird update` keeps the script current.

Done when the command prints this, and you then open a new terminal.

```text
Installed tab completion for {shell}:
  {path}
  {rc} sources it
Open a new terminal.
```

A second run prints "Tab completion for {shell} was installed already; its script is current:" and the same two paths.
`dockingbird clean --all` removes the script but not the two lines. Delete them yourself if you like.

heading: Install > A bare install is wrong
summary: Never run `uv tool install dockingbird` without `--index`.
text:
Never run `uv tool install dockingbird` without `--index`.
That name on PyPI is not this product, so a bare install puts a different program on your computer.
If you ran it, run `uv tool uninstall dockingbird`, then the install line for your platform.

heading: Install > A failed install
summary: The index serves an active license only.
text:
The index serves an active license only.
A wrong key, a license that is not active, or a trial gives uv an authentication error, and no `dockingbird` command appears.
The error text is uv's own and is not a Dockingbird message, so it has no message id.
Copy the key from your purchase email again and run the install line again.

heading: Install > When it fails
summary: - [`COMPLETION_ALREADY`](../troubleshooting.md#completion_already) says completion was installed already and its script is current.
text:
- [`COMPLETION_ALREADY`](../troubleshooting.md#completion_already) says completion was installed already and its script is current. Nothing is wrong.
- [`COMPLETION_SHELL_UNKNOWN`](../troubleshooting.md#completion_shell_unknown) means `$SHELL` names a shell Dockingbird has no completion for. Name one, as in `dockingbird completion --install zsh`.
- [`COMPLETION_RC_REFUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#completion_rc_refused) means Dockingbird could not write your shell's startup file. The script was written, and the startup file is unchanged.

heading: Activate
summary: This page gives this computer its seat with `dockingbird license activate`, or starts a trial, and shows how to read the result.
text: This page gives this computer its seat with `dockingbird license activate`, or starts a trial, and shows how to read the result.

heading: Activate > Before you start
summary: - `dockingbird --version` prints a line that starts with `dockingbird`.
text:
- `dockingbird --version` prints a line that starts with `dockingbird`. [Install](install.md) covers it.
- Your license key is in your purchase email. With no key, use the trial in step 3.

heading: Activate > What a seat is
summary: A seat is one person, who may link up to three computers.
text:
A seat is one person, who may link up to three computers.
A laptop, a desktop and a cloud VM are one seat.
A second Dockingbird home on the same computer, set with another `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`, shares that computer.
Agents, containers and repos are never counted.
Licensing sends Zeusfyi nothing from a repo or an agent.

Refusing a start for a missing or ended license is not yet available.
In this release every start goes ahead, and a start prints one line when licensing has something to say.
Only a new agent's start ever concerns the license. `sync`, `stop`, `clean`, `status`, `update` and every running agent never stop for it.

heading: Activate > 1. Activate with a key
summary: Dockingbird asks for the key and does not show it.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license activate
```

Dockingbird asks for the key and does not show it.
Without a terminal it reads the key from standard input, so `pbpaste | dockingbird license activate` works too.
The key is never read from the command line.

Two options help a scripted install.
`--label TEXT` names this computer in the list of computers, by default its host name.
`--accept-terms VERSION` accepts the agreement's version.

Done when the command prints the activated line, with the count of linked computers under it.
Then it prints the line that names the terms.

```text
This computer is activated: {plan}, {seats}, {term}.
  Computers linked: 4 of 30 (10 seats, 3 computers each)
```

```text
You use Dockingbird under its terms: {link}
```

The link is the address of Zeusfyi's end-user license agreement.
Activating again on a computer that is already linked keeps its link.

heading: Activate > 2. Read the status
summary: Done when the first line reads "Licensed: {plan}, {seats}, {term}."
text:
```bash
dockingbird license status
```

Done when the first line reads "Licensed: {plan}, {seats}, {term}."
Under it come how many computers one seat may link, this computer's label, the day the lease ends and the last check-in.
These come from the license file on this computer, with no network.
`dockingbird license status --refresh` checks in with Zeusfyi first.
`dockingbird status` also shows the state in one line once this computer has a license file.

heading: Activate > 3. Start a trial instead
summary: A trial needs no key, and each computer gets one.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license trial
```

A trial needs no key, and each computer gets one.

Done when the command prints this line, then the terms line.

```text
The trial started on this computer: {plan}, {term}.
```

A second run prints "This computer has had its trial already." and names `dockingbird license activate`.
A trial has these limits.

- It cannot install from the index, which serves an active license only.
- It is not an activation. On an index install, `dockingbird update` answers "Updating Dockingbird needs this computer's license" until you activate with a key.

heading: Activate > 4. A key typed as a word
summary: A key on the command line is refused, because your shell history and other programs can read it.
text:
A key on the command line is refused, because your shell history and other programs can read it.
Nothing runs, and the exit status is 2.

```text
A license key never goes on the command line, where your shell
history and other programs can read it.
Paste it when asked: dockingbird license activate
```

heading: Activate > 5. Seats full, and freeing one
summary: When every computer the license admits is linked, activation stops with exit 1.
text:
When every computer the license admits is linked, activation stops with exit 1.
It says "Every computer this license admits is linked, so this one can't join." and lists each linked computer with its id.
`dockingbird license activations` lists the computers, and `--release ID` frees one.

```bash
dockingbird license activations --release ID
```

Done when it prints "The seat of activation {id} is free again.", then lists the rest.
Run `dockingbird license activate` again and this computer joins.
`dockingbird license deactivate` gives this computer's own seat back and prints "This computer no longer uses a seat of the license."
`dockingbird clean --all` does the same first.

A computer rebuilt with a new identifier is a new computer each time.
A re-imaged VM, a cloud instance recreated on each deploy, and a container without a machine id are examples.
Run `dockingbird license deactivate` before you destroy one. An unreleased seat stops counting by itself after 90 days.

heading: Activate > Where Dockingbird keeps it
summary: The license file is `license.json` in the Dockingbird home, readable by you alone.
text:
The license file is `license.json` in the Dockingbird home, readable by you alone.
It holds the license document, this computer's id and label, the last check-in, the terms accepted and the download token.
`dockingbird update` uses that token as the index's password, so an activated computer updates with no key.
The first `license` command also downloads Zeusfyi's license program, `zeusfyi-license`, into the `bin` folder of the home.
A computer offline, or an outage at Zeusfyi, interrupts nothing, because the license keeps working for its lease.

heading: Activate > When it fails
summary: - Typing the key after the command name gives [`LICENSE_KEY_IN_ARGV`](../troubleshooting.md#license_key_in_argv) and exit 2.
text:
- Typing the key after the command name gives [`LICENSE_KEY_IN_ARGV`](../troubleshooting.md#license_key_in_argv) and exit 2. Nothing ran.
- A key the license server has never seen gives [`LICENSE_KEY_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#license_key_invalid). Copy it again from the email.
- When every computer of the license is linked, activation ends with [`LICENSE_SEATS_FULL`](../troubleshooting.md#license_seats_full). Free one with `--release ID` and retry.
- A second `license trial` on the same Mac gives [`LICENSE_TRIAL_USED`](../troubleshooting.md#license_trial_used), because each computer gets one trial.
- `update` on an index install with no activation stops with [`LICENSE_UPDATE_NEEDS_LICENSE`](../troubleshooting.md#license_update_needs_license).
- With the license server unreachable you get [`LICENSE_AUTHORITY_UNAVAILABLE`](../troubleshooting.md#license_authority_unavailable). Nothing changed, so retry once you are online.
- `clean --all` offline leaves the seat in use and prints [`LICENSE_SEAT_STILL_HELD`](../troubleshooting.md#license_seat_still_held). Free it from another Mac.

heading: First run
summary: Pick a git repository you work in, run `dockingbird init` there, then start `claude-1` and sign it in.
text: Pick a git repository you work in, run `dockingbird init` there, then start `claude-1` and sign it in. Each step below shows the lines Dockingbird prints when it worked.

heading: First run > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is installed and activated.
text:
- Dockingbird is installed and activated. `dockingbird --version` prints a version, and `dockingbird license status` prints "Licensed: ..." or the trial line. See [install](install.md) and [activate](activate.md).
- Docker answers. `docker version` prints without an error.
- You are in a git repository with at least one commit on a branch. Agents start from your last commit, never from uncommitted edits.

heading: First run > 1. Make the repository ready
summary: `dockingbird init` runs anywhere inside a repository, and it writes these files.
text:
```bash
cd your-repo
dockingbird init
```

`dockingbird init` runs anywhere inside a repository, and it writes these files.

- `.dockingbird/project.toml` holds the project's slug, the release that wrote it, its rules file, and each shipped role's harness, model and effort.
- `.dockingbird/rules.md` holds the lines every agent of the project gets after Dockingbird's own rules.
- `.dockingbird/swarms/example/` holds an example swarm.
- `.agents/skills/` holds this release's skills, and `.claude/skills` is a link to them.
- `.claude/agents/` holds the agent definitions.
- `.dockingbird/skills.lock` lists every installed file with its digest.

The slug is `--project SLUG`, else the name of the `origin` remote, else the folder's name.
Without an `origin` remote, `init` says so and names the project after the folder.

Done when `init` prints this and exits 0.

```text
Set up {project} for Dockingbird {release}: the project file, its rules,
an example swarm, the skills and their agents. Keep them in git:
git add .dockingbird .agents .claude && git commit
Then start an agent: dockingbird claude
```

Two more lines follow, about running the example swarm on the fleet once its hosts are filled in.

Commit the files now, so the agents' copy of the branch holds them.

```bash
git add .dockingbird .agents .claude && git commit
```

Without an org login on this computer, `init` also says the project is not in your organisation's store.
It still exits 0. `dockingbird init --no-register` skips that step.

A later run changes only what a new release changed.
It keeps an installed file you edited and names it, and `--force` replaces it.
It never rewrites `project.toml`, `rules.md` or a swarm.
`dockingbird init --check` writes nothing and exits 1 when an installed file is not the running release's.
It prints "{project} is not set up for Dockingbird {release}: init would change it." and "To change it: dockingbird init".
When nothing differs, `init` prints "{project} is set up for Dockingbird {release}: nothing to change."

heading: First run > 2. Start the first agent
summary: The command does five things in order.
text:
```bash
dockingbird claude
```

The command does five things in order.

1. It checks your branch. A symlink that leaves the repo, a submodule or a Git LFS file gets the branch refused in seconds. Each file is named, and nothing is set up.
2. It checks the platform and starts Docker Desktop if needed.
3. It builds the image on your computer. This takes about 5 minutes, downloads about 1 GB, and happens once.
4. It starts Dockingbird and copies your branch for the agents.
5. It downloads Claude Code's latest release the first time, then starts `claude-1` in its container.

On a terminal, each wait is one line redrawn in place.
In a pipe or a file, the build prints its heading at once, then a progress line at most once a minute.

```text
Setting up Dockingbird, first time only (about 5 min):
still setting up: step 12 of 41, 3 min so far
```

The copy and the start print these lines.

```text
Copying your-repo (main) for the agents ({size}) ... done ({elapsed})
Starting claude-1 on your-repo (main). Claude will show a sign-in link:
open it on this Mac, sign in, then paste the code here. Only this once.
```

On a terminal, the last line is "To leave it working, close this window."
Done when `AGENT_STARTING` or `SIGNIN_FIRST_TIME` has printed and `claude-1` shows its sign-in, or its prompt when a login already exists.

The agent works in its own copy of your branch, mounted at `/work/your-repo` in its container.
It never sees your uncommitted edits.

heading: First run > 3. Sign in
summary: Dockingbird reads the Claude Code or Codex login already on this computer, and keeps a copy.
text:
Dockingbird reads the Claude Code or Codex login already on this computer, and keeps a copy.
Without a login, each tool signs in once, inside its container.

- Claude shows a link. Open it on this Mac, sign in, and paste the code back.
- Codex, started with `dockingbird codex`, shows a link and a one-time code. Open the link and enter the code. If device code login is off, turn it on in ChatGPT's security settings.
- With no Claude or ChatGPT account, quit the sign-in and run `dockingbird login claude --api-key` or `dockingbird login codex --api-key`.

Quitting the sign-in ends the agent and prints these lines.

```text
Claude isn't signed in yet. Run dockingbird claude again to sign in.
Or use an API key: dockingbird login claude --api-key
```

The agent's empty copy is removed, and the next start shows the sign-in again.
Done when the agent starts and `dockingbird status` shows `claude-1` working.
The first line of `status` reads "Dockingbird {version}, signed in to Claude and Codex".

heading: First run > 4. What the repo's own settings do
summary: Every checkout is trusted.
text:
Every checkout is trusted.
The repo's own hooks, settings and MCP servers run inside the agent, and Claude does not ask whether to trust `/work/your-repo`.
`dockingbird trust --off` marks a checkout untrusted, which keeps those settings off.
[Trust and repo settings](../guides/trust-and-repo-settings.md) says what then changes.

heading: First run > 5. Leave, return and stop
summary: Closing the window leaves `claude-1` working.
text:
Closing the window leaves `claude-1` working.
A bare `dockingbird claude` in that repo reconnects to the one Claude without a terminal. `dockingbird claude --as claude-1` reconnects to it by name.
When the tool ends, Dockingbird prints what was shared.

```text
claude-1 is done: 2 commits shared on main. Get them: dockingbird sync
```

Dockingbird turns itself off after 30 minutes with no agent, and the next command turns it back on.
`dockingbird stop` stops every agent and prints "Stopped {names}. Dockingbird is off until you next use it."
Nothing is lost.

[Choose a topology](choose-a-topology.md) covers a second computer or a team pool, and the [quickstart](../quickstart.md) continues with the daily loop.

heading: First run > When it fails
summary: - No `docker` command gives [`DOCKER_NOT_INSTALLED`](../troubleshooting.md#docker_not_installed).
text:
- No `docker` command gives [`DOCKER_NOT_INSTALLED`](../troubleshooting.md#docker_not_installed). Install Docker Desktop, or Docker on Linux.
- A Docker that has not started in time gives [`DOCKER_NOT_RUNNING`](../troubleshooting.md#docker_not_running). Start it and run the command again.
- A missing buildx plugin stops the build with [`DOCKER_BUILDX_MISSING`](../troubleshooting.md#docker_buildx_missing).
- Files that Dockingbird did not make in the home folder give [`HOME_NOT_EMPTY`](../troubleshooting.md#home_not_empty). Unset `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`, or point it at an empty folder.
- Ctrl-C during the build gives [`SETUP_INTERRUPTED`](../troubleshooting.md#setup_interrupted). Nothing changed, so run the command again.
- A build that fails gives [`IMAGE_BUILD_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#image_build_failed), names the step, and shows Docker's own output with `--verbose`.
- A command run outside a git repo gives [`NOT_A_GIT_REPO`](../troubleshooting.md#not_a_git_repo). `cd` into your project first.
- A symlink out of the repo, a submodule or a Git LFS file gives [`LINK_TREE_POLICY`](../troubleshooting.md#link_tree_policy). Fix the files named, commit, and run the command again.
- Running inside a submodule gives [`SUBMODULE_NOT_YET`](../troubleshooting.md#submodule_not_yet). `cd` into the main repo.
- `init` outside a git repo gives [`INIT_NOT_A_CHECKOUT`](../troubleshooting.md#init_not_a_checkout), and writes nothing.
- `init` inside the Dockingbird home gives [`INIT_INSIDE_HOME`](../troubleshooting.md#init_inside_home), and writes nothing.
- A tool without a sign-in gives [`SIGNIN_NEEDED`](../troubleshooting.md#signin_needed). Run `dockingbird claude` again, or use an API key.

heading: Choose a topology
summary: This page helps you pick where your agents run, from one Mac to a team pool.
text:
This page helps you pick where your agents run, from one Mac to a team pool. It names the pages and the example each choice needs.
Every choice starts with the one-computer set-up, so finish [first run](first-run.md) first.

heading: Choose a topology > Before you start
summary: - `dockingbird claude` has started an agent on this computer.
text:
- `dockingbird claude` has started an agent on this computer. [First run](first-run.md) shows the lines that prove it.
- You know how many computers should run agents, and whether one person or a team uses them.

heading: Choose a topology > The four choices
summary: The license does not depend on the topology: one seat is one person with up to three computers.
text:
| Choice | Use it when | What you add | Example | Pages |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| One computer | One person, one Mac | Nothing | [One Mac](../../examples/one-mac/README.md) | [Quickstart](../quickstart.md), [daily loop](../guides/daily-loop.md) |
| Two computers over ssh | You have a second Mac or Linux host you reach with ssh | A host, with `dockingbird fleet hosts set NAME --ssh DEST` | [Two Macs](../../examples/two-macs-ssh/README.md) | [Hosts](../guides/hosts.md), [hosts file](../reference/files/hosts-file.md) |
| A cloud VM | The second computer is a Compute Engine VM | A host, with `dockingbird fleet hosts set NAME --gcloud VM --zone ZONE --project PROJECT` | [Cloud VM](../../examples/cloud-vm-gcloud/README.md) | [Cloud VMs](../guides/cloud-vms.md), [hosts](../guides/hosts.md) |
| A team pool | Several people share hosts and a queue of swarms | A PostgreSQL 18 store, an org login, a worker on each host | [Team fleet](../../examples/team-fleet/README.md) | [Team fleet](../guides/team-fleet.md), [fleet scheduler](../guides/fleet-scheduler.md), [swarms](../guides/swarms.md) |

The license does not depend on the topology: one seat is one person with up to three computers.
[Activate](activate.md) explains seats.

heading: Choose a topology > 1. One computer
summary: Install, activate, make the repo ready and run `dockingbird claude`.
text:
Install, activate, make the repo ready and run `dockingbird claude`.
Every agent runs in its own container on this computer, and its work reaches you only as commits through `dockingbird sync`.
Nothing else is needed, and this setup is the base of the other three.

Done when `dockingbird status` lists your agents.

heading: Choose a topology > 2. Two computers over ssh
summary: You keep working on your first computer, and agents also run on a second one.
text:
You keep working on your first computer, and agents also run on a second one.
The second computer needs Docker, and your own ssh must reach it without asking.
A Mac whose login does not find Docker Desktop's `docker` needs `--path PATH`, and Docker Desktop's socket needs `--docker-host URL`.
A Linux host is added the same way, with Docker Engine there.

`dockingbird fleet hosts set NAME --ssh DEST` first reads the host over your ssh. It writes the host into `hosts.toml` only when that read works.
`dockingbird fleet agents --host NAME` then lists the agents running there.

Done when `fleet hosts set` prints this line, where the host's rows follow.

```text
{host}: {route} {target}, saved in {path}.
```

If the host cannot be read, the command saves nothing and prints the ssh check to try first.

heading: Choose a topology > 3. A cloud VM
summary: A Compute Engine VM is added through your own `gcloud compute ssh`, with `--gcloud VM --zone ZONE --project PROJECT`.
text:
A Compute Engine VM is added through your own `gcloud compute ssh`, with `--gcloud VM --zone ZONE --project PROJECT`.
Another cloud's VM is a host over ssh, so it follows choice 2.
Start a stopped VM first, because `fleet hosts set` cannot read it.
The VM needs the same things as any host: arm64, Docker Engine with buildx, uv and git.

Done when `fleet hosts set` prints its "saved in" line, as in choice 2.

heading: Choose a topology > 4. A team pool
summary: A pool shares hosts across people.
text:
A pool shares hosts across people.
It queues swarms and starts each where it fits.
It needs a PostgreSQL 18 store that your organisation runs. It also needs one admin, and a login for each host's worker and for each person.
Each computer logs in once with `dockingbird org login HOST:PORT --as user --role ROLE`, and `dockingbird fleet submit` queues a swarm.

Computers can also join a control plane, so agents on different computers can message each other. The control plane is a home of its own, made with `dockingbird cp init`.
Each joining computer runs `dockingbird node join` with a bundle the control plane makes for it.

A store that Zeusfyi hosts for you is not yet available.
[Team fleet](../guides/team-fleet.md) installs the store and both features, in order.

Done when `dockingbird org login` ends 0 on a computer, and `dockingbird org status` checks the login.

heading: Choose a topology > When it fails
summary: - A host that ssh, gcloud or Docker cannot reach ends `fleet hosts set` with [`FLEET_HOSTS_NOT_REACHED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_not_reached).
text:
- A host that ssh, gcloud or Docker cannot reach ends `fleet hosts set` with [`FLEET_HOSTS_NOT_REACHED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_not_reached). Nothing is saved, and the message prints the command to try by hand.
- A `hosts.toml` that cannot be read gives [`FLEET_HOSTS_FILE_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_file_invalid). The message names the line to fix.
- `fleet agents --host NAME` with a name the file lacks gives [`FLEET_HOST_UNKNOWN`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_host_unknown), plus the `set` command that adds it.
- A fleet command on a computer with no org login gives [`ORG_NOT_CONFIGURED`](../troubleshooting.md#org_not_configured). Run `dockingbird org login HOST --as user --role ROLE`.
- Logging in as the wrong kind for a command gives [`ORG_ROLE_MISSING`](../troubleshooting.md#org_role_missing). The message prints the login that command needs.

heading: Agent set-up prompt
summary: The block below is a prompt for Claude Code or Codex on the computer that will run Dockingbird.
text:
The block below is a prompt for Claude Code or Codex on the computer that will run Dockingbird. Clone this
repository on that computer, open your coding agent in the clone, and paste the whole block as your first message.
The agent reads the quickstart and the prerequisites, checks Docker, uv, git, the disk and the platform, and then
waits while you install and activate. After that it runs `dockingbird init` in your repository, starts one agent
with `dockingbird start`, proves a message round trip and ends with a table of every step and its done line.

```text

1. Who you are

You are setting up Dockingbird on this computer with its owner. The owner types the license key and does any

sign-in; you run every other step, and only after the checks below pass.

Each step ends with its done line: the exact line Dockingbird prints when the step worked. A step that prints a

message id instead stops the setup. Open the id's entry in docs/troubleshooting.md (its anchor is the id in lower

case), show the owner its "Next step:", and report it.

2. Read first

Read these files of this repository: llms.txt, docs/quickstart.md, docs/getting-started/prerequisites.md and

templates/AGENTS.md. Once the owner names the topology in step 4, read its page too:

  one Mac              examples/one-mac/README.md

  two Macs over ssh    examples/two-macs-ssh/README.md

  a cloud VM           examples/cloud-vm-gcloud/README.md

  a team fleet         examples/team-fleet/README.md

Read, do not skim: the done line of each step is on those pages.

3. Check before you act

Run each check and report it as pass or fail, with the command you used.

  Platform: uname -m prints arm64 (an Apple silicon Mac) or aarch64 (arm64 Linux). Intel Macs, x86 Linux and

    Windows are not supported.

  Docker: docker buildx version prints the plugin's version, and docker version answers without an error. On a Mac

    a stopped Docker Desktop passes, because Dockingbird starts it.

  uv: uv --version prints its version.

  git: /usr/bin/git --version prints its version.

  Disk: df -h ~ shows room for the first build, which downloads about 1 GB and fills a 441 MB package folder.

  Home: ls -A "${DOCKINGBIRD_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share/dockingbird}" prints nothing, or the folder does not exist.

    Files there that Dockingbird did not make stop the first start with HOME_NOT_EMPTY.

Stop on any fail. Show the owner the entry the prerequisites page names for it, and report.

4. Hand the key steps to the owner

heading: Agent set-up prompt
summary: Ask the owner which repository to set up, and which topology this is: one Mac, two Macs over ssh, a cloud VM or
text:
Ask the owner which repository to set up, and which topology this is: one Mac, two Macs over ssh, a cloud VM or

a team fleet. Then ask the owner to run these two steps at their own terminal:

  the install line for this platform from docs/getting-started/install.md, with the key from the purchase email;

  dockingbird license activate, which asks for the key at a hidden prompt.

Never ask for the key: a key pasted into this chat lands in your transcript. Go on once the owner says both ran.

5. Check the owner's steps

  dockingbird --version

Done when it prints a line that starts with dockingbird and a version. When the shell finds no dockingbird, the

owner runs uv tool update-shell and opens a new terminal.

  dockingbird license status

Done when the first line reads "Licensed: {plan}, {seats}, {term}." (LICENSE_SHOWN). Any other first line means

the activation did not take: show it to the owner and go back to step 4.

6. Make the repository ready

cd into the repository the owner named, then run:

  dockingbird init

Done when it prints "Set up {project} for Dockingbird {release}: the project file, its rules," and exits 0

(INIT_DONE). Without an org login a line follows saying the project is not in your organisation's store

(INIT_NOT_REGISTERED); both mean success. A repository set up before prints "{project} is set up for Dockingbird

{release}: nothing to change." instead, which is also success. Outside a git repository init stops with

INIT_NOT_A_CHECKOUT.

Agents start from the last commit. Show the owner the files init wrote and, on their word, commit them:

  git add .dockingbird .agents .claude && git commit -m "Add the Dockingbird project files"

7. First start

  dockingbird start "say hello and stop"

Add --harness codex when the owner uses Codex. Run it in the background, or with a 10-minute timeout: the first

start builds the image (about 5 minutes and about 1 GB, once) and takes the Claude Code or Codex sign-in that this

computer already has. Done when it prints these two lines (AGENT_STARTED_BUS):

  {name} started on {repo} ({branch}).

  Thread {thread}. Watch: dockingbird wait {name}

Use the name it printed, claude-1 on a new computer, in every step below. Then run:

  dockingbird status

  dockingbird wait {name}

Done when status lists the agent and wait prints "{kind} from {name}: {subject}" (WAIT_DELIVERY). A wait that

heading: Agent set-up prompt
summary: prints "Nothing arrived" or "Nothing new" has used its 25 seconds; run it again.
text:
prints "Nothing arrived" or "Nothing new" has used its 25 seconds; run it again.

On SIGNIN_NEEDED or START_NO_SIGNIN_BUS, stop. The owner signs in at their terminal with dockingbird login claude

(or dockingbird login codex), and then you run this step again.

8. Prove it

  dockingbird status --json

Done when it exits 0 and one line of JSON has "name" set to the agent and "state" set to working or idle.

  dockingbird license status

Done when the first line starts with "Licensed:".

  dockingbird send {name} "Reply with the word ready."

Done when it prints "Sent {kind} to {name} (message {value})." (SENT).

  dockingbird wait {name}

  dockingbird read {index}

Done when wait prints "Read it: dockingbird read {index}" and read prints "{kind} from {name}, {priority}:

{subject}" (READ_HEADER), with the agent's reply under it.

9. Optional topology

For a second computer the owner reaches with ssh, or a Compute Engine VM:

  dockingbird fleet hosts set NAME --ssh DEST

  dockingbird fleet hosts set NAME --gcloud VM --zone ZONE --project PROJECT

Done when it prints "{host}: {route} {target}, saved in {path}." (FLEET_HOSTS_SET).

For a team fleet the owner logs this computer in to the organisation's store, at their terminal, because it asks

for a password at a hidden prompt:

  dockingbird org login HOST:PORT --as user --role ROLE

Done when dockingbird org status, which you run, ends 0.

10. Report

End with a table of every step: the command, the done line you saw and the exit status. Under it, list each

message id you met with its troubleshooting entry, then your own next step.

11. Never

  ask for the key, or read it from the clipboard, a file or this chat;

  put the key in a command line, the shell history, a file or the report;

  run uv tool install dockingbird without the --index part of the install line;

  edit files outside the repository being set up;

  run dockingbird clean --all without the owner's word.

```

You run four commands at your own terminal: the install line with your key and `dockingbird license activate` in step 4, `dockingbird login claude` or `dockingbird login codex` when step 7 stops for a sign-in, and `dockingbird org login` in step 9 for a team fleet.

heading: Frequently asked questions
summary: Thirteen questions, three lines each.
text: Thirteen questions, three lines each. The questions cover the prerequisites and the key, what the agent sees, sync, two agents on one branch, a shared key, the slow first start, a closed lid, Claude Code against Codex, support, a new laptop, a trial and offline use. The last line of each answer is a link.

heading: Frequently asked questions > What do I need: Mac or Linux, Docker, uv, git, disk?
summary: You need an Apple silicon Mac or arm64 Linux, Docker Desktop (Docker Engine with buildx on Linux), uv, and git at `/usr/bin/git`.
text:
You need an Apple silicon Mac or arm64 Linux, Docker Desktop (Docker Engine with buildx on Linux), uv, and git at `/usr/bin/git`.
Intel Macs, x86 Linux and Windows are not supported. The first run downloads about 1 GB once and takes about 5 minutes.
See [prerequisites](getting-started/prerequisites.md).

heading: Frequently asked questions > Where does the key go, and how do I know the install worked?
summary: The key goes to uv through the environment variable `UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD`, then to `dockingbird license activate`, which asks for it hidden.
text:
The key goes to uv through the environment variable `UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD`, then to `dockingbird license activate`, which asks for it hidden.
The install worked when `dockingbird --version` prints a version and activation prints `This computer is activated:`.
See [install](getting-started/install.md).

heading: Frequently asked questions > What does the agent see of my computer and my repo?
summary: Each agent runs in its own container, on its own copy of your last commit.
text:
Each agent runs in its own container, on its own copy of your last commit. It never sees your uncommitted edits.
A connection you name is the only way a folder, a database or a secret reaches it.
See [the security model](concepts/security-model.md).

heading: Frequently asked questions > Where are the agent's changes, and what if we both committed?
summary: The agents' work reaches you only as commits, when you run `dockingbird sync`.
text:
The agents' work reaches you only as commits, when you run `dockingbird sync`.
`sync` never rewrites history and keeps your uncommitted edits. When both sides have new commits, it offers a merge.
See [the sync model](concepts/sync-model.md).

heading: Frequently asked questions > Can two agents work on one branch at once?
summary: Yes.
text:
Yes. Each agent has its own copy of your branch, so two agents never overwrite each other's files.
Start each with `dockingbird claude` or `dockingbird codex` in its own terminal, or with `dockingbird start` for a task on the bus.
See [the sync model](concepts/sync-model.md).

heading: Frequently asked questions > Can my colleague use my key?
summary: No.
text:
No. A seat is one person, who may link up to three computers, so a colleague needs a seat of their own.
A fourth computer on a one-seat license stops at activation with `LICENSE_SEATS_FULL`, and the key is never shown or printed.
See [what a seat is](guides/licensing.md#what-a-seat-is).

heading: Frequently asked questions > Why is the first start slow, and how much disk does it take?
summary: The first start builds Dockingbird's image on your computer, about 1 GB of downloads and about 5 minutes, once.
text:
The first start builds Dockingbird's image on your computer, about 1 GB of downloads and about 5 minutes, once.
Each agent's copy holds your repo's history, and `dockingbird clean` frees the copies you no longer need.
See [first run](getting-started/first-run.md).

heading: Frequently asked questions > What happens when I close the lid or lose the network?
summary: Closing the terminal leaves the agent working, and a bare `dockingbird claude` in that repo reconnects to it.
text:
Closing the terminal leaves the agent working, and a bare `dockingbird claude` in that repo reconnects to it.
When Docker Desktop was asleep, the screen shows `Waking Docker ...` and the command goes on once Docker answers.
See [the daily loop](guides/daily-loop.md).

heading: Frequently asked questions > Claude Code or Codex, and how do I pick the model?
summary: Run `dockingbird claude` for Claude Code or `dockingbird codex` for Codex.
text:
Run `dockingbird claude` for Claude Code or `dockingbird codex` for Codex. Each signs in once, inside its container.
`dockingbird set NAME --model MODEL --effort LEVEL` changes the model and effort of a running agent.
See [Claude Code and Codex](concepts/claude-code-and-codex.md).

heading: Frequently asked questions > Something failed: where do I ask, and what do I send?
summary: Every message says what to do next, and the [catalogue](troubleshooting.md) lists them all by id.
text:
Every message says what to do next, and the [catalogue](troubleshooting.md) lists them all by id.
To ask for help, send `dockingbird --version`, the output of `dockingbird status --json` and the message id.
See [SUPPORT.md](../SUPPORT.md).

heading: Frequently asked questions > How do I move to a new laptop?
summary: Free the old computer's seat with `dockingbird license deactivate`, or with `dockingbird license activations --release ID` if it is lost.
text:
Free the old computer's seat with `dockingbird license deactivate`, or with `dockingbird license activations --release ID` if it is lost.
Then install Dockingbird on the new laptop and run `dockingbird license activate`.
See [move your seat](../examples/move-your-seat/README.md).

heading: Frequently asked questions > Can I try it without a key?
summary: Yes.
text:
Yes. `dockingbird license trial` starts a trial on this computer with no key, once per computer.
A trial cannot install from the release index and cannot update, so an install needs a key.
See [start a trial](guides/licensing.md#start-a-trial).

heading: Frequently asked questions > What happens when the computer is offline or the term ends?
summary: `dockingbird license status` reads a file on the computer and needs no network, and without a check-in the license keeps working for its lease.
text:
`dockingbird license status` reads a file on the computer and needs no network, and without a check-in the license keeps working for its lease.
After a term ends the installed version keeps working, and new releases need a renewed license.
See [offline behavior](guides/licensing.md#offline-behavior-and-day-counts).

heading: Architecture
summary: Dockingbird starts every agent in a Docker container on your Mac or Linux computer.
text: Dockingbird starts every agent in a Docker container on your Mac or Linux computer. A folder called a home holds the state of those containers. This page shows how a host, a home and an agent relate, and what carries an agent's commits back to you.

heading: Architecture > Hosts, homes and containers
summary: A host is a computer that runs the `dockingbird` command.
text: A host is a computer that runs the `dockingbird` command. Each host holds one or more homes. A home is a folder, `~/.local/share/dockingbird` by default, together with the Docker containers, volumes and image that belong to it. A home runs one coordinator container and one container for each running agent. Every agent works in its own copy of your branch, so two agents never overwrite each other and none touches your files.

heading: Architecture > How it behaves
summary: The command on the host talks to the home's coordinator.
text:
The command on the host talks to the home's coordinator. `dockingbird claude` starts Docker Desktop when it is off, builds the image once (about 5 minutes), starts the home, and then starts an agent named `claude-1` in its own container.

Each agent's copy starts from your last commit and sits at `/work/<repo-name>` in the container. The agent never sees edits you have not committed. It runs without permission prompts, because the container is its sandbox.

An agent shares its commits, and `dockingbird sync` brings them to your branch. [The sync model](sync-model.md) describes that path. Your own checkout changes only through `sync` and a few lines Dockingbird adds to `.git/config` and to the ref `dockingbird/<branch>`.

A home turns itself off after 30 minutes with no agent. The next command turns it back on. `dockingbird status` only looks, so it never starts Docker or the home.

A second home on the same computer is a second, separate installation. Run it with `dockingbird --home NAME` or with `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` set to another folder. It has its own containers, volumes and image tag, and it shares the computer's seat.

Other computers join the picture through `hosts.toml`, which names each one by an ssh destination or a Compute Engine VM. `dockingbird fleet agents --host NAME` then reads that computer's agents, and the fleet pages explain the rest. [Fleet and hosts](fleet-and-hosts.md) covers them.

heading: Architecture > Does it need the cloud
summary: Agents run in containers on your computer.
text: Agents run in containers on your computer. Each agent's tool calls its own model API, Anthropic's for Claude Code and OpenAI's for Codex. License check-ins go to the publisher, and the licensing note lists what they send: nothing from a repo or an agent. The [security model](security-model.md) lists what an agent can reach.

heading: Architecture > What it never does
summary: - It mounts nothing from your computer into an agent except the folders you connect by name.
text:
- It mounts nothing from your computer into an agent except the folders you connect by name.
- It never gives an agent your uncommitted edits, your home folder, your keychain or your other repos.
- It never pushes a branch you did not connect, and it never runs on a platform other than Apple silicon Macs and arm64 Linux.
- It never starts Docker or a home from `dockingbird status`, which only looks.

heading: Architecture > The picture
summary: Text alternative.
text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph host["Host: one computer"]
    cli["dockingbird CLI"]
    repo["Your checkout, branch main"]
    subgraph home1["Home: default"]
      coord1["coordinator container"]
      a1["agent container claude-1"]
      a2["agent container codex-1"]
    end
    subgraph home2["Home: lab, from --home lab"]
      coord2["coordinator container"]
      a3["agent container claude-1"]
    end
  end
  cli -->|"claude, status, send"| coord1
  cli -->|"--home lab"| coord2
  coord1 --- a1
  coord1 --- a2
  coord2 --- a3
  a1 -->|"commits, over sync"| repo
  a2 -->|"commits, over sync"| repo
```

Text alternative. One host runs the `dockingbird` command and holds your checkout. The host has two homes, the default one and `lab`. Each home has a coordinator container and one container per agent. The command talks to each home's coordinator. The agents' commits reach your checkout only through `dockingbird sync`.

text:
| Guide | What it adds |
|---|---|
| [First run](../getting-started/first-run.md) | Starts the first agent and builds the image. |
| [The daily loop](../guides/daily-loop.md) | Starts agents, reads status, syncs and stops. |
