heading: Glossary
summary: The entries below are in the order a new user meets them: one computer first, then messages, then teams, then licensing.
text: The entries below are in the order a new user meets them: one computer first, then messages, then teams, then licensing. Each entry says what the word names in two sentences and links to the page that explains it.

heading: Glossary > home
summary: A home is the folder `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`, `~/.local/share/dockingbird` by default, with the containers, volumes and image that belong to it.
text:
A home is the folder `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`, `~/.local/share/dockingbird` by default, with the containers, volumes and image that belong to it. `dockingbird --home NAME` runs a command in a second home on the same computer.

Explained in [Architecture](architecture.md).

heading: Glossary > agent
summary: An agent is one Claude Code or Codex process that runs in its own container with its own copy of a branch.
text:
An agent is one Claude Code or Codex process that runs in its own container with its own copy of a branch. Dockingbird names agents `claude-1`, `codex-1` and so on, or by the name you give with `--as`.

Explained in [Agents and the bus](agents-and-the-bus.md).

heading: Glossary > the bus
summary: The bus is the message system you and your agents use to pass tasks, questions, answers and files.
text:
The bus is the message system you and your agents use to pass tasks, questions, answers and files. The commands `send`, `inbox`, `read`, `wait` and `results` move messages on it.

Explained in [Agents and the bus](agents-and-the-bus.md).

heading: Glossary > turn
summary: A turn is the work an agent does between one message and its report.
text:
A turn is the work an agent does between one message and its report. After each turn an agent on the bus sends you a status message such as `turn 3`, at priority P3.

Explained in [Agents and the bus](agents-and-the-bus.md).

heading: Glossary > delivery
summary: A delivery is one message waiting in an inbox, yours or an agent's.
text:
A delivery is one message waiting in an inbox, yours or an agent's. `dockingbird inbox claude-2` lists the deliveries waiting for that agent, and `dockingbird read ID` reads one.

Explained in [Agents and the bus](agents-and-the-bus.md).

heading: Glossary > question row
summary: A question row is one line of `dockingbird questions`, a question an agent asks you.
text:
A question row is one line of `dockingbird questions`, a question an agent asks you. It keeps its row number until you answer it with `dockingbird answer ROW`.

Explained in [Agents and the bus](agents-and-the-bus.md).

heading: Glossary > config
summary: A config is a small TOML file that adds a command of your own, such as `dockingbird review`, which runs Claude Code or Codex with settings you chose.
text:
A config is a small TOML file that adds a command of your own, such as `dockingbird review`, which runs Claude Code or Codex with settings you chose. It lives in the `.dockingbird/` folder of a repo or is copied in with `dockingbird config add`.

Explained in [Your own commands](../guides/your-own-commands.md).

heading: Glossary > skill
summary: A skill is a folder holding a `SKILL.md` and the files it uses, named by its folder, which an agent's tool lists as its own.
text:
A skill is a folder holding a `SKILL.md` and the files it uses, named by its folder, which an agent's tool lists as its own. A config's `[skills]` table, `--skills` on a start and `dockingbird set NAME --skills` give an agent skills.

Explained in [Give agents skills](../guides/skills.md).

heading: Glossary > fallback tool
summary: A fallback tool is the other tool, Claude Code or Codex, that a bus agent moves to with its conversation when a rule of its `[fallback]` table says so.
text:
A fallback tool is the other tool, Claude Code or Codex, that a bus agent moves to with its conversation when a rule of its `[fallback]` table says so. The same table sets which failed turns are tried again and which are reported.

Explained in [Your own commands](../guides/your-own-commands.md#a-fallback-tool).

heading: Glossary > connection
summary: A connection is a named grant of one outside thing: a GitHub branch, a folder, a database, a service, an MCP server or a browser.
text:
A connection is a named grant of one outside thing: a GitHub branch, a folder, a database, a service, an MCP server or a browser. Dockingbird holds the secret, and the agent only asks for the thing by its name.

Explained in [Security model](security-model.md).

heading: Glossary > host
summary: A host is a computer your `dockingbird` command reaches, named in `hosts.toml` by an ssh destination or a Compute Engine VM.
text:
A host is a computer your `dockingbird` command reaches, named in `hosts.toml` by an ssh destination or a Compute Engine VM. This computer is always the host called `local`.

Explained in [Fleet and hosts](fleet-and-hosts.md).

heading: Glossary > pool
summary: The pool is the set of hosts the fleet scheduler may place swarms on, kept in your organisation's PostgreSQL store.
text:
The pool is the set of hosts the fleet scheduler may place swarms on, kept in your organisation's PostgreSQL store. Each pool host has cores, memory, a rank and an agent cap.

Explained in [Fleet scheduler](fleet-scheduler.md).

heading: Glossary > swarm
summary: A swarm is a team of agents started together from one definition file, with a count for each role.
text:
A swarm is a team of agents started together from one definition file, with a count for each role. `dockingbird fleet submit` queues it.

Explained in [Swarms and roles](swarms-and-roles.md).

heading: Glossary > role
summary: A role is one kind of agent in a swarm definition, such as a reviewer, a tester or a builder.
text:
A role is one kind of agent in a swarm definition, such as a reviewer, a tester or a builder. It names the tool, the model, the effort, the count, a brief and the roles its agents may message.

Explained in [Swarms and roles](swarms-and-roles.md).

heading: Glossary > role library
summary: A role library is a folder of role files, `.dockingbird/roles/`, that a swarm's role names with `use` and overrides key by key.
text:
A role library is a folder of role files, `.dockingbird/roles/`, that a swarm's role names with `use` and overrides key by key. Dockingbird ships six roles, which `dockingbird init` copies there.

Explained in [Swarms and roles](swarms-and-roles.md).

heading: Glossary > parameter
summary: A parameter is a value a swarm definition declares in `[params]` and writes as `{{name}}`, given at submit with `--set` or `--values`.
text:
A parameter is a value a swarm definition declares in `[params]` and writes as `{{name}}`, given at submit with `--set` or `--values`. The built-ins, such as `{{swarm}}` and `{{branch}}`, need no declaration.

Explained in [Swarm definition file](../reference/files/swarm-definition.md#parameters).

heading: Glossary > workload
summary: A workload is what the fleet scheduler queues: a swarm or a lease.
text:
A workload is what the fleet scheduler queues: a swarm or a lease. It has an id, a priority from P0 to P3 and an age.

Explained in [Swarms and roles](swarms-and-roles.md).

heading: Glossary > control plane
summary: The control plane is a Dockingbird home of its own that other computers join with `node join`.
text:
The control plane is a Dockingbird home of its own that other computers join with `node join`. Once a computer has joined, its agents get a fleet inbox and can message agents on other computers.

Explained in [Control plane](control-plane.md).

heading: Glossary > seat
summary: A seat is one person's share of a license.
text:
A seat is one person's share of a license. One seat may link up to three computers.

Explained in [Licensing model](licensing-model.md).

heading: Glossary > computer
summary: A computer, for licensing, is one machine linked to a seat by `dockingbird license activate`.
text:
A computer, for licensing, is one machine linked to a seat by `dockingbird license activate`. A second home on the same computer shares its link, and agents, containers and repos are never counted.

Explained in [Licensing model](licensing-model.md).

heading: Glossary > lease
summary: A lease is a claim on a host's cores and memory that a command holds while it runs, made with `dockingbird fleet run`.
text:
A lease is a claim on a host's cores and memory that a command holds while it runs, made with `dockingbird fleet run`. The scheduler waits for a host with room, then runs the command there.

Explained in [Fleet scheduler](fleet-scheduler.md).

heading: Glossary > admitter
summary: The admitter is the long-running `dockingbird fleet admitter` command that decides which host each queued workload goes to.
text:
The admitter is the long-running `dockingbird fleet admitter` command that decides which host each queued workload goes to. It runs on one machine of the pool that stays awake.

Explained in [Fleet and hosts](fleet-and-hosts.md).

heading: Glossary > worker
summary: A worker is the long-running `dockingbird fleet worker --host NAME` command, one for each machine of the pool.
text:
A worker is the long-running `dockingbird fleet worker --host NAME` command, one for each machine of the pool. It reports the machine's load every 30 seconds and starts and watches the agents placed there.

Explained in [Fleet and hosts](fleet-and-hosts.md).

heading: Glossary > egress mode
summary: An egress mode sets how far an agent's network reaches.
text:
An egress mode sets how far an agent's network reaches. The four modes are `full`, `allowlist`, `models` and `none`.

Explained in [Security model](security-model.md).

heading: Glossary > kept copy
summary: A kept copy is the copy of your branch that an agent leaves behind when it stops with work not yet shared.
text:
A kept copy is the copy of your branch that an agent leaves behind when it stops with work not yet shared. `dockingbird claude --as NAME` picks it up, and `dockingbird clean` asks before it removes one.

Explained in [Sync model](sync-model.md).

heading: Agents and the bus
summary: You hand a delegated agent a task, and it works in the background while you do something else.
text: You hand a delegated agent a task, and it works in the background while you do something else. Everything between you and that agent travels on one message bus. This page follows a task from `start` to the saved results.

heading: Agents and the bus > What the bus is
summary: Besides `dockingbird claude` and `dockingbird codex`, which you work in, Dockingbird runs agents that you give a task and then talk to by message.
text: Besides `dockingbird claude` and `dockingbird codex`, which you work in, Dockingbird runs agents that you give a task and then talk to by message. Each one has its own container and its own copy of the branch. Every exchange command acts as one client of yours on this computer, the host client. A question an agent asks you therefore waits in a single inbox, and every message you send names you as its sender, so the agent can answer you.

heading: Agents and the bus > How a message travels
summary: `dockingbird start "Fix the failing test"` starts the agent and returns once it runs, in about half a minute.
text:
`dockingbird start "Fix the failing test"` starts the agent and returns once it runs, in about half a minute. It prints `claude-1 started on myapp (main).` and then `Thread <id>. Watch: dockingbird wait claude-1`. The task is the first message of the agent's thread. Every later task you send continues that thread.

The agent works through a turn. After each turn it sends you a status message such as `turn 3` with its final text, at priority P3, the lowest. An error arrives at once at P1, so it sorts before every summary, task and question. You read what came back with `wait`, `inbox` and `read`, and you save the files with `results`.

| Command | What it moves |
|---|---|
| `start "TASK"` | Starts an agent and delivers the task as the first message of its thread. |
| `send NAME TEXT` | Delivers a message. It answers the agent's one open question, or it is a new task when none is open. |
| `send NAME --withdraw N` | Takes a message back. An agent that already accepted it is asked to stop that work. |
| `wait NAME` | Returns at once with a message you have not seen, or waits for the next one, 25 seconds by default. |
| `inbox` | Lists the messages waiting for you, each priority's newest first, 20 to a page. |
| `read N` | Shows one message whole and marks it read. `--keep` leaves it unread. |
| `results NAME` | Saves the files attached in the agent's task thread under `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/results/NAME/`. |
| `inbox NAME` | Lists what other agents and you sent to that agent. Nothing is copied into your inbox. |

heading: Agents and the bus > Questions and deliveries
summary: A delivery is one message in an inbox.
text:
A delivery is one message in an inbox. A question row is one line of `dockingbird questions`: a question an agent asks you, with the number it got when you first saw it. The number stays until you answer. `dockingbird answer 3 --option 2` or `dockingbird answer 3 "Use Vue."` answers it.

A question can come from a choice the tool put up, a plan to approve, the end of a Codex turn at a terminal, or a message the agent sent you with kind `question`. An agent that asks and waits shows `asks` in `dockingbird status` and does not go on until you answer. An agent that asks without waiting keeps working, and its question stays listed. A question a stopped agent asked is withdrawn.

heading: Agents and the bus > Between agents
summary: An agent sends to another agent of the project by name, with `to=<name>` in its `bus_send`.
text:
An agent sends to another agent of the project by name, with `to=<name>` in its `bus_send`. Dockingbird delivers the message to that inbox. A name no agent has, or an agent that has ended, is refused with `AGENT_UNKNOWN` or `AGENT_ENDED`. An agent in a swarm role that names `send_to` can reach only its parent and the roles listed, and any other send is refused with `FORBIDDEN` and the reason `NOT_IN_SEND_RULES`.

Agents on the same repository and branch hear of each other. The first delivery names the others, and `Agent <name> joined your work` and `Agent <name> left your work` follow. You can read what they send each other with `dockingbird inbox claude-2`, and reading changes nothing for that agent.

heading: Agents and the bus > What it never does
summary: - It never lets an agent reach another agent by any path but the bus.
text:
- It never lets an agent reach another agent by any path but the bus. Each agent has its own network, and a proxy refuses every address that is not public.
- It never deletes a message. `dockingbird inbox --clear` marks a stopped agent's notices read and closes its open questions, and every message still reads by its id.
- It never applies `set` to a turn in flight. A new model, effort or compact point takes effect from the agent's next turn.
- It never types a message into an agent's screen while you have unsent text there.
- It never brings an agent's commits to you on the bus. With the default `tools = "bus"`, an agent reports by messages and files, and its commits do not reach `sync`.

heading: Agents and the bus > An agent's life
summary: In `status --json`, an agent's `state` is one of `working`, `idle`, `waiting`, `preparing`, `stopped` or `crashed`.
text:
In `status --json`, an agent's `state` is one of `working`, `idle`, `waiting`, `preparing`, `stopped` or `crashed`. The human screen adds `asks`, with a count, for an agent that waits on your answer. The diagram below shows which command moves an agent from one state to the next.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> preparing: start
  preparing --> working: tool starts
  working --> idle: turn ends
  idle --> working: send
  working --> asking: agent asks and waits
  asking --> working: answer
  working --> stopped: stop
  idle --> stopped: stop
  working --> crashed: tool exits with an error
  stopped --> preparing: start --as NAME
  crashed --> preparing: claude --as NAME
```

Text alternative. `start` puts the agent in `preparing`, and it becomes `working` once its tool runs. When a turn ends it is `idle`, and `send` makes it `working` again. A question it waits on shows as `asking` until you `answer`. `stop` ends it as `stopped`, and a tool that exits with an error leaves it `crashed`. Picking either up with `--as NAME` sends it back to `preparing`.

heading: Agents and the bus > The path of a message
summary: Text alternative.
text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph host["Host"]
    send["start, send"]
    wait["wait"]
    read["inbox, read"]
    results["results"]
  end
  bus(["the bus"])
  subgraph box["Agent container"]
    inbox["agent inbox"]
    turn["a turn"]
  end
  send -->|"task or reply"| bus
  bus --> inbox
  inbox --> turn
  turn -->|"status, question, files"| bus
  bus --> wait
  bus --> read
  bus --> results
```

Text alternative. The host commands `start` and `send` put a task or a reply on the bus. The bus delivers it to the agent's inbox, and the agent works a turn. The agent sends back a status, a question or files over the same bus. The host reads them with `wait`, `inbox` and `read`, and saves files with `results`. Nothing reaches an agent except through the bus.

heading: The sync model
summary: You and your agents each hold a branch of the same project, and `dockingbird sync` is the one command that moves commits between them.
text: You and your agents each hold a branch of the same project, and `dockingbird sync` is the one command that moves commits between them. It works in both directions, as git bundles. This page describes what it does in each situation and what it refuses to carry.

heading: The sync model > Where the commits live
summary: Each agent works in its own copy of your branch, made from your last commit.
text:
Each agent works in its own copy of your branch, made from your last commit. It never sees edits you have not committed. When an agent shares commits, they collect on the agents' side. `dockingbird sync` runs on the branch you are on, in the checkout you run it in, and brings those commits over as a git bundle. Git reads the bundle with `index-pack --strict` into the ref `dockingbird/<branch>`.

Sync names each commit with the agent that shared it. It takes that name from Dockingbird's own record and never from the commit's author field. Two agents on one branch each work in their own copy, and sync names the agent behind every commit it brings.

heading: The sync model > What sync does in each case
summary: Your uncommitted edits stay as they are.
text:
| Situation | What sync does |
|---|---|
| You are behind | Fast-forwards your branch at once and lists each commit with its agent. |
| You are ahead | Sends your commits as a bundle, only what the agents lack. |
| Both sides moved, at a terminal | Asks `Merge theirs into yours now? [Y/n]`. Yes runs your own `git merge` with sync's protections, then sends the merge. |
| Both sides moved, no terminal | Prints the look-first command `git log -p main..dockingbird/main` and `When you are ready: git merge dockingbird/main, then dockingbird sync`. |
| The merge conflicts | Leaves the merge for you to finish. A merge in progress stops every later `sync` and `start` until you commit it. |
| The agents' copy was changed outside Dockingbird | Pauses sharing and loses nothing. `dockingbird sync --accept COMMIT` goes on from the commit sync names. |
| You made the branch again under its old name | `dockingbird sync --let-go` asks once, names what goes, and makes your branch the branch. |

Your uncommitted edits stay as they are. Only when the agents changed a file you are editing, ignored files included, does sync change nothing and name the files. Commit or stash them and run it again. After a good sync, each other linked branch of the same checkout that lacks the agents' commits gets one line with the step that takes them.

heading: The sync model > Turning a commit down
summary: Don't want an agent's commit? Commit its opposite.
text: Don't want an agent's commit? Commit its opposite. `git revert COMMIT` writes the revert on your branch, and the next `dockingbird sync` sends it to the agents. A reset or a deleted branch removes nothing. The agents' copy still holds the commit, so the following sync brings it back to you.

heading: The sync model > What is refused before anything is bundled
summary: Sync refuses a branch that holds a symlink to an absolute path, one that leaves the repo or points into `.git`, a chain of symlinks that is too long or loops, a symlink with an unusable target, a submodule or a Git LFS file.
text: Sync refuses a branch that holds a symlink to an absolute path, one that leaves the repo or points into `.git`, a chain of symlinks that is too long or loops, a symlink with an unusable target, a submodule or a Git LFS file. It names each file with its kind, at most 100 at a time. A symlink whose relative target stays inside the repo goes through as it is. When the commits sync takes add a symlink or change where one points, it notes each one with its target.

heading: The sync model > The protections your git runs with
summary: Every git call sync makes in your checkout runs `/usr/bin/git` with a scrubbed environment.
text:
Every git call sync makes in your checkout runs `/usr/bin/git` with a scrubbed environment. Hooks are off through `core.hooksPath=/dev/null`, and so are fsmonitor, submodule recursion and git's automatic gc. No transport is allowed, and `GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1` keeps an LFS download or hook from running here.

Like your own `git pull`, sync follows the agents' `.gitattributes`, so a filter or merge driver your git config defines runs when they name it. When your hooks folder sits inside the work tree and the incoming commits change it, sync merges nothing and names the files. When the agents changed `.gitattributes`, `.gitmodules` or `.lfsconfig`, sync shows the new lines. Review the agents' commits before you build or run them.

heading: The sync model > Kept copies
summary: An agent that stops with work not shared keeps its copy and holds its name.
text: An agent that stops with work not shared keeps its copy and holds its name. `dockingbird status` lists it under "Needs your attention" with the command that picks it up, and `dockingbird claude --as NAME` continues it. A copy kept on another branch gets a step such as `git switch feature/r7, then dockingbird claude --as keep7`. `dockingbird clean` removes a provably empty copy at once and asks about every other one, with the default answer No.

heading: The sync model > What it never does
summary: - It never changes your uncommitted edits.
text:
- It never changes your uncommitted edits.
- It never runs your git hooks, an LFS download or a submodule update during a sync.
- It never merges on a terminal without asking, and Ctrl-C at the question merges nothing and exits 130.
- It never drops an agent's commit because you reset your branch.
- It never takes the author field as the agent's name.

heading: The sync model > The picture
summary: Text alternative.
text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph you["Your checkout"]
    main["branch main"]
    ref["ref dockingbird/main"]
  end
  subgraph agents["Agents' side"]
    a1["claude-1 copy"]
    a2["claude-2 copy"]
    shared["shared branch main"]
  end
  a1 -->|"shares commits"| shared
  a2 -->|"shares commits"| shared
  shared -->|"sync: git bundle"| ref
  ref -->|"you are behind: fast-forward"| main
  ref -.->|"both sides moved: merge offer"| main
  main -->|"sync: bundle of your commits"| shared
```

Text alternative. Two agents each work in their own copy and share commits to the shared branch on the agents' side. `sync` carries that branch to your checkout as a bundle and lands it in the ref `dockingbird/main`. From there it fast-forwards `main` when you are behind, or offers a merge when both sides moved. Your own commits travel back to the shared branch in a bundle.

| [Clean and uninstall](../guides/clean-and-uninstall.md) | Frees disk and removes kept copies. |
| [SYNC_UPDATED](../troubleshooting.md#sync_updated) | The line printed when sync took the agents' commits. |

| [SYNC_CONFLICTS](../troubleshooting.md#sync_conflicts) | The line printed when the merge stops on conflicts. |
| [SYNC_TREE_POLICY](../troubleshooting.md#sync_tree_policy) | The refusal for a symlink, a submodule or an LFS file. |

heading: Claude Code and Codex
summary: Dockingbird runs two coding tools, Claude Code and Codex, and treats them alike wherever it can.
text: Dockingbird runs two coding tools, Claude Code and Codex, and treats them alike wherever it can. This page lists the places where they differ, as the operator guide states them: how each signs in, which flags each takes, and which figures each reports.

heading: Claude Code and Codex > What the two share
summary: Both tools run in a container with their own copy of your branch.
text:
Both tools run in a container with their own copy of your branch. Both use the bus, `sync`, trust marks and egress modes in the same way. A config's command runs Claude Code or Codex and never any other program. Everything below is a difference, so a row that is missing is the same for both.

| Topic | Claude Code | Codex |

|---|---|---|

| Start at a terminal | `dockingbird claude` | `dockingbird codex` |

| One-shot form | `dockingbird claude -p "..."`, which a pick-up runs after `--resume <id>` | `dockingbird codex exec "..."`, which a pick-up runs as `exec resume <id>` |

| First sign-in | Its own `claude auth login` runs in the container: open the link, sign in, paste the code | `codex login --device-auth` runs: open the link and enter the one-time code |

| Login reused from your computer | Claude's default profile: a token in `~/.claude/settings.json`, then the Keychain item, then `~/.claude/.credentials.json` | The `auth.json` Codex uses |

| Token from another sign-in | `pbpaste \| dockingbird login claude --oauth-token -` after `claude setup-token` | `cat ~/.codex/auth.json \| dockingbird login codex --auth-json -` |

| API key | `dockingbird login claude --api-key`, an Anthropic key, read through its `apiKeyHelper` | `dockingbird login codex --api-key`, an OpenAI key, taken with `codex login --with-api-key` |

| Gateway for `--base-url` | The origin, to which Claude adds `/v1/...` | A URL that ends in `/v1`, to which Codex adds `/responses` and `/models` |

| Refreshing a sign-in | One live session holds the refresh lease, and the others get a copy without the refresh token | Each session gets the whole `auth.json`, and the last writer wins |

| Your rules file | `--agent-md` and `--claude-md` | `--agent-md` only, because `dockingbird codex --claude-md PATH` is refused |

| `harness_args` in a config | `--model`, `--fallback-model`, `--max-turns` and `--effort` | `--model`, `-m` and `-c model_reasoning_effort=LEVEL` |

| Effort levels | `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max` | The levels its model takes |

| Effort word checked | By Dockingbird, against those five words, in a config's `harness_args`, in `set --effort` and at a swarm submit | By Codex, at the agent's first request; Dockingbird passes the word as `-c model_reasoning_effort=LEVEL` and refuses only one with `=` in it |

| Compact point | 100K to 1M | Any count of tokens |

heading: Claude Code and Codex > What the two share
text:
| `set` on a running agent | A running Claude gets `/model`, `/effort` and `/autocompact` before its next turn | At a terminal Codex takes no typed command, so `set` names the stop and the pick-up that apply the change |

| Where it reads the skills Dockingbird gives | `~/.claude/skills`, where Claude Code finds personal skills | `~/.agents/skills`, where Codex finds a user's |

| How it lists skills | In its Skill tool and its `/` menu, within 1% of its context window, each description cut at 1,536 characters | For its `$` mention, within 2% of its context window (8,000 characters when it doesn't know the window), each description cut at 1,024 characters; Dockingbird sets its `skills.max_context_tokens` to 10,000 tokens for an agent with skills |

| A `SKILL.md` with no frontmatter `description` | One with no frontmatter is listed among its slash commands | Not listed |

| A skill `set --skills` adds | On the bus it is told `/reload-skills` before its next turn; with its screen running it is typed `/reload-skills` at its next idle prompt; at a terminal its own watcher lists the skill within seconds | On the bus it reads the skill when its next turn starts; with its screen running it reads it again itself at its next idle prompt; at a terminal its own re-read lists it within seconds |

| `pin` | `pin claude 2.1.285`, and `"stable"` is its slower channel | `pin codex 0.162.1` |

| Cost in `status --json` | `result_cost_usd`, Claude Code's own estimate, in US dollars | None, because Codex names no cost |

heading: Claude Code and Codex > Signing in
summary: Dockingbird reuses the Claude and Codex logins already on your computer.
text:
Dockingbird reuses the Claude and Codex logins already on your computer. The first start that needs one reads it and keeps a copy in the coordinator's store, and `dockingbird login claude --here` does the same on demand. When you quit a first sign-in, the agent ends with `Claude isn't signed in yet. Run dockingbird claude again to sign in.` Codex ends with the same first sentence, then `(If device code login is off, turn it on in ChatGPT's security settings.)`. Both lines add the API key route.

`dockingbird login claude` or `dockingbird login codex` signs in again, for an expired sign-in or another account, and refuses while that tool's agents run. The last login wins, so either form removes that tool's saved API key. `dockingbird logout claude` and `dockingbird logout codex` remove a sign-in and a saved key.

heading: Claude Code and Codex > Names and one-shots
summary: A name belongs to the tool that first used it.
text: A name belongs to the tool that first used it. `dockingbird codex --as keep7` for a Claude agent is refused, with the step that picks that agent up. A one-shot prints only the tool's answer on stdout. Without a terminal and without a sign-in it refuses and points at `dockingbird login claude`. A script that pipes nothing into a one-shot closes its input with `< /dev/null`, or Codex waits for input that never ends.

heading: Claude Code and Codex > Choosing the tool
summary: `dockingbird start` runs Claude unless `--harness codex` says otherwise.
text:
`dockingbird start` runs Claude unless `--harness codex` says otherwise. A config's `harness` key takes `claude` or `codex`, defaults to `claude`, and is fixed once set, so `--harness` cannot change it. A swarm role names its `harness` too. Dockingbird downloads each tool into its program store at the first start and keeps the version you pin in `versions.toml`. `dockingbird pin --clear claude` follows the latest release again.

An agent on the bus can move to the other tool after a failed turn, with its conversation, when its `[fallback]` table says so. By default only a turn a safety system refused moves it, and it moves once at most. [Your own commands](../guides/your-own-commands.md#a-fallback-tool) sets the table up.

heading: Claude Code and Codex > Model and effort per role
summary: A swarm role's model and effort come from the project, never from Dockingbird: `[roles.NAME]` in `.dockingbird/project.toml`, your organisation's store (`dockingbird org roles set NAME --harness H --model M --effort E`), the role's own `model` and `effort`, or `fleet submit --set ROLE.model=M --set ROLE.effort=E` for one swarm.
text:
A swarm role's model and effort come from the project, never from Dockingbird: `[roles.NAME]` in `.dockingbird/project.toml`, your organisation's store (`dockingbird org roles set NAME --harness H --model M --effort E`), the role's own `model` and `effort`, or `fleet submit --set ROLE.model=M --set ROLE.effort=E` for one swarm. [The swarms guide](../guides/swarms.md#choose-each-roles-model-and-effort) recommends a kind of model and an effort for each role. For a project that has set nothing yet, these are the models of each kind for each tool.

| Role | Claude Code model | Codex model | Effort |
|---|---|---|---|
| coordinator | `claude-opus-5-5` | `gpt-6.1-sol` | `xhigh` |
| implementer | `claude-opus-5-5` | `gpt-6.1-sol` | `medium`; `high` for a fix in existing code, concurrency, or a task left to its judgment |
| reviewer | `claude-fable-5-1` | `gpt-6-astra` | `high`; `xhigh` for concurrency, security, query generation or ranking, or a large diff |
| tester | `claude-sonnet-5-5` | `gpt-6-luna` | `high`; on Claude Code, `xhigh` when it must judge a flaky or partial result |
| reader | `claude-sonnet-5-5`, or `claude-haiku-5-5` for inventories, extraction and short rewrites | `gpt-6-luna` | `medium`; on Claude Code, `high` for strict instruction following |
| hands | `claude-opus-5-5` | `gpt-6.1-sol` | `max` on Claude Code; `high` on Codex |

The Codex column maps the same kinds onto Codex's models by Codex's own descriptions, so measure it on your work before you rely on it. An account sees the models its plan or API organisation offers, so check Codex's `/model` before a submit. A `[roles.NAME]` table answers a role only when its `harness` is the role's, and the project file holds one table per name. A project that runs both tools keeps the second tool's rows in the store, one row per name and tool.

heading: Claude Code and Codex > What it never does
summary: - It never lends a refresh token to an agent.
text:
- It never lends a refresh token to an agent. The copy of a Keychain or login-file sign-in leaves the refresh token out.
- It never answers the trust question of a tool for a checkout you marked untrusted. Claude may ask once per repo, and Codex shows its folder notice each time.
- It never sums the figures a tool reports. Each `result_*` value is the tool's own.
- It never lets `--claude-md` reach Codex, which does not read `CLAUDE.md` at startup.
- It never accepts a `harness_args` flag outside the lists in the table.

heading: Claude Code and Codex > The picture
summary: Text alternative.
text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  cmd["Your command"] --> pick{"Which tool?"}
  pick -->|"claude, start, config harness claude"| claude["Claude Code in a container"]
  pick -->|"codex, start --harness codex, config harness codex"| codex["Codex in a container"]
  store["Coordinator store: sign-in or API key"] -->|"link and pasted code, or key"| claude
  store -->|"device code, or key"| codex
```

Text alternative. Your command picks the tool: `claude`, a plain `start` and a config with `harness = "claude"` run Claude Code, and `codex`, `start --harness codex` and a config with `harness = "codex"` run Codex. Each tool runs in its own container. The coordinator's store holds the sign-in or API key, and each agent asks it for its own tool's credential at start.

text:
| Guide | What it adds |

| [Sign-in and API keys](../guides/sign-in-and-api-keys.md) | Signs in, signs out and saves a key for either tool. |

heading: Swarms and roles
summary: You describe a team of agents in one TOML file, for example four builders, a reviewer and a tester.
text: You describe a team of agents in one TOML file, for example four builders, a reviewer and a tester. The fleet scheduler then starts that team on a host of your pool. Below are the parts of the file, the values you give at submit, and the workload that results.

heading: Swarms and roles > The definition
summary: A definition is a TOML file at `schema = 1`.
text: A definition is a TOML file at `schema = 1`. It names a `project`, a `priority` from P0 to P3, the `[source]` repository and branch the agents work on, and an optional `[placement]` list of hosts. Each kind of agent is one `[[role]]` table. A `key` makes the definition repeatable: a second submit with the same key answers the swarm that was queued first. Without a `key`, every submit queues a new swarm, keyed by its name and the UTC time. The [team fleet example](../../examples/team-fleet/swarm.toml) places a reviewer, a tester and two builders.

heading: Swarms and roles > Roles
summary: A role is one kind of agent.
text:
A role is one kind of agent. It names a `harness` (`claude` or `codex`), a `count`, and a `brief`, a Markdown file that is the agent's first task. It may add `min` and `max`, the fewest agents a retire leaves and the most an add reaches. Both default to the count. A role marks its job with `reviews` or `tests`, which name the roles whose commits it checks.

The model and the effort come from the first place that gives them: a value given at submit, the role, its library role, then `[roles.<name>]` in `.dockingbird/project.toml` when its harness is the role's, then your organisation's store. A role that none of them covers is refused. The name the last two are read by is the role's `kind`, else `reviewer` when it reviews, `tester` when it tests and `implementer` otherwise, the names the library's `index.toml` gives. A role that uses a library role, or names another new key, tries its own name and its library role's name first. [The definition reference](../reference/files/swarm-definition.md#where-a-roles-model-and-effort-come-from) gives the whole order, and [the swarms guide](../guides/swarms.md#choose-each-roles-model-and-effort) recommends a model and an effort for each kind of role.

A role can take its settings from a library. `use = "<name>"` reads `.dockingbird/roles/<name>.toml` in the project. `use = "dockingbird/<name>"` reads one of the roles Dockingbird ships: `coordinator`, `implementer`, `reviewer`, `tester`, `reader` and `hands`. None of them names a model or an effort. `dockingbird init` copies those into the project, and a copy you edited survives a later `init`. Each key the swarm gives replaces the library role's, but `needs` and a subagent's table, which merge field by field.

A role can also name a fallback tool, a `[role.fallback]` table with the keys of a config's `[fallback]`. After a failed turn its agents retry, report, or move to the other tool with their conversation, as the table's rules say.

A role's `send_to` lists the roles whose agents it may message besides its parent. An empty list means the parent alone. Leaving it out lets the agent message any agent of the project. Any other send is refused with `FORBIDDEN`.

heading: Swarms and roles > Values at submit
summary: A definition may declare `[params]`, each an `int`, a `choice` or a `text` with a default and bounds, and write `{{name}}` in its roles' values and texts.
text:
A definition may declare `[params]`, each an `int`, a `choice` or a `text` with a default and bounds, and write `{{name}}` in its roles' values and texts. The submit also supplies built-ins: `{{swarm}}`, `{{project}}`, `{{repository}}` and `{{branch}}`, and in a text alone `{{roles}}` and `{{params}}`. `dockingbird fleet submit NAME --set N=4` gives one value, and `--set grader.count=6` sets a role's count. `--values FILE` takes a JSON document shaped `{"params": {...}, "roles": {"<role>": {...}}}`. A `--set` beats the file for the same key.

A submit may set a role's `count`, `min`, `max`, `model`, `effort`, `compact_at` and `session_hours`, a subagent's `model`, `effort` and `max`, and a role's fallback `harness`, `model`, `effort` and `placement`. `dockingbird fleet describe NAME` prints every parameter and settable field as JSON and connects to nothing. A submit checks every rule before it stores anything, prints each refusal as `refused: <field>: <rule>`, and exits 1. `fleet queue` and `fleet why` show the values a swarm was given.

heading: Swarms and roles > What a workload is
summary: A workload is the unit the scheduler queues, and it is either a swarm or a lease.
text:
A workload is the unit the scheduler queues, and it is either a swarm or a lease. A successful submit prints `<id> pending, position <n>`, and that id names the workload in every later command. The controls `hold`, `release`, `pause`, `resume`, `cancel` and `done` take it. [The fleet scheduler](fleet-scheduler.md) explains how a workload waits and how it is admitted.

Agents the fleet starts get `--compact-at 500000` and `--session-hours 48` unless their role names its own. An agent that hands its parent a message beginning `status: done` is retired on its own word.

heading: Swarms and roles > What it never does
summary: - It never stops an agent during a turn.
text:
- It never stops an agent during a turn. `pause`, `cancel`, `done` and `retire` each wait for the running turn to end.
- It never queues a definition that breaks a rule. Nothing is stored when a refusal prints.
- It never starts a second swarm for a repeated `key`.
- It never places a swarm on a host whose home has no checkout of the repository, and `fleet why` names that hold `no_seed`.
- It never lets a role drop a tool of the bus set.
- It never moves one agent between its tools more often than the installation allows, once by default, so an agent never moves back and forth.

heading: Swarms and roles > The picture
summary: Text alternative.
text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  vals["--set builder.count=4"] -->|"values at submit"| def["Definition: swarm.toml"]
  subgraph roles["Roles and counts, an example"]
    coord["coordinator x1"]
    build["builder x4"]
    rev["reviewer x1"]
    test["tester x1"]
  end
  def --- roles
  coord -->|"send_to"| build
  build -->|"send_to"| rev
  build -->|"send_to"| test
  def -->|"fleet submit"| wl["Workload: pending"]
  wl -->|"placed on a host"| run["Running swarm"]
  run -->|"done or cancel"| fin["Ended"]
```

Text alternative. A definition lists its roles and their counts, here one coordinator, four builders, one reviewer and one tester. The `send_to` edges show who may message whom: the coordinator reaches the builders, and the builders reach the reviewer and the tester. Values such as `--set builder.count=4` enter at submit. `fleet submit` turns the definition into a pending workload, the scheduler places it on a host, and `done` or `cancel` ends it.

text:
| Guide | What it adds |
|---|---|
| [Swarms](../guides/swarms.md) | Writes a definition, submits it and changes a running swarm. |
| [The fleet scheduler](../guides/fleet-scheduler.md) | Follows the queue and uses the controls. |
| [Team fleet](../guides/team-fleet.md) | Installs the store, the worker and the admitter first. |
| [Swarm definition](../reference/files/swarm-definition.md) | Lists every key of a definition. |
| [Roles and connections](../reference/files/roles-and-connections.md) | Lists the keys of a library role. |

heading: Fleet and hosts
summary: Dockingbird keeps two lists of computers, and they do different jobs.
text: Dockingbird keeps two lists of computers, and they do different jobs. The hosts file names the computers your own command reaches. The pool names the hosts a team's scheduler may start swarms on. This page separates them and explains the one name that ties them together.

heading: Fleet and hosts > The hosts file and the pool
summary: Start with `hosts.toml`, a file in your Dockingbird home.
text:
Start with `hosts.toml`, a file in your Dockingbird home. It holds one `[[host]]` table per other computer you reach, and each table has a `name` and one route. The route is `ssh`, with an optional `path` and `docker_host`, or `gcloud` with a `zone` and a `project`. You read a host's agents with `dockingbird fleet agents --host NAME` and open one with `dockingbird fleet attach`. Your own computer is always `local`, and it never appears in the file.

The pool is a separate record. An admin enrols each host in the organisation's PostgreSQL store with `dockingbird fleet hosts add`, and gives it cores, memory, a load line, a rank, an agent cap and a power setting. The scheduler places swarms on pool hosts only. A pool host missing from your file appears in `fleet queue`, but not in `fleet hosts` or `fleet agents`.

heading: Fleet and hosts > The one-name rule
summary: A host has one name across your hosts file, the pool and every swarm definition.
text:
A host has one name across your hosts file, the pool and every swarm definition. The pool host's name is the `--host` its worker runs under, so set the host in `hosts.toml` under that same name. An admitter that starts a stopped Compute Engine VM finds it by that name in its own `hosts.toml`.

`fleet hosts rename` and `fleet hosts forget` change the file alone. They never touch the pool's records or a swarm definition. With a `fleet.toml` in your home, each refuses a host the pool holds, so you drain and remove it there, rename it in the file, and enrol it again under the new name. A computer's control plane label is a second name, chosen apart, and it may differ from the host name.

heading: Fleet and hosts > Placement order
summary: The pool orders its hosts by `--rank`, with 1 first and unranked hosts after the ranked ones by name.
text: The pool orders its hosts by `--rank`, with 1 first and unranked hosts after the ranked ones by name. A definition's `[placement] hosts` lists its preferred hosts. When it leaves `[placement]` out, the swarm may go to every pool host that takes swarms, in pool order. Inside a host, the scheduler picks a home that has a checkout of the repository first, then the home with the fewest running agents, then the first by path. A host whose placed home has no checkout is held with the reason `no_seed`.

heading: Fleet and hosts > The control plane's home
summary: The control plane is a second feature that shares the word fleet.
text: The control plane is a second feature that shares the word fleet. One Dockingbird home turns into the control plane with `cp init`, and its hub listens on port 4222 of that computer's loopback until you serve it to a private network. Every other computer joins with a bundle from `cp token` and the command `node join`. After that, an agent on one computer can message an agent on another by its fleet name, which is the computer's label, a dash and the agent's name. A team may use the control plane, the scheduler, or both. [The control plane](control-plane.md) has the details.

heading: Fleet and hosts > Worker and admitter
summary: Two long-running commands do the fleet's work, each under the machine's own service manager.
text:
Two long-running commands do the fleet's work, each under the machine's own service manager. That is a LaunchAgent on a Mac and a systemd user unit on Linux, with `loginctl enable-linger` set so it runs while nobody is logged in.

`dockingbird fleet worker --host NAME` runs once on each machine of the pool. It publishes the machine's sample every 30 seconds and runs the start jobs the admitter gives it. Each agent starts through its home's own `dockingbird start`. The worker then watches what it started. When pause, cancel or done asks, it stops each agent after its running turn.

`dockingbird fleet admitter` runs once, on one machine that stays awake. It admits workloads after every change to the queue or the pool, and at least every 30 seconds. It also does the housekeeping on the same beat: stale hosts, stalled workers, expired leases, and a stopped `gcloud` VM that work is waiting for. When the database does not answer, each command ends with exit 69 and its service manager starts it again. A login the database turns down ends with exit 78.

heading: Fleet and hosts > What it never does
summary: - It never lets `hosts.toml` hold a pool record.
text:
- It never lets `hosts.toml` hold a pool record. The file names routes, and the pool lives in the store.
- It never saves a host from `fleet hosts set` before it has read that host's Docker and homes.
- It never starts or changes anything on a host when `fleet agents` reads it. The read uses Docker alone.
- It never keeps a database password in `org.toml`. Each role's password is a line of `~/.pgpass`.

summary: Text alternative.
text:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
  you["Your computer: hosts.toml"]
  store[("Org store, PostgreSQL 18")]
  adm["admitter, on one machine kept awake"]
  subgraph pool["Pool: placement in rank order"]
    h1["host lab, rank 1, worker"]
    h2["host cloud, rank 2, worker"]
  end
  subgraph cpg["Control plane home"]
    hub["hub, port 4222"]
  end
  m1["member computer, label lab"]
  m2["member computer, label cloud"]
  h1 -->|"sample every 30 s"| store
  h2 -->|"sample every 30 s"| store
  adm -->|"start jobs"| store
  store -->|"start jobs to the worker"| h1
  you -.->|"ssh or gcloud: fleet agents --host"| h1
  m1 -->|"node join"| hub
  m2 -->|"node join"| hub
```

The admitter, on one machine that stays awake, writes start jobs and the workers run them, in the pool's order. Separately, member computers join the control plane's hub with `node join`. Your computer reaches a host over ssh or gcloud through `hosts.toml`.

heading: The fleet scheduler
summary: This page is for teams.
text:
This page is for teams. It explains what the fleet scheduler is, what it decides and what it never does. The commands that run it are on [the fleet scheduler guide](../guides/fleet-scheduler.md).

The fleet scheduler is a pool of hosts and a queue of work, both kept in your organisation's PostgreSQL 18 store. Work is either a swarm (a team of agents from a definition) or a lease (cores and memory for one command). Each host runs a worker. One host of the pool runs the admitter, which looks at the queue and the hosts and starts each workload on a host with room. Every person and every service reaches the store with a login of their own, made with `org login`.

The word "fleet" names two features in Dockingbird. This page is the first, the scheduler behind `dockingbird fleet`. The second is [the control plane](control-plane.md), which lets agents on different computers message each other. A team can use either alone or both together.

heading: The fleet scheduler > The pool and its hosts
summary: A host joins the pool when the admin enrols it with `fleet hosts add`.
text:
A host joins the pool when the admin enrols it with `fleet hosts add`. A host has one name everywhere: its `[[host]]` name in `hosts.toml`, its name in the pool and the `--host` its worker runs under.

| Property | What it sets |
|---|---|
| cores and memory | the share of the host the scheduler may reserve for workloads |
| gate lines | a live reading each (idle CPU, free memory, disk or I/O pressure) with a bound and a clear value, green or red |
| rank | the host's place in the order the scheduler tries hosts, 1 first, unranked hosts after by name |
| agent cap | the most agents the fullest home on the host may run |
| takes swarms | whether the host accepts swarms or only leases |
| power | `gcloud` lets the admitter start a stopped Compute Engine VM when work waits for it |

A worker publishes its host's sample every 30 seconds: load, free memory and the checkouts its homes link. A host with no sample for 180 seconds is stale, and the swarms placed on it are interrupted until its worker publishes again.

heading: The fleet scheduler > Workloads
summary: A workload carries a project, a priority from P0 to P3, a reservation and an age.
text:
A workload carries a project, a priority from P0 to P3, a reservation and an age. The reservation is the cores, memory and agents the workload needs. A swarm's reservation comes from its roles. A lease's comes from the `--cores` and `--memory` you gave `fleet run`.

The states of a workload are pending, held, admitted, running, paused, interrupted, done and cancelled. A command moves it from one state to the next, except that the admitter moves a pending workload to admitted and a stale host interrupts a swarm. [The fleet scheduler guide](../guides/fleet-scheduler.md) shows the commands for each move.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> pending: fleet submit or fleet run
    pending --> held: fleet hold
    held --> pending: fleet release
    pending --> admitted: the admitter finds a host with room
    admitted --> running: the agents start
    admitted --> held: a start is refused
    running --> paused: fleet pause
    paused --> running: fleet resume
    running --> interrupted: the host goes stale
    interrupted --> running: the host worker returns
    running --> done: fleet done
    running --> cancelled: fleet cancel
    paused --> cancelled: fleet cancel
    admitted --> cancelled: fleet cancel
    interrupted --> cancelled: fleet cancel
    done --> [*]
    cancelled --> [*]
```

A workload is submitted, waits as pending, is admitted onto one host, runs, and ends as done or cancelled. `fleet hold` keeps a pending workload out of every pass and `fleet release` puts it back. The scheduler also holds a swarm whose start it refuses, such as one with no checkout, until you fix the cause and release it. `fleet pause` and `fleet resume` stop and restart a running team, each agent stopping after its running turn. A host that stops reporting makes a running swarm interrupted until its worker publishes again. A lease takes `cancel` only. `fleet set --priority` changes a priority in any state but an ended one and keeps the workload's age.

heading: The fleet scheduler > How the scheduler decides
summary: The admitter admits workloads by priority first, then by age, oldest first.
text:
The admitter admits workloads by priority first, then by age, oldest first. It places a workload on the first host of its placement order that has the room, green gate lines and a home with a checkout of the repository. A swarm without a `[placement]` goes to every pool host that takes swarms, in pool rank order.

A swarm is admitted once the fewest agents of each role (`min`) fit. Agents above that count wait as fill rows and start once the host has room, before any new swarm is admitted. A running swarm therefore grows ahead of a waiting one of any priority.

heading: The fleet scheduler > Why a workload waits
summary: A workload waits while no host passes every check: its gate lines are green, the host has the cores and memory, a home has room under the agent cap, and a home links a checkout of the repository.
text:
A workload waits while no host passes every check: its gate lines are green, the host has the cores and memory, a home has room under the agent cap, and a home links a checkout of the repository. `fleet why ID` names the first check each host fails, with the figures. A hold is a reason in its own right. Some holds clear when you fix the cause and run `fleet release`.

| Hold | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `no_seed` | the host's placed home has no checkout of the swarm's repository |
| `no_checkout` | the start found no checkout to use, or the fetch into a clone failed |
| a missing connection | the placed home has no enabled connection of a name one of its roles lists, so no agent started (`fleet why` says which) |
| your own hold | you ran `fleet hold ID --reason TEXT` |

heading: The fleet scheduler > What it never does
summary: - It never stops an agent during a turn.
text:
- It never stops an agent during a turn. Pause, cancel, done, retire and replace each wait for the running turn to end.
- It never moves a running agent to another host.
- It never holds a password. Each role's password stays in the line of the `~/.pgpass` file on the computer that logs in.
- It never runs a command when the store turns the login down. `fleet run` ends 78 and runs nothing, while a store that does not answer at all makes it run the command without a lease and say so on one line.

heading: The control plane
summary: This page is for teams.
text:
This page is for teams. It explains what the control plane is, how a computer joins it and what it holds. The commands are on [the team fleet guide](../guides/team-fleet.md).

A control plane is one Dockingbird home that you turn into the fleet's meeting point with `cp init`. Other computers join it from one of their own homes with `node join`. Once a computer has joined, each agent started on it gets a fleet inbox on the control plane, beside the inbox on its own home. Through that inbox an agent can message an agent on another computer. The control plane and the [fleet scheduler](fleet-scheduler.md) are separate features. A team can use either alone or both together.

heading: The control plane > How a computer joins
summary: The control plane's hub listens on a TCP port, 4222, on the control plane's computer.
text:
The control plane's hub listens on a TCP port, 4222, on the control plane's computer. Docker publishes that port on the loopback address only. Until you serve the port to your private network, no other computer reaches it.

`cp token` adds one computer. You give it a label and a platform, and it prints one line, the bundle. The bundle holds the computer's hub address, node id, label, key and token. The control plane shows it once and stores it nowhere. You paste the bundle into `node join` on that computer's home. Each bundle joins once.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Control plane home
    participant M as Member computer home
    participant H as Hub on port 4222
    A->>A: cp token --host LABEL
    A-->>M: the bundle, pasted into node join
    M->>H: node join, over the private network
    H-->>M: the computer is in the fleet as LABEL
    M->>H: dockingbird start opens a fleet session
    H-->>M: the agent gets a fleet inbox
```

Text alternative. On the control plane's home, `cp token --host LABEL` prints a bundle once. You paste it into `node join` on the member computer's home, which reaches the hub on port 4222 over your private network. After that, each `dockingbird start` on the member opens a fleet session on the control plane, and the agent gets a fleet inbox beside its own.

heading: The control plane > What a member's agents get
summary: A member's agent is named in the fleet by the computer's label, a dash and the agent's name, such as `lab-notes-1`.
text:
A member's agent is named in the fleet by the computer's label, a dash and the agent's name, such as `lab-notes-1`. A label is one to eight lowercase letters or digits and starts with a letter. An agent whose tools include `bus_send` gets ten fleet tools, listed in [the fleet tools reference](../reference/fleet-tools.md).

An agent reads both inboxes and takes the more urgent delivery first. A choice its tool puts up, or a plan to approve, is asked on the control plane first. When the control plane does not take the question, it is asked on the agent's own home.

When the control plane does not answer at the start, the agent starts all the same and works on its own home. It gets its fleet inbox once the control plane answers.

heading: The control plane > What the control plane keeps
summary: For each computer it keeps the computer's public key and a digest of its token.
text:
For each computer it keeps the computer's public key and a digest of its token. It never keeps the bundle, the computer's private key or the token itself.

A message to a fleet agent whose home is asleep or offline waits on the control plane until that home reads it. At most 200 deliveries wait for one agent.

heading: The control plane > What crosses and what stays
summary: A home's work, runs, claims and publication stay on the home.
text: A home's work, runs, claims and publication stay on the home. A fleet thread and a home thread are two threads. A message sent in one is never seen in the other, and a home's own `questions` list shows none of the fleet's.

heading: The control plane > What it never does
summary: - It never lets one computer read another computer's inboxes.
text:
- It never lets one computer read another computer's inboxes.
- It never changes a running agent. `cp remove` ends a computer's fleet sessions, and the agents keep running there without the fleet.
- It never accepts a bundle twice. Joining again takes `cp remove`, a new `cp token` and `node leave` first.
- It never protects a frame better than your network does. Frames between computers are as private as the tailnet or network that carries them.

A computer that was removed or lost its home joins again with a new bundle. The first `dockingbird cp status` after the control plane's computer restarts starts the control plane again. The fleet sessions survive as rows, and every member reconnects by itself.

heading: Licensing model
summary: You buy seats, one for each person.
text: You buy seats, one for each person. Each seat links up to three of that person's computers, for example a laptop, a desktop and a cloud VM. The sections below cover how a computer is counted, how check-ins and offline days work, and why this release never blocks your work.

heading: Licensing model > Seats and computers
summary: A seat is one person.
text:
A seat is one person. A laptop, a desktop and a cloud VM can all belong to that seat, on arm64, the only platform Dockingbird runs on. A second Dockingbird home on the same computer, made with another `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`, shares that computer's link. Agents, containers and repos are never counted.

`dockingbird license activate` links the computer you run it on. It asks for your key with the typing hidden, or reads it from standard input, and it refuses a key given as a word on the command line with exit 2. A computer is known by an identifier kept in its license file. A re-imaged VM, a cloud instance recreated on every deploy, and a container or CI runner without a machine id each get a new identifier, so each counts as a new computer every time.

When all the computers a license admits are linked, activation refuses with exit 1. Free one with `dockingbird license activations --release ID`. Better, run `dockingbird license deactivate` or `dockingbird clean --all` before you destroy a computer. A link nobody released stops counting by itself after 90 days. `dockingbird license trial` starts a trial on a computer with no key, once per computer.

heading: Licensing model > Check-ins and offline use
summary: This release does not enforce licensing.
text:
This release does not enforce licensing. A start reaches no network and downloads nothing. It runs the license client only when one is already on the computer, prints one line for any state but a valid license or none, such as `agents start because licensing isn't enforced yet`, and then the agent starts.

Once licensing is enforced, a start whose last check-in is older than a day checks in with the publisher first. A failed check-in never stops the start. Without a check-in, the license keeps working for its lease, so a computer that is offline, or an outage at the publisher, interrupts nothing.

When the term nears its end, when a computer has been offline a while, or when the term has ended and its grace period runs, a start prints one line and the agent starts. Past the grace period, a start is refused before anything runs, with exit 1, the reason, and the next step. The step is `dockingbird license activate`, `dockingbird license status --refresh` or `dockingbird update`. `dockingbird license status` shows when the lease ends.

heading: Licensing model > The end of a term
summary: `dockingbird license status` shows the state, the plan, the seats and the end of the term from the license file, with no network.
text: `dockingbird license status` shows the state, the plan, the seats and the end of the term from the license file, with no network. `--refresh` checks in first. After a term ends, the installed version keeps working. New releases need the license renewed, because the release index serves current licenses only.

heading: Licensing model > Three ways to run it
summary: Today you run the organisation's store and your hosts yourself.
text: Today you run the organisation's store and your hosts yourself. Two other arrangements are planned, one where the publisher runs the store and one that mixes the two, and neither is available yet. [Hosting paradigms](hosting-paradigms.md) sets the three side by side.

heading: Licensing model > What it never does
summary: Ten commands ignore licensing: `sync`, `stop`, `clean`, `status`, `results`, `read`, `inbox`, `serve`, `update` and `login`.
text: Ten commands ignore licensing: `sync`, `stop`, `clean`, `status`, `results`, `read`, `inbox`, `serve`, `update` and `login`. You always get your work back. A running agent keeps running, and reconnecting to it is not a new start. Nothing from a repo or an agent goes to the publisher. A key never travels on the command line, so it stays out of your shell history and out of `ps`.

heading: Licensing model > The picture
summary: Text alternative.
text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  key["License key"] --> seat["Seat: one person"]
  seat --> c1["Computer 1: laptop"]
  seat --> c2["Computer 2: desktop"]
  seat --> c3["Computer 3: cloud VM"]
  c1 --> home1["Home: default"]
  c1 --> home2["Home: lab, shares the computer"]
  c1 -->|"license activate, then check-in"| pub["Publisher's license check"]
  c1 -.->|"license activations --release ID"| freed["Link freed"]
  pub -->|"lease"| offline["Works offline until the lease ends, then a grace period"]
```

Text alternative. One key gives a seat to one person. The seat links up to three computers, here a laptop, a desktop and a cloud VM. Two homes on the laptop share its single link. A computer activates and checks in with the publisher's license check, which gives it a lease. The computer works offline until the lease ends, then a grace period runs. `license activations --release ID` frees a link.

heading: Hosting paradigms
summary: Dockingbird's team features keep their records in one PostgreSQL store, and someone has to run that store.
text: Dockingbird's team features keep their records in one PostgreSQL store, and someone has to run that store. This page names the three ways to arrange it, says who runs the store and the hosts in each, and marks the one you can use today.

heading: Hosting paradigms > The three paradigms
summary: In all three, the seat is one person with up to three computers, and license check-ins go to the publisher.
text:
| Paradigm | Who runs the store | Who runs the hosts | Available |
|---|---|---|---|
| Run it yourself | Your organisation, on its own machines or cloud | Your organisation | Yes, today |
| The publisher runs the store | The publisher | Not stated yet | Not yet available |
| A mix | The publisher | Your organisation's own hosts | Not yet available |

In all three, the seat is one person with up to three computers, and license check-ins go to the publisher.

heading: Hosting paradigms > Run it yourself
summary: This is the one arrangement you can use today.
text:
This is the one arrangement you can use today. Your organisation runs a PostgreSQL 18 store and creates its schemas with `dockingbird org create`, run as the `fleet_admin` role. `dockingbird org login` points each computer at the store, and the login's password stays in `~/.pgpass`, never in the pointer file. Each pool machine runs a worker, and one machine that stays awake runs the admitter. Your own computers or cloud VMs are the hosts, reached over your own ssh or gcloud.

You do not need the store for every setup. One computer needs nothing beyond `dockingbird claude`. A second computer needs only a `hosts.toml` entry and an ssh or gcloud route. The store matters when a team shares a queue and a pool.

| Your setup | What you need |
|---|---|
| One computer | The install and a license seat. |
| Two or more computers you reach yourself | A `hosts.toml` entry for each, over ssh or gcloud. |
| A team that shares a queue of swarms | The store, a worker on each host and one admitter. |

heading: Hosting paradigms > The two arrangements that are not yet available
summary: In one, the publisher runs the store.
text: In one, the publisher runs the store. In the other, a mix, the publisher runs the store and your own hosts run the agents. Neither is available yet, and no guide covers them.

heading: Hosting paradigms > What it never does
summary: This page documents only the first arrangement, because the other two do not work in the current release.
text: This page documents only the first arrangement, because the other two do not work in the current release. No arrangement sends the contents of a repo or an agent's output to the publisher through licensing. Today the publisher sees license check-ins and nothing else of yours, since you run the store.

```mermaid
    h2["Hosts: not stated yet"]
  end

    h3["Hosts: your organisation"]
  end

```

heading: Security model
summary: A coding agent runs commands you never typed, so Dockingbird runs each agent inside its own Docker container.
text: A coding agent runs commands you never typed, so Dockingbird runs each agent inside its own Docker container. This page lists what that container can reach, what it cannot, where secrets live, and what `dockingbird clean --all` takes away.

heading: Security model > What an agent can reach
summary: An agent reaches its own container and its own copy of one branch at `/work/<repo-name>`.
text:
An agent reaches its own container and its own copy of one branch at `/work/<repo-name>`. It also reaches the folders you connected by name, read-only unless a config grants write, and the message bus. It can read its tool's own sign-in or saved API key, but it cannot change it. Its network depends on the egress mode.

| Egress mode | What the agent reaches |
|---|---|
| `full`, the default | Its own network with NAT out and no proxy, so any host. |
| `allowlist` | Its tool's own hosts, the hosts of its presets and the hosts of its config's `allow`, through a proxy of its own. The presets are `registries` and `github`. |
| `models` | Its tool's own hosts alone, through a proxy of its own. |
| `none` | No network at all, the model API included. |

You set the mode with `--egress MODE` on a start, with `egress` in a config, or for new agents with `dockingbird egress MODE`. A host outside the list gets the proxy's `407` and a message that names Dockingbird and the way out. The proxy tunnels TLS and sees only the host name and port. In both proxy modes it refuses every address that is not public, so an agent cannot reach your Mac, your LAN or another agent through it. A proxy mode needs Docker Engine 28 or later.

heading: Security model > What an agent cannot reach
summary: No agent has a bind mount except the folders you connected.
text: No agent has a bind mount except the folders you connected. Your home folder, your keychain and your other repos are therefore out of reach. Nothing under `~/.claude` is mounted for it, and the refresh token of your Mac's own login never leaves your Mac. Your claude.ai connectors never load in an agent, in any egress mode. Each agent sits on a network of its own, so two agents share no channel except the bus.

heading: Security model > Where secrets live
summary: A connection holds the secret and the agent holds only the name.
text:
A connection holds the secret and the agent holds only the name. A GitHub key, a database password and a vault passphrase stay inside Dockingbird. The coordinator is the only container that holds them, and it has no network except ssh to the hosts of your connections. An agent asks it for a fetch, a push or one SQL statement, and never gets the key or the password.

Each tool's sign-in and saved API key live in a Docker volume that no agent mounts. An agent asks the coordinator for its own tool's credential at its start. A key you save goes through a container's standard input and never appears in an argument, a container environment, `docker inspect`, a log or a file on your Mac.

heading: Security model > What stays open
summary: The default mode `full` lets a hijacked agent send out the repo it works on and its own Docker sign-in or key to any host.
text: The default mode `full` lets a hijacked agent send out the repo it works on and its own Docker sign-in or key to any host. `dockingbird egress allowlist` closes that for agents you start from then on. An `allowlist` entry names a host and not a port, so an allowed host is open on every port. Prompt injection through repo content is not addressed. Every container runs as your uid, and an agent can fill its copy or Docker's disk until `clean` frees it. A browser you lend with `serve` loads pages through your computer's network, and in your own browser the agent acts as you on every site you are signed in to.

heading: Security model > What clean removes
summary: `dockingbird clean --all` removes this installation's containers, its five volumes, every agent's dependency cache and its images.
text: `dockingbird clean --all` removes this installation's containers, its five volumes, every agent's dependency cache and its images. The volumes hold every agent's copy and history, the sign-ins and the saved key, the tools' store and the toolchains. It also removes the links Dockingbird added to your checkouts' `.git/config` and the refs `dockingbird/<branch>`, and the files in the home. It gives the seat back first. A `config.toml` you wrote stays, and so does the empty `logs/` folder. Before it removes anything, it lists each agent still working and each copy that holds work. `dockingbird disconnect NAME` removes one connection's copy of a key.

heading: Security model > What it never does
summary: Dockingbird mounts no home folder, keychain or other repo into an agent.
text: Dockingbird mounts no home folder, keychain or other repo into an agent. No command of it shows a secret on a screen, in a log or on a command line. Your claude.ai connectors stay off in every agent. The proxy tunnels an agent's TLS traffic without opening it, so the tool's own certificate check runs against the real server.

heading: Security model > The picture
summary: Text alternative.
text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph box["Agent container"]
    agent["agent: Claude Code or Codex"]
    copy["its copy of the repo"]
    cred["its tool's sign-in"]
  end
  agent --- copy
  agent --- cred
  agent -->|"allowlist or models"| proxy["its own proxy"]
  proxy --> hosts["model API and allowed hosts"]
  agent -->|"full"| net["any host"]
  agent -->|"asks by name"| coord["coordinator"]
  coord -->|"ssh through the relay"| gh["GitHub branch you connected"]
  subgraph never["Never reached"]
    home["your home folder"]
    key["your keychain"]
    other["your other repos"]
    conn["your claude.ai connectors"]
  end
```

Text alternative. The agent container holds the agent, its copy of the repo and its tool's sign-in. In `allowlist` and `models` the agent's traffic leaves through its own proxy to the model API and the allowed hosts. In `full` it goes to any host. For a connection the agent asks the coordinator by name, and the coordinator reaches the GitHub branch you connected over ssh. Your home folder, your keychain, your other repos and your claude.ai connectors are never reached.

heading: Observability
summary: This page explains where Dockingbird's figures come from, how fresh each source is, and what none of them hold.
text: This page explains where Dockingbird's figures come from, how fresh each source is, and what none of them hold. Three sources exist. An agent reports its own context, turns and cost. A host reports its load and memory. The fleet scheduler's admitter reports the queue and the room left on each host. All three use the Prometheus text format, so any Prometheus can collect them and any Grafana can draw them.

heading: Observability > The three sources
summary: Every agent container serves its figures at `GET /metrics` on port 9464, inside its own container network.
text:
| Source | What it holds | How fresh | How you read it |
|---|---|---|---|
| An agent | Its model and effort, turns, context in use against the window and the compact point, compactions, changed and untracked paths, sign-in and token trouble, bus losses, API retries, tokens and cost per model, and its last result | As old as the last figures its container wrote: its last turn's end, its last renewal or its last change, seconds to a minute behind | `dockingbird fleet scrape` on the host |
| A host | Cores, load against the load line, idle cores, free memory, swap, Docker's CPUs and memory, containers running, and each kind of process with its CPU, memory and count | As old as the run that read it | `dockingbird fleet probe` on a Mac |
| The admitter | Queue depth by priority, reserved and spare room per host, red gate lines, stale hosts, interrupted workloads, holds by reason, counters of admissions, starts, queue wait and agent seconds | Updated by each admission pass, which runs after every change to the queue and at least every 30 seconds | `dockingbird fleet queue --metrics`, or the admitter's own port |

Every agent container serves its figures at `GET /metrics` on port 9464, inside its own container network. On Docker no port of the computer reaches that port. The host renders the same text itself with `fleet scrape`, from the home's `status`, and connects to no container. Each line carries the labels `profile` (the home), `agent`, `session` and `tool`. An agent of a swarm also carries `team` and `role`.

The agent families are gauges. Cost and tokens count from the start of an agent's process for Claude, or of its thread for Codex. They fall back to zero when it restarts. A window query on them therefore uses `delta()` or `deriv()`, and a restart shows as a negative step. `rate()` and `increase()` fit only the counters that end in `_total`, which the admitter serves.

Codex reports less than Claude. Its agents show no cost and no API retries, and its per-model tokens and compactions stay empty until its rollout has been read. [The metrics reference](../reference/metrics.md) lists every family with its type and labels.

heading: Observability > What stays out
summary: No source holds the text of a message, the content of a repository, or a name that a program printed.
text: No source holds the text of a message, the content of a repository, or a name that a program printed. The probe shows numbers and kinds of process only. The agent figures carry an agent's name, session and tool as labels and nothing it wrote. Reading figures starts, stops and changes nothing: `fleet probe`, `fleet read-home` and `fleet scrape` only look.

heading: Observability > The metrics path
summary: Text alternative.
text:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph host["Host"]
    subgraph net["Agent container network, no published port"]
      agent["agent /metrics, port 9464"]
    end
    status["home status"]
    scrape["fleet scrape"]
    probe["fleet probe"]
    exporter["exporter, one HTTP port"]
  end
  admitter["fleet admitter, its own port"]
  prom["Prometheus"]
  graf["Grafana"]
  agent -. same figures .-> status
  status --> scrape
  scrape --> exporter
  probe --> exporter
  exporter -->|"scraped every 30 s"| prom
  admitter -->|"scraped every 60 s"| prom
  prom --> graf
```

Text alternative. Inside the host, an agent's container serves `/metrics` on a port that only its own container network reaches. The agent's figures also reach the home's status. `fleet scrape` reads that status and renders the same text, and `fleet probe` reads the host. A small exporter on the host joins the two and serves one page on one HTTP port. Prometheus scrapes that page every 30 seconds and the admitter's port every 60 seconds. Grafana reads from Prometheus. Nothing is published from the container.

heading: Observability > Guides that use it
summary: - [Read the figures by hand](../guides/metrics.md) shows each command and its output.
text:
