- [Read the figures by hand](../guides/metrics.md) shows each command and its output.
- [Collect them with Prometheus](../guides/prometheus.md) runs the exporter and the two scrape jobs.
- [Draw them in Grafana](../guides/grafana.md) imports the default dashboard and sets three alerts.
- [The fleet scheduler](fleet-scheduler.md) explains the admitter that serves the third source.
- [The architecture](architecture.md) shows hosts, homes and containers.

heading: The daily loop
summary: This page walks through one normal day: start an agent at your terminal, read what it is doing, take its commits, and stop.
text: This page walks through one normal day: start an agent at your terminal, read what it is doing, take its commits, and stop. It also says what resumes by itself and what needs a command when a laptop sleeps, a terminal closes or an agent ends with work not shared.

heading: The daily loop > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird --version` prints a version. The first start is in [first run](../getting-started/first-run.md).
- Docker Desktop is running. `docker version` answers.
- You stand in a git repository with at least one commit. `git log -1` prints it. Agents start from your last commit and never see uncommitted edits.

heading: The daily loop > 1. Start an agent
summary: Use `dockingbird codex` for Codex.
text:
```bash
cd myapp
dockingbird claude
```

Use `dockingbird codex` for Codex. The first agent is `claude-1`, and the numbers climb across the whole installation, so the next one is `claude-2`. `--as NAME` picks a name made of lowercase letters, digits and `-`. `--new` always starts a new agent instead of reconnecting to one.

The agent works in its own copy of your branch, in its own container. The last start line is the done line.

```text
To leave it working, close this window.
```

Message id `AGENT_LEAVE_HINT`. The agent keeps working when you close the window.

heading: The daily loop > 2. Read status
summary: `status` only looks.
text:
```bash
dockingbird status
```

`status` only looks. It starts nothing and waits at most 10 seconds for Docker. Its first line names the version and the sign-ins.

```text
Dockingbird 0.15.3, signed in to Claude and Codex
```

Each repo and branch lists its agents, how long each has worked, how far behind you are and the step that fixes it. An agent that asks you something shows "asks you" with the count; answer it as [delegating tasks](delegating-tasks.md) says. An agent that reported on its task shows idle until you run `dockingbird stop NAME`. The last line is the done line.

```text
Nothing needs your attention.
```

Anything under "Needs your attention" comes with its own command.

heading: The daily loop > 3. Take the agents' commits
summary: `sync` works on the branch you are on, in the checkout you run it in.
text:
```bash
dockingbird sync
```

`sync` works on the branch you are on, in the checkout you run it in. Agents' commits arrive on the ref `dockingbird/<branch>`. The model is on [the sync model](../concepts/sync-model.md). The result is one of these lines.

```text
myapp (main): up to date.
myapp (main): sent your 1 commit to the agents. They'll build on it.
Updated your main to 5555555. Review them: git log -p 1111111..5555555
```

When you are behind, `sync` fast-forwards your branch and names each commit with the agent that shared it. Message ids `SYNC_UP_TO_DATE`, `SYNC_SENT` and `SYNC_UPDATED`. Run `git log -p` as the last line says before you build or run anything.

heading: The daily loop > 3. Take the agents' commits > You and the agents both have new commits
summary: On a terminal, `sync` shows the commits and asks.
text:
On a terminal, `sync` shows the commits and asks.

```text
myapp (main): you and the agents both have new commits.
Merge theirs into yours now? [Y/n]
```

Yes runs a git merge with sync's protections, then sends the merge to the agents. The done line follows.

```text
Merged, and sent the merge to the agents. Review: git log -p 1111111..main
```

A conflict stops the merge with `Fix them, commit, then run this again.` (`SYNC_CONFLICTS`). Finish the merge, commit, and run `dockingbird sync` again. Starting an agent on such a branch offers the same merge first (`START_MERGE_OFFER`). Without a terminal, `sync` prints the look-first command and `git merge dockingbird/main`.

heading: The daily loop > 3. Take the agents' commits > Edits you have not committed
summary: Your open edits stay as they are.
text: Your open edits stay as they are. When the agents changed a file you are editing, `sync` merges nothing and names the files (`SYNC_OVERLAP`). Commit or stash them, then run it again.

heading: The daily loop > 3. Take the agents' commits > Turning a commit down
summary: Undo an agent's commit with a commit of your own, then sync.
text:
Undo an agent's commit with a commit of your own, then sync.

```bash
git revert COMMIT
dockingbird sync
```

Resetting or deleting your branch does not remove it. The agents' copy keeps the commit, and the next sync brings it back.

heading: The daily loop > 3. Take the agents' commits > A paused branch
summary: When the agents' copy of a branch changed outside Dockingbird, sharing pauses and nothing is lost (`SYNC_PAUSED`).
text:
When the agents' copy of a branch changed outside Dockingbird, sharing pauses and nothing is lost (`SYNC_PAUSED`).

```bash
dockingbird status --verbose
dockingbird sync --accept 5555555
```

The first command shows what changed. The second goes on from the commit `sync` named.

heading: The daily loop > 3. Take the agents' commits > A branch made again under its old name
summary: If you deleted a branch and made it again, and you do not want the agents' commits on it, `dockingbird sync --let-go` asks once and names what goes.
text:
If you deleted a branch and made it again, and you do not want the agents' commits on it, `dockingbird sync --let-go` asks once and names what goes.

```text
Let go of 2 commits the agents made on feature/x and make yours the branch? [y/N]
```

Answer y and yours is the branch (`SYNC_LET_GO_DONE`). The agents' copies keep their work, but a copy built on the commits let go cannot share until it syncs onto yours.

heading: The daily loop > 4. Stop
summary: With agents working, `stop` asks first.
text:
```bash
dockingbird stop
```

With agents working, `stop` asks first. `--yes` skips the question, and without a terminal it refuses without `--yes`.

```text
Stop claude-1 (working) and turn Dockingbird off?
Its work is kept. [y/N]
```

Done when the command prints this line. Nothing is lost.

```text
Stopped claude-1. Dockingbird is off until you next use it.
```

`dockingbird stop claude-1` stops one agent. Its work is kept, and `dockingbird claude --as claude-1` picks it up. Dockingbird also turns itself off after 30 minutes with no agent, and the next command turns it back on.

heading: The daily loop > Reconnect, or start a new agent
summary: Close the terminal and the agent keeps working (`AGENT_KEEPS_WORKING`).
text:
Close the terminal and the agent keeps working (`AGENT_KEEPS_WORKING`).

```text
claude-1 keeps working without a terminal: dockingbird claude --as claude-1
```

A bare `dockingbird claude` in that repo reconnects to the one Claude that has no terminal, and lists them when there are two. `dockingbird claude --as claude-1` reconnects to that agent from any branch or checkout. When another terminal shows it, this terminal takes it over, and the other one says `claude-1 is now shown in another terminal. It keeps working.` `dockingbird claude --new` starts a fresh agent. Arguments for the tool and `--egress` never reconnect, because an agent's egress is fixed at its start.

heading: The daily loop > When the laptop sleeps or the network drops
summary: No behaviour is documented yet for a sleeping laptop, for a network drop during a model call, or for the recovery of an unreachable host.
text:
| Situation | What resumes by itself | What needs a command |
|---|---|---|
| A closed terminal | The agent keeps working | `dockingbird claude --as NAME` to show its screen again |
| Docker Desktop waking from Resource Saver | The command waits and prints `Waking Docker ...` (`DOCKER_WAKING`) | Past 2 minutes it ends with "Docker is answering slowly." or "Docker isn't running."; restart Docker Desktop and run the command again |
| `status` while Docker is slow | It prints what it last knew (`STATUS_DOCKER_SLOW`) | Run it again in a moment |
| A restart of Docker or Dockingbird | Nothing: the agent is stopped and its copy may hold work (`STATUS_STOPPED_BY_RESTART`) | The pick-up command on its status row |
| The laptop sleeps | Not documented yet | Not documented yet |
| The network drops during an agent's model call | Not documented yet | Not documented yet |
| A host unreachable over ssh | Not documented yet | `fleet agents` prints `Couldn't read lab: ...` (`FLEET_HOST_NOT_READ`); fix the route, see [hosts](hosts.md) |

No behaviour is documented yet for a sleeping laptop, for a network drop during a model call, or for the recovery of an unreachable host. The rows say so instead of guessing.

heading: The daily loop > An agent that ended with work not shared, or crashed
summary: Agents say how they ended.
text:
Agents say how they ended. A tool that exits cleanly with commits shared prints the first line. A tool that ended with a copy kept prints one of the next two.

```text
claude-1 is done: 2 commits shared on main. Get them: dockingbird sync
claude-1 stopped, with 2 commits not shared yet. Pick it up:
dockingbird claude --as claude-1
```

A crash, most likely the out-of-memory killer, keeps the copy every time and says so (`AGENT_CRASHED`).

```text
claude-1 crashed 3 min ago, probably out of memory (more memory: Docker
Desktop > Settings > Resources). Its copy is kept and may hold work:
dockingbird claude --as claude-1
Log: logs/agents/claude-1-<stamp>.log
```

The word "may" means Dockingbird could not count the copy's own commits, usually because the branch moved on since the copy started. `dockingbird status` lists every kept copy under "Needs your attention" with its pick-up command, from where you stand: `git switch feature/r7, then dockingbird claude --as keep7` when the copy is on another branch.

The kept copy lives in the Docker volume `dockingbird-state`, never on your Mac. `dockingbird status claude-1` names its commits and files not shared, at most 5 of each, and where the log is.

Pick it up with `dockingbird claude --as claude-1`. The tool resumes its conversation. When nothing of the conversation could be kept, one line says "The earlier conversation couldn't be restored, so this is a new one." Its copy's commits then reach you through `dockingbird sync`.

heading: The daily loop > An agent that ended with work not shared, or crashed > What clean asks
summary: `dockingbird clean` removes an empty copy at once and asks about every other one.
text:
`dockingbird clean` removes an empty copy at once and asks about every other one. The default answer is no.

```text
claude-1 left 2 commits not shared yet. Remove its copy anyway? [y/N]
```

Message id `CLEAN_ASK_UNSHARED`. Answer y only when you have taken the work or do not want it. `dockingbird clean claude-1` deletes one stopped agent whole, with its copy, results and history, after the same question. See [clean and uninstall](clean-and-uninstall.md).

heading: The daily loop > When it fails
summary: Sixteen messages can show up in a normal day.
text:
Sixteen messages can show up in a normal day. Most only inform, and each one names its own next command.

- A sync that took the agents' commits ends with [`SYNC_UPDATED`](../troubleshooting.md#sync_updated) and the `git log -p` line to review them.
- When you committed on the branch too, [`SYNC_BOTH_MOVED`](../troubleshooting.md#sync_both_moved) asks whether to merge. Starting an agent on such a branch shows [`START_MERGE_OFFER`](../troubleshooting.md#start_merge_offer) with the same question.
- A merge that hits conflicts stops with [`SYNC_CONFLICTS`](../troubleshooting.md#sync_conflicts). Fix the files, commit, and run `dockingbird sync` again.
- An agent edited a file that you are editing and have not committed: [`SYNC_OVERLAP`](../troubleshooting.md#sync_overlap) names it. Commit or stash it first.
- Someone changed the agents' copy of a branch outside Dockingbird, so [`SYNC_PAUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#sync_paused) pauses sharing. `dockingbird sync --accept COMMIT` goes on from there.
- Without a terminal, `dockingbird stop` prints [`STOP_REFUSED_NO_TTY`](../troubleshooting.md#stop_refused_no_tty). Add `--yes`.
- Docker Desktop asleep gives [`DOCKER_WAKING`](../troubleshooting.md#docker_waking) while the command waits, and `status` shows [`STATUS_DOCKER_SLOW`](../troubleshooting.md#status_docker_slow) when Docker is too slow to answer.
- Closing a terminal leaves [`AGENT_KEEPS_WORKING`](../troubleshooting.md#agent_keeps_working) on screen with the command that reconnects.
- A restart of Docker or Dockingbird shows [`STATUS_STOPPED_BY_RESTART`](../troubleshooting.md#status_stopped_by_restart) on the agent's row, with its pick-up command.
- An agent that ended with a copy kept prints [`AGENT_STOPPED_NOT_SHARED`](../troubleshooting.md#agent_stopped_not_shared), and a killed one prints [`AGENT_CRASHED`](../troubleshooting.md#agent_crashed). Both give the pick-up command.
- `dockingbird clean` asks [`CLEAN_ASK_UNSHARED`](../troubleshooting.md#clean_ask_unshared) before it deletes a copy that holds commits. The default answer is no.
- `dockingbird status NAME` can print [`STATUS_KEPT_WORKTREE`](../troubleshooting.md#status_kept_worktree) when the kept copy has a worktree with commits on no branch. A start under that name then gets a fresh copy.
- A host that ssh cannot reach shows up as [`FLEET_HOST_NOT_READ`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_host_not_read) in `dockingbird fleet agents`.

heading: Delegating tasks
summary: Give an agent a task, then do something else.
text: Give an agent a task, then do something else. The agent runs in its own container on a copy of your branch, with no terminal of its own. It tells you what it did in messages, and they wait in your inbox until you read them. All the commands below speak as one client of yours, the host client, so a question from any agent shows up in one inbox and your replies carry your name.

heading: Delegating tasks > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up and Docker Desktop is running.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up and Docker Desktop is running. `dockingbird status` prints a first line such as `Dockingbird 0.15.3, signed in to Claude and Codex`.
- The tool you delegate to has a sign-in or a saved API key. An agent without a terminal cannot sign in, so `start` refuses a tool that has neither (`SIGNIN_NEEDED`). Fix it with [sign-in and API keys](sign-in-and-api-keys.md).
- You stand in a git repository with a commit. The agent starts from your last commit.

heading: Delegating tasks > 1. Hand over the task
summary: The command prints a line for each step it waits on, then returns once the agent runs, about half a minute later.
text:
```bash
dockingbird start "Fix the failing test"
```

The command prints a line for each step it waits on, then returns once the agent runs, about half a minute later. It runs Claude unless you add `--harness codex`. `--task -` reads the task from standard input, and `--file PATH` attaches a text file (repeatable). Done when it prints the agent, the thread and the way to follow it.

```text
claude-1 started on myapp (main).
Thread <id>. Watch: dockingbird wait claude-1
```

Message id `AGENT_STARTED_BUS`. Without a task the agent starts idle and says `Send it a task: dockingbird send claude-1 TEXT` (`AGENT_STARTED_IDLE`). `--cpus 2` and `--memory 4g` limit the agent's container. `--as NAME` names the agent. A name whose agent ended picks up where it left off.

heading: Delegating tasks > 2. Wait for it
summary: `wait` returns at once with a message from the agent that you have not seen yet.
text:
```bash
dockingbird wait claude-1
```

`wait` returns at once with a message from the agent that you have not seen yet. Otherwise it waits for the next one, 25 seconds by default, or the `--seconds N` you give. Each message is told once. Done when it prints the kind, the sender and the subject.

```text
status from claude-1: turn 1
Read it: dockingbird read 1
```

Message id `WAIT_DELIVERY`. After each turn an agent sends a status message with its final text at priority P3, the lowest. An error comes at once at P1, so it sorts before every summary, task and question. When time runs out, `wait` says so and counts what waits (`WAIT_TIMED_OUT`).

```text
Nothing new in 45 s. 2 messages wait in your inbox: dockingbird inbox
```

heading: Delegating tasks > 3. Read the inbox
summary: Messages sort by priority, from P0 down to P3, and the newest comes first inside a priority.
text:
```bash
dockingbird inbox
```

Messages sort by priority, from P0 down to P3, and the newest comes first inside a priority. You see one page at a time. Each message gets a row number the first time you see it, and it keeps that number while it waits. Reading or answering other messages never renumbers it. The numbers start again at 1 once the inbox is empty. A row looks like this.

```text
  1  claude-1  status  P3  turn 1  2 min ago
```

When nothing waits, the line is `Nothing is waiting in your inbox.` (`INBOX_EMPTY`).

| Option | What it shows |
|---|---|
| `--priority P1` | Only messages of that priority, `P0` to `P3` |
| `--questions` | Only the questions your agents asked |
| `--page 2` | The second page of 20 |
| `--all` | Every row |
| `dockingbird inbox claude-2` | What other agents and you sent that agent, with no row numbers |
| `--clear` | Marks the notices of stopped agents read and closes their open questions; nothing is deleted |

heading: Delegating tasks > 4. Read a message
summary: Done when the header line prints, followed by the whole body and the files it names.
text:
```bash
dockingbird read 1
```

Done when the header line prints, followed by the whole body and the files it names.

```text
status from claude-1, P3: turn 1
```

Message id `READ_HEADER`. Reading marks the message read. A notice that needs no answer then leaves your inbox, unless you add `--keep`, which shows it and leaves it unread.

Looking for an old message? `dockingbird search "closed issues"` lists the newest messages, in every thread of your agents, whose subject or body holds all the words. It prints no body. Take the row's sender and subject, then use `read` for what came to you.

heading: Delegating tasks > 5. Answer a question
summary: A question an agent asks you leads `dockingbird status` until you answer it.
text:
A question an agent asks you leads `dockingbird status` until you answer it. List the open ones, then answer one.

```bash
dockingbird questions
dockingbird answer 3 --option 2
dockingbird answer 3 "Use Vue."
```

`questions` prints one page, oldest first, with each row's agent, kind, first line, choices and age. `dockingbird questions 3` shows one whole. When none waits, the line is `No agent is waiting for your answer.` (`QUESTIONS_EMPTY`). `answer` takes an option number or your own words and prints the answer it recorded.

```text
claude-1's question 3 answered by you: Use Vue.
```

Message id `ANSWERED`. An agent at a terminal shows its tool's own dialog on its screen, where you pick the answer with the arrow keys and Enter, and `answer` says so. A question an agent asked over the bus gets your answer as a reply it reads like any other.

heading: Delegating tasks > 6. Send more work
summary: A plain message answers the agent's one open question, or is a new task when it asked none.
text:
```bash
dockingbird send claude-1 "Yes, include the closed ones."
```

A plain message answers the agent's one open question, or is a new task when it asked none. Two open questions are refused (`SEND_AMBIGUOUS`): say which with `--reply-to ROW`, where ROW is the question's row in `dockingbird inbox`, not its number in `questions`. `--file PATH` attaches a text file. `dockingbird send claude-1 --withdraw 3` takes a message back. Done when the line names the kind, the agent and the message.

```text
Sent {kind} to claude-1 (message {value}).
```

Message id `SENT`. `{kind}` is the message kind and `{value}` identifies the message. An agent that has ended gets the message when you continue it with the command the line names.

heading: Delegating tasks > 7. Save its files
summary: `results` saves the files the agent attached in its task thread under `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/results/claude-1/`.
text:
```bash
dockingbird results claude-1 --to ../handoff
```

`results` saves the files the agent attached in its task thread under `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/results/claude-1/`. Each file is named by the first 16 hex digits of its SHA-256 and its name, readable only by you, and never overwritten. `--to DIR` also copies them into a folder of yours outside `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`. Done when each saved file prints its type and path, and the copy line follows.

```text
The copy in {where} is yours, outside dockingbird clean.
```

Message ids `RESULTS_WRITTEN` and `RESULTS_COPY_OWN`. `{where}` is the folder you gave. The thread is the one the start opened, so a follow-up's files are saved too. An agent's "done" is its own report, never Dockingbird's check: read its results before you rely on them.

heading: Delegating tasks > 8. Change its model or effort
summary: The change applies from the agent's next turn, never to one in flight.
text:
```bash
dockingbird set claude-1 --effort xhigh
```

The change applies from the agent's next turn, never to one in flight. Claude's levels are `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max`. `--model NAME` and `--compact-at 600k` work the same way. Done when the line prints.

```text
claude-1: model {model}, effort xhigh; applies from its next turn.
See it: dockingbird status claude-1
```

Message id `SET_DONE`. A change lasts only while the agent runs.

heading: Delegating tasks > 8. Change its model or effort > Give it more skills
summary: `--skills` names skill folders, comma-separated, or a skills folder, as a start does, and goes alone, beside no other change.
text:
```bash
dockingbird set claude-1 --skills .agents/skills/a
```

`--skills` names skill folders, comma-separated, or a skills folder, as a start does, and goes alone, beside no other change. A skill of a name the agent has is replaced, and none is removed. Done when the line names the skills added.

```text
claude-1: skills added: a; its tool lists them from its next turn.
```

Message id `SET_SKILLS_DONE`. The skills do not outlive a stop. [Give agents skills](skills.md) has the rules and the other two endings of the line.

heading: Delegating tasks > 9. Stop it
summary: The agent stops.
text:
```bash
dockingbird stop claude-1
```

The agent stops. Its thread, its files and its results stay.

heading: Delegating tasks > One-shot answers
summary: `dockingbird claude -p "Summarize the open TODOs"` and `dockingbird codex exec "Fix the tests"` resume or start an agent that takes exactly those arguments and print only the tool's answer on standard output.
text: `dockingbird claude -p "Summarize the open TODOs"` and `dockingbird codex exec "Fix the tests"` resume or start an agent that takes exactly those arguments and print only the tool's answer on standard output. Dockingbird's own lines go to standard error. A script that pipes nothing into a one-shot closes its input with `< /dev/null`, or Codex waits for input that never ends. With `--json` before the tool's name, the final envelope is JSON, described in [the envelope](../reference/integration/json.md). An agent sends to another agent by name; to read what they sent each other, `dockingbird inbox claude-2`. The model is in [agents and the bus](../concepts/agents-and-the-bus.md).

heading: Delegating tasks > When it fails
summary: - A start for a tool with no sign-in or key ends with [`SIGNIN_NEEDED`](../troubleshooting.md#signin_needed).
text:
- A start for a tool with no sign-in or key ends with [`SIGNIN_NEEDED`](../troubleshooting.md#signin_needed). Run `dockingbird login claude` first.
- When Dockingbird refuses the task after the agent is already running, [`AGENT_STARTED_TASK_REFUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#agent_started_task_refused) says the agent runs without it. Send it a task with `dockingbird send`, or stop it.
- Nothing arrived while `wait` ran: [`WAIT_TIMED_OUT`](../troubleshooting.md#wait_timed_out). Run `wait` again.
- [`INBOX_EMPTY`](../troubleshooting.md#inbox_empty) says no message waits for you, or none matches your `--priority` or `--questions`.
- Two open questions make a plain `send` ambiguous. [`SEND_AMBIGUOUS`](../troubleshooting.md#send_ambiguous) asks for `--reply-to` with the question's row in `dockingbird inbox`.
- Sending to an agent that runs at a terminal with no bus tools prints [`SEND_NOT_ON_BUS`](../troubleshooting.md#send_not_on_bus). Start one with `dockingbird start`.
- An agent with no attached files gives [`RESULTS_NONE`](../troubleshooting.md#results_none).
- When a file name in your folder is taken by something else, [`RESULTS_TAKEN`](../troubleshooting.md#results_taken) saves nothing there. Use another folder with `--to`.
- A `--to` folder that does not exist, or lies inside Dockingbird's own folder, prints [`RESULTS_TO_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#results_to_invalid).
- `dockingbird set` on an agent that has stopped prints [`SET_NOT_RUNNING`](../troubleshooting.md#set_not_running). Pick the agent up first.

heading: Connections
summary: A connection hands an agent one thing of yours, such as a branch, a folder or a database, and keeps the key or password inside Dockingbird.
text: A connection hands an agent one thing of yours, such as a branch, a folder or a database, and keeps the key or password inside Dockingbird. Below are the seven kinds, each linked to its page, and the commands that record, list, revoke and serve a connection.

heading: Connections > What a connection is
summary: You record a connection once with `dockingbird connect NAME`.
text:
You record a connection once with `dockingbird connect NAME`. The name is lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. Dockingbird keeps whatever opens the thing: a copy of an ssh key, a database password, a vault passphrase. The agent never sees it. When an agent needs the thing, it asks Dockingbird for one action through `bus_request`, such as a fetch, a query or a run. Dockingbird does it and sends back the result.

A config lists the connections its agents may use, as `connections = ["github"]`. Only a config you added with `dockingbird config add` may do that. A repo's own config that names a connection is refused when it starts, and the refusal names the step to add it instead. Each start of an added config's command grants its connections to that agent's session for at most its `session_hours`. A name you have not recorded, or have disabled, stops the start.

heading: Connections > The seven kinds
summary: A GitHub connection copies your ssh key, without its passphrase, into Dockingbird's own volume, or uses your Mac's ssh-agent.
text:
| Kind | Command | What the agent gets | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| GitHub repo | `connect NAME --github OWNER/REPO` | a fetch and a push of one branch | [github.md](github.md) |
| Folder | `connect NAME --folder PATH` | a folder of this computer, read-only unless the config says `write` | this page |
| Database | `connect NAME --database URL` | one SQL statement at a time, and its rows | [databases.md](databases.md) |
| Service | `connect NAME --service FILE` | a run of your program with arguments you allow | [mcp-and-services.md](mcp-and-services.md) |
| MCP server | `connect NAME --mcp URL` | the server's tools inside the agent's harness | [mcp-and-services.md](mcp-and-services.md) |
| Browser | `connect NAME --browser chrome` | Chrome, Firefox or Safari of this Mac, lent while you serve it | [mcp-and-services.md](mcp-and-services.md) |
| Vault | `connect NAME --vault gopass` | a sign-in that Dockingbird types into the lent browser | [secrets-vault.md](secrets-vault.md) |

A GitHub connection copies your ssh key, without its passphrase, into Dockingbird's own volume, or uses your Mac's ssh-agent. Agents fetch and push the one branch you connected and never hold the key. The page [github.md](github.md) covers deploy keys, grants and a push that stopped midway.

A folder connection mounts one folder of this computer at `/dockingbird/folders/NAME` from the agent's next start. The agent reads there and cannot write, rename or delete unless its config holds a `[folders]` table with `NAME = "write"`. Reads are not logged, the grant is. The details follow in the steps below.

A database connection is PostgreSQL only. Dockingbird keeps the role's password and opens the database itself, so the agent sends a statement and reads rows from a file. A role that can write is refused unless you register the database with `--writes`. The page [databases.md](databases.md) has the role's SQL and the write path.

A service connection names a program of yours in a TOML file. The program runs on this computer, as you, only while `dockingbird serve NAME` runs, with the arguments the file allows. The page [mcp-and-services.md](mcp-and-services.md) shows the file.

An MCP server connection registers a streamable-HTTP server by URL for the roles of a swarm that list its name. Each of their agents gets the server's tools beside Dockingbird's own at every start.

heading: Connections > The seven kinds
summary: A browser connection lends Chrome, Firefox or Safari of this Mac to one agent at a time.
text:
A browser connection lends Chrome, Firefox or Safari of this Mac to one agent at a time. An added config with `browser = "chrome"` instead gets a Chrome of Dockingbird's own in a container, with no connection and nothing on your Mac.

A vault connection points at a gopass store. Dockingbird types the stored password and one-time code into the lent browser, and the agent sees neither. The page [secrets-vault.md](secrets-vault.md) shows the store.

heading: Connections > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird status` must not print "Dockingbird isn't set up yet."; `dockingbird login claude` does the set-up from any folder.
- A GitHub connection runs inside a git checkout, on the branch the agents work on. Every other kind runs from any folder.
- A folder connection needs the folder under a path Docker Desktop shares, which its Settings > Resources > File sharing lists.

heading: Connections > Steps
text:
1. Record a folder of this computer. Dockingbird refuses a link, the root of the disk and its own folder.

   ```bash
   dockingbird connect notes --folder ../notes
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints these lines.

   ```text
   Connected notes: agents of a config that names it read it, read-only unless
   the config gives them write access, at /dockingbird/folders/notes.
   ```

2. Write a config that names it. In this file the agents get write access to the folder and work in an empty scratch folder.

   ```toml
   command = "analyst"
   workspace = "scratch"
   connections = ["notes"]

   [folders]
   notes = "write"
   ```

3. Add the config, then start its command. Dockingbird locks nothing in a folder, so when two agents hold write access to it, the last write wins.

   ```bash
   dockingbird config add analyst.toml
   dockingbird start --command analyst "Read /dockingbird/folders/notes and write analysis.md there."
   ```

   The step is done when the two commands print these lines.

   ```text
   Registered analyst: dockingbird analyst "task" (connections: notes)
   analyst-1 started in a scratch folder.
   ```

4. List your connections. Bare `connections` prints each enabled name. Give it a name and it adds the permitted operations, each agent's grant and expiry, and the newest requests.

   ```bash
   dockingbird connections
   dockingbird connections notes
   ```

   The second command is done when it prints the folder's line, then one `Agent:` line for each agent granted it.

   ```text
   Read-only: <path>
   Agent: analyst-1; <state>; until <time>
   ```

5. Take a connection from one agent, or from everyone. A revoke refuses that agent's new and waiting requests, and an agent already running finishes. A disconnect stops new grants and deletes Dockingbird's copy of any key. Your own key files stay.

   ```bash
   dockingbird revoke notes --to analyst-1
   dockingbird disconnect notes
   ```

   A folder cannot be taken from a running agent, so for a folder both commands stop the agent and name the command that continues it. The revoke prints these lines.

   ```text
   Revoked analyst-1's access to notes and stopped analyst-1: a folder can't be
   taken away from a running agent.
   Continue it: dockingbird analyst --as analyst-1
   ```

   For any other kind, `revoke` prints `Revoked analyst-1's access to NAME.` and `disconnect` prints `Disconnected NAME.`

6. Serve a service, a browser or a vault as yourself. Until this runs in a terminal, `dockingbird status` shows the agent's request as waiting.

   ```bash
   dockingbird serve convert
   ```

heading: Connections > Steps
summary: The step is done when the command prints this line.
text:
The step is done when the command prints this line. The page [mcp-and-services.md](mcp-and-services.md) covers `serve --all` and `serve --unit`, which keep serving with no terminal open.

   ```text
   Serving convert: agents' requests to it run here, as you, one at a time.
   Ctrl-C stops it.
   ```

7. Watch the browser of an agent whose config says `browser = "chrome"`. The command prints a `vnc://127.0.0.1` address and the browser's own password, then opens Screen Sharing. The agent can read anything you type there.

   ```bash
   dockingbird watch surf-1
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints these lines. Close the viewer or press Ctrl-C to stop.

   ```text
   Opening surf-1's browser, vnc://127.0.0.1:<port>, in your VNC viewer.
   Anything you type or paste into this browser is visible to the agent surf-1,
   which reads the page. Sign in to nothing you would not hand it.
   VNC password: <the browser's own password>
   ```

heading: Connections > Grants to a swarm role
summary: Dockingbird also grants and denies a connection by the role of a swarm, for the agents of one swarm or all of them.
text:
Dockingbird also grants and denies a connection by the role of a swarm, for the agents of one swarm or all of them.

```bash
dockingbird connect scores --revoke --role grader
dockingbird connect scores --to-role grader --until 2026-12-01T00:00:00+00:00
```

The first command stops every running agent of the role from using `scores` at its next request, with no restart. It also keeps the connection from any agent of the role that starts later. The second lifts that denial and grants the connection to the role's running agents until the time you give. Add `--swarm KEY` to narrow either one to a single swarm. Done when they print `scores: denied to role grader` and `scores: granted to role grader until <time>, <n> running agents`.

heading: Connections > When it fails
summary: - [`CONNECTION_UNKNOWN_CONNECTION`](../troubleshooting.md#connection_unknown_connection): the config names a connection that `dockingbird connections` does not list, so the start stopped.
text:
- [`CONNECTION_UNKNOWN_CONNECTION`](../troubleshooting.md#connection_unknown_connection): the config names a connection that `dockingbird connections` does not list, so the start stopped.
- [`CONNECTION_INVALID_NAME`](../troubleshooting.md#connection_invalid_name): the name holds a capital, a space or a character beyond letters, digits and hyphens.
- [`CONNECTION_CONFIG_CHANGED`](../troubleshooting.md#connection_config_changed): you connected an existing name again with another repo, branch or key. Run `dockingbird disconnect NAME` first.
- [`CONNECTION_UNKNOWN_AGENT`](../troubleshooting.md#connection_unknown_agent): no running agent has that name. `dockingbird status` lists the running ones.
- [`CONNECTION_UNKNOWN_GRANT`](../troubleshooting.md#connection_unknown_grant): the agent holds no unrevoked grant for that connection, so `revoke` had nothing to take.
- [`CONNECTION_INVALID_UNTIL`](../troubleshooting.md#connection_invalid_until): the `--until` time is past, or lacks a timezone such as `+00:00`.
- [`CONNECT_FOLDER_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_folder_invalid): the path is missing, a link, the whole disk or Dockingbird's own folder.
- [`WATCH_NO_BROWSER`](../troubleshooting.md#watch_no_browser): the agent has no browser running in a container. Its config asks for none, or its container stopped.
- [`START_FOLDER_MISSING`](../troubleshooting.md#start_folder_missing): the folder moved or was deleted since you connected it. Connect it again at its new path.
- [`CONNECT_ARGUMENTS_REQUIRED`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_arguments_required): `connect` got no name, or two kinds at once.
- [`CONFIG_INVALID_FILE`](../troubleshooting.md#config_invalid_file): a repo's own config names a connection. Move the file out of `.dockingbird/` and run `dockingbird config add` on it.

Related pages: [your-own-commands.md](your-own-commands.md) for configs, [delegating-tasks.md](delegating-tasks.md) for the tasks agents get, and [../concepts/security-model.md](../concepts/security-model.md) for what agents can reach.

heading: Your own commands
summary: A config is a small TOML file that adds a command to Dockingbird, such as `dockingbird review "Check the login flow"`.
text:
A config is a small TOML file that adds a command to Dockingbird, such as `dockingbird review "Check the login flow"`. Each command runs Claude Code or Codex with the settings you chose filled in. This page writes one, runs it, makes it the default, shares it across repos and removes it. Every key is in [the app config reference](../reference/files/app-config.md).

A command is a preset. `dockingbird review "Check the login flow"` is `dockingbird start --command review "Check the login flow"`, and the agent it starts is a delegated agent, named `review-1`, `review-2` and so on. Dockingbird ships no such command. The names `review`, `triage` and `notes` here are examples, and none exists until a config of yours adds it.

heading: Your own commands > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird status` must not print "Dockingbird isn't set up yet."
- You stand in a git checkout when the config lives in the repo. A config with `workspace = "scratch"` needs none.
- `dockingbird config list` runs. A home with no config prints the first line below.

```text
No configs yet. Put one in this repo's .dockingbird/ folder,
or add one: dockingbird config add PATH
```

heading: Your own commands > Steps
text:
1. Write the config in the repo's `.dockingbird/` folder. Each `*.toml` file there is a config, and its commands exist in that checkout with nothing to register. Dockingbird reads the file at every start, so an edit counts from the next one. Every key is optional.

   ```toml
   # .dockingbird/review.toml
   command = "review"
   summary = "Review this branch and list what to fix"
   skill = "skills/review.md"
   instructions = "review-role.md"
   tools = "bus"
   workspace = "repo"
   mode = "bus"
   context = "fresh"
   ```

   The skill file becomes the agent's first turn on the bus, with the task put where `$TASK` stands. The instructions file is role text that follows Dockingbird's own rules. Both paths start from the config's folder.

   ```markdown
   Review the changes on this branch for this task:

   $TASK

   List what to fix, file by file, in a Markdown file you attach, then mark the task done.
   ```

2. Check that Dockingbird sees it. The list shows this repo's configs first. Each row gives the config's source, commands, workspace, mode and connections, and the start of its digest, with the summary under it.

   ```bash
   dockingbird config list
   ```

   The step is done when a row names review with the source "this repo". Below the rows, the list names each config, key or command that cannot run, with its file and key and never a value. The top help screen lists the command after the everyday ones, with its summary and file.

3. Run the command. It takes every option of `start` except `--command`, among them `--terminal`, `--harness`, `--as`, `--new`, `--file` and `--task -`.

   ```bash
   dockingbird review "Check the login flow"
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints these lines. From there the agent behaves like any delegated agent: wait, inbox, read and results work on it, and its status row shows its command and mode.

   ```text
   review-1 started on myapp (main).
   Thread <id>. Watch: dockingbird wait review-1
   ```

heading: Your own commands > The four keys that decide what a command does
summary: The file can also pin start flags.
text:
| Key | Values | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `tools` | `bus` (default), `default`, `full` | `bus` moves messages and files only, and no commits reach `sync`. `default` and `full` let the agent's commits reach you through `dockingbird sync`. |
| `workspace` | `repo` (default), `scratch` | `repo` is a copy of the repo. `scratch` is an empty folder of its own, needs no git repo, and an added config's command then runs from any folder. |
| `mode` | `bus` (default), `terminal` | `bus` runs the agent in the background through messages. `terminal` runs it at your terminal. A `mode` you write is fixed, and `--terminal` or `--bus` that disagrees is refused. |
| `context` | `kept` (default), `fresh` | `kept` is one conversation for every task delivery. `fresh` starts a new conversation for each, under the same rules. Bus only. |

The file can also pin start flags. Write harness, mode, a limit or a fallback key in it, and a start that asks for something else is refused before anything starts. A key left out stays open to its flag.

| File key | Flag it fixes |
|---|---|
| `harness` | `--harness` |
| `mode` | `--terminal` and `--bus` |
| `[limits]` `cpus`, `memory`, `session_hours` | `--cpus`, `--memory`, `--session-hours` |
| `[fallback]` `harness`, `model`, `effort`, `placement` | `--fallback TOOL`, `--fallback-model`, `--fallback-effort`, `--fallback-placement` |

```text
review runs with mode = bus: .dockingbird/review.toml says so.
Drop the flag, or change the file.
```

The skill is different: only a bus agent takes it as a first turn, and a terminal agent receives the task as a plain message.

heading: Your own commands > The default command
summary: One command of a repo's configs may say `default = true`.
text:
One command of a repo's configs may say `default = true`. In that checkout, `dockingbird start "Check the login flow"` with no `--command` then runs it and says so first.

```text
Using review from .dockingbird/review.toml for this checkout
```

Two configs that each mark one command cancel each other out. A config that marks two commands is refused whole. A default in an added config is ignored, and `dockingbird claude` and `dockingbird codex` never use one.

heading: Your own commands > Share a config across repos
summary: Adding a config copies it, with the files it names, into Dockingbird, and its commands then work in every repo.
text:
Adding a config copies it, with the files it names, into Dockingbird, and its commands then work in every repo. The copy is what runs, so add the file again after each change. The config takes its file's name unless you pass `--name NAME`.

```bash
dockingbird config add agents/triage.toml
dockingbird config remove triage
```

The step is done when these lines print. The "Replaced" line appears instead of "Registered" when you add a name you added before.

```text
Registered triage: dockingbird triage "task"
Replaced triage (was 7608094fd9980624)
Removed triage.
```

Agents already running keep the config they started with. Cleaning everything removes the added configs and never touches a repo's `.dockingbird/` folder.

| Case | What wins |
|---|---|
| A name in the repo's config and in an added one | the repo's own command, in that checkout; `dockingbird -h` says so |
| A name in two of the repo's own configs | neither runs |
| A name Dockingbird keeps, such as `status`, `start` or `claude` | the config is refused whole, and `config add` refuses it |

One file can hold several commands, each in a `[commands.NAME]` table, in place of the top-level `command`, `default` and `skill`. A table sets its own summary, default, skill and instructions, and may override any other key. The top instructions come before each command's own, and a top summary reaches no command.

heading: Your own commands > Skills
summary: A config's `[skills]` table gives each agent of its commands skills its tool lists as its own.
text:
A config's `[skills]` table gives each agent of its commands skills its tool lists as its own. The `skill` key, singular, is another key: the first turn's text.

```toml
# Skills its tool lists (Claude Code's Skill tool and / menu, Codex's $ mention): one skills folder, or skill folders, each a path from this checkout's top. Default: none.
[skills]
path = ".agents/skills"
# Where they go in the agent's home: both (~/.claude/skills and ~/.agents/skills), claude or agents. Default: both.
into = "both"
```

A repo's own config's skills apply only in a checkout you have not marked untrusted. An added config's paths are relative to its file's folder, and `config add` copies them with it, so its skills are the ones it had when you added it, until you add it again. `--skills PATHS` on a start does the same for that start, and a skill it names replaces the config's skill of the same name. [Give agents skills](skills.md) has every rule, the bounds and how each tool lists the skills.

heading: Your own commands > A fallback tool
summary: A config's `[fallback]` table sets what a failed turn of its agents does: try it again, report it, or move the agent to the other tool with its conversation.
text:
A config's `[fallback]` table sets what a failed turn of its agents does: try it again, report it, or move the agent to the other tool with its conversation. Without the table every failure is reported.

1. Add the table. This one moves a Claude agent to Codex when a safety system refuses a turn, and retries every other failure that can pass, such as a rate limit or a provider outage.

   ```toml
   # .dockingbird/review.toml
   command = "review"
   harness = "claude"

   [fallback]
   harness = "codex"

   [fallback.on]
   refusal = "fallback"
   server = "retry"
   ```

   Those two rules are the defaults with a `harness`, written out. Keep transient classes on `retry`: a move changes the model in the middle of a task. [The app.toml reference](../reference/files/app-config.md#keys-of-fallback) lists every key, every error class and each default.

2. Start the command on the bus. The step is done when it prints its start lines.

   ```text
   review-1 started on myapp (main).
   Thread <id>. Watch: dockingbird wait review-1
   ```

   When this computer has no Codex sign-in, the agent starts with its move off and says so once. Its rules then only retry and report.

   ```text
   review-1 starts with its fallback off: no Codex sign-in here.
   ```

3. Read the inbox after a failed turn. A retry shows under "Needs your attention" in `dockingbird status` while it waits. A move stops the agent after its turn, keeps its copy, and sends you one message at `P1`.

   ```text
   review-1 is retrying after rate_limit (1 of 3), next in 5 min.
   review-1 stopped after refusal: moving to Codex
   ```

4. Pick the agent up on the fallback tool when Dockingbird does not. On this computer its fallback watcher runs the pick-up itself, at most three times for one agent, and `dockingbird status` names the command when nothing picks the agent up.

   ```bash
   dockingbird review --as review-1 --fallback
   ```

   The step is done when the start lines print. The agent goes on with its conversation and the messages that waited for it, under the fallback's model and effort. Afterwards the agent keeps the tool it ran last, so a later pick-up by its name runs it on Codex. By default an agent moves once at most.

heading: Your own commands > A fallback tool
summary: `dockingbird start` fills the table's keys a config leaves unset: `--fallback TOOL`, `--fallback-model MODEL`, `--fallback-effort LEVEL` and `--fallback-placement any` or `require-login`.
text: `dockingbird start` fills the table's keys a config leaves unset: `--fallback TOOL`, `--fallback-model MODEL`, `--fallback-effort LEVEL` and `--fallback-placement any` or `require-login`. A flag that differs from a value the file sets is refused. So are a model or an effort with no tool to move to, and any of the four flags for an agent at a terminal, which runs no rules.

heading: Your own commands > Trust, tool arguments and secrets
summary: A repo's own config comes with the repo, so whoever can push to it decides what it says.
text:
A repo's own config comes with the repo, so whoever can push to it decides what it says. In a checkout you marked untrusted with `dockingbird trust --off`, five keys are off: `harness_args`, `[env]`, `[skills]`, `harness_config` and `repo_settings = true`. An added config's `harness_args`, `[env]`, `[skills]` and `harness_config` apply everywhere, since you chose to add it. The page [trust-and-repo-settings.md](trust-and-repo-settings.md) has the whole trust model.

`harness_args` take only Claude Code's `--model`, `--fallback-model`, `--max-turns` and `--effort`, with `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `max` as the effort. For Codex they take `--model`, `-m` and `-c model_reasoning_effort=LEVEL`. Anything else is refused, and the refusal names the allowed flags.

Only an added config may name `connections` and `browser`, and only by the names of connections you recorded with `dockingbird connect`, never as a value. See [connections.md](connections.md). A value in any config's `[env]` flows into the agent's environment, where the agent can read it. A key or a password therefore goes in an added config and never in the repo's file. Dockingbird refuses a config that holds one of its own tokens, or a sign-in or API key it keeps.

Your own Claude Code or Codex can start these commands too, through `dockingbird mcp`. See [mcp-server.md](mcp-server.md).

heading: Your own commands > When it fails
summary: - [`CONFIG_INVALID_FILE`](../troubleshooting.md#config_invalid_file) refuses a file or a start.
text:
- [`CONFIG_INVALID_FILE`](../troubleshooting.md#config_invalid_file) refuses a file or a start. The line names the key and why, in words such as "a name Dockingbird keeps", "not an allowed value" or "only for a config you added", and never shows the value.
- [`CONFIG_PROBLEM_ROW`](../troubleshooting.md#config_problem_row) is one row of `dockingbird -h` or `config list` for a config, key or command that does not apply, such as `.dockingbird/review.toml: harness_args applies after dockingbird trust`.
- [`CONFIG_READ_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#config_read_failed) means Dockingbird could not read the configs. Its own commands still work.
- [`CONFIG_NOT_REGISTERED`](../troubleshooting.md#config_not_registered) means `config remove` found no added config of that name. `config list` shows the names.
- [`START_COMMAND_UNKNOWN`](../troubleshooting.md#start_command_unknown) means no config here gives that command. The message lists the ones that do.
- [`START_CONFIG_FIXED`](../troubleshooting.md#start_config_fixed) means a flag such as `--harness` or `--terminal` disagrees with a key the file fixes. Drop the flag or change the file.
- [`START_SKILLS_REFUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#start_skills_refused) means a start's `--skills` names what Dockingbird cannot use, such as a path with no skill or a link. Nothing was started. Fix that skill folder, or leave it out of `--skills`.
- [`START_FALLBACK_NO_HARNESS`](../troubleshooting.md#start_fallback_no_harness) means `--fallback-model` or `--fallback-effort` came with no fallback tool, from the flag or the file. Nothing was started. Add `--fallback TOOL`, or a `harness` to the `[fallback]` table.
- [`START_FALLBACK_TERMINAL`](../troubleshooting.md#start_fallback_terminal) means a fallback flag came with an agent at a terminal, which runs no rules. Nothing was started. Drop the flag, or start the agent on the bus.
- [`FALLBACK_OFF_HERE`](../troubleshooting.md#fallback_off_here) says the agent started with its move off, because this computer has no sign-in for the fallback tool. Sign that tool in with `dockingbird login`, then pick the agent up.
- [`FALLBACK_NO_LOGIN`](../troubleshooting.md#fallback_no_login) means the pick-up, or a start under `placement = "require-login"`, needs the fallback tool signed in here. Nothing was started. Run the `dockingbird login` the line names.
- [`FALLBACK_NONE`](../troubleshooting.md#fallback_none) means the agent recorded no tool to move to. Name one, as in `--fallback codex`.
- [`FALLBACK_MAX`](../troubleshooting.md#fallback_max) means the agent has moved as often as one agent may. Pick it up on the tool it runs now, without `--fallback`.
- [`STATUS_FALLBACK_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#status_fallback_failed) says every pick-up the fallback watcher tried was refused, and names the last refusal. Mend its cause, then run the `--fallback` pick-up the note names.

heading: Give agents skills
summary: A skill is a folder holding a `SKILL.md` and the files it uses (scripts, references, Codex's `agents/openai.yaml`), named by its folder.
text: A skill is a folder holding a `SKILL.md` and the files it uses (scripts, references, Codex's `agents/openai.yaml`), named by its folder. Dockingbird gives an agent skills its tool lists as its own: Claude Code in its Skill tool and its `/` menu, Codex for its `$` mention. This page shows four ways to give an agent skills: at one start, from a config, on a running agent and for a swarm role. A config's `skill` key, singular, is another key: the text of the agent's first turn, which [your own commands](your-own-commands.md) covers.

heading: Give agents skills > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird status` must not print "Dockingbird isn't set up yet."
- You stand in the git checkout that holds the skill folders. The examples use two skills in `.agents/skills`:

  ```text
  .agents/skills/a/SKILL.md
  .agents/skills/b/SKILL.md
  ```

- Each `SKILL.md` has a frontmatter that names a `description`. Codex lists no skill whose `SKILL.md` lacks one. Claude Code lists a skill with no frontmatter among its slash commands.

heading: Give agents skills > 1. Give skills at one start
summary: `--skills PATHS` names skill folders, comma-separated, or a skills folder, each path relative to the folder you run the command in, or absolute.
text:
```bash
dockingbird start --skills .agents/skills "Fix the failing test"
dockingbird start --skills .agents/skills/a,.agents/skills/b "Fix the failing test"
```

`--skills PATHS` names skill folders, comma-separated, or a skills folder, each path relative to the folder you run the command in, or absolute. The first line gives the agent every skill of `.agents/skills`, the second those two. `dockingbird claude`, `dockingbird codex` and every config's command take the same option. A skill it names replaces a config's skill of the same name. Done when the start prints the agent, the thread and the way to follow it.

```text
claude-1 started on myapp (main).
Thread <id>. Watch: dockingbird wait claude-1
```

Message id `AGENT_STARTED_BUS`. A path Dockingbird cannot use stops the start, and nothing is started.

heading: Give agents skills > 2. Name them in a config
summary: A config's `[skills]` table gives the skills to every start of its command.
text:
A config's `[skills]` table gives the skills to every start of its command. Add the table to any config; [your own commands](your-own-commands.md) writes one step by step.

```toml
# .dockingbird/app.toml
command = "review"

[skills]
path = ".agents/skills"
into = "both"
```

- `path` is one skills folder, each of whose folders holding a `SKILL.md` is one skill (`path = ".agents/skills"`), or a list of folders, each one skill or a skills folder (`path = [".agents/skills/review", "tools/skills"]`). A repo's own config names paths from the checkout's top.
- `into` is where they go in the agent's home. `both`, the default, writes each skill to `~/.claude/skills`, where Claude Code finds personal skills, and to `~/.agents/skills`, where Codex finds a user's. `claude` or `agents` writes only that one.
- A repo's own config's skills apply only in a checkout you have not marked untrusted with `dockingbird trust --off`. An added config's skills, and the ones `--skills` names, apply everywhere.
- An added config's paths are relative to its file's folder, and `config add` copies them with it. Its skills are the ones it had when you added it, until you add it again.

Run the command. Done when it prints its start lines.

```bash
dockingbird review "Check the login flow"
```

```text
review-1 started on myapp (main).
Thread <id>. Watch: dockingbird wait review-1
```

In a checkout you marked untrusted, the command runs without the skills, and `dockingbird config list` and `dockingbird -h` say so in a row: `.dockingbird/app.toml: skills applies after dockingbird trust` (`CONFIG_PROBLEM_ROW`).

heading: Give agents skills > 3. Add skills to a running agent
summary: `set` names the skills as `--skills` names them at a start, and reads them on this computer first.
text:
```bash
dockingbird set claude-1 --skills .agents/skills/a
```

`set` names the skills as `--skills` names them at a start, and reads them on this computer first. When one cannot be read, nothing changes. A skill of a name the agent has is replaced, and none is removed. Done when the line names the skills added.

```text
claude-1: skills added: a; its tool lists them from its next turn.
```

Message id `SET_SKILLS_DONE`. The end of the line says when the agent's tool lists them.

| The agent runs | Its tool lists the skills | The line ends |
|---|---|---|
| on the bus | from its next turn: Claude Code is told `/reload-skills` before that turn, and Codex reads them when its next turn starts | `its tool lists them from its next turn.` |
| on the bus, with its screen running | from its next idle prompt, where Claude Code is typed `/reload-skills` and Codex reads them again itself | `its tool lists them from its next idle prompt.` |
| at a terminal | within seconds, through Claude Code's own watcher or Codex's own re-read | `its tool lists them within seconds.` |

`--skills` goes alone. Beside another change, such as `--model`, `set` refuses both and changes nothing. The skills do not outlive a stop: a pick-up has the skills its own start names. A Codex agent started with no skill lists the skills added later within Codex's own budget, 2% of its context window, since Dockingbird sets its `skills.max_context_tokens` only at a start with skills.

heading: Give agents skills > 4. Give a swarm role skills
summary: A swarm's `[[role]]`, or a library role, may name `skills`, a table as a config's `[skills]` takes it.
text:
A swarm's `[[role]]`, or a library role, may name `skills`, a table as a config's `[skills]` takes it. `path` is one skill or skills folder or a list of them, each a path from the top of the swarm's source, a library role's too. `into` is `both`, `claude` or `agents`.

```toml
[[role]]
name = "builder"
harness = "claude"
count = 2
brief = "briefs/builder.md"

[role.skills]
path = "tools/skills"
into = "both"
```

`fleet submit` reads the paths from the top of the checkout the definition is in, by a config's rules: no link, no hidden entry, the skills' bounds. It refuses `skills` in a swarm with no `[source]`, which has no clone. `fleet describe` reads no tree. Every start of the role's agents reads the trees from the swarm's clone, where its agents run, and places them as a config's skills are placed. The example names `tools/skills`, outside the clone's own `.agents/skills`, so a Codex role lists each skill once ([How each tool lists them](#how-each-tool-lists-them)).

A `[[role]]` entry's `skills` replaces its library role's whole table, so name every path the role needs in one place. `fleet submit --set` cannot set `skills`. A skill of a plugin, or one in a person's own skills folder, is not reachable by its install name: copy its folder into the repository first, under `.agents/skills/` or in a `skills/` folder of the definition's own.

Give a role a skill only when its task needs that skill's method, such as a SQL skill for the builder and the reviewer of a migration, or a verification skill for a tester. Each skill an agent has sits in its tool's listing for every agent of the role, for the whole swarm. A fact only one swarm needs, such as a table's name or a command's flags, goes in the role's brief. A role whose task needs no skill gets no `skills` key, and its library role's rules and its brief are its whole context.

```bash
dockingbird fleet submit NAME
```

Done when the swarm is queued.

```text
{id} pending, position {position}
```

Message id `FLEET_SUBMITTED`. What the submit cannot read is refused at its key, one `FLEET_REFUSED` line each: `role[N].skills.path`, `role[N].skills.<name>` for one skill, or `role[N].skills` for the set's bounds.

```text
refused: role[N].skills.path: not a skills table: path (skill or skills folders of the source checkout), into (both, claude or agents)
```

heading: Give agents skills > 4. Give a swarm role skills
summary: A start whose clone lacks a path, as when its branch moved after the submit, holds the swarm.
text:
A start whose clone lacks a path, as when its branch moved after the submit, holds the swarm. The worker's log names the agent, its role, the key and the cause, and `fleet why` names the hold.

```bash
dockingbird fleet why ID
```

```text
{id} is held: skills_refused
```

Message id `FLEET_WHY_STATE`. Push the fix to the swarm's branch, then release the swarm.

```bash
dockingbird fleet release ID
```

Done when the line names the state the swarm entered.

```text
{id} {state}
```

Message id `FLEET_STATE_NOW`. Every start attempt of a swarm in a clone of the worker's own, the one `fleet release` makes included, first fetches and fast-forwards that clone from its `origin`, so the fix you pushed reaches the start. A clone that cannot fast-forward, because it holds commits not yet pushed, is used as it is, and the worker's log says so. A checkout your home links by hand is never fetched.

heading: Give agents skills > How each tool lists them
summary: Dockingbird places each `SKILL.md` as it is, its frontmatter and any hooks it names included.
text:
Dockingbird places each `SKILL.md` as it is, its frontmatter and any hooks it names included.

| Topic | Claude Code | Codex |
|---|---|---|
| Where `into` writes them | `~/.claude/skills`, where Claude Code finds personal skills (`both` or `claude`) | `~/.agents/skills`, where Codex finds a user's (`both` or `agents`) |
| How it lists them | in its Skill tool and its `/` menu | in a table of its skill roots, each with an alias (`r0`, `r1`, ...), `~/.agents/skills` among them, and one line per skill naming its `SKILL.md` under its root's alias |
| Listing budget | 1% of its context window | 2% of its context window, or 8,000 characters when it doesn't know the window; for an agent started with skills, the 10,000 tokens Dockingbird sets (below) |
| Each description cut at | 1,536 characters | 1,024 characters |
| A `SKILL.md` without a frontmatter `description` | listed among its slash commands when it has no frontmatter | not listed |
| A skill of the same name in the checkout's own `.claude/skills` or `.agents/skills`, which the tool loads | lists only the one in your personal folder, the one Dockingbird wrote | lists both |

Past its budget, Codex shortens the descriptions, then leaves out whole skills, user skills (the ones in `~/.agents/skills`) first. For an agent with skills, Dockingbird sets Codex's `skills.max_context_tokens` to its cap, 10,000 tokens. A skill whose `agents/openai.yaml` turns implicit use off (`allow_implicit_invocation: false`) is left out of Codex's list and reached by a `$` mention alone. A Codex role whose `path` is the clone's own `.agents/skills` lists each skill twice, the placed copy and the repository's; name a folder outside it to list each once.

heading: Give agents skills > Bounds
summary: A refusal past a bound names the key that went over.
text:
| Bound | Figure |
|---|---|
| A skill's name | its folder's: 1 to 63 lowercase letters, digits and `-`, a letter or a digit first, no `--` and no `-` at the end; never `synced` |
| Entries in one `skills.path` or one `--skills` | 16 |
| Skills of one agent, a config's and a start's together | 32 |
| Files in one skill | 64 |
| Depth of a file under its skill folder | 8 path parts |
| One file of a skill | 1 MiB |
| One agent's skills together, as Dockingbird records them | 4 MiB |
| Codex's `skills.max_context_tokens` for an agent with skills | 10,000 tokens |

A refusal past a bound names the key that went over.

heading: Give agents skills > When it fails
summary: - [`START_SKILLS_REFUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#start_skills_refused) stops a start whose `--skills` names what Dockingbird cannot use: an empty path between commas, a path with no skill, a link, a skill named twice, a skill folder named `synced` (Claude Code's folder of synced skills), or a file it can't read safely.
text:
- [`START_SKILLS_REFUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#start_skills_refused) stops a start whose `--skills` names what Dockingbird cannot use: an empty path between commas, a path with no skill, a link, a skill named twice, a skill folder named `synced` (Claude Code's folder of synced skills), or a file it can't read safely. The line `--skills: {key}: {cause}` names the key and why, and nothing was started. Fix that skill folder, or leave it out of `--skills`.
- [`SET_SKILLS_REFUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#set_skills_refused) refuses `set --skills` for the same causes, or when the agent's skills with those added would be more, or larger, than an agent may have. The line `--skills: {key}: {cause}; nothing was changed.` names the key and why. Fix that skill folder, or leave it out of `--skills`.
- [`CONFIG_INVALID_FILE`](../troubleshooting.md#config_invalid_file) refuses a config whose `[skills]` table Dockingbird cannot use. The line names the key, such as `skills.path`, and why, and never shows the value. Fix that, then run the command again.
- [`OPTIONS_NOT_BOTH`](../troubleshooting.md#options_not_both) means `set --skills` came with another change, such as `--model`. Nothing changed. Give `--skills` in a `set` of its own.
- [`FLEET_REFUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_refused) names a role's `skills` key that `fleet submit` could not read, such as `role[N].skills.path`, or `skills` in a swarm with no `[source]`. Fix the folder or the key, then submit again.
- [`FLEET_WHY_STATE`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_why_state) prints `{id} is held: skills_refused` when a start's clone lacks a path a role's `skills` names. Push the fix, then run `dockingbird fleet release ID`.

heading: Toolchains and dependencies
summary: Each agent runs the language versions your repo already names, where production reads them.
text:
Each agent runs the language versions your repo already names, where production reads them. This page shows which versions agents get, installs them ahead of a start, locks them for every computer, and changes one.

Dockingbird reads none of the version files itself. [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev) reads them in a container of Dockingbird's own and installs each version once per Mac, into a store every agent mounts read-only. The files it reads are `mise.toml`, `.tool-versions`, and the version files that `mise.toml` enables under `[settings]`. For example, `idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools = ["node", "python"]` makes mise read `.nvmrc` and `.python-version`. A `mise.lock` decides over them, as mise decides.

heading: Toolchains and dependencies > Before you start
summary: - You stand in a git repo.
text:
- You stand in a git repo. Outside one, `dockingbird env` says so and exits 1.
- Docker runs. With Docker off, `env` shows the heading and the store's line from its last record, and says the versions need Dockingbird running.
- To change a version, you can commit `mise.toml` and `mise.lock` in the repo.

heading: Toolchains and dependencies > Steps
text:
1. Read what agents get. The table lists each tool the repo's files name, with the request and its file, beside the version agents get. A version is marked "(locked)" when `mise.lock` names it, and "(not installed yet)" when no start has installed it. Below come the image's Python, Node and Go, where nothing names them, and the count of toolchains this Mac holds. The command runs in a container with your checkout mounted read-only, so it writes nothing there.

   ```bash
   dockingbird env
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints a table like this one.

   ```text
   myapp (main)   repo wants         agents get
     Python       3.12 (mise.toml)   3.12.7 (locked)
     Node         20 (.nvmrc)        20.18.1
     Go           nothing named      1.27.2 (the image's)
   Dependencies: none preinstalled (no lock file).
   Downloaded: 2 toolchains. Unused ones go with: dockingbird clean
   Change one: dockingbird env use TOOL VERSION
   ```

   With `--json`, each line is one envelope, and a tool's row adds `tool_word`, `locked` and `installed`.

2. Install those versions now, so the next start waits for none. This writes nothing in your checkout.

   ```bash
   dockingbird env install
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints this line, or when the versions were installed already.

   ```text
   Lock them so every machine gets the same: dockingbird env lock
   ```

3. Lock the versions. Each exact version goes into `mise.toml` and is locked in `mise.lock`. Once you commit both, every Mac and every agent gets the same versions.

   ```bash
   dockingbird env lock
   git add mise.toml mise.lock
   ```

   The step is done when the first command prints these lines.

   ```text
   Locked Python and Node in mise.toml and mise.lock. Commit them so every machine
   gets the same: git add mise.toml mise.lock
   ```

4. Change one version. The tool is python, node, go, java, rust, ruby, bun, deno, zig, pnpm, yarn or npm. The version is a number such as 22, 3.12 or 1.82.0. Go also takes prefix:1.20, and Java takes temurin-21, or 21 for mise's default vendor. The words lts and latest are refused. Any other tool that mise knows goes into `mise.toml` by hand.

   ```bash
   dockingbird env use node 22
   ```

   The command writes the version into `mise.toml`, creating the file when the repo has none, and installs it. The step is done when it prints this line. A line for each running agent follows, because those agents keep their old version until you restart them.

heading: Toolchains and dependencies > Steps
text:
```text
   Wrote mise.toml: node = "22" (was .nvmrc: 20; mise.toml wins now). Agents started from now get Node 22.11.0.
   ```

5. Start with the image's versions for one start only. Neither flag is remembered. The first skips the repo's versions, and the second keeps the toolchain and skips the dependency install.

   ```bash
   dockingbird claude --no-toolchain
   dockingbird claude --no-deps
   ```

   The first line of a start says what the agent gets. Both flags also work on `codex` and `start`.

   ```text
   Toolchain for myapp: Python 3.12.7 (mise.toml) and Node 20.18.1 (.nvmrc).
   Toolchain for myapp: nothing named; agents get the image's versions.
   ```

heading: Toolchains and dependencies > What a start does about versions
summary: A start installs a version that is not in the store yet, with a live line, before anything else starts.
text:
A start installs a version that is not in the store yet, with a live line, before anything else starts. A second agent on the same repo prints the first line alone. An install that fails stops the start before anything is made, with mise's last lines. Ctrl-C during an install ends the start with exit 130 and leaves the install going, so the next start uses it. A running agent keeps the versions it started with, and `dockingbird status` says when its repo now asks for others.

```text
Installing Node 20.18.1 ... {elapsed}: <mise's latest line>
Installed Node 20.18.1 ({elapsed}).
```

heading: Toolchains and dependencies > Dependencies
summary: Before its tool starts, an agent whose repo names a toolchain installs the repo's dependencies in its own copy, from the lock files at the repo's top, with the toolchain's own package managers.
text:
Before its tool starts, an agent whose repo names a toolchain installs the repo's dependencies in its own copy, from the lock files at the repo's top, with the toolchain's own package managers. A repo that names no toolchain gets the image's versions and installs nothing.

| Lock file | Command the agent runs |
|---|---|
| `uv.lock` | `uv sync --locked` |
| `package-lock.json` | `npm ci` |
| `pnpm-lock.yaml` | `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` |
| `yarn.lock` | `yarn install --immutable` (Yarn 2 and later) or `yarn install --frozen-lockfile` (Yarn 1) |
| `go.sum` | `go mod download` |
| `Cargo.lock` | `cargo fetch --locked` |
| `Gemfile.lock` | `BUNDLE_FROZEN=true bundle install` |

A lock file that does not match its manifest fails the install, as it would in production. A Maven or Gradle build, and a `requirements.txt` without a lock file, get nothing. The agent prints `Installing myapp's dependencies: uv sync --locked (uv.lock)`, the command's own lines, then `Dependencies installed ({elapsed}).` On the bus these lines go to its log, and `dockingbird status` shows "preparing: installing dependencies".

npm's, uv's and Go's downloads go to a cache of the agent's own, the Docker volume `dockingbird-cache-<agent>` at `/dockingbird/cache`. A restart of the same agent keeps it. `dockingbird clean` removes an agent's cache with its kept copy, `clean NAME` with the agent, and `clean --all` removes them all. `clean` also removes the versions no running agent and no repo's last look names, and clears mise's download cache.

An agent whose egress is `none` or `models` reaches no registry, so it runs each command's offline form, such as `uv sync --locked --offline`, from what is cached. See [egress-and-network.md](egress-and-network.md).

heading: Toolchains and dependencies > Trust
summary: A repo's mise config can do more than name versions.
text:
A repo's mise config can do more than name versions. Its `[env]` sets variables and its `[settings]` change how mise installs. Those load only in a checkout you trust, which is every checkout unless you ran `dockingbird trust --off` or made untrusted the default. In an untrusted checkout, a mise config that needs trust stops the start and `env`, with mise's own words. A `mise.toml` of plain versions, a `.tool-versions` and the version files need no trust. An untrusted agent gets its toolchain alone and prints `Dependencies: skipped (untrusted checkout; dockingbird trust allows them).` The page [trust-and-repo-settings.md](trust-and-repo-settings.md) covers trust.

A config's `[env]` arrives through mise before the repo's own, so the repo's `mise.toml` entry of a name wins. A config's `mise_env`, such as `"ci"`, makes mise read `mise.ci.toml` over `mise.toml`, for the install and for the agent's environment. See [your-own-commands.md](your-own-commands.md).

heading: Toolchains and dependencies > When it fails
summary: - [`TOOLCHAIN_INSTALL_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#toolchain_install_failed) shows mise's last lines when a version does not exist, a download failed or a checksum did not match.
text:
- [`TOOLCHAIN_INSTALL_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#toolchain_install_failed) shows mise's last lines when a version does not exist, a download failed or a checksum did not match. No agent started. Fix the file that names the version, or start with `--no-toolchain`.
- [`TOOLCHAIN_LOOK_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#toolchain_look_failed) means mise could not read the repo's versions. An invalid `mise.toml` is one cause, and an untrusted checkout whose mise config needs trust is the other.
- [`TOOLCHAIN_LOOK_UNAVAILABLE`](../troubleshooting.md#toolchain_look_unavailable) appears when Docker is off, so `env` cannot read the versions agents get. The exit status is 0.
- [`TOOLCHAIN_LOCK_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#toolchain_lock_invalid) says `mise.lock` is unreadable and ignored. `dockingbird env lock` writes it again.
- [`TOOLCHAIN_RUNNING_DIFFERS`](../troubleshooting.md#toolchain_running_differs) appears in `status` for an agent that runs an older version than the repo now asks for. Stop it and start it again under its name.
- [`TOOLCHAIN_INTERRUPTED`](../troubleshooting.md#toolchain_interrupted) follows a Ctrl-C during an install. The install carries on and no agent started.
- [`ENV_NOT_A_REPO`](../troubleshooting.md#env_not_a_repo) means you ran `env` outside a git repo.
- [`ENV_USE_NOT_A_NUMBER`](../troubleshooting.md#env_use_not_a_number) refuses `lts` and `latest` and names an example number for the tool.
- [`ENV_USE_UNKNOWN_TOOL`](../troubleshooting.md#env_use_unknown_tool) lists the twelve tools `env use` takes.
- [`ENV_USE_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#env_use_failed) means mise could not install that version, offline or because it does not exist.
- [`DEPS_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#deps_failed) ended the agent because the install command failed. Fix what the last lines say, or pick the agent up with `--no-deps`.
- [`DEPS_OFFLINE_REFUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#deps_offline_refused) ended the agent because its egress reaches no registry and the packages are not cached. Pick it up with `--egress full`, or with `--no-deps`.

heading: Trust and repo settings
summary: This page explains which checkouts are trusted and what that changes inside an agent.
text: This page explains which checkouts are trusted and what that changes inside an agent. A trusted checkout lets the repo's own settings, hooks and MCP servers load, as Claude Code and Codex load them outside Dockingbird. An untrusted one gets none of them, because a cloned repo can use them to run code before an agent does anything. The marks live on your Mac, so no agent can change them.

heading: Trust and repo settings > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird --version` prints a version.
- You know the repo's folder. Trust is per checkout, and `dockingbird trust` with no path acts on the repo you stand in.

heading: Trust and repo settings > What trust changes
summary: Every checkout is trusted unless you mark it untrusted, or make untrusted the default.
text:
Every checkout is trusted unless you mark it untrusted, or make untrusted the default. The table shows what each state gives an agent.

| Item | Trusted checkout | Untrusted checkout |
|---|---|---|
| The repo's Claude Code and Codex settings, hooks and MCP servers | Load | Stay off |
| The repo's rules file, `.dockingbird/rules.md` by default | Read at each start | Not read |
