| Claude's project `CLAUDE.md` and skills | Load with the settings | Stay off |
| Codex's `AGENTS.md` | Read | Read, through Codex's global instructions file; its `.codex/config.toml`, hooks and exec policies stay off |
| The repo's mise `[env]` and `[settings]` | Load | A config that needs them stops the start |
| Dependency installs from lock files | Run | Skipped: the agent gets its toolchain alone |
| Claude's question whether to trust `/work/<repo-name>` | Dockingbird answers it | Claude may ask once per repo; Dockingbird never answers |
| Codex's folder-access notice | Not shown | Shown at each screen; one Enter opens its copy restricted |

A plain version in `mise.toml`, a `.tool-versions` file and the version files need no trust. See [toolchains](toolchains.md).

heading: Trust and repo settings > 1. Mark a checkout untrusted
summary: `--off` and `--forget` are the same.
text:
```bash
dockingbird trust --off
```

`--off` and `--forget` are the same. Name another folder to mark it: `dockingbird trust --off ../cloned-app`. Done when the line prints.

```text
Not trusted: {path}. Its own settings, hooks and MCP servers stay off
in agents started here.
```

Message id `TRUST_FORGOTTEN`. `{path}` is the checkout's path on your Mac. Agents already running keep what they started with.

heading: Trust and repo settings > 2. Trust a checkout again
summary: This removes the mark `--off` left and marks the checkout trusted, whatever the default says.
text:
```bash
dockingbird trust
```

This removes the mark `--off` left and marks the checkout trusted, whatever the default says. Done when the line prints.

```text
Trusted {path}. This checkout's own settings, hooks and MCP servers
load in agents started here.
```

Message id `TRUSTED`. A tool loads them only once Dockingbird has proven they cannot redirect its sign-in, and today that holds for both Claude Code and Codex. For a tool where it does not yet hold, the command adds `Claude Code keeps them off for now: Dockingbird has not yet proven they can't redirect its sign-in.` (`TRUST_PIN_UNPROVEN`).

heading: Trust and repo settings > 3. Make untrusted the default
summary: Open `config.toml` in `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` and put one line at the top.
text:
Open `config.toml` in `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` and put one line at the top.

```toml
trust = "untrusted"
```

`trust = "trusted"`, or no line, is the default. A checkout you marked with `dockingbird trust` or `dockingbird trust --off` keeps its mark whatever the line says. The marks are files under `trust/` and `untrusted/` in `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`. You edit the line by hand: there is no command or flag for it. Dockingbird changes nothing else in that file except its own `last_build_seconds` line, and a `config.toml` holding anything of yours stays through `dockingbird clean --all`. You can write the line before the first start, because a fresh home holding only your `config.toml` is Dockingbird's to use.

The command prints no done line. Check the line by starting a Codex agent in a repo you never marked: it shows the untrusted note before Codex opens.

```text
Codex may ask for folder access to /work/myapp: that is its copy of this repo.
```

Message id `TRUST_NOTE`. Any other `trust` value, or a `config.toml` that is not TOML, is refused by every command that reads trust (`TRUST_CONFIG_INVALID`). A start stops before anything runs.

heading: Trust and repo settings > 4. What an untrusted checkout looks like at a start
summary: Claude may ask once per repo whether to trust its copy.
text:
Claude may ask once per repo whether to trust its copy. Codex shows its folder-access notice each time it opens its screen. Dockingbird answers neither, and whatever you answer turns nothing on. At a terminal, Dockingbird prints its note before each such Codex start and waits for Enter.

```text
Press Enter to open Codex.
```

Press Enter before you type. `n`, `q`, `2` or Esc at Codex's notice close Codex and end the agent. Ctrl-C there ends the start before Codex runs. A start whose input or output is a pipe prints Codex's note on the first start only and never waits. An agent started with `dockingbird start` in an untrusted repo runs without a screen, because its tool would ask about trust (`START_NO_SCREEN_TRUST`).

Dependency installs are skipped, and the agent says so.

```text
Dependencies: skipped (untrusted checkout; dockingbird trust allows them).
```

Message id `DEPS_SKIPPED_UNTRUSTED`. When the repo's mise config needs trust, the start stops. Two ways on: `dockingbird trust`, or a start with the image's versions.

```bash
dockingbird claude --no-toolchain
```

`--no-toolchain` is for that one start and is not remembered. Also on `codex` and `start`.

heading: Trust and repo settings > 5. A trusted repo's Codex config that sets `developer_instructions`
summary: Dockingbird's rules reach a Codex agent through the `developer_instructions` key.
text:
Dockingbird's rules reach a Codex agent through the `developer_instructions` key. A trusted repo whose `.codex/config.toml` sets that key would replace them, so the start is refused on this Mac before anything runs, exit 2.

```text
.codex/config.toml sets developer_instructions, which replaces the agent's
Dockingbird rules in a trusted checkout, so nothing was started.
Remove the key, or run untrusted: dockingbird trust --off
```

Message id `START_PROJECT_RULES_REPLACED`. The same line shows when the file cannot be read (a link, over its size bound, not TOML). It also answers a bare `dockingbird codex` that would reconnect to a running agent: the agent keeps working, and you reach it again once the key is gone. Claude is not affected, and an untrusted repo's file is never read.

heading: Trust and repo settings > 6. Rules of your own for every agent
summary: Agents get Dockingbird's built-in rules for the coordination tools.
text:
Agents get Dockingbird's built-in rules for the coordination tools. To add your own for every agent in this home, write one file per tool in the home's `instructions/` folder.

```bash
mkdir -p "$DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/instructions"
$EDITOR "$DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/instructions/claude.md"
```

With no `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` set, the home is `~/.local/share/dockingbird`. The files are `claude.md` and `codex.md`. Dockingbird copies a changed file into Docker the way it copies a key, read-only to agents, and never mounts it. A repo has its own rules too: the file that `[rules] file` names in `.dockingbird/project.toml` is read from the checkout at each start, `.dockingbird/rules.md` when the key is unset. It reaches Claude and Codex after Dockingbird's rules and before a config's own instructions.

A rules file the project names that is missing, a link, not UTF-8 text or holding a Dockingbird credential stops the start. So does a total of rules longer than 64 KB. In an untrusted repo the project's file is not read. These commands print no done line. Start an agent and ask it to quote its rules.

heading: Trust and repo settings > When it fails
summary: - [`TRUST_FORGOTTEN`](../troubleshooting.md#trust_forgotten): the checkout is marked untrusted.
text:
- [`TRUST_FORGOTTEN`](../troubleshooting.md#trust_forgotten): the checkout is marked untrusted.
- [`TRUST_NOTE`](../troubleshooting.md#trust_note): the first attached start in a checkout whose settings are off; the tool may ask about trust, and the answer turns nothing on.
- [`TRUST_CONFIG_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#trust_config_invalid): the `trust` line of `config.toml` is not `"trusted"` or `"untrusted"`, or the file is not TOML.
- [`TRUST_NOT_A_CHECKOUT`](../troubleshooting.md#trust_not_a_checkout): the path is not in a git repo; name one with `dockingbird trust PATH`.
- [`TRUST_PIN_UNPROVEN`](../troubleshooting.md#trust_pin_unproven): a tool keeps the repo's settings off for now, trusted or not.
- [`START_NO_SCREEN_TRUST`](../troubleshooting.md#start_no_screen_trust): an agent without a terminal runs without a screen, because its tool would ask about trust.
- [`DEPS_SKIPPED_UNTRUSTED`](../troubleshooting.md#deps_skipped_untrusted): dependencies were not installed in an untrusted checkout.
- [`START_PROJECT_RULES_REPLACED`](../troubleshooting.md#start_project_rules_replaced): a trusted repo's Codex config would replace Dockingbird's rules.

heading: Sign-in and API keys
summary: Agents need a Claude or a Codex sign-in, and Dockingbird has three ways to give one.
text: Agents need a Claude or a Codex sign-in, and Dockingbird has three ways to give one. It can follow the login that your own Claude Code or Codex already holds on this computer. It can run a separate sign-in inside Docker. Or it can store an API key. Whichever you set up last is the one in use, and each step below ends with the line that proves it.

heading: Sign-in and API keys > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird --version` prints a version.
- For a sign-in, a terminal. `login` without one stops with `LOGIN_NEEDS_TERMINAL`, and an API key does not need a terminal.
- None of that tool's agents is running. `login` and `logout` refuse while they run. `dockingbird status` lists them.

heading: Sign-in and API keys > 1. Let the first start reuse your computer's login
summary: The first start that needs a sign-in reads the login Claude Code or Codex already uses on this computer, keeps a copy in Dockingbird's store and follows it from then on.
text:
The first start that needs a sign-in reads the login Claude Code or Codex already uses on this computer, keeps a copy in Dockingbird's store and follows it from then on. When it finds one, it says so.

```text
Claude uses this computer's login from now on (dockingbird logout claude stops that).
```

Message id `LOGIN_HERE_ADOPTED`. Claude's login is looked for in three places, in the order Claude Code uses them: a token in the `env` block of Claude Code's `settings.json`, the macOS Keychain item, then the login file `.credentials.json`. From `settings.json` only the token and its gateway address are read. For Codex it reads `auth.json`. When the computer has no login, the start runs the tool's own sign-in inside the agent's container: open the link it shows on this computer, sign in, and paste the code. Only the first time.

heading: Sign-in and API keys > 2. Use your computer's login on demand
summary: Run it again whenever you like; when nothing changed it says so.
text:
```bash
dockingbird login claude --here
```

Run it again whenever you like; when nothing changed it says so. Done when the line prints.

```text
Claude uses this computer's login now, and Dockingbird follows it.
```

Message id `LOGIN_HERE_DONE`. The copy leaves out the refresh token, which never leaves your computer, so no agent can renew or sign out your login. Your own Claude Code or Codex keeps it fresh by being used. When Dockingbird is on, it copies a renewed login at once. A gateway in `settings.json` must be an `https://` address, or an address of this computer itself. Dockingbird refuses to send a token to any other plain `http://` gateway (`LOGIN_HERE_GATEWAY_NOT_HTTPS`). If macOS asks whether security may read the login, choose Always Allow.

heading: Sign-in and API keys > 3. Sign in again, or as someone else
summary: This runs the tool's sign-in in a login container, for an expired or revoked sign-in or another account.
text:
```bash
dockingbird login claude
dockingbird login codex
```

This runs the tool's sign-in in a login container, for an expired or revoked sign-in or another account. The first line says what it will ask.

```text
Signing in to Claude. Open the link it shows, sign in, then paste the code here.
```

Message id `SIGNIN_START`. Codex shows a device code instead: open the link on this computer and enter the code. If Codex's device code login does not finish, turn on device code login in ChatGPT's security settings. Done when the line prints.

```text
Claude is signed in.
```

Message id `SIGNIN_DONE`. A sign-in that does not finish changes nothing, and names the API key route (`SIGNIN_FAILED`). Press Ctrl-C to quit one; only those two lines follow.

heading: Sign-in and API keys > 4. Reuse a sign-in you made elsewhere
summary: For Claude, run `claude setup-token` in a terminal and copy the token it shows.
text:
For Claude, run `claude setup-token` in a terminal and copy the token it shows. For Codex, keep the file `auth.json` of a Codex sign-in.

```bash
pbpaste | dockingbird login claude --oauth-token -
cat auth.json | dockingbird login codex --auth-json -
```

Both forms read the value from the pipe only. It never appears in a command line, a log or a file on your computer. Clear the clipboard afterwards with `pbcopy < /dev/null`. Done when the line prints.

```text
Saved. Claude will use this token.
```

Message id `LOGIN_IMPORTED`. A Claude token is the subscription's credential, not an API key: `status` says "signed in". Both forms refuse while that tool's agents run.

heading: Sign-in and API keys > 5. Use an API key
summary: The command asks for an Anthropic API key and hides what you type.
text:
```bash
dockingbird login claude --api-key
```

The command asks for an Anthropic API key and hides what you type. `dockingbird login codex --api-key` does the same for an OpenAI key. Without a terminal it reads the key from standard input.

```text
Paste your Anthropic API key (hidden):
```

Message id `API_KEY_PROMPT`. Done when the line prints.

```text
Saved. Claude will use this key; your Claude sign-in is not used.
```

Message id `API_KEY_SAVED`. While a key is saved, `dockingbird status` says "Claude uses an API key". The key goes from the prompt through a container's standard input into the tool's volume, mode 0600. It is never in an argument list, a container environment, a log or a file on your computer. An agent asks Dockingbird for its own tool's key at its start and cannot change it or read the other tool's. `--base-url URL`, with an `https://` address, sends that tool's requests to a gateway of yours. Give Codex's URL in the form of `OPENAI_BASE_URL`, ending in `/v1`.

A key the provider refuses is refused in seconds ("its provider refused the saved Claude key"), never after the tool's own timeout.

heading: Sign-in and API keys > 6. The last login wins
summary: A plain `login` after `--api-key` removes the key once the sign-in succeeds.
text:
A plain `login` after `--api-key` removes the key once the sign-in succeeds.

```text
Claude is signed in. Your saved Claude API key is removed.
```

Message id `SIGNIN_DONE_KEY_REMOVED`. `--api-key` in turn replaces the sign-in, and either token form removes the saved key. The tool uses whatever you did last.

heading: Sign-in and API keys > 7. Sign out
summary: This removes that tool's sign-in and saved API key from Dockingbird's store.
text:
```bash
dockingbird logout claude
dockingbird logout codex
```

This removes that tool's sign-in and saved API key from Dockingbird's store. When Dockingbird followed your computer's login, it stops following it and leaves your own login unchanged. Done when the line prints.

```text
Signed out of Claude. Dockingbird has no Claude sign-in or key now.
```

Message id `SIGNED_OUT`. With neither there, the line is `Claude wasn't signed in. Nothing to do.` (`LOGOUT_NOT_SIGNED_IN`, exit 0). A sign-out revokes nothing at Anthropic or OpenAI. If an agent may have copied the sign-in, also sign out in your account. To follow your computer's login again, run `dockingbird login claude --here`.

heading: Sign-in and API keys > Where the sign-in lives
summary: Each tool has a Docker volume, `dockingbird-home-claude` and `dockingbird-home-codex`, that holds its credentials store and the saved key.
text: Each tool has a Docker volume, `dockingbird-home-claude` and `dockingbird-home-codex`, that holds its credentials store and the saved key. Dockingbird itself mounts them. No agent does: an agent asks for its sign-in at its start and runs with a private home folder. An agent that works without a terminal takes a changed sign-in within about 20 seconds. Claude restarts between two tasks to use it and resumes its conversation. An agent at a terminal gets the new copy within the same time. Dockingbird writes nothing into your own Claude or Codex folders. See [data and privacy](data-and-privacy.md).

heading: Sign-in and API keys > When it fails
summary: - A tool with no sign-in at a start gives [`SIGNIN_NEEDED`](../troubleshooting.md#signin_needed).
text:
- A tool with no sign-in at a start gives [`SIGNIN_NEEDED`](../troubleshooting.md#signin_needed). The line names the command to run.
- Quitting the sign-in before it finishes ends with [`SIGNIN_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#signin_failed), which says nothing changed. Run the sign-in again or use an API key.
- A sign-in that finished but could not be stored prints [`SIGNIN_NOT_SAVED`](../troubleshooting.md#signin_not_saved). Run `login` again.
- `login` in a script, with no terminal, prints [`LOGIN_NEEDS_TERMINAL`](../troubleshooting.md#login_needs_terminal). Save an API key instead.
- Both `login` and `logout` refuse while an agent of that tool runs: [`LOGIN_AGENTS_RUNNING`](../troubleshooting.md#login_agents_running) and [`LOGOUT_AGENTS_RUNNING`](../troubleshooting.md#logout_agents_running) name the agent. Stop it, then run the command again.
- A computer with no Claude Code or Codex login gives [`LOGIN_HERE_NOT_FOUND`](../troubleshooting.md#login_here_not_found) for `--here`. Sign in with the tool itself first.
- A login that has expired gives [`LOGIN_HERE_EXPIRED`](../troubleshooting.md#login_here_expired). Use Claude Code once so it renews, then run `--here` again.
- A gateway in Claude Code's `settings.json` that starts with `http://` gives [`LOGIN_HERE_GATEWAY_NOT_HTTPS`](../troubleshooting.md#login_here_gateway_not_https).
- A piped token with spaces or an unreadable `auth.json` gives [`LOGIN_IMPORT_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#login_import_invalid).
- An empty key, or a Ctrl-C at the prompt, gives [`API_KEY_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#api_key_invalid). A key that could not be stored gives [`API_KEY_NOT_SAVED`](../troubleshooting.md#api_key_not_saved).
- When signing out stops half way, [`LOGOUT_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#logout_failed) says whether the saved key is still in use. Run `logout` again.

heading: Egress and what agents can reach
summary: Egress is how far an agent's network reaches, and Dockingbird's own default is `full`, which has no limit at all.
text: Egress is how far an agent's network reaches, and Dockingbird's own default is `full`, which has no limit at all. Below you pick a mode for new agents, for one start and for one config. You also see what a blocked host looks like from inside the agent, and what an allowlist still leaves open.

heading: Egress and what agents can reach > The four modes
summary: Under `full`, a hijacked agent can send out the repo it works on, and its own Docker sign-in or key, to any host.
text:
| Mode | What the agent reaches | How |
|---|---|---|
| `allowlist` | its tool's own hosts (the model API and the sign-in), the hosts of its presets, and the hosts of the config's `allow` | through a proxy container of its own, and nothing else |
| `models` | its tool's own hosts alone | through the same proxy |
| `none` | nothing, not even the model's API | no network at all |
| `full` | the whole internet | the agent's own network with NAT out, and no proxy |

Under `full`, a hijacked agent can send out the repo it works on, and its own Docker sign-in or key, to any host. `allowlist` closes that: with the registries and GitHub allowed, installing dependencies and reading GitHub's content still work, while sending something out needs a credential the agent does not hold.

| Preset | Hosts it covers |
|---|---|
| `registries` | the package registries of the ecosystems GitHub's recommended allowlist names: npm and Yarn, PyPI, crates.io, the Go module proxy and checksum database, RubyGems, Maven Central and the Gradle plugin portal, NuGet, Packagist, pub.dev and Hex |
| `github` | `github.com`, `api.github.com`, `codeload.github.com` and `*.githubusercontent.com` |

heading: Egress and what agents can reach > Before you start
summary: - Docker Engine 28 or later runs for `allowlist` and `models`.
text:
- Docker Engine 28 or later runs for `allowlist` and `models`. `docker version` prints the Engine's version, and an older one needs a Docker Desktop update first. The mode `full` works on any version.
- About 30 Docker networks fit in Docker's default address pools, shared by every Docker network on the computer. A start with no range left is refused.

Dockingbird checks no Engine version. Engine 27 refuses the agent's network with Docker's own error, shown as `EGRESS_PROXY_FAILED`. Engine 26 or older ignores the isolated-gateway option, so the agent's internal network keeps an address on the Docker host, and the agent can reach what listens there. Update Docker Desktop first.

heading: Egress and what agents can reach > Steps
text:
1. See what new agents get. The output also says whether a file named `egress.toml` in Dockingbird's folder sets it, or it is Dockingbird's own default.

   ```bash
   dockingbird egress
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints one of these two forms.

   ```text
   Egress for new agents: full.
   Nothing is set: this is Dockingbird's own default.
   ```

2. Set the default for new agents on this Mac. An allowlist given no entries takes the two presets. One given entries is exactly those entries plus the tool's own hosts, so name both presets again to keep them. An entry is a host like docs.python.org, a wildcard like *.corp.example for every name under it, or a preset.

   ```bash
   dockingbird egress allowlist --allow registries --allow github --allow docs.python.org
   ```

   Agents already running keep what they started with. The step is done when the command prints these lines, with your list in the brackets.

   ```text
   Egress for new agents is now allowlist (<the allow list>).
   Agents already running keep theirs.
   ```

3. Change one start. The flag exists on `claude`, `codex` and `start`. An agent you pick up again keeps the mode of its last start.

   ```bash
   dockingbird claude --egress models
   dockingbird start --egress none "Summarise the README"
   ```

   A config can set the same thing with the keys `egress` and `allow`, and a start flag cannot override them. Configs are covered on [your-own-commands.md](your-own-commands.md).

   ```toml
   command = "review"
   egress = "allowlist"
   allow = ["registries", "github", "docs.python.org"]
   ```

4. Remove the setting, so new agents get Dockingbird's own default again.

   ```bash
   dockingbird egress --reset
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints these lines.

   ```text
   Egress for new agents is Dockingbird's own default: full.
   Agents already running keep theirs.
   ```

heading: Egress and what agents can reach > What a blocked host sees
summary: A host outside the list gets the proxy's `407` and a message that names Dockingbird and the way out, so a tool fails with its own proxy-refused error and not a timeout.
text:
A host outside the list gets the proxy's `407` and a message that names Dockingbird and the way out, so a tool fails with its own proxy-refused error and not a timeout.

```text
Dockingbird's egress proxy refuses with 407 a host that is not in the allow list or whose address is not public, and a request that names an upstream proxy of its own: allow a public host with allow in the config, or start with --egress full. A host in the list whose name does not resolve, or that does not answer, gets 502, 504 or 500 instead.
```

An allowed host whose name does not resolve gets the proxy's `502`, as the lookup would fail anywhere. TLS is never opened. The proxy tunnels the connection, sees the host name and the port and nothing inside, and the tool's own certificate check runs against the real server.

In `allowlist` and `models`, a tool that ignores the proxy fails and does not get around it. The agent's network has no route out, no gateway and no IPv6. Its only resolver, Docker's, answers the names of containers on that network and no outside name. A connection to an IP address, to an IPv6 literal, or any other traffic such as UDP, QUIC or ping, has no route or is refused at the proxy.

heading: Egress and what agents can reach > What the list does not limit
summary: - An entry names a host, not a port.
text:
- An entry names a host, not a port. An admitted host is open on every port, and a host you allow is a host the agent can post to. Allow only hosts you would let it send the repo to.
- A `*.` entry admits every name under the domain, and the proxy's lookup of the name the agent picks reaches that domain's own nameservers.
- An internationalized name, with an `xn--` label, is not admitted yet. An `allow` entry holding one is refused when the config is read.
- The proxy refuses every address that is not public, whether or not the name is allowed. A connection to your Mac, your LAN, `host.docker.internal`, Docker's own ranges or another agent's address gets the same `407`. A name in the list that resolves to one of them is refused too. `--egress full` is the way to reach them.
- Under `full` there is no proxy, so an agent's own browser reaches this Mac's loopback services through `host.docker.internal`. A browser agent that must not reach them uses `allowlist` or `models`.
- Behind a proxy that every connection must use, only `--egress full` works.
- A project config in a checkout you marked untrusted can only narrow egress, with `none`, `models` or a list the default already covers. Anything wider is refused, and the step is `dockingbird trust`.

Your claude.ai connectors never load in an agent. The image's managed settings turn them off in every mode, `--egress full` included, and a repo's or an agent's own settings cannot turn them back on. An agent gets a document by `send --file` or an artifact, never through your accounts.

The agents' own networks are separate. Each agent gets a network named `dockingbird-net-<name>` that no other agent joins. Under `allowlist` and `models` its proxy, `dockingbird-proxy-<name>`, sits on that network and on the shared `dockingbird-out` bridge. Under `none` there is no network.

heading: Egress and what agents can reach > When it fails
summary: - A start that prints [`EGRESS_PROXY_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#egress_proxy_failed) found the proxy of a `models` or `allowlist` agent dead or silent.
text:
- A start that prints [`EGRESS_PROXY_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#egress_proxy_failed) found the proxy of a `models` or `allowlist` agent dead or silent. The start removed everything it made. Run it again.
- Docker has no address range left when you see [`START_NETWORK_POOLS_FULL`](../troubleshooting.md#start_network_pools_full). List the networks with `docker network ls`, free them with `docker network prune`, or add pools through Docker's `default-address-pools` setting.
- [`EGRESS_FILE_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#egress_file_invalid) blocks every new agent while `egress.toml` is unreadable. Repair the file, or delete it with `dockingbird egress --reset`.
- An `--allow` entry that is no host, wildcard name or preset draws [`EGRESS_ENTRY_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#egress_entry_invalid).
- An untrusted checkout whose config asks for more than the default allows stops with [`START_EGRESS_UNTRUSTED`](../troubleshooting.md#start_egress_untrusted). Narrow the entry, or run `dockingbird trust`.
- [`START_CONFIG_FIXED`](../troubleshooting.md#start_config_fixed) says the `--egress` you typed disagrees with the `egress` in the config file. Drop the flag or edit the file.
- [`BROWSER_STORE_NO_EGRESS`](../troubleshooting.md#browser_store_no_egress) refuses egress `none` for a config that installs Web Store extensions, since Chrome downloads them from Google.

heading: Hosts
summary: This page adds a second computer to your Dockingbird, over ssh or through gcloud.
text: This page adds a second computer to your Dockingbird, over ssh or through gcloud. It then reads the agents that run there and opens one of them in your terminal. A host is a computer with Dockingbird homes of its own. Your own computer never needs an entry in the file, because every fleet line already calls it `local`.

heading: Hosts > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is installed and set up on the host, as on this computer.
text:
- Dockingbird is installed and set up on the host, as on this computer. Check on the host with `dockingbird --version`.
- Docker answers on the host. Check from here with `ssh lab.example docker version`, or for a Compute Engine VM with `gcloud compute ssh cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project -- docker version`.
- Your own ssh reaches the host without asking a question. Check with `ssh lab.example true`, which returns at once. Dockingbird runs your own ssh with your own configuration and agent, and never copies a key. A host that does not answer within 15 seconds is not reached.
- A cloud VM that is stopped must be started first. A stopped VM cannot be read.
- Networking, if the host is not on your LAN: [networking](networking.md), [Tailscale](tailscale.md), [other networks](other-networks.md).

heading: Hosts > Add a host over ssh
summary: The command reaches the host and reads its Docker and its Dockingbird homes.
text:
```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts set lab --ssh lab.example
```

The command reaches the host and reads its Docker and its Dockingbird homes. That is the same read the agents listing makes, and it starts and changes nothing on the host. Only after the read succeeds does the command write the host into your hosts file and print the rows it read. The last line is the done line.

```text
lab: 2 agents running in 1 home
...
lab: ssh lab.example, saved in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml.
```

That last line is message `FLEET_HOSTS_SET`. Run the command again with a name the file already holds, and it replaces the route while it keeps the host's home tables and its place in the file. The done line then ends with the words `updated in`, which is `FLEET_HOSTS_UPDATED`. A name is lowercase letters, digits and dashes, at most 56 characters, and never `local`.

heading: Hosts > Add a Compute Engine VM through gcloud
summary: Dockingbird reaches the VM through your own gcloud.
text:
```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts set cloud --gcloud cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project
```

Dockingbird reaches the VM through your own gcloud. It uses the one on your search path, or else the one the Google Cloud SDK installs. When yours lives somewhere else, write its absolute path into the host's table by hand, under the key `gcloud_program`. A VM of another cloud is a host over ssh instead. The done line has the same shape as the ssh one.

```text
cloud: gcloud cloud-1, saved in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml.
```

The guide on [cloud VMs](cloud-vms.md) covers the VM itself.

heading: Hosts > Fix a host that cannot be read
summary: When the read fails, nothing is saved.
text:
When the read fails, nothing is saved. The command ends 1 and prints the command to try yourself first. Run that command, fix what it shows, then run `set` again.

| What ssh or Docker shows | Fix | Then |
|---|---|---|
| `docker` is not found over ssh, while it works in a terminal on the host | give the commands a `PATH` with the folder that holds `docker` | add `--path PATH` |
| Docker Desktop's socket is not the default one | give the commands that socket as `DOCKER_HOST` | add `--docker-host unix://SOCKET` |
| the host does not answer | start the host, check the route | run `set` again |

On a Mac, the folder is usually Docker Desktop's.

```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts set lab --ssh lab.example --path /Applications/Docker.app/Contents/Resources/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
```

`--path` writes the `path` key and `--docker-host` writes the `docker_host` key. Both apply only to the ssh route. `--home HOME` adds a table for one of the host's homes by name, without checking that it exists.

heading: Hosts > Read the hosts and their agents
summary: The first command prints one line per host in the file, in the file's order (`FLEET_HOSTS_ROW`).
text:
```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts
dockingbird fleet agents --host lab
dockingbird fleet agents
```

The first command prints one line per host in the file, in the file's order (`FLEET_HOSTS_ROW`).

```text
lab: ssh lab.example
cloud: gcloud cloud-1
```

The agents listing covers every Dockingbird agent on one computer, in every home and on every version. It reads Docker alone, runs no Dockingbird command in those homes, and changes nothing. Without a host option it reads this computer, so a fresh install shows `local` with nothing written in any file. A host that cannot be read ends with exit 1 and the line `Couldn't read NAME`, then the cause (`FLEET_HOST_NOT_READ`). Each read gets at most 20 seconds.

| Line | What it shows |
|---|---|
| `lab: 2 agents running in 1 home` | the first line: how many agents in how many homes (`FLEET_HOST_ROW`) |
| a home row | the home's folder, its version, whether it is running, how many agents run in it (`FLEET_HOME_ROW`) |
| an agent row | the name, `bus` or `terminal`, `screen` or `no screen`, and its state (`FLEET_AGENT_ROW`) |
| a swarm row | how many agents of a swarm run and wait, with its project, priority and state (`FLEET_SWARM_ROW`) |

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `working` | its home's coordinator reports it at work |
| `idle` | its home's coordinator reports it idle |
| `asks` with a number | it waits for that many questions to be answered |
| `unknown` with a reason | `no-coordinator`, `timeout`, `refused`, `unexpected-shape`, `not-read` or `no-session` |

A script reads the same rows with `--json`, one envelope per line, and each agent's full container id is in them. In that output the `host` of a row of this computer is `null`.

heading: Hosts > Attach to an agent
summary: The first command lists every agent as JSON, with the full container id of each, 64 letters and digits.
text:
```bash
dockingbird --json fleet agents --host lab
dockingbird fleet attach --host lab --container ID
```

The first command lists every agent as JSON, with the full container id of each, 64 letters and digits. The second opens one agent in your terminal, so it needs a real terminal, and it prints its done line before it hands you the agent's screen.

```text
Opening claude-1 on lab. Ctrl-] then Ctrl-\ leaves it running.
```

That line is `FLEET_ATTACHING`. Some agents have no screen. You then see the agent's log as it grows, and each line you type and send with Enter reaches the agent as a message (`FLEET_FOLLOWING`). Press Ctrl-C to close that view. The agent keeps working either way.

Messages to an agent with no screen are sent by its home's own `dockingbird send`. The hosts file must therefore name that program for the home, and [the hosts file](../reference/files/hosts-file.md) shows how. On another host, the log may end with a line from ssh itself, `Connection to NAME closed.`

heading: Hosts > Rename or forget a host
summary: The first line is `FLEET_HOSTS_RENAMED`, with a second line saying that swarm definitions and pool records that name `lab` are not changed.
text:
```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts rename lab bench
dockingbird fleet hosts forget bench
```

```text
lab is now bench in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml.
bench is forgotten: its entry is removed from ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml.
```

The first line is `FLEET_HOSTS_RENAMED`, with a second line saying that swarm definitions and pool records that name `lab` are not changed. The second is `FLEET_HOSTS_FORGOTTEN`. Both change only the file, and nothing on the host. A host that the fleet pool holds is refused with `FLEET_HOSTS_IN_USE`: drain it and remove it there first (`dockingbird fleet hosts drain NAME`, then `dockingbird fleet hosts remove NAME`), then rename it here, then enrol it again under its new name. A host has one name across your file, the pool and swarm definitions ([fleet scheduler](fleet-scheduler.md)).

heading: Hosts > Read one Mac's load
summary: `fleet probe` reads this Mac and its Docker once and prints a line per figure: cores, memory, load against the load line, CPU, swap, GPU, Docker's VM, containers, networks, then each kind of process with its CPU, memory and count.
text:
```bash
dockingbird fleet probe
```

`fleet probe` reads this Mac and its Docker once and prints a line per figure: cores, memory, load against the load line, CPU, swap, GPU, Docker's VM, containers, networks, then each kind of process with its CPU, memory and count. It first prints `This Mac:` with the cores and memory. It shows numbers and kinds only, never a program's name. With `--json` it prints one line holding every container of every home. `--disk` also reads Docker's disk use, which is slow on a large image store.

It starts, stops and changes nothing, gives each read at most 20 seconds and the whole run 60, and ends 0 with whatever it read. A part it could not read says `unread`, and the screen ends `Not read: ...` (`FLEET_PROBE_UNREAD`). It runs on a Mac only. On Linux it ends 1 with `The fleet probe reads macOS only` (`FLEET_PROBE_NOT_MACOS`), and it reads this computer, never a host. To read a Mac host, run it on that Mac.

The GUI that lists every host in one window is not yet available.

heading: Hosts > When it fails
summary: Each message id below links to its entry in the catalogue.
text:
Each message id below links to its entry in the catalogue.

- [`FLEET_HOSTS_NOT_REACHED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_not_reached) means `set` could not read the host. It saved nothing, and the message prints the command to try yourself.
- [`FLEET_HOST_NOT_READ`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_host_not_read) means the agents listing could not read the host, or `local`. The line ends with the error that ssh, gcloud or Docker printed.
- [`FLEET_HOST_UNKNOWN`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_host_unknown) means the `--host` name is not in the file. `fleet hosts` lists the names, and the message prints the `set` line that adds it.
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_ROUTE_NEEDED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_route_needed) means `set` got no route, or got both. Give `--ssh DEST`, or `--gcloud VM` with `--zone` and `--project`. It exits 2.
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_NAME_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_name_invalid) means the name is not lowercase letters, digits and dashes. It exits 2, and nothing was read or written.
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_LOCAL_FIXED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_local_fixed) means no host may take the name `local`, which every computer uses for itself. It exits 2.
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_NAME_TAKEN`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_name_taken) means `rename` asked for a name the file already holds. It exits 2.
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_IN_USE`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_in_use) means the fleet pool still lists the host, so `rename` and `forget` wait until you drain and remove it there.
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_BUSY`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_busy) means another command was writing the file at that moment. Run yours again.
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_FILE_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_file_invalid) means the file breaks a rule. The message names the key and never a value, and no host is read until you fix it.
- [`FLEET_ROWS_SKIPPED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_rows_skipped) means some rows of the host's Docker listing could not be read. The rest is shown.
- [`FLEET_ATTACH_NO_CONTAINER`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_attach_no_container) means `attach` got no `--container`. It exits 2.
- [`FLEET_ATTACH_BAD_CONTAINER`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_attach_bad_container) means the value is not a full container id. It exits 2.
- [`FLEET_ATTACH_NOT_A_TERMINAL`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_attach_not_a_terminal) means the input or output went to a file or a pipe. Run it in a terminal.
- [`FLEET_ATTACH_GONE`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_attach_gone) means the agent ended after the list was read. Nothing was opened.
- [`FLEET_ATTACH_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_attach_failed) means Docker, ssh, gcloud or the home's own `dockingbird` would not start. The line ends with the system's words.
- [`FLEET_PROBE_NOT_MACOS`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_probe_not_macos) means the probe ran on a computer that is not a Mac. It exits 1.
- [`FLEET_PROBE_NO_SYSCTL`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_probe_no_sysctl) means the probe could not read this Mac's cores, so it stopped. It exits 1.

Every key of `hosts.toml` is in [the hosts file](../reference/files/hosts-file.md). Two worked examples are [two Macs over ssh](../../examples/two-macs-ssh/README.md) and [a cloud VM over gcloud](../../examples/cloud-vm-gcloud/README.md).

heading: Licensing
summary: Take a seat, read it, free it, move it to a new laptop, give it back.
text: Take a seat, read it, free it, move it to a new laptop, give it back. Each of those is one command under dockingbird license, and each is below with the line it prints when it worked. After them come the trial, the offline behavior and a table of every license message. This release does not enforce licensing, so no start is refused for a license. A refused start and its grace periods are not yet available.

heading: Licensing > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is installed.
text:
- Dockingbird is installed. Check with `dockingbird --version`, which prints a version. If it is not, see [install fails](../troubleshooting/install-fails.md).
- You have the license key from your purchase email. Dockingbird never prints it back.
- The computer can reach the license server. The first `dockingbird license` command downloads a small license program from it, so an offline first run stops with `LICENSE_AUTHORITY_UNAVAILABLE`.

heading: Licensing > What a seat is
summary: A seat is one person.
text:
A seat is one person. That person may link up to three computers to it, for example a laptop, a desktop and a cloud VM. A license with 10 seats admits 30 computers.

A second Dockingbird home on the same computer shares that computer's link. Agents, containers and repos are never counted. A computer rebuilt with a new identifier counts as a new computer each time. That covers a re-imaged VM, a cloud instance recreated on each deploy, and a container or CI runner with no machine id.

Licensing only concerns a new agent's start. `sync`, `stop`, `clean`, `status`, `results`, `read`, `inbox`, `update` and every running agent never wait on it, so your work always comes back.

heading: Licensing > Activate a computer
summary: The command asks for the key with the input hidden.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license activate
```

The command asks for the key with the input hidden. Without a terminal it reads the key from standard input, so a clipboard works on a Mac.

```bash
pbpaste | dockingbird license activate
```

A key typed as an argument is refused with exit 2 before anything runs. That keeps it out of your shell history and out of `ps`. The refusal is `LICENSE_KEY_IN_ARGV`.

The step is done when the product prints this line, then the terms line and a count of linked computers.

```text
This computer is activated: {plan}, {seats:seat|seats}, {term}.
You use Dockingbird under its terms: {link}
  Computers linked: 4 of 30 (10 seats, 3 computers each)
```

Two options help a scripted install. `--label TEXT` names this computer in the list, and its default is the hostname. `--accept-terms VERSION` accepts that version of the agreement without a prompt. Activating again on a linked computer keeps its link.

heading: Licensing > Read the status
summary: This reads the license file on the computer and uses no network.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license status
```

This reads the license file on the computer and uses no network. It shows the state, the plan, the seats and the end of the term. Then it shows how many computers one seat may link, this computer's label, the end of its lease and the last check-in.

```bash
dockingbird license status --refresh
```

With `--refresh` the command checks in with the license server first. Use it after you renew a license, after you free a seat from another computer, and after coming back online.

`dockingbird status` shows the license state in one line once the computer has a license file. With `--json`, status prints its values as fields a script can read.

heading: Licensing > List the computers on a seat
summary: The command asks for the key, as `activate` does, and prints the count line and one line per linked computer.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license activations
```

The command asks for the key, as `activate` does, and prints the count line and one line per linked computer. The list holds at most 80 computers, those seen longest ago first. When there are more, a line above it says how many it shows.

```text
{label}: activated {activated}, last seen {seen}, id {id}
Free a seat: dockingbird license activations --release ID
```

heading: Licensing > Free a seat with --release
summary: The list above gives each computer an id.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license activations --release ID
```

The list above gives each computer an id. Pass the id of the computer you want to free. The product prints this line when it worked, then lists the computers that remain.

```text
The seat of activation {id} is free again.
```

Use this for a laptop that was lost or wiped. A seat that nobody frees stops counting after 90 days.

heading: Licensing > Move a seat to a new laptop
summary: You change laptops, and the license already links three computers.
text:
You change laptops, and the license already links three computers. The seat moves in four steps. The [cookbook](../../examples/move-your-seat/README.md) shows each one with its output.

1. On the old laptop, if you still have it, run `dockingbird license deactivate`. Skip this step when the old laptop is lost.
2. On the new laptop, install Dockingbird as the [install guide](../getting-started/install.md) describes.
3. Run `dockingbird license activate` on the new laptop. With the old link still held, it prints `LICENSE_SEATS_FULL` and names every linked computer with its id.
4. Free the old laptop with `dockingbird license activations --release ID`, then run `dockingbird license activate` again.

Run `dockingbird license status --refresh` on the new laptop to confirm. If the old laptop is still on, the same command there prints `This computer's seat was freed from another computer.` and the next step `dockingbird license activate`.

heading: Licensing > Give a seat back
summary: This frees the seat this computer holds and removes its license file.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license deactivate
```

This frees the seat this computer holds and removes its license file. It is done when the product prints this line.

```text
This computer no longer uses a seat of the license.
```

`dockingbird clean --all` gives the seat back first, then removes everything Dockingbird made. When the license server does not answer, `clean --all` still finishes and prints `LICENSE_SEAT_STILL_HELD`. Free that seat from another computer with `dockingbird license activations`. Run one of these two commands before you destroy a computer, a VM or a runner.

heading: Licensing > Start a trial
summary: A trial needs no key and is allowed once per computer.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license trial
```

A trial needs no key and is allowed once per computer. The step is done when the product prints this line.

```text
The trial started on this computer: {plan}, {term}.
```

A second trial on the same computer prints `LICENSE_TRIAL_USED`, and the next step is `dockingbird license activate` with a key. A trial cannot install from the release index and cannot update. `dockingbird update` on an index install needs an activation and says so with `LICENSE_UPDATE_NEEDS_LICENSE`.

heading: Licensing > Offline behavior and day counts
summary: `dockingbird license status` needs no network, so it works anywhere.
text:
`dockingbird license status` needs no network, so it works anywhere. A command that asks the license server, such as `--refresh`, `activations` or `deactivate`, prints `LICENSE_AUTHORITY_UNAVAILABLE` when the server is out of reach. It exits 1 and changes nothing.

Without a check-in the license keeps working for its lease, so an offline computer or an outage at the license server interrupts nothing. The status screen names the stage the computer is in.

| What status prints | What it means | What you run |
|---|---|---|
| `The license server hasn't answered lately; agents start while the lease lasts.` | The last check-in is old. The lease still holds. | `dockingbird license status --refresh` |
| `It ends soon: renew it to keep starting new agents after that.` | The term ends within the warning window. | Renew the license. |
| `The license's term ended.` | The term is over. The installed version keeps working. New releases need a renewed license. | Renew, then `dockingbird license status --refresh` |
| `The license server hasn't answered for too long.` | The offline gap passed the limit. | Get online, then `dockingbird license status --refresh` |

Four figures are each the term the license names. They are the warning window, the length of a lease, the offline limit and the grace after a term ends. The status screen prints the lease end as `Lease until` and the last check-in as `Last check-in`. The one fixed figure on a customer page is 90 days for a seat nobody released.

heading: Licensing > What each message means
summary: A message id also arrives as `id` in `--json` output.
text:
A message id also arrives as `id` in `--json` output. The links lead to the catalogue entry with the full text.

| Message id | What it means | Exit |
|---|---|---|
| `LICENSE_KEY_IN_ARGV` | The key was typed as an argument. Nothing ran. | 2 |
| `LICENSE_KEY_INVALID` | The license server does not know that key, or the text is not a key. | 1 |
| `LICENSE_SEATS_FULL` | Every computer the license admits is linked. Free one. | 1 |
| `LICENSE_TRIAL_USED` | This computer has had its trial. Activate with a key. | 1 |
| `LICENSE_UPDATE_NEEDS_LICENSE` | An index install updates only on an activated computer. | 1 |
| `LICENSE_AUTHORITY_UNAVAILABLE` | The license server was out of reach. Nothing changed. | 1 |
| `LICENSE_AUTHORITY_REFUSED` | The server refused for a reason with no wording of its own. | 1 |
| `LICENSE_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED` | The license program runs on Apple silicon Macs and arm64 Linux only. | 1 |
| `LICENSE_SEAT_STILL_HELD` | `clean --all` could not reach the server, so the seat is held. | 0 |
| `LICENSE_OPTION_INVALID` | A `--label`, `--accept-terms` or `--release` value has a character it does not take. | 2 |

Four more ids mean the license program is missing or damaged: `LICENSE_CLIENT_DAMAGED`, `LICENSE_CLIENT_UNAVAILABLE`, `LICENSE_CLIENT_DIGEST_MISMATCH` and `LICENSE_CLIENT_PATH_INVALID`. Each prints its next step. Run `dockingbird update` for the damaged and digest ids, `dockingbird license status` for the unavailable one, and unset the variable the message names for the path one.

heading: Licensing > When it fails
summary: For the story of each refusal in the order a reader meets it, see [license refused](../troubleshooting/licence-refused.md).
text:
| Message id | What it means and the fix |
|---|---|
| [LICENSE_KEY_IN_ARGV](../troubleshooting.md#license_key_in_argv) | Paste the key when asked. |
| [LICENSE_KEY_INVALID](../troubleshooting.md#license_key_invalid) | Check the key from your purchase email. |
| [LICENSE_SEATS_FULL](../troubleshooting.md#license_seats_full) | Free a computer with `--release ID`. |
| [LICENSE_TRIAL_USED](../troubleshooting.md#license_trial_used) | Activate with a key. |
| [LICENSE_UPDATE_NEEDS_LICENSE](../troubleshooting.md#license_update_needs_license) | Activate, then update again. |
| [LICENSE_AUTHORITY_UNAVAILABLE](../troubleshooting.md#license_authority_unavailable) | Get online and run the command again. |
| [LICENSE_AUTHORITY_REFUSED](../troubleshooting.md#license_authority_refused) | Read the detail line the server returned. |
| [LICENSE_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED](../troubleshooting.md#license_platform_unsupported) | Use an Apple silicon Mac or arm64 Linux. |
| [LICENSE_SEAT_STILL_HELD](../troubleshooting.md#license_seat_still_held) | Free the seat from another computer. |
| [LICENSE_OPTION_INVALID](../troubleshooting.md#license_option_invalid) | Run `dockingbird license -h`. |
| [LICENSE_CLIENT_UNAVAILABLE](../troubleshooting.md#license_client_unavailable) | Run `dockingbird license status` to download the program again. |
| [LICENSE_CLIENT_DAMAGED](../troubleshooting.md#license_client_damaged) | Run `dockingbird update`. |

For the story of each refusal in the order a reader meets it, see [license refused](../troubleshooting/licence-refused.md). The idea behind seats is on the [licensing model](../concepts/licensing-model.md) page.

heading: Updates
summary: A Dockingbird home takes a new release in one of a few ways, and this page walks through each.
text: A Dockingbird home takes a new release in one of a few ways, and this page walks through each. `dockingbird update` fetches the latest Dockingbird, Claude Code and Codex. When agents are running, the home switches in place. Each agent picks up the new code at its next stopping point and keeps its conversation. Later sections cover version pins, homes on other versions, a repo's own files and a whole fleet.

heading: Updates > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is installed from Zeusfyi's release index and this computer is activated.
text:
- Dockingbird is installed from Zeusfyi's release index and this computer is activated. `dockingbird license status` shows the license. Without an activation, `update` stops with `LICENSE_UPDATE_NEEDS_LICENSE` and says `Activate it: dockingbird license activate`.
- Dockingbird is set up. Before the first run, `update` upgrades only the command and prints `Dockingbird isn't set up yet; the first dockingbird claude will set it up.`
- No other `update` runs on this computer. A second one stops with `Another dockingbird update is under way here.` (`UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS`).

heading: Updates > 1. Check for a newer release
summary: `--check` changes nothing.
text:
```bash
dockingbird update --check
```

`--check` changes nothing. Done when the line says a newer one is out.

```text
A newer Dockingbird is out. Get it: dockingbird update
```

Message id `UPDATE_AVAILABLE`. If the network is down, the check names the source it could not read and exits 1 (`UPDATE_CHECK_FAILED`).

heading: Updates > 2. Update with no agent running
summary: `update` upgrades the command, puts the release's code in the home's code store, and rebuilds the image only when the image's base changed: its operating system, its toolchains, its locked Python packages or its launcher.
text:
```bash
dockingbird update
```

`update` upgrades the command, puts the release's code in the home's code store, and rebuilds the image only when the image's base changed: its operating system, its toolchains, its locked Python packages or its launcher. Then it fetches the latest of each tool you have used. A tool you never used is not fetched. The lines run in this order.

```text
Getting the latest Dockingbird ... done (0.15.2 -> 0.15.3)
Rebuilding Dockingbird (about 5 min) ... done (4 min)
Claude Code 2.1.296 is the latest.
Dockingbird 0.15.3 is installed and takes over now. Your repos, history and your saved Claude API key are kept.
```

Done when the last line prints, or `Up to date.` when nothing changed (`UPDATE_DONE`). Message ids `UPDATE_GETTING`, `UPDATE_REBUILDING`, `UPDATE_TOOLS` and `UPDATE_ROLLING`. The rebuild line appears only when the image's base changed. A tool that `update` had to fetch says `Got Claude Code 2.1.296.` instead. When the new release changes Dockingbird's records, `update` first says so, because there is no way back.

```text
This update changes Dockingbird's records.
Once it takes over, it can't go back to 0.15.2.
```

On a Mac, `update` then tries to put the Dockingbird GUI in place. The GUI is not yet available to customers, so this step can fail after Dockingbird itself updated. `update` says so, ends with the GUI message and exits 1. The update is done. See [the GUI](gui.md).

heading: Updates > 3. Update with agents running
summary: Run the same command.
text:
Run the same command.

```bash
dockingbird update
```

The new code takes over at once and Dockingbird's coordinator is replaced in the background. Your agents keep working through it. Done when the line names them.

```text
Dockingbird 0.15.3 is installed and takes over now.
claude-1 and codex-1 take it at their next stopping point.
```

Message id `UPDATE_ROLLING`. An agent switches in place: the same container, session and conversation, with its deliveries and open questions kept. Before its next prompt, at no cost of a turn, its tool is told `Dockingbird updated from 0.15.2 to 0.15.3 and resumed your conversation. Continue where you were.` A command you run meanwhile waits for the switch, minutes at most, and prints `Switching Dockingbird to 0.15.3 ...` (`UPDATE_SWITCHING`).

heading: Updates > 3. Update with agents running > When an agent switches
summary: `dockingbird status` says how far the roll got and what holds each agent back.
text:
| Agent | Switches |
|---|---|
| On the bus | Between two turns, never inside a turn or a tool call |
| With a screen of its own on the bus | At its open gate, once your turn has ended |
| At a terminal | Never: it keeps its code until its terminal closes, and `update` never asks it |
| A Claude agent with background work | After the work ends, up to 30 minutes; past that the work is ended and the agent is told |
| An agent asked to stop after its turn | Ends as asked and never switches |

`dockingbird status` says how far the roll got and what holds each agent back.

```text
Dockingbird 0.15.3 is taking over: claude-1 and codex-1 take it at their next stopping point.
claude-1 takes 0.15.3 at the end of its turn (asked 2 min ago).
claude-2 on 0.15.2 keeps its own until its terminal closes.
```

Message ids `STATUS_UPDATE_ROLLING` and `STATUS_UPDATE_STRAGGLERS`. An idle agent that does not answer its ask in 10 minutes is left on its code. The roll waits for such agents, its stragglers, up to 24 hours, then ends, and `status` names the ones still running. A later `dockingbird update` asks the bus and screen stragglers again. To move an agent at a terminal, stop it and start it again.

```bash
dockingbird stop claude-2
dockingbird claude --as claude-2
```

Done when `update`, run again for the same version, prints this line.

```text
Dockingbird 0.15.3 is in place, and no agent is waiting to take it.
```

An update that changes Dockingbird's engine, the image's base, also rolls. Each bus or screen agent moves to a new container at its next stopping point, keeping its name, session and conversation, and `update` names those agents apart. The cookbook [update with agents running](../../examples/update-with-agents-running/README.md) runs this end to end.

heading: Updates > 3. Update with agents running > A roll that fails
summary: `status` shows it under "Needs your attention" with the fix.
text:
`status` shows it under "Needs your attention" with the fix.

```text
Dockingbird didn't switch to 0.15.3, so 0.15.2 still runs.
See why and try again: dockingbird update
```

Message id `UPDATE_SWITCH_FAILED`. Run `dockingbird update` again. A roll stops if Dockingbird here or its code cannot be read for 30 minutes, and the next command here resumes it.

heading: Updates > 3. Update with agents running > A home too old to roll
summary: A home whose running Dockingbird predates rolling updates waits once, for its first update to a release that rolls.
text:
A home whose running Dockingbird predates rolling updates waits once, for its first update to a release that rolls. The agents keep their code until they end.

```text
Dockingbird here is too old to take 0.15.3 while agents run,
so claude-1 on 0.15.2 keeps its own until it ends.
```

Message id `UPDATE_NO_ROLL_FLOOR`. `status` says what waits (`STATUS_UPDATE_STAGED`). Once the last agent ends, Dockingbird switches by itself, with no command typed. After that, updates reach working agents at their stopping points.

heading: Updates > 4. Pin a tool version
summary: `pin` writes the version into `versions.toml` in the home.
text:
```bash
dockingbird pin claude 2.1.285
dockingbird pin --clear claude
```

`pin` writes the version into `versions.toml` in the home. The next start downloads it if it is missing. Agents already running keep their version. Done when the line prints.

```text
Claude Code will run 2.1.285 from its next start; agents already running keep theirs.
Claude Code follows the latest release from its next start.
```

Message ids `PIN_DONE` and `PIN_FOLLOWS`. `dockingbird --version` shows a pin as `Claude Code 2.1.285 (pinned)`. A start or an update never changes a pinned version. `latest` and `--clear` follow the latest release. `stable` is Claude Code's slower channel and Codex has none. See [lock the tools your agents run](../../examples/lock-tool-versions/README.md).

heading: Updates > 5. Read homes on other versions
summary: A home runs the Dockingbird it was last started or updated with, which may not be the one on your path.
text:
A home runs the Dockingbird it was last started or updated with, which may not be the one on your path.

```bash
dockingbird homes
dockingbird inspect swarm
```

`homes` prints one line per home on this computer.

```text
default (default): Dockingbird running, version 0.15.3, this home
```

Message id `HOMES_ROW`. `inspect swarm` reads one home's agents and who may message whom, without starting, updating or locking anything.

| Home | `homes` says | A command from here |
|---|---|---|
| Runs the image this Dockingbird would run | Its line, readable | Runs as usual |
| Runs 0.6.2 or later, an older image | `readable for inspection; a command from here would update it` | Updates its coordinator; its running agents follow |
| Runs a newer Dockingbird | `readable for inspection; commands from here are refused: it is newer, update this computer's Dockingbird` | Refused |
| Runs older than 0.6.2 | `not readable from here` | Updates it; with agents running, it switches once they end |
| Its coordinator is stopped | `not readable from here: a command from here would start it` | Starts it |

Three refusals name both sides. `INSPECT_NOT_SUPPORTED` is fixed by updating that home: `dockingbird --home lab update` for the home named `lab`. `STATE_NEWER` and `INSPECT_SCHEMA_NEWER` are fixed by updating this computer with `dockingbird update`.

heading: Updates > 6. Check a repo after an update
summary: `init --check` writes nothing and exits 1 when an installed file is not the running release's.
text:
```bash
dockingbird init --check
```

`init --check` writes nothing and exits 1 when an installed file is not the running release's.

```text
myapp is not set up for Dockingbird 0.15.3: init would change it.
To change it: dockingbird init
```

Message id `INIT_OUT_OF_DATE`. Run `dockingbird init`: a file you edited is kept and named, and `--force` replaces it. Done when the check prints `myapp is set up for Dockingbird 0.15.3: nothing to change.` (`INIT_CURRENT`).

heading: Updates > 7. Move a fleet to a release
summary: For a team whose computers form a pool, an admin moves every host with one command.
text:
For a team whose computers form a pool, an admin moves every host with one command.

```bash
dockingbird fleet update --release 0.15.3
```

Only a member of `fleet_admin` may run it; any other login ends 77. Each host needs a live worker and a `repoint` line in its `[[host]]` table of `hosts.toml`: your own command that restarts that host's Dockingbird services and returns without waiting. See [the hosts file](../reference/files/hosts-file.md). The command installs the release host by host, updates each home, moves the services and waits for the worker to report the release. Done when the last line prints.

```text
Dockingbird 0.15.3 runs on lab and local.
```

Message id `FLEET_UPDATE_DONE`. A step that fails stops the command with the host and its words, exit 1, and leaves later hosts as they are. Fix it and run the same command again: hosts done are skipped. `--host NAME` moves one host. Before a release that needs a newer store, an admin runs `dockingbird org create`; a worker or admitter of the new release refuses to start against an older store (`FLEET_STORE_BEHIND`) until then.

heading: Updates > When it fails
summary: - Never activated? On an index install, `update` stops at [`LICENSE_UPDATE_NEEDS_LICENSE`](../troubleshooting.md#license_update_needs_license) and tells you to run `dockingbird license activate`.
text:
- Never activated? On an index install, `update` stops at [`LICENSE_UPDATE_NEEDS_LICENSE`](../troubleshooting.md#license_update_needs_license) and tells you to run `dockingbird license activate`.
- A dead network turns `update --check` into [`UPDATE_CHECK_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#update_check_failed).
- If uv cannot fetch the release, [`UPDATE_UV_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#update_uv_failed) prints the exact command that failed. Run it yourself to read uv's reason.
- A second `update` started during the first prints [`UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS`](../troubleshooting.md#update_in_progress). Wait for the first to end.
- The new coordinator may not come up. [`UPDATE_SWITCH_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#update_switch_failed) then says the old version still runs, and `dockingbird update` shows why.
- On a Dockingbird from before rolling updates, [`UPDATE_NO_ROLL_FLOOR`](../troubleshooting.md#update_no_roll_floor) says the agents keep their code until they end.
- Before a release that changes the records takes over, you read [`UPDATE_MIGRATES`](../troubleshooting.md#update_migrates). The old version cannot run on those records.
- Reading a home that predates inspection yields [`INSPECT_NOT_SUPPORTED`](../troubleshooting.md#inspect_not_supported); a home that a newer Dockingbird wrote yields [`STATE_NEWER`](../troubleshooting.md#state_newer). Update that home in the first case and this computer in the second.
- After an update, `init --check` exits 1 with [`INIT_OUT_OF_DATE`](../troubleshooting.md#init_out_of_date) if a repo's installed files are older. `dockingbird init` brings them up.
- `pin claude 2.1` is refused with [`PIN_INVALID_VERSION`](../troubleshooting.md#pin_invalid_version), and a well formed number the vendor never published gives [`TOOL_PIN_NOT_FOUND`](../troubleshooting.md#tool_pin_not_found).
- For a fleet, a host lacking its `repoint` line stops `fleet update` before it touches anything ([`FLEET_UPDATE_NO_REPOINT`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_update_no_repoint)). A step that breaks on one host prints [`FLEET_UPDATE_HOST_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_update_host_failed), and the same command, run again, resumes.
- A worker that meets an org store without the newest change is refused with [`FLEET_STORE_BEHIND`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_store_behind), until an admin runs `dockingbird org create`.

heading: Start agents from your own Claude Code or Codex
summary: `dockingbird mcp` is an MCP server, over stdio, for the Claude Code or Codex you work in on this computer.
text: `dockingbird mcp` is an MCP server, over stdio, for the Claude Code or Codex you work in on this computer. Through eleven tools your harness starts agents in Dockingbird, sends them messages, reads what they send back, saves their results and stops them. Your harness starts the server. You never run it yourself. The tool table and arguments are also on [the integration reference](../reference/integration/mcp.md).

heading: Start agents from your own Claude Code or Codex > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird status` must not print "Dockingbird isn't set up yet."
- Claude Code or Codex is installed, so `command -v claude` or `command -v codex` prints a path. Another harness takes step 3 instead.
- Your harness runs in the checkout whose configs you want, because the server works in whatever folder the harness runs in.

heading: Start agents from your own Claude Code or Codex > Steps
text:
1. Connect Dockingbird's tools to each harness it finds. For each one the command runs that harness's own `mcp add`, records the result, and prints the undo.

   ```bash
   dockingbird mcp install
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints these lines, once for each harness found.

   ```text
   Connected Dockingbird's tools to Claude Code: <path>
   To undo: claude mcp remove --scope user dockingbird
   ```

2. Check the recorded connections. The command reports a harness that lost them, a program that left your `PATH`, or a hand-made connection it cannot check.

   ```bash
   dockingbird mcp install --check
   ```

   The step is done when each harness reports this line and no "no longer has" line appears.

   ```text
   Claude Code already has Dockingbird's tools; nothing changed.
   ```

3. Connect another harness by hand. The definition below goes into that tool's MCP settings, and stdio carries the traffic. Afterwards you record it under the harness's name.

   ```bash
   dockingbird mcp install --show
   dockingbird mcp install --connected NAME
   ```

   Showing the definition connects nothing. A home other than the default adds an `env` entry with `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` to it. The step is done when the first command prints this line, then the definition.

   ```json
   {"command": "dockingbird", "args": ["mcp"]}
   ```

   ```text
   Dockingbird's MCP server (stdio), for any tool's MCP settings:
   ```

4. Ask your harness to start an agent. It calls `agent_start` with a task, then `agent_wait`, `agent_read` and `agent_results` for the answer. Leave out `command` and Dockingbird chooses as `dockingbird start` does, taking the checkout's default command, else the default environment.

   ```text
   agent_start {"command": "review", "task": "Check the login flow"}
   ```

   The step is done when the reply names the new agent, such as review-1, and the command that applied.

heading: Start agents from your own Claude Code or Codex > The eleven tools
text:
| Tool | Required | Optional | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `agent_start` | none | `command`, `task`, `name`, `harness` (`claude` or `codex`), `idempotency_key` | starts an agent, or continues one that ended when `name` names it; `task` is its first message |
| `agent_list` | none | `cursor` | one page of your agents with name, state, mode, model, effort and inbox counts |
| `agent_status` | `agent` | none | one agent: its last turn, model and effort, pending obligations and kept results |
| `agent_send` | `agent`, `text` | `kind`, `reply_to`, `artifacts`, `payload`, `idempotency_key` | sends a new task (`task_request`, the default) or answers a question with `reply_to`; the first line of `text` is the subject |
| `agent_inbox` | none | `agent`, `cursor` | one page of the deliveries your agents sent you, or with `agent` the deliveries to that agent |
| `agent_read` | `delivery_id` | `cursor`, `idempotency_key` | one page of a delivery's body and its artifact ids, and records your read |
| `agent_wait` | none | `agent`, `timeout_s` (1 to 45) | waits for the next delivery from `agent` or from any agent; a timeout cancels nothing |
| `agent_results` | `agent` | `cursor` | one page of the agent's artifacts saved under `results/<agent>/` in Dockingbird's folder, small text inline |
| `agent_stop` | `agent` | `idempotency_key` | stops one agent's container; its results are kept |
| `agent_set` | `agent` | `model`, `effort`, `idempotency_key` | changes a running agent's model or effort from its next turn |
| `agent_artifact_put` | `agent`, `name`, `content` | `media_type`, `idempotency_key` | stores a document as an artifact and returns the id that `agent_send` takes in `artifacts` |

heading: Start agents from your own Claude Code or Codex > How the server behaves
summary: - The harness can name a command, a task, an agent's name and its tool.
text:
- The harness can name a command, a task, an agent's name and its tool. It can never name a path, a config's content, a mount or an environment.
- Everything an agent writes comes back framed as data, with `from`, `kind`, `provenance` and `body`, and control characters escaped. Dockingbird never acts on it. Whether your harness does is the harness's own setting.
- A tool that changes something takes an `idempotency_key` of the form `YYYYMMDD/uuid4` and returns it. A retry with the same key and arguments gets the first answer back without running again. The same key with other arguments is refused with `IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT`.
- The server keeps the last 256 answers while it runs and writes nothing to disk. A retry after an unknown outcome, or after the server restarted, runs again, so a message can then arrive twice.
- `agent_inbox` and `agent_wait` share their rows with `dockingbird inbox` and `dockingbird wait`. A delivery one of them showed does not show again as new in the others.
- The server reads the checkout's `.dockingbird/` configs and the configs `config add` registered, once, when it starts. Its instructions name the commands they add, the default first. See [your-own-commands.md](your-own-commands.md).
- `agent_start` first makes Dockingbird ready as `dockingbird start` does, starting Docker and Dockingbird when they are off. It never waits for a toolchain. While the repo's versions install it answers `PROJECT_BUSY` with the cause `TOOLCHAIN_FETCHING`, and the harness tries again. See [toolchains.md](toolchains.md).
- Apart from that, the server never starts Docker or Dockingbird. While Dockingbird is off, its reads say it is unavailable, and `dockingbird sync`, `claude` or `codex` turns it back on.
- It starts agents without a terminal only. The tool names, their arguments and `idempotency_key` are under [the compatibility promise](../reference/integration/compatibility.md).

heading: Start agents from your own Claude Code or Codex > Undo
summary: Run the undo line from step 1 to remove the tools from one harness.
text:
Run the undo line from step 1 to remove the tools from one harness. A full clean does it for every harness that `mcp install` connected, using each harness's own remove command, and prints one line for each.

```text
Disconnected Claude Code from Dockingbird.
```

A harness you connected by hand keeps its settings. The clean prints the remove command for you to run.

heading: Start agents from your own Claude Code or Codex > When it fails
summary: - With no usable `claude` or `codex` on your `PATH`, `install` prints [`MCP_NOT_FOUND`](../troubleshooting.md#mcp_not_found), connects nothing, and shows the definition for another tool.
text:
- With no usable `claude` or `codex` on your `PATH`, `install` prints [`MCP_NOT_FOUND`](../troubleshooting.md#mcp_not_found), connects nothing, and shows the definition for another tool.
- [`MCP_CONNECT_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#mcp_connect_failed) means the tool's own `mcp add` failed or did not answer. Run the `mcp add` command the message gives, then `dockingbird mcp install --connected claude` to record it.
- [`MCP_CHECKED`](../troubleshooting.md#mcp_checked) is what `--check` prints for a harness that lost the tools, a program missing from `PATH`, a hand-made connection, or an empty record.
- Running `install` twice gives [`MCP_ALREADY_CONNECTED`](../troubleshooting.md#mcp_already_connected), and nothing changes.
- During a full clean, [`MCP_DISCONNECT_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#mcp_disconnect_failed) means a harness's remove command failed. Run the printed command yourself.
- [`TOOLCHAIN_FETCHING`](../troubleshooting.md#toolchain_fetching) is the cause behind `PROJECT_BUSY`, because the repo's versions are still installing. Call `agent_start` again.

heading: Clean and uninstall
summary: This page shows how to get disk back from Dockingbird, from a light clean up to removing the tool.
text: This page shows how to get disk back from Dockingbird, from a light clean up to removing the tool. `clean` never touches your code, `~/.claude`, `~/.codex` or any object that does not carry this installation's labels. The order matters at the end: run `dockingbird clean --all` before `uv tool uninstall dockingbird`.

heading: Clean and uninstall > Before you start
summary: - Docker Desktop is running.
text:
- Docker Desktop is running. `docker version` answers.
- Work you want is taken. Run `dockingbird sync` in each repo first, and `dockingbird results NAME --to DIR` for files you want to keep ([delegating tasks](delegating-tasks.md)). Copies made with `--to` are yours and `clean` never removes them.
- You can read the list of kept copies. `dockingbird status` shows each under "Needs your attention".

heading: Clean and uninstall > What takes the disk
summary: Each agent's copy holds the repo's history.
text:
Each agent's copy holds the repo's history. Dockingbird keeps five Docker volumes: the state volume with every agent's copy and history, one volume each for the Claude and Codex sign-ins, the program store with each downloaded tool version, and the toolchain store. An agent also has a dependency cache, the volume `dockingbird-cache-<agent>`. Docker keeps the build cache of Dockingbird's image, shared with every other project's. A first run downloads about 1 GB. How much a week of use takes is not documented yet. Docker's own summary shows what is used now.

```bash
docker system df
```

`clean` prints the size it freed. That figure does not count Docker's build cache.

heading: Clean and uninstall > 1. Free disk
summary: `clean` removes old images of this installation, versions of toolchains that no running agent and no repo names, and the copies agents left behind.
text:
```bash
dockingbird clean
```

`clean` removes old images of this installation, versions of toolchains that no running agent and no repo names, and the copies agents left behind. It removes a copy that is provably empty at once and asks about every other one. The default answer is no.

```text
claude-1 left 2 commits not shared yet. Remove its copy anyway? [y/N]
```

Message ids `CLEAN_ASK_UNSHARED`, `CLEAN_ASK_CHANGED` for files not committed, and `CLEAN_ASK_CRASHED` for a crash. A copy's results go with the copy and the question covers both (`CLEAN_RESULTS_QUESTION`). `--yes` removes without asking. Without a terminal, or with `--json`, `clean` without `--yes` keeps each copy it would ask about and exits 1. Ctrl-C at a question is a no for it and every question after it, and the command exits 130. Done when it names what it freed.

```text
Removed 2 copies (reviewer: 1 commit not shared; rev2: empty) and temporary files: 300 MB freed.
```

Message id `CLEAN_DONE`. A copy you said no to is named: `Kept claude-1's copy. Nothing else to clean.` (`CLEAN_KEPT`). Below a megabyte it says `under 1 MB freed`.

heading: Clean and uninstall > 2. Delete a stopped agent by name
summary: This deletes the agent whole: its kept copy, its results folder and its history.
text:
```bash
dockingbird clean codex-1
dockingbird clean codex-1 claude-2
```

This deletes the agent whole: its kept copy, its results folder and its history. `status` no longer lists it and its name is free for a new agent. It asks first about a copy or results that may hold work. It deletes an agent whole or not at all, so a no, or a copy it could not remove, keeps everything of that agent. Done when the line prints.

