```text
Deleted codex-1: its copy (1 commit not shared), its results and its history; 300 MB freed.
```

Message id `CLEAN_NAME_DELETED`. A working agent is refused: `codex-1 is running. To delete it, stop it first: dockingbird stop codex-1` (`CLEAN_NAME_RUNNING`). An agent with nothing left says `Nothing to delete: codex-1 has no kept copy, results or history.` (`CLEAN_NAME_NOTHING`). Names and `--all` do not go together (`CLEAN_NAMES_WITH_ALL`).

heading: Clean and uninstall > 3. Remove everything Dockingbird made
summary: This removes this installation's containers, its five volumes, every agent's dependency cache, its images, every link in your checkouts' `.git/config`, the refs `refs/remotes/dockingbird/*` in each linked checkout and its files in `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`.
text:
```bash
dockingbird clean --all
```

This removes this installation's containers, its five volumes, every agent's dependency cache, its images, every link in your checkouts' `.git/config`, the refs `refs/remotes/dockingbird/*` in each linked checkout and its files in `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`. Harbor's install and jobs go with them. It gives this computer's seat back first. It lists what is lost, every item named, before it asks.

```text
claude-1 is working now: it will be stopped and its copy removed.
keep8 stopped with 1 file not committed: its copy will be removed.
myapp (main): 2 commits the agents shared that you haven't synced.
To keep them: git switch main, then dockingbird sync
This removes everything Dockingbird made: every agent and its copy, their
history, and the settings and logs in DOCKINGBIRD_HOME.
Your code is untouched. Type delete to go on:
```

Message ids `CLEAN_ALL_WORKING`, `CLEAN_ALL_KEPT`, `CLEAN_ALL_UNSYNCED` and `CLEAN_ALL_CONFIRM`. Take the commits the list names before you type `delete`. Any other answer prints `Nothing removed.` and exits 1 (`CLEAN_ALL_DECLINED`). `--yes` accepts the loss and afterwards names the working agents it stopped. Without a terminal and without `--yes` it refuses (`CLEAN_ALL_NEEDS_TERMINAL`). Done when the last lines print.

```text
Removed everything Dockingbird made ({freed}). Your code is untouched.
To remove the command too: uv tool uninstall dockingbird
```

Message id `CLEAN_ALL_DONE`. `{freed}` is the size. If it could not remove everything, it says so and the next run finishes the job (`CLEAN_ALL_INCOMPLETE`). If the license server did not answer, the seat is still held: `Free it from another computer: dockingbird license activations` (`LICENSE_SEAT_STILL_HELD`).

heading: Clean and uninstall > 3. Remove everything Dockingbird made > What stays
summary: Delete the empty `logs/` folder after uninstalling, once Docker Desktop has restarted, if you like.
text:
| Kept | Why |
|---|---|
| Your code, `~/.claude` and `~/.codex` | Dockingbird never touches them |
| A `config.toml` holding anything you wrote, your `trust` line among it | It is yours |
| Your `instructions/` folder; `versions.toml` under `--yes` | They are yours. Without `--yes`, the list names `versions.toml` and it goes |
| Your `vaults/` folder when anything is in it | Your vault connections' stores (`CLEAN_ALL_VAULTS_KEPT`) |
| The empty `logs/` folder | Docker Desktop can refuse a shared folder deleted and made again, so the next start would fail |
| Other homes, clones, installs and caches in the default home | `CLEAN_KEPT_FOLDERS` names them |
| Docker's build cache | It carries no labels and is shared with other projects |

Delete the empty `logs/` folder after uninstalling, once Docker Desktop has restarted, if you like. A second `dockingbird clean --all` finds nothing to clean.

heading: Clean and uninstall > 4. Uninstall the tool
summary: uv prints its own confirmation.
text:
```bash
uv tool uninstall dockingbird
command -v dockingbird
```

uv prints its own confirmation. Done when `command -v dockingbird` prints nothing. Uninstalling first would leave Dockingbird's containers, volumes and image behind. `dockingbird completion --install` added two lines to your shell's startup file. `clean --all` removes the completion script but not those lines, so delete them yourself.

heading: Clean and uninstall > 5. Prune Docker's build cache
summary: This removes the unused build cache of every project on this Docker, not only Dockingbird's.
text:
```bash
docker builder prune
```

This removes the unused build cache of every project on this Docker, not only Dockingbird's. Run it only if that is what you want. Docker asks before it removes anything and prints its own total. The cookbook [uninstall completely](../../examples/uninstall-completely/README.md) strings these steps together.

heading: Clean and uninstall > When it fails
summary: - `dockingbird clean` asks before it deletes a copy.
text:
- `dockingbird clean` asks before it deletes a copy. [`CLEAN_ASK_UNSHARED`](../troubleshooting.md#clean_ask_unshared) is for commits not shared, [`CLEAN_ASK_CHANGED`](../troubleshooting.md#clean_ask_changed) for files not committed, and [`CLEAN_ASK_CRASHED`](../troubleshooting.md#clean_ask_crashed) for a crashed agent whose work could not be counted. Answer y only when you no longer want that work.
- In a script, `clean` without `--yes` keeps those copies and prints [`CLEAN_KEPT_NO_TERMINAL`](../troubleshooting.md#clean_kept_no_terminal).
- `dockingbird clean codex-1` for a running agent gives [`CLEAN_NAME_RUNNING`](../troubleshooting.md#clean_name_running). Stop the agent, then clean it.
- A name together with `--all` gives [`CLEAN_NAMES_WITH_ALL`](../troubleshooting.md#clean_names_with_all) and exit 2.
- Without a terminal, `clean --all` prints [`CLEAN_ALL_NEEDS_TERMINAL`](../troubleshooting.md#clean_all_needs_terminal). Add `--yes`.
- Any answer except `delete` ends with [`CLEAN_ALL_DECLINED`](../troubleshooting.md#clean_all_declined), and nothing is removed.
- A removal that could not finish prints [`CLEAN_ALL_INCOMPLETE`](../troubleshooting.md#clean_all_incomplete). Run `dockingbird clean --all` again.
- An image that another build uses stays, with [`CLEAN_ALL_IMAGE_LEFT`](../troubleshooting.md#clean_all_image_left).
- A license server that does not answer leaves the seat held: [`LICENSE_SEAT_STILL_HELD`](../troubleshooting.md#license_seat_still_held). Free it from another computer.

heading: Backup and restore
summary: This page says what Dockingbird keeps on your computer and in Docker, which of it you should save before replacing a computer, and how to start fresh on the new one.
text: This page says what Dockingbird keeps on your computer and in Docker, which of it you should save before replacing a computer, and how to start fresh on the new one. A restore of a copied home is not documented yet: a procedure is written here only after a run proves it.

heading: Backup and restore > What a home holds
summary: A home is the folder `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`, `~/.local/share/dockingbird` by default.
text:
A home is the folder `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`, `~/.local/share/dockingbird` by default. Other homes live in `homes/NAME` below it. The folder holds the files below, and Docker holds the rest in five volumes. See [the home layout](../reference/files/home-layout.md) for every file.

| Where | What it holds | Who writes it |
|---|---|---|
| `config.toml` | The image tag, the last build's duration and your `trust` line | You and Dockingbird |
| `hosts.toml`, `fleet.toml` | The other computers you reach, and the fleet database and your role | You, or `fleet hosts` |
| `versions.toml`, `egress.toml` | Tool pins, and what new agents may reach | `pin`, `egress` |
| `instructions/` | Your rules for every agent: `claude.md`, `codex.md` | You |
| `configs/` | A copy of each config you added with `config add`, and `configs/index.json` | `config add` |
| `results/<agent>/` | Files `dockingbird results` saved, one folder per agent | `results` |
| `connections/`, `vaults/` | The catalogs of your connections; the stores of vault connections | `connect` |
| `logs/` | Each agent's log, copied when it ends, and Dockingbird's own log | Dockingbird |
| `bin/`, `license.json` | The license client, the license file and the GUI link | `license`, `ui --install` |
| Docker volume `dockingbird-state` | Every agent's copy and history, and the protected copy of each linked branch | Dockingbird |
| Docker volumes `dockingbird-home-claude`, `dockingbird-home-codex` | The sign-ins and the saved API keys | `login` |
| Docker volume `dockingbird-tools` and the toolchain store | Downloaded versions of Claude Code and Codex, and the language versions agents get | Dockingbird |

The sign-ins live in the volumes, so a copy of the folder carries none. Sign in again on the new computer, as [sign-in and API keys](sign-in-and-api-keys.md) says. Dockingbird refuses to run in a folder that holds files but no marker, apart from the files it lists as yours: `logs/`, `instructions/`, `vaults/`, `versions.toml`, `config.toml`, `hosts.toml` and `fleet.toml`.

heading: Backup and restore > Before you start
summary: - The old computer still runs Dockingbird.
text:
- The old computer still runs Dockingbird. `dockingbird --version` prints a version.
- You have a folder outside `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` for what you save. `dockingbird results --to` refuses a folder inside it (`RESULTS_TO_INVALID`).

heading: Backup and restore > 1. Take the agents' work
summary: In each repo, take the commits the agents shared, and stop what runs.
text:
In each repo, take the commits the agents shared, and stop what runs.

```bash
dockingbird sync
dockingbird stop
```

Done when `sync` prints `myapp (main): up to date.` or the `Updated your main to ...` line, and `stop` prints `Stopped claude-1. Dockingbird is off until you next use it.` See [the daily loop](daily-loop.md). An agent's copy is in the state volume, not on your computer, so work not shared is lost with the volume. `dockingbird status` lists every kept copy under "Needs your attention".

heading: Backup and restore > 2. Save the results
summary: Run it once per agent.
text:
```bash
dockingbird results claude-1 --to ../save/claude-1
```

Run it once per agent. Done when each file prints its type and path, then this line.

```text
The copy in {where} is yours, outside dockingbird clean.
```

Message id `RESULTS_COPY_OWN`. `{where}` is the folder you gave. An agent with no files says `claude-1's task thread has no artifacts yet.` (`RESULTS_NONE`).

heading: Backup and restore > 3. Save your configs
summary: `config list` prints one row for each config: where it comes from, its commands, how it runs, the connections it may use and the start of its fingerprint.
text:
```bash
dockingbird config list
```

`config list` prints one row for each config: where it comes from, its commands, how it runs, the connections it may use and the start of its fingerprint.

```text
  {name}  {scope}  {commands}  {workspace}  {mode}  {connections}  {digest}
```

Message id `CONFIG_LIST_ROW`. Each field is one cell of the row. Keep the TOML files you added from. `config add` copied them into the home, and you can add them again on the new computer. A repo's own `.dockingbird/` folder is in the repo, so git carries it.

heading: Backup and restore > 4. Save your own files
summary: Copy `hosts.toml`, `fleet.toml`, `versions.toml`, `config.toml`, the `instructions/` folder and any `vaults/` you want to keep into the save folder.
text:
Copy `hosts.toml`, `fleet.toml`, `versions.toml`, `config.toml`, the `instructions/` folder and any `vaults/` you want to keep into the save folder. `dockingbird homes` lists every home on this computer, one line each, so you can do the same for each named home.

```bash
dockingbird homes
```

```text
default (default): Dockingbird stopped, version 0.15.3, this home
```

Message id `HOMES_ROW`. A connection's catalog in `connections/` names each key's path. The key's copy lives in a Docker volume, not in that folder, so the folder alone does not carry it.

heading: Backup and restore > 5. Give the seat back
summary: Done when the line prints.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license deactivate
```

Done when the line prints.

```text
This computer no longer uses a seat of the license.
```

Message id `LICENSE_RELEASED`. `dockingbird clean --all` gives the seat back first too. If you wiped the old computer without doing either, free it from another computer with `dockingbird license activations --release ID`. The cookbook [move your seat to a new laptop](../../examples/move-your-seat/README.md) shows both.

heading: Backup and restore > 6. Start fresh on the new computer
summary: Install Dockingbird as [install](../getting-started/install.md) says.
text:
Install Dockingbird as [install](../getting-started/install.md) says. Then take a seat.

```bash
dockingbird license activate
```

Done when the line prints.

```text
This computer is activated: {plan}, {seats:seat|seats}, {term}.
```

Message id `LICENSE_ACTIVATED`. Create the home folder if it does not exist, and copy your saved `hosts.toml`, `fleet.toml`, `versions.toml`, `config.toml` and `instructions/` into it before the first start. A folder holding only those files is Dockingbird's to use. Then add your configs again with `dockingbird config add`. The first start in a repo sets up the rest and signs in. The cookbook [before you replace a computer](../../examples/before-you-replace-a-computer/README.md) runs steps 1 to 6 in order.

Agents' copies and histories do not move. Restoring a whole copied home, folder and volumes together, is not documented yet.

heading: Backup and restore > When it fails
summary: - A `--to` folder inside the Dockingbird home, or one that does not exist, gives [`RESULTS_TO_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#results_to_invalid).
text:
- A `--to` folder inside the Dockingbird home, or one that does not exist, gives [`RESULTS_TO_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#results_to_invalid).
- A file name in the save folder that already holds something else gives [`RESULTS_TAKEN`](../troubleshooting.md#results_taken). Save into a new folder.
- A license server that does not answer at `license deactivate` or `clean --all` leaves the seat held, and [`LICENSE_SEAT_STILL_HELD`](../troubleshooting.md#license_seat_still_held) says so. Free it from the new computer.
- A license with every computer linked refuses the new one with [`LICENSE_SEATS_FULL`](../troubleshooting.md#license_seats_full). `dockingbird license activations --release ID` frees one.
- A home folder that holds other files and no marker gives [`HOME_NOT_EMPTY`](../troubleshooting.md#home_not_empty). Point `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` at an empty folder.

heading: Data and privacy
summary: This page lists what leaves your computer when you use Dockingbird, where each kind of data is kept and how to see it.
text: This page lists what leaves your computer when you use Dockingbird, where each kind of data is kept and how to see it. It lists every kind of traffic the documentation names. For what an agent can reach and what it cannot, see [the security model](../concepts/security-model.md).

heading: Data and privacy > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird --version` prints a version.
- You know which egress mode your agents use. `dockingbird egress` prints it.

heading: Data and privacy > What leaves the computer
summary: Dockingbird pushes no image to a registry, and its own pulls need no login.
text:
| Traffic | To whom | When |
|---|---|---|
| The agent's own tool, Claude Code or Codex, sending its requests | Anthropic or OpenAI, or the gateway you set with `--base-url` | Whenever an agent works, under your sign-in or your API key |
| The tool's sign-in | The tool's own sign-in hosts | When you sign in |
| Downloads of Claude Code and Codex | Their vendors | The first start of each tool, and `dockingbird update` |
| Dockingbird's own releases | Zeusfyi's release index, with this computer's activation as the password | `dockingbird update` and `update --check` |
| License actions | Zeusfyi's license server | `license activate`, `license trial`, `license status --refresh`, `license activations`, `license deactivate`, and `clean --all`, which gives the seat back first |
| The license client download | Zeusfyi, checked against a SHA-256 Dockingbird pins | The first `license` command |
| The image build | Pinned public base images and Ubuntu packages, pulled without your login | The first start and a rebuild after an update |
| A fetch or a push of a connection's branch | The hosts of the connections you registered | Only when an agent asks for it and a config names that connection |

Dockingbird pushes no image to a registry, and its own pulls need no login. Licensing sends nothing from a repo or an agent to Zeusfyi, and Zeusfyi's privacy note lists what it does send. The note is not yet published in this repository.

heading: Data and privacy > What leaves the computer > Licensing in this release
summary: This release does not enforce licensing.
text: This release does not enforce licensing. A start reaches no network for licensing and downloads no license client. It runs the license client only when one is already on the computer. The daily check-in that an enforced start would make, and the refusals that follow it, are not yet available. Until then the only license traffic is what you start yourself with a `license` command.

heading: Data and privacy > What leaves the computer > What an agent can send
summary: An agent reaches the network by its egress mode, which you set with [egress and network](egress-and-network.md).
text:
An agent reaches the network by its egress mode, which you set with [egress and network](egress-and-network.md).

| Mode | What an agent reaches |
|---|---|
| `allowlist` | Its tool's own hosts, the presets and hosts you allow, through a proxy that sees only host names and ports |
| `models` | Its tool's own hosts alone |
| `none` | Nothing, the model API included |
| `full` | The whole network, with no list. This is Dockingbird's default |

Under `full`, a hijacked agent can send out the repo it works on and its own Docker sign-in or key to any host. `dockingbird egress allowlist` closes that for the agents you start afterwards. An agent can read its own tool's sign-in or saved key and cannot change it. It cannot read the other tool's, and nothing it does touches your computer's own sign-in. Your claude.ai connectors, such as Gmail and Drive, never load in an agent in any mode.

heading: Data and privacy > Where data is kept
summary: Docker runs every Dockingbird command with its own configuration folder, so your saved registry logins and credential helper are never used.
text:
| Data | Where | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Your repo's history in each agent's copy | The Docker volume `dockingbird-state` | Never on your computer's disk as a folder you open |
| Sign-ins and saved API keys | The Docker volumes `dockingbird-home-claude` and `dockingbird-home-codex` | A key is mode 0600, never in an argument list, a container environment, a log or a file on your computer |
| Files an agent attached | `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/results/<agent>/` | Mode 0700, files 0600 |
| Each agent's log | `logs/agents/<name>-<stamp>.log` | Dockingbird's own events, never the tool's output |
| Unexpected errors | `logs/dockingbird.log` | Redacted, rotated |
| The license | `license.json` in `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` | The license document, this computer's id and label, the last check-in, the terms accepted and the download token; mode 0600 |
| Your connections' keys | A Docker volume, never the folder | An agent asks for a fetch or a push, never for the key |
| Links and refs in your checkout | `branch.<branch>.dockingbird` in `.git/config` and `refs/remotes/dockingbird/<branch>` | `clean --all` removes them |

Docker runs every Dockingbird command with its own configuration folder, so your saved registry logins and credential helper are never used. A `proxies` setting of yours reaches every container Dockingbird creates, with any user name and password in the proxy URL.

heading: Data and privacy > How to see it
summary: `license status` reads the license file with no network.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license status
dockingbird license status --refresh
dockingbird egress
```

`license status` reads the license file with no network. Done when the line prints.

```text
Licensed: {plan}, {seats:seat|seats}, {term}.
```

Message id `LICENSE_SHOWN`. `--refresh` checks in with Zeusfyi first, so it is the one status command that sends something. `dockingbird egress` prints what new agents may reach and whether `egress.toml` sets it.

```text
Egress for new agents: full.
Nothing is set: this is Dockingbird's own default.
```

Message id `EGRESS_SHOWN`. `dockingbird status` repeats it as `Egress for new agents: full`. To remove what Dockingbird made, `dockingbird clean --all` removes the containers, volumes, images and files, and your code stays untouched. See [clean and uninstall](clean-and-uninstall.md).

heading: Data and privacy > When it fails
summary: - [`LICENSE_AUTHORITY_UNAVAILABLE`](../troubleshooting.md#license_authority_unavailable): the license server did not answer.
text:
- [`LICENSE_AUTHORITY_UNAVAILABLE`](../troubleshooting.md#license_authority_unavailable): the license server did not answer.
- [`LICENSE_CLIENT_DIGEST_MISMATCH`](../troubleshooting.md#license_client_digest_mismatch): the downloaded client did not match its pinned checksum; nothing was kept.
- [`EGRESS_FILE_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#egress_file_invalid): `egress.toml` cannot be read, so no new agent starts until you fix or reset it.

heading: Networking
summary: Dockingbird uses a network in three ways, and each needs one thing reachable.
text: Dockingbird uses a network in three ways, and each needs one thing reachable. This page names the three, shows the check for each, and lists what no route needs. Pick the guide for your network from the table at the foot.

heading: Networking > The three routes
summary: Text alternative: the CLI reaches a host over ssh or gcloud.
text:
| Route | Who talks to whom | Carried by | What must be reachable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Host route | the CLI on this computer to a host's Docker | your own ssh, or your own `gcloud compute ssh` | the host's ssh, as your own configuration reaches it |
| Hub route | a member computer's fleet-link to the control plane's hub | TCP, port 4222 | the control plane computer's hub port, served to your private network |
| Egress route | an agent's tool to the internet | the agent's own network, through a proxy in the proxy modes | the hosts the egress mode allows |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  CLI[CLI on this computer] -- "ssh or gcloud" --> HOST[Host with Docker]
  MEM[Member computer] -- "TCP 4222" --> HUB[Control plane hub]
  AG[Agent container] -- "egress mode" --> NET[Internet]
  HUB -. "loopback only until served" .- CPC[Control plane computer]
```

Text alternative: the CLI reaches a host over ssh or gcloud. A member computer reaches the control plane's hub on TCP port 4222, which Docker publishes on the control plane computer's loopback until you serve it to your private network. An agent reaches the internet only as far as its egress mode allows.

A team that runs the fleet scheduler has a fourth route, from each host to the fleet's PostgreSQL database. It uses the `host` and `port` of the org login, and a host that cannot reach it ends its fleet commands with exit 69 ([team fleet](team-fleet.md)).

heading: Networking > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is installed on each computer.
text:
- Dockingbird is installed on each computer. `dockingbird --version` prints a version when it is.
- You know which routes you need. One Mac on its own talks to no other computer, so it needs only the egress route.
- You know what private network joins your computers. It may be a tailnet, a plain VPN, a bastion, a cloud network or Compute Engine, and the table at the foot names the guide for each.

heading: Networking > Check the host route
summary: The first command is the one Dockingbird runs itself, so a problem shows there first.
text:
```bash
ssh lab.example docker version
dockingbird fleet hosts set lab --ssh lab.example
```

The first command is the one Dockingbird runs itself, so a problem shows there first. The second adds the host once a read has worked, and its last line is the done line.

```text
lab: ssh lab.example, saved in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml.
```

A Compute Engine VM goes through your own gcloud in the same two steps.

```bash
gcloud compute ssh cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project -- docker version
dockingbird fleet hosts set cloud --gcloud cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project
```

Neither route needs anything beyond what your own ssh or gcloud already uses. Dockingbird waits 15 seconds for a host to answer, and each read of its agents gets 20 seconds.

heading: Networking > Check the hub route
summary: `cp init` turns one home into the control plane, given the address at which the other computers reach its hub.
text:
`cp init` turns one home into the control plane, given the address at which the other computers reach its hub.

```bash
dockingbird cp init --hub-address <ipv4>
dockingbird cp token --host lab --platform linux
dockingbird node join
dockingbird cp status
```

Run `cp init` and `cp token` on the control plane's home, and `node join` on the member's home. The done lines follow.

```text
This home is now the fleet's control plane, at <ipv4>:4222.
This computer joined the fleet as lab (node NODE_ID).
```

The first is `CP_INITIALIZED` and the second `NODE_JOINED`. `cp status` then lists the computer with its state, its version and how long ago the control plane heard from it. The hub listens on port 4222 of the control plane's computer. Docker publishes that port on the computer's loopback only, so nothing on the network reaches it until you serve it ([Tailscale](tailscale.md) shows the serve line; [other networks](other-networks.md) says what is documented for a plain VPN). Frames between computers are as private as the network you serve the port to.

A member that loses the hub finds it within 40 seconds, then reconnects by itself. Fleet calls are refused at once meanwhile, and a call waits at most 30 seconds for its answer. The agents keep working on their own home. The hub takes at most 1024 connections, one for each member and one for the control plane.

heading: Networking > Check the egress route
summary: With nothing set, it prints Dockingbird's own default.
text:
```bash
dockingbird egress
```

With nothing set, it prints Dockingbird's own default.

```text
Egress for new agents: full.
Nothing is set: this is Dockingbird's own default.
```

| Mode | What the agent reaches |
|---|---|
| `full` | the agent's own network with NAT out, no proxy; the default |
| `allowlist` | its tool's own hosts, the hosts of its presets and of its config's `allow`, through a proxy container |
| `models` | its tool's own hosts alone |
| `none` | no network at all, the model API included |

Two presets exist, `registries` and `github`, and [ports and hosts](../reference/ports-and-hosts.md) lists the hosts each one covers.

```bash
dockingbird egress allowlist --allow docs.python.org
```

That command sets the default for new agents, and agents already running keep theirs (`EGRESS_SET`). To change one start only, give `--egress MODE` to `claude`, `codex` or `start`.

A host outside the list gets a `407` from the proxy. The tool then fails with its own proxy-refused error, and not with a timeout. The proxy also refuses every address that is not public, so your LAN and `host.docker.internal` fail even when you list them. A proxy mode needs Docker Engine 28 or later, and the full rules are in [egress and network](egress-and-network.md).

heading: Networking > What nothing else needs
summary: - No route between agents.
text:
- No route between agents. Each agent is on a network of its own that no other agent joins, and its one channel to another agent is Dockingbird's message bus.
- No published port for an agent's metrics. Each agent's container serves `/metrics` on port 9464 inside its own network, and no port of the computer reaches it.
- No public port on the control plane's computer. Docker publishes the hub's port on loopback, and you choose the network that reaches it.
- No copy of an ssh key. Dockingbird runs your own ssh and gcloud with your own configuration.

[Ports and hosts](../reference/ports-and-hosts.md) lists every port and host in one table.

text:

heading: Networking > When it fails
summary: - [`FLEET_HOSTS_NOT_REACHED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_not_reached): the host route failed; the message gives the command to try.
text:
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_NOT_REACHED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_not_reached): the host route failed; the message gives the command to try.
- [`FLEET_HOST_NOT_READ`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_host_not_read): `fleet agents` could not read the host.
- [`CP_ALREADY_INITIALIZED`](../troubleshooting.md#cp_already_initialized): this home is already the control plane; nothing changed.
- [`MODE_CHANGE_AGENTS_RUNNING`](../troubleshooting.md#mode_change_agents_running): `cp init` and `node join` need the home's agents stopped.
- [`NATS_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE`](../troubleshooting.md#nats_server_unavailable): the hub did not answer in time; run the command again.
- [`FLEET_SESSION_NOT_OPENED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_session_not_opened): an agent started without a fleet inbox because the control plane was asleep, unreachable, at another version or refused the credential.
- [`FLEET_LINK_START_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_link_start_failed): Docker refused to run the fleet-link; the next command tries again.
- [`NODE_VERSION_MISMATCH`](../troubleshooting.md#node_version_mismatch): the member and the control plane run different versions; update the one behind.
- [`EGRESS_PROXY_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#egress_proxy_failed): the proxy of an `allowlist` or `models` start did not come up; run again.
- [`START_NETWORK_POOLS_FULL`](../troubleshooting.md#start_network_pools_full): Docker has no address range left for the agent's network.
- [`EGRESS_ENTRY_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#egress_entry_invalid): an `--allow` entry is not a host or a preset. Exit 2.
- [`EGRESS_FILE_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#egress_file_invalid): `egress.toml` cannot be read, so no new agent starts until `dockingbird egress --reset`.

heading: Tailscale
summary: This page puts the fleet on a tailnet.
text: This page puts the fleet on a tailnet. The control plane's tailnet address becomes the hub address, `tailscale serve` puts the hub's port on the tailnet, a grant lets a tagged VM reach it, and MagicDNS names reach each host over ssh. Dockingbird publishes no port to the internet for any of this. Its hub port is on loopback until you serve it.

heading: Tailscale > Before you start
summary: - Every computer of the fleet is a device of your tailnet.
text:
- Every computer of the fleet is a device of your tailnet. Check on each with `tailscale ip -4`, which prints the device's IPv4 address.
- Dockingbird is installed on each computer. Check with `dockingbird --version`.
- No agent runs in the home that becomes the control plane, or in a home that joins. `cp init` and `node join` refuse with `MODE_CHANGE_AGENTS_RUNNING` until `dockingbird stop` has stopped them.
- MagicDNS is on, if you want to type host names. Tailnets created on or after October 20, 2022 have it on by default.
- For a member in a cloud under a tag, the tag exists in your tailnet policy. Tags are defined by their owners in the `tagOwners` section.

heading: Tailscale > Find the control plane's tailnet address
summary: Run this on the computer that holds the control plane's home.
text:
Run this on the computer that holds the control plane's home.

```bash
tailscale ip -4
```

It prints that device's IPv4 address, and no IPv6 address. The steps below call it `<ipv4>`. In a policy, the name `control-plane.example` stands for the same device.

heading: Tailscale > Make the home the control plane
summary: That output is `CP_INITIALIZED`.
text:
```bash
dockingbird cp init --hub-address <ipv4>
```

```text
This home is now the fleet's control plane, at <ipv4>:4222.
Make a bundle for each computer that joins:
dockingbird cp token --host LABEL --platform PLATFORM
```

That output is `CP_INITIALIZED`. The home keeps the control plane's key beside the hub's address. Run `cp init` on a home that is already the control plane, and it changes nothing and prints `CP_ALREADY_INITIALIZED`.

heading: Tailscale > Serve the hub's port to the tailnet
summary: The hub listens on port 4222 of the control plane's computer, and Docker publishes that port on the computer's loopback only.
text:
The hub listens on port 4222 of the control plane's computer, and Docker publishes that port on the computer's loopback only. This line, run on that computer, forwards the tailnet's port 4222 to it.

```bash
tailscale serve --bg --tcp 4222 tcp://127.0.0.1:4222
```

Tailscale describes `--bg` as running the command as a background process and `--tcp=<port>` as a raw TCP forwarder on that port. Tailscale's page does not quote an output line for it, so the proof is the join below. Frames between computers are as private as the tailnet.

heading: Tailscale > Let a tagged member reach the hub
summary: A member that is your own device on the tailnet needs no grant.
text:
A member that is your own device on the tailnet needs no grant. A member that is not your device, such as a VM in a cloud under a tag, needs this grant in your tailnet's policy, with its tag and the control plane's device in place of the placeholders.

```json
{"src": ["tag:lab"], "dst": ["control-plane.example"], "ip": ["tcp:4222"]}
```

Tailscale grants deny by default. A grant has a source, a destination and an `ip` field that names a protocol and a port, so this one admits devices tagged `lab` to TCP port 4222 of the control plane's device, and to no other port. Adding a tag to a device removes its associated user, so a tagged VM needs a grant of its own. [Cloud VMs](cloud-vms.md) lists the conditions a cloud member meets.

heading: Tailscale > Add each computer
summary: On the control plane's home, make one bundle for each computer.
text:
On the control plane's home, make one bundle for each computer. The label is one to eight lowercase letters and digits, starting with a letter.

```bash
dockingbird cp token --host lab --platform linux
```

```text
lab is enrolled as node NODE_ID (linux).
Its bundle is the next line, shown once and not kept here:
paste it into dockingbird node join on that computer.
```

The control plane keeps only the computer's public key and its token's digest, never the bundle. A bundle joins once and decodes to at most 4096 bytes. On that computer's home, run `node join` and paste the bundle in, since the command reads standard input.

```bash
dockingbird node join
```

```text
This computer joined the fleet as lab (node NODE_ID).
Each agent started here from now on gets a fleet inbox.
```

Those two outputs are `CP_TOKEN_ISSUED` and `NODE_JOINED`. Back on the control plane's home, list the computers.

```bash
dockingbird cp status
```

Each computer gets one row. The row holds its label, node id and platform, then whether it joined, is waiting to join or was removed. It ends with the computer's version, its fleet inboxes and how long ago the control plane last heard from one of them. If you see `No computer has joined the fleet yet.` (`CP_STATUS_EMPTY`), no bundle was made or every computer was removed.

heading: Tailscale > Reach hosts by MagicDNS name
summary: MagicDNS gives each device a fully qualified name made of its machine name and your tailnet's DNS name, and adds search domains so the machine name alone reaches it.
text:
MagicDNS gives each device a fully qualified name made of its machine name and your tailnet's DNS name, and adds search domains so the machine name alone reaches it. Tailscale's own example is `ssh username@monitoring`. Dockingbird takes the same destination.

```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts set lab --ssh lab
```

```text
lab: ssh lab, saved in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml.
```

That is `FLEET_HOSTS_SET`. The destination is any word your own ssh reaches without asking, with no whitespace and no leading dash. Dockingbird copies no key, so the name only has to reach a host your own ssh accepts.

heading: Tailscale > Use Tailscale SSH instead of keys
summary: Tailscale SSH lets the tailnet itself decide who may open an ssh connection.
text:
Tailscale SSH lets the tailnet itself decide who may open an ssh connection. People are known by their tailnet identity, so no key has to sit on the host. To switch it on, run the command below on the host.

```bash
tailscale up --ssh
```

After that, your policy needs two entries. The first lets the source reach the destination on port 22. The second is an ssh rule with an action, and the action is either `accept` or `check`. Accept lets in anyone already signed in to the tailnet. Check asks people to sign in again once per check period, which is 12 hours unless you change it.

A prompt would stop Dockingbird, because its ssh must reach the host without asking. Choose accept for the user that runs Dockingbird. If your policy says check, open a terminal, run `ssh lab true`, sign in, and add the host before the period ends.

heading: Tailscale > After a restart and an update
summary: After the control plane's computer restarts, the first `dockingbird cp status` on its home starts the control plane and its hub again, and every member's fleet-link reconnects by itself.
text:
After the control plane's computer restarts, the first `dockingbird cp status` on its home starts the control plane and its hub again, and every member's fleet-link reconnects by itself. To update, run `dockingbird update` on the control plane's home first, then on each member. A member that is behind has its fleet frames refused with `NODE_VERSION_MISMATCH` until the versions match, and its agents keep working on their own home.

To join a computer again after a lost home or a removal, run `dockingbird cp remove lab` and `dockingbird cp token --host lab --platform linux` on the control plane's home, then `dockingbird node leave` and `dockingbird node join` on the computer.

heading: Tailscale > When it fails
summary: - [`CP_ALREADY_INITIALIZED`](../troubleshooting.md#cp_already_initialized): the home is already the control plane, so nothing changed.
text:
- [`CP_ALREADY_INITIALIZED`](../troubleshooting.md#cp_already_initialized): the home is already the control plane, so nothing changed. `cp status` lists the computers it holds.
- [`MODE_CHANGE_AGENTS_RUNNING`](../troubleshooting.md#mode_change_agents_running): agents still run in the home. Stop them with `dockingbird stop`, then try again.
- [`NATS_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE`](../troubleshooting.md#nats_server_unavailable): the hub took too long to answer. Everything else on the home works, so run the command again.
- [`NODE_ALREADY_ENROLLED`](../troubleshooting.md#node_already_enrolled): the control plane already used this bundle. Run `cp remove`, then `cp token` to get a new bundle.
- [`NODE_ALREADY_JOINED`](../troubleshooting.md#node_already_joined): the home is in the fleet already, so run `node leave` before you join again.
- [`RPC_PEER_HOST_MISMATCH`](../troubleshooting.md#rpc_peer_host_mismatch): you pasted a bundle made for another computer. Leave the fleet, then join with the bundle made for this one.
- [`FLEET_SESSION_NOT_OPENED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_session_not_opened): the control plane did not open an agent's fleet inbox. The agent works as usual. Check the serve line and the grant.
- [`NODE_VERSION_MISMATCH`](../troubleshooting.md#node_version_mismatch): the member and the control plane run different versions, so fleet messages wait. Update whichever is behind.
- [`NODE_SESSIONS_LIVE`](../troubleshooting.md#node_sessions_live): `node leave` found agents that still use the fleet. Stop them first.
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_NOT_REACHED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_not_reached): the host route failed. Run `ssh lab docker version` yourself to see why.

The cookbook for [a fleet on a tailnet](../../examples/fleet-on-a-tailnet/README.md) runs these steps in order, and [networking](networking.md) names the three routes.

heading: Other networks
summary: Not every team runs a tailnet.
text: Not every team runs a tailnet. Some reach their hosts through a bastion, over WireGuard, or in a cloud network with no public addresses. This page shows all three. Each one has the setup you do outside Dockingbird, the `fleet hosts set` line, and the table that line writes. Dockingbird runs your own ssh or gcloud, so any route those two can take works.

heading: Other networks > Before you start
summary: - The host runs Docker, and Dockingbird is set up on it ([hosts](hosts.md)).
text:
- The host runs Docker, and Dockingbird is set up on it ([hosts](hosts.md)).
- Your ssh reaches the host without a question, so every key is loaded in your ssh agent. A passphrase prompt is a question. Check with `ssh lab true`, which must return at once.
- For gcloud, the Google Cloud SDK is on this computer and signed in. Check with `gcloud compute ssh cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project -- true`.
- [Networking](networking.md) names the three routes and what each needs.

heading: Other networks > A bastion with ProxyJump
summary: A bastion is one host that your network lets you reach, and that reaches the others.
text:
A bastion is one host that your network lets you reach, and that reaches the others. `ProxyJump` in `~/.ssh/config` tells ssh to connect through it. OpenSSH describes the value as one or more jump proxies in the form `[user@]host[:port]`, separated by commas and visited in order. This entry reaches `lab-1.internal.example` through the bastion.

```text
Host bastion
  HostName bastion.lab.example
  User ops

Host lab
  HostName lab-1.internal.example
  ProxyJump bastion
```

First make ssh itself work, since Dockingbird runs exactly this.

```bash
ssh lab docker version
```

It prints Docker's client and server versions. Then give the entry's name to Dockingbird as the destination.

```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts set lab --ssh lab
```

```text
lab: ssh lab, saved in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml.
```

That line is `FLEET_HOSTS_SET`, and the table it writes follows.

```toml
[[host]]
name = "lab"
ssh = "lab"
```

When your terminal on the host finds `docker` and the ssh login does not, add `--path`; [hosts](hosts.md) shows the fix. The cookbook [a host behind a bastion](../../examples/host-behind-a-bastion/README.md) runs this in order.

heading: Other networks > A WireGuard mesh
summary: A WireGuard mesh gives each computer an address on its own interface.
text:
A WireGuard mesh gives each computer an address on its own interface. WireGuard's quick start adds that address with `ip address add dev wg0 ADDRESS/MASK`, makes keys with `wg genkey` and `wg pubkey`, and brings an interface up with `wg-quick`. The mesh is set up outside Dockingbird. Once the computers reach each other on it, ssh works over it like over any network.

Name the peer in `~/.ssh/config` with its WireGuard address, or use a name your DNS resolves to it.

```text
Host lab
  HostName <wireguard address of lab>
```

```bash
ssh lab docker version
dockingbird fleet hosts set lab --ssh lab
```

The done line and the table are the same as for the bastion. The host route is all this release's guide documents for a mesh. The hub route (a member joining a control plane) is documented for a tailnet only: `cp init --hub-address` is described there with a tailnet address, and the hub's port is on loopback until a forwarder you provide serves it. The guide does not say that a WireGuard address works as the hub address. Ask through [SUPPORT.md](../../SUPPORT.md) before you join computers over a mesh.

heading: Other networks > A Compute Engine VM with no public IP
summary: Google's documentation says that if the instance does not have an external IP address, `gcloud compute ssh` automatically uses IAP TCP tunneling.
text:
Google's documentation says that if the instance does not have an external IP address, `gcloud compute ssh` automatically uses IAP TCP tunneling. Dockingbird runs that same command, so the VM needs these on the Google side.

- A firewall rule that allows ingress from the IAP range `35.235.240.0/20` to port 22.
- The role `roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor` for the account that runs `gcloud`.

```bash
gcloud compute ssh cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project -- docker version
dockingbird fleet hosts set cloud --gcloud cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project
```

```text
cloud: gcloud cloud-1, saved in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml.
```

```toml
[[host]]
name = "cloud"
gcloud = "cloud-1"
zone = "europe-west1-b"
project = "example-project"
```

The VM must be running. A stopped VM cannot be read, and the refusal says so. When your `gcloud` is neither on your `PATH` nor in the SDK's usual places, write its absolute path into the table as `gcloud_program`. [Cloud VMs](cloud-vms.md) covers the VM itself.

heading: Other networks > What each route writes
summary: An `ssh` value is not empty, has no leading dash and no whitespace.
text:
| Network | `fleet hosts set` | Keys in `hosts.toml` |
|---|---|---|
| bastion with `ProxyJump` | `--ssh lab` | `name`, `ssh` |
| WireGuard mesh | `--ssh lab` | `name`, `ssh` |
| VM with no public IP | `--gcloud cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project` | `name`, `gcloud`, `zone`, `project` |
| a host that needs a `PATH` | add `--path PATH` | `path` |
| Docker on a non-default socket | add `--docker-host URL` | `docker_host` |

An `ssh` value is not empty, has no leading dash and no whitespace. The `gcloud`, `zone` and `project` values are lowercase letters, digits, dashes, dots and colons. [The hosts file](../reference/files/hosts-file.md) has every rule.

heading: Other networks > When it fails
summary: - [`FLEET_HOSTS_NOT_REACHED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_not_reached) means the read through the route failed and nothing was saved.
text:
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_NOT_REACHED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_not_reached) means the read through the route failed and nothing was saved. The message prints the command to try yourself, and it says when this computer has no gcloud.
- [`FLEET_HOST_NOT_READ`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_host_not_read) means the agents listing could not read a host you saved earlier.
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_ROUTE_NEEDED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_route_needed) means `set` needs `--ssh DEST`, or `--gcloud VM` with `--zone` and `--project`. It exits 2.
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_FILE_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_file_invalid) means a value in `hosts.toml` breaks a rule. The message names its place and never the value.
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_NAME_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_name_invalid) means the host's name holds a character a name cannot have. It exits 2.

heading: Other networks > Sources
text:
| Topic | Page |
|---|---|
| `ProxyJump` | https://man.openbsd.org/ssh_config |
| WireGuard | https://www.wireguard.com/quickstart/ |
| IAP TCP forwarding for `gcloud compute ssh` | https://docs.cloud.google.com/iap/docs/using-tcp-forwarding |

heading: Cloud VMs
summary: This page makes a Linux VM a Dockingbird host.
text: This page makes a Linux VM a Dockingbird host. It lists what the VM needs, adds it, reads its agents, starts it from the fleet pool when it is stopped, sizes its disk and, if you want, joins it to a control plane. The examples use a Compute Engine VM, `cloud-1`, in the zone `europe-west1-b` of the project `example-project`. A VM of another cloud is a host over ssh ([hosts](hosts.md)).

heading: Cloud VMs > Before you start
summary: Run these checks on the VM.
text:
Run these checks on the VM.

| Needs | Check |
|---|---|
| arm64 Linux, the only Linux platform; x86 Linux is not supported | `uname -m` prints `aarch64` |
| Docker Engine, version 28 or later if agents use the `allowlist` or `models` egress modes | `docker version` prints a client and a server |
| Docker's buildx plugin, from the `docker-buildx-plugin` package | `docker buildx version` prints a version |
| uv | `uv --version` prints a version |
| git at `/usr/bin/git` | `/usr/bin/git --version` prints a version |
| Dockingbird, installed and set up ([install](../getting-started/install.md)) | `dockingbird --version` prints a version |

A VM is one of the up to three computers of a seat. A VM re-imaged or recreated on each deploy counts as a new computer each time, so avoid re-imaging it ([licensing](licensing.md)). The first start on a computer builds Dockingbird's image, which takes about 5 minutes once.

On your own computer, the Google Cloud SDK is signed in. `gcloud compute ssh cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project -- docker version` must print Docker's versions.

heading: Cloud VMs > Start the VM
summary: A stopped VM cannot be read.
text:
A stopped VM cannot be read.

```bash
gcloud compute instances start cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project
```

heading: Cloud VMs > Add the VM
summary: The command reaches the VM through your own `gcloud compute ssh`, reads its Docker and its homes, saves the host only after that succeeds, and prints the rows it read.
text:
```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts set cloud --gcloud cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project
```

The command reaches the VM through your own `gcloud compute ssh`, reads its Docker and its homes, saves the host only after that succeeds, and prints the rows it read.

```text
cloud: 4 agents running in 2 homes
...
cloud: gcloud cloud-1, saved in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml.
```

The last line is `FLEET_HOSTS_SET`. The gcloud route writes `name`, `gcloud`, `zone` and `project` into the host's table. When your `gcloud` is neither on your `PATH` nor where the SDK installs it, add its absolute path by hand as `gcloud_program`. A later `set` of the same host over gcloud keeps it.

heading: Cloud VMs > Fix a login that does not find docker
summary: The gcloud route has no `path` key.
text:
The gcloud route has no `path` key. When `gcloud compute ssh cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project -- docker version` fails with `docker` not found, find where it is on the VM.

```bash
gcloud compute ssh cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project -- 'command -v docker'
```

Either make the VM's login find it, so that the first command succeeds, or reach the VM over ssh and give the commands there a `PATH`.

```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts set cloud --ssh cloud.example --path /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
```

`--path` holds the folders that contain `docker`. `--docker-host URL` sets `DOCKER_HOST` for a Docker whose socket is not the default one. Moving a host from `--gcloud` to `--ssh` drops its gcloud keys, `gcloud_program` included.

heading: Cloud VMs > Read the VM's agents
summary: That is `FLEET_HOST_ROW`, followed by a row for each home and agent.
text:
```bash
dockingbird fleet agents --host cloud
```

```text
cloud: 4 agents running in 2 homes
```

That is `FLEET_HOST_ROW`, followed by a row for each home and agent. A stopped VM reads as `Couldn't read cloud: ...` (`FLEET_HOST_NOT_READ`) until it runs again.

`dockingbird fleet probe` reads a Mac only, so it cannot read the VM's load. On Linux it ends 1 with `FLEET_PROBE_NOT_MACOS`. In a fleet pool, the VM's worker publishes its host sample every 30 seconds.

heading: Cloud VMs > Let the pool start a stopped VM
summary: A team that runs the fleet scheduler can leave the VM stopped between jobs.
text:
A team that runs the fleet scheduler can leave the VM stopped between jobs. The admin enrols it in the pool with `--power gcloud`. This line is the one the team fleet example uses; its gate lines depend on your VM, and [fleet scheduler](fleet-scheduler.md) explains each flag.

```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts add cloud --os linux --cores 60 --memory 230g --line idle_millicores=4000,8000 --line free_mib=16384,32768 --line psi_io_full=1500,1200 --power gcloud
```

With `--power gcloud`, the pool's admitter starts the stopped VM when work waits for it. The admitter finds the VM by the pool's name in its own `hosts.toml`, so the admitter's home must hold a `[[host]]` named `cloud` with the gcloud route above. The admitter runs on one machine of the pool that stays awake, and not on the VM. A host has one name across your file, the pool and swarm definitions.

heading: Cloud VMs > Size the disk
summary: The sources give no single size, so measure it.
text:
The sources give no single size, so measure it. Each agent's copy holds its repo's history, and Dockingbird keeps five Docker volumes, a toolchain store and Docker's build cache.

```bash
docker system df
dockingbird clean
```

`docker system df` shows what Docker's data uses, and `dockingbird clean` frees disk and prints the sizes it freed. A start offers to run `clean` when Docker is almost out of space. Read both after the first start and again after a week of real use, then size the boot disk with room to spare. [Clean and uninstall](clean-and-uninstall.md) has the rest.

heading: Cloud VMs > Join the VM to a control plane
summary: A VM may join a control plane like any other computer ([Tailscale](tailscale.md) shows the commands), on these conditions.
text:
A VM may join a control plane like any other computer ([Tailscale](tailscale.md) shows the commands), on these conditions.

- Its credential acts for its own home only. It opens fleet sessions under its own label and reads the replies to its own inbox.
- The credential lives only in `<home>/fleet/container/` and in the fleet-link's read-only bind. It is never in an agent's container, a log or a command line.
- `dockingbird cp remove LABEL` on the control plane cuts the VM off at once, with no precondition, and `dockingbird node leave` on the VM removes the credential.
- Its fleet sessions expire with their hours.

A compromised member can send instructions to any agent of the fleet, including agents whose grants reach repositories, and can read what is addressed to its own agents, attachments included. It cannot read another computer's inboxes, the harness's sign-in or either database.

heading: Cloud VMs > When it fails
summary: - [`FLEET_HOSTS_NOT_REACHED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_not_reached): `set` could not read the VM and saved nothing.
text:
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_NOT_REACHED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_not_reached): `set` could not read the VM and saved nothing. The message gives `gcloud compute ssh cloud-1 -- docker version` to try, and says a stopped VM must be started first. It also says when this computer has no `gcloud`.
- [`FLEET_HOST_NOT_READ`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_host_not_read): `fleet agents` could not read the VM.
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_ROUTE_NEEDED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_route_needed): `--gcloud VM` needs `--zone` and `--project`. Exit 2.
- [`FLEET_HOSTS_IN_USE`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_in_use): the pool holds the VM; drain and remove it there before renaming it here.
- [`DOCKER_NOT_INSTALLED`](../troubleshooting.md#docker_not_installed): there is no `docker` command on the VM.
- [`DOCKER_BUILDX_MISSING`](../troubleshooting.md#docker_buildx_missing): install the `docker-buildx-plugin` package.
- [`FLEET_PROBE_NOT_MACOS`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_probe_not_macos): the probe reads macOS only.
- [`NODE_SESSIONS_LIVE`](../troubleshooting.md#node_sessions_live): `node leave` needs the agents that use the fleet stopped.

The worked example is [a Mac and a cloud VM over gcloud](../../examples/cloud-vm-gcloud/README.md). [Other networks](other-networks.md) covers a VM with no public IP.

heading: Connect agents to GitHub
summary: This page connects one branch of a GitHub repo to your agents.
text: This page connects one branch of a GitHub repo to your agents. They fetch and push that branch through Dockingbird, and none of them ever holds the key. The model behind it is on [connections.md](connections.md).

heading: Connect agents to GitHub > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird status` must not print "Dockingbird isn't set up yet."
- You stand in a checkout of the repo, on the branch the agents work on. `git branch --show-current` prints it.
- GitHub accepts a key of yours. `ssh -G github.com` lists the key files your ssh would try, in order, and Dockingbird tries the same ones.
- To limit the connection to one repository, you hold a deploy key with write access to it. Step 2 makes one.
- To use the ssh-agent, you run Docker Desktop. The plain Docker Engine forwards no agent.

heading: Connect agents to GitHub > Steps
text:
1. Connect with the key your own ssh uses for GitHub. Here `github` is only the connection's name. Dockingbird copies your branch first when no agent has copied it yet, as a start does, and then connects that branch.

   ```bash
   dockingbird connect github --github example-org/example-app
   ```

   To connect another branch, switch to it and run the same command there, or add `--branch NAME` for a branch Dockingbird has already copied. A key with a passphrase makes ssh-keygen ask for it once, on your terminal, so it can write Dockingbird's copy without one. Dockingbird never sees the passphrase. The step is done when the command prints these lines.

   ```text
   Connected github: example-org/example-app (main) over SSH as somebody, with a copy of
   ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (no passphrase) kept in Dockingbird until you disconnect.
   A config that names it: connections = ["github"]
   ```

2. Limit the connection to one repository with a deploy key. Add the public half to the repo as a deploy key with write access, then name the private file. Only you may read that file, it cannot be a link, and it cannot sit inside Dockingbird's folder.

   ```bash
   ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -f ~/.ssh/dockingbird_github
   dockingbird connect github --github example-org/example-app --key ~/.ssh/dockingbird_github
   ```

   The step is done when the same "Connected github" lines print. A key of your account reaches every repository your account does, while a deploy key reaches the one repo.

3. Use your Mac's ssh-agent instead of a copy of a key. Docker Desktop forwards the agent into Dockingbird's coordinator, so no key is copied anywhere. Docker Desktop opened from the Dock has no agent in its session. Open it from a terminal, and load your key first.

   ```bash
   open -a Docker
   ssh-add --apple-use-keychain ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
   dockingbird connect github --github example-org/example-app --agent
   ```

   When no agent is forwarded yet, Dockingbird restarts itself to take it and prints a line for that. The step is done when the command prints these lines.

   ```text
   Restarting Dockingbird to use your Mac's ssh-agent ... done
   ```

   ```text
   Connected github: example-org/example-app (main) over SSH as somebody, with your Mac's
   ssh-agent; no key is copied.
   A config that names it: connections = ["github"]
   ```

heading: Connect agents to GitHub > Steps
summary: Every key in the agent reaches every repository your account does.
text:
Every key in the agent reaches every repository your account does. Running `ssh-add -D`, or quitting Docker Desktop, ends that at once. If your Mac's agent restarts, requests fail with "your Mac's ssh-agent isn't reachable". Then `dockingbird stop`, followed by any command, binds the socket again.

4. Name the connection in a config you add. Agents ask for a fetch or a push with a `bus_request`, and Dockingbird's coordinator runs it. A push sends the head the agents published. A command that pushes therefore needs a `tools` setting of `default` or `full`, since `bus` shares no commits.

   ```toml
   command = "fixer"
   connections = ["github"]
   tools = "default"
   ```

   ```bash
   dockingbird config add fixer.toml
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints this line.

   ```text
   Registered fixer: dockingbird fixer "task" (connections: github)
   ```

5. See what the connection lets agents do. The `status` screen lists each connection after the sign-in line. `dockingbird status fixer-1` adds that agent's last request and, when it failed, the reason in plain words.

   ```bash
   dockingbird connections github
   ```

   The step is done when the output holds this line, followed by one `Agent:` line for each grant.

   ```text
   Fetch and push example-org/example-app (main)
   ```

heading: Connect agents to GitHub > How a fetch and a push work
summary: A fetch leaves the branch as a bundle file in the agent's log folder, with its SHA-256.
text:
A fetch leaves the branch as a bundle file in the agent's log folder, with its SHA-256. A push needs a fetch of the same connection first. It fails when GitHub's branch holds commits the published head lacks. The agent then merges its newest fetch into its work, shares it, and pushes again. It fetches again first when GitHub's branch moved since the last fetch.

Dockingbird checks the copy of your key against GitHub's own host keys from this computer before it says done. `--known-hosts PATH` names a file of host keys to trust instead. Fetch and push over SSH are all that connections run today. HTTPS tokens are not yet available.

heading: Connect agents to GitHub > Grants, revoke and a stuck push
summary: Each start of an added config's command grants its connections to that agent for at most its `session_hours`.
text:
Each start of an added config's command grants its connections to that agent for at most its `session_hours`. Take the connection from one agent with `dockingbird revoke github --to fixer-1`, from a swarm role with `dockingbird connect github --revoke --role grader`, or from everyone with `dockingbird disconnect github`. The disconnect also deletes Dockingbird's copy of the key. `dockingbird clean --all` removes it too. Your own key file stays where it is. The commands and their done lines are on [connections.md](connections.md).

A push that stopped midway, after which GitHub's branch moved, has a result Dockingbird cannot tell. It holds every other push back and lists the case under "Needs your attention" in `dockingbird status`. Open the branch on GitHub, check whether the push landed, then release it.

```bash
dockingbird connections --release
```

The command is done when it prints these lines. The next push starts with a fresh fetch.

```text
Released the push to example-org/example-app whose result was unknown.
The next push starts with a fresh fetch.
```

heading: Connect agents to GitHub > When it fails
summary: - [`CONNECT_NOT_IN_REPO`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_not_in_repo): you ran `connect` outside a checkout, or `--branch` names a branch Dockingbird has not copied.
text:
- [`CONNECT_NOT_IN_REPO`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_not_in_repo): you ran `connect` outside a checkout, or `--branch` names a branch Dockingbird has not copied. Switch to the branch and run it again.
- [`CONNECT_GITHUB_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_github_invalid): the value after `--github` is not an owner and a name joined by one slash.
- [`CONNECT_NO_KEY`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_no_key): none of the key files `ssh -G github.com` lists exists. Pass `--key PATH`, or make the deploy key of step 2.
- [`CONNECT_KEY_UNREADABLE`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_key_unreadable): the key file is missing, a link, readable by others, or inside Dockingbird's folder.
- [`CONNECT_KEY_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_key_invalid): the file is not a private key, for example the `.pub` file. Name the one without `.pub`.
- [`CONNECT_KEY_HARDWARE`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_key_hardware): the key lives on a security key and cannot be copied. A deploy key works.
- [`CONNECT_PASSPHRASE_WRONG`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_passphrase_wrong): `ssh-keygen` could not unlock the key. Run the command again, or make a deploy key.
- [`CONNECT_PASSPHRASE_NEEDS_TERMINAL`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_passphrase_needs_terminal): the key has a passphrase and the command has no terminal to ask on.
- [`CONNECT_KEY_REFUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_key_refused): GitHub refused every key tried. Add the key's `.pub` to your account, or to the repo as a deploy key with write access.
- [`CONNECT_GITHUB_UNREACHABLE`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_github_unreachable): this computer could not reach GitHub. Nothing was saved.
- [`CONNECT_HOST_KEY_MISMATCH`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_host_key_mismatch): GitHub answered with a host key Dockingbird does not hold. Run `dockingbird update`.
- [`CONNECT_KEY_CHANGED`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_key_changed): the connection keeps a different key than the file holds now. Disconnect it, then connect again.
- [`CONNECT_NO_AGENT`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_no_agent), [`CONNECT_AGENT_REFUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_agent_refused), [`CONNECT_AGENT_NO_DESKTOP`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_agent_no_desktop): `--agent` found no ssh-agent, an agent without a key GitHub knows, or a Docker that is not Docker Desktop.
- [`CONNECT_AGENT_UNREACHABLE`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_agent_unreachable) and [`CONNECT_AGENT_EMPTY`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_agent_empty): the connection is saved, but Docker Desktop reaches no agent, or an agent with no key. Both exit 0.
- [`STATUS_PUSH_UNRESOLVED`](../troubleshooting.md#status_push_unresolved): a push ended with an unknown result. Check the branch on GitHub, then run `dockingbird connections --release`.

heading: MCP servers, services and browsers for agents
summary: Agents can call an MCP server by its URL, run a program of yours with arguments you allow, and drive a browser.
text: Agents can call an MCP server by its URL, run a program of yours with arguments you allow, and drive a browser. This page connects each one, then shows how `serve` runs the program or lends the browser as you, by hand or from a unit that starts at login. The model behind all of them is on [connections.md](connections.md).

heading: MCP servers, services and browsers for agents > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird status` must not print "Dockingbird isn't set up yet."
- For a service, you hold the program, the checkout it lives in, and the commit that checkout is at. `git rev-parse HEAD` in the checkout prints the commit.
- For a browser of this Mac, you use a Mac with Google Chrome installed. Lending Chrome, Firefox or Safari works on a Mac only.
- For a browser in Docker, you need nothing on the Mac. The first start builds the browser's image once.

heading: MCP servers, services and browsers for agents > An MCP server by URL
summary: An MCP connection registers a streamable-HTTP server for the roles of a swarm that list its name in `connections`.
text:
An MCP connection registers a streamable-HTTP server for the roles of a swarm that list its name in `connections`. Each of their agents gets the server's tools beside Dockingbird's own at every start.

```bash
dockingbird connect search --mcp https://mcp.example/mcp
```

The URL is `https`, with a lowercase host, an optional port, a path and a query, no user name and no fragment, at most 2048 characters. Dockingbird keeps nothing else, and a server that needs a key is not yet available. The catalogue lists no done line for this form. The step is done when the command exits 0 and `dockingbird connections` lists `search`.

heading: MCP servers, services and browsers for agents > A program as a service
summary: A service file says what runs and what an agent may choose.
text:
A service file says what runs and what an agent may choose. It must be a file of yours that only you can read, not a link, and not inside Dockingbird's folder. The file below is `convert.toml`.

```toml
# What dockingbird serve convert runs when an agent asks.
# The program, and the checkout it lives in at this commit (both or neither).
# serve will not run it once the checkout moved.
program = "/path/to/convert/bin/convert"
checkout = "/path/to/convert"
commit = "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567"
# The most seconds one run may take; then it is stopped.
timeout_s = 600
# Its words: {output} is the folder it writes its result to (once),
# each {NAME} is an argument declared below.
argv = ["--pages", "{pages}", "--mode", "{mode}", "{output}"]

# A whole number from 1 to 500.
[arguments.pages]
type = "int"
minimum = 1
maximum = 500

# One of these words.
[arguments.mode]
type = "choice"
choices = ["fast", "best"]
```

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `program` | the program to run, with `checkout` and `commit` to pin the code it runs |
| `timeout_s` | most seconds one run may take, then `SIGTERM`, and `SIGKILL` 10 seconds later |
| `argv` | the program's words, each `{NAME}` replaced by a declared argument and `{output}` by the output folder |
| `uses` | the database connection whose credential each run gets, such as `uses = ["scores"]` |
| `[call]` | in place of `argv`, a Python function in the checkout, named by `python`, `module` and `function` |
| `[arguments.NAME]` | one argument an agent may fill in |

The same keys are listed in [the roles and connections reference](../reference/files/roles-and-connections.md).

| Argument `type` | Keys it takes | What the agent may send |
|---|---|---|
| `int` | `minimum`, `maximum` | a whole number between the two bounds |
| `choice` | `choices` | one word from the list |
| `text` | `max_chars` | text up to that many characters, passed on as typed |

A `text` argument reaches the program as the agent typed it. If the program reads one as a path or a command's name, the agent gains that reach. Declare `choice` or `int` where the program takes a path, a name or a mode.

heading: MCP servers, services and browsers for agents > A program as a service
text:
1. Connect the file. Dockingbird checks every key, checks that `argv` uses each declared argument, and checks that the checkout is at the commit. It runs nothing.

   ```bash
   dockingbird connect convert --service ./convert.toml
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints these lines.

   ```text
   Connected convert: agents of a config that names it run /path/to/convert/bin/convert here, as you,
   with the arguments it declares, when you run dockingbird serve convert.
   A config that names it: connections = ["convert"]
   ```

2. Serve it. An agent of a config that names `convert` asks for a run with `bus_request`. Its request waits in `dockingbird status` until this runs.

   ```bash
   dockingbird serve convert
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints this line. Each request then prints how its run ended.

   ```text
   Serving convert: agents' requests to it run here, as you, one at a time.
   Ran convert for runner-1: done in 3 s.
   ```

A run starts the program alone, never through a shell. It gets the file's words with the checked arguments in place and runs in its checkout. It sees five variables and nothing else of your shell: `PATH`, your `HOME`, `LANG=C.UTF-8`, a `TMPDIR` of its own and `DOCKINGBIRD_SERVICE_OUTPUT`, the output folder's path. The output folder is the result. It holds what the program wrote plus `stdout.txt` and `stderr.txt`, at most 64 MiB and 10,000 entries, with links left out. It lands in the agent's log folder under `log/connections/<job>/`.

Before each run, `serve` checks the request again. It refuses a request that came too late or names a program or arguments the file does not allow. It also refuses when the checkout moved, or the program is gone, a link, or writable by anyone else. Ctrl-C, closing the terminal or ending `serve` stops the run, and the agent learns its request did not run.

A service that needs a database gets its credential through `uses`. The broker puts `PGHOST`, `PGPORT`, `PGDATABASE`, `PGUSER` and `PGPASSWORD` into that run's environment alone, never into a file, a log or an agent. A `uses` that names more than one connection, or one that is not an enabled database, is declined before the run starts. The agent needs no grant on that database, because its grant is the service's. The worked case is [the database cookbook](../../examples/database-without-the-password/README.md).

heading: MCP servers, services and browsers for agents > A browser of this Mac
summary: An agent of a config that names `chrome` asks for the browser and waits until `serve` runs in a terminal on this Mac.
text:
```bash
dockingbird connect chrome --browser chrome
dockingbird serve chrome
```

An agent of a config that names `chrome` asks for the browser and waits until `serve` runs in a terminal on this Mac. `serve` lends it to one agent at a time, either your own browser with its logins, cookies and open tabs, or a fresh one that exists for that session alone. Each request picks, and your own is the default. `firefox` and `safari` work the same way after `connect NAME --browser firefox` or `--browser safari`.

| Browser | One-time set-up for your own profile |
|---|---|
| Chrome | open `chrome://inspect/#remote-debugging`, turn remote debugging on, keep Chrome running, and click Allow when it asks, which it does for each use |
| Firefox | quit Firefox before the first request; `serve` starts it with remote control on and closes it when `serve` stops, and a Firefox you opened by hand is refused |
| Safari | in Settings > Advanced turn on "Show features for web developers", then in Settings > Developer turn on "Allow Remote Automation" and "Allow JavaScript from Apple Events", and click OK when macOS asks |

In your own browser the agent can act as you on every site you are signed in to, and Dockingbird restricts nothing it does on any website. The browser loads pages with your Mac's network, so the agent's egress setting does not limit what it reaches there. A fresh browser has none of your logins and is removed afterwards. The agent keeps the browser until it lets go, its container ends, the browser closes, the session's time limit passes, or you press Ctrl-C.

Clicks, typing, scrolling and dragging are real mouse and keyboard input on this Mac when the browser has a window. That needs Accessibility for the app you run `serve` from, under System Settings > Privacy & Security > Accessibility. Start `serve` from Terminal. A `serve` started by an agent app counts as its own program, which no app's switch covers. A screenshot of your own Safari needs Screen Recording the same way. Moving the pointer into a corner of the screen stops an input.

The step is done when the command prints this line.

```text
Google Chrome is open for review-1 (own profile) until review-1 lets it go,
its container ends, or Ctrl-C.
```

heading: MCP servers, services and browsers for agents > A browser of its own, in Docker
summary: An added config with `browser = "chrome"` gives each of its agents a Google Chrome of Dockingbird's own.
text:
An added config with `browser = "chrome"` gives each of its agents a Google Chrome of Dockingbird's own. It runs headed on a virtual screen, in a container beside the agent's, behind the agent's egress proxy. No `connect` or `serve` is needed, nothing runs on your Mac, and none of your logins is in it. A repo's own config that asks for one is refused at its start.

```toml
command = "surf"
workspace = "scratch"
browser = "chrome"
egress = "allowlist"
allow = ["registries", "github"]
```

A start prints a line for each wait, then the agent runs.

```text
Building the agent's browser ... done ({elapsed})
Starting the agent's browser ... done ({elapsed})
```

`dockingbird watch surf-1` shows that screen in your VNC viewer, Screen Sharing on a Mac, and lets you take over. The address it prints, `vnc://127.0.0.1:<port>`, takes connections from this Mac alone. Anything you type or paste there, the agent can read. The command is done when it prints these lines, and `--no-open` prints the address and opens no viewer.

```text
Opening surf-1's browser, vnc://127.0.0.1:<port>, in your VNC viewer.
Anything you type or paste into this browser is visible to the agent surf-1,
which reads the page. Sign in to nothing you would not hand it.
VNC password: <the browser's own password>
```

heading: MCP servers, services and browsers for agents > Serve every connection of a home
summary: `dockingbird serve --all` serves every service and browser connection of the home in one process.
text:
`dockingbird serve --all` serves every service and browser connection of the home in one process. `dockingbird serve --unit` prints the unit that keeps it running, a launchd property list on a Mac and a systemd user unit on Linux, and installs nothing. Save the text as the unit's file and install it the way your system does. A home started with a folder rather than a name needs `dockingbird --home NAME serve --unit`.

```bash
dockingbird serve --all
dockingbird serve --unit
```

`serve --all` never starts Docker or Dockingbird. While Docker does not answer, or no coordinator runs, it exits 1, and the unit starts it again every 10 seconds until they answer. `dockingbird stop` ends it with exit 0, and the unit leaves it stopped. Browsers are lent from a Mac only, so a Linux unit serves services.

heading: MCP servers, services and browsers for agents > When it fails
summary: - [`CONNECT_MCP_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_mcp_invalid): the URL is not an `https` address with a lowercase host, no user and no fragment, or it is too long.
text:
- [`CONNECT_MCP_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_mcp_invalid): the URL is not an `https` address with a lowercase host, no user and no fragment, or it is too long.
- [`CONNECT_SERVICE_INVALID`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_service_invalid): the service file is missing, readable by others, a link, too large, or holds a key to fix. The line names the key and never its value.
- [`CONNECT_SERVICE_CHECKOUT_MOVED`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_service_checkout_moved): the checkout is not at the file's commit. Check that commit out, or write the commit it is at.
- [`SERVE_NOT_A_SERVICE`](../troubleshooting.md#serve_not_a_service): the name is a GitHub repo, a folder or a database, which `serve` does not run.
- [`SERVE_CHECKOUT_MOVED`](../troubleshooting.md#serve_checkout_moved): the checkout moved since `connect`, and nothing ran. Connect the service again.
- [`SERVE_COORDINATOR_GONE`](../troubleshooting.md#serve_coordinator_gone): Dockingbird stopped while `serve` waited. Start `serve` again.
- [`SERVE_ALL_NONE`](../troubleshooting.md#serve_all_none): the home has no service or browser connection to serve.
- [`SERVE_UNIT_UNNAMED`](../troubleshooting.md#serve_unit_unnamed): the home has no name, so the unit cannot start it. Pass `--home NAME`.
- [`CONNECT_BROWSER_UNSUPPORTED`](../troubleshooting.md#connect_browser_unsupported): `--browser` takes `chrome`, `firefox` or `safari`.
- [`SERVE_BROWSER_MAC_ONLY`](../troubleshooting.md#serve_browser_mac_only) and [`SERVE_BROWSER_MISSING`](../troubleshooting.md#serve_browser_missing): the computer is not a Mac, or Chrome is not installed where the line says.
- [`SERVE_BROWSER_NOT_ENABLED`](../troubleshooting.md#serve_browser_not_enabled): Chrome's remote debugging is off. Turn it on once and the next request works.
- [`SERVE_BROWSER_ACCESSIBILITY`](../troubleshooting.md#serve_browser_accessibility): Accessibility is off for the app running `serve`, so the agent's clicks are refused while serving goes on.
