summary: Each row of `status --json` is an envelope of its own.
text:
```bash
dockingbird --json status
```

Each row of `status --json` is an envelope of its own. A running agent's row carries the figures its supervisor writes: `phase`, `turns`, `turn_running`, `last_turn_at`, `last_turn`, `context_window`, `compact_at_asked`, `changed`, `untracked`, `screen_held`, `token_failed`, `sign_in_retry`, `bus_losses`, the `result_` figures of the last result, `model_usage` per model, `compactions` and `api_retries`. Scrape turns these rows into the metric families. A value the tool did not report is `null`.

heading: Read the metrics by hand > The labels
text:
| Label | What it names | Where it appears |
|---|---|---|
| `profile` | The home | Every agent line |
| `agent` | The agent's name | Every agent line |
| `session` | The agent's session | Every agent line |
| `tool` | `claude` or `codex` | Every agent line |
| `team`, `role` | The swarm and the role of a fleet agent | An agent of a swarm |

heading: Read the metrics by hand > The JSON forms for a script
summary: [The example exporter](../../examples/observability/exporter.py) reads these envelopes with the standard library alone.
text:
| Command | `id` | What `fields` hold |
|---|---|---|
| `fleet probe --json` | `FLEET_PROBE` | Each figure by name, the kinds of process, `unread` |
| `fleet read-home --json` | `FLEET_HOME` | The home's agents, state counts, inbox rows, `unread` |
| `fleet scrape --json` | `FLEET_SCRAPE` | `read_at`, the agents, `exposition` |
| `fleet queue --metrics` | none | Prints text only, with no `--json` form |

[The example exporter](../../examples/observability/exporter.py) reads these envelopes with the standard library alone. [The metrics reference](../reference/metrics.md) lists every family. To collect the figures on a schedule, go on to [the Prometheus guide](prometheus.md).

heading: Read the metrics by hand > When it fails
summary: - [`FLEET_PROBE_NOT_MACOS`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_probe_not_macos): the probe reads macOS only and ends 1.
text:
- [`FLEET_PROBE_NOT_MACOS`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_probe_not_macos): the probe reads macOS only and ends 1. Run it on a Mac.
- [`FLEET_PROBE_NO_SYSCTL`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_probe_no_sysctl): the probe could not read the Mac's cores and stopped. Ends 1.
- [`FLEET_PROBE_UNREAD`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_probe_unread): a part could not be read. The rest is printed and the command ends 0.
- [`FLEET_HOME_NO_STATUS`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_home_no_status): the home's own `status` failed, so `read-home` stops. Ends 1.
- [`FLEET_HOME_UNREAD`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_home_unread): the inbox could not be read, so it is `unread`. Ends 0.
- [`FLEET_SCRAPE_NO_STATUS`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_scrape_no_status): the home's status failed or Dockingbird is not ready there, so no figures print. Ends 1.
- [`FLEET_SCRAPE_NO_DISK`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_scrape_no_disk) and [`FLEET_HOME_NO_DISK`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_home_no_disk): `--disk` belongs to the probe. Both end 2.
- [`ORG_NOT_CONFIGURED`](../troubleshooting.md#org_not_configured): this computer has no org login, which `fleet queue --metrics` needs. Run `dockingbird org login`.
- [`FLEET_DB_UNREACHABLE`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_db_unreachable): the fleet database did not answer. Ends 69.
- [`FLEET_DB_REFUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_db_refused): the database turned the login down. Ends 78.

heading: Collect the metrics with Prometheus
summary: This page puts a host's agent figures, the host's own load and the fleet queue into a Prometheus you run.
text: This page puts a host's agent figures, the host's own load and the fleet queue into a Prometheus you run. Prometheus is yours to install. The [official install page](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/installation/) covers every platform. [The observability page](../concepts/observability.md) shows how the pieces connect: an agent's container serves its figures only inside its own network, so a small exporter on the host serves them for Prometheus.

heading: Collect the metrics with Prometheus > Before you start
summary: - You have read the figures once by hand, as [the metrics guide](metrics.md) shows.
text:
- You have read the figures once by hand, as [the metrics guide](metrics.md) shows. Check with `dockingbird fleet scrape`, which ends with a `# EOF` line.
- Python 3.12 on each host. Check with `python3 --version`.
- Prometheus installed, on any computer that reaches your hosts. Check with `prometheus --version`.
- For the fleet job, a running admitter and its metrics port. [The fleet scheduler guide](fleet-scheduler.md) starts it.

heading: Collect the metrics with Prometheus > Copy the exporter to each host
summary: Put [exporter.py](../../examples/observability/exporter.py) on each host that runs homes.
text: Put [exporter.py](../../examples/observability/exporter.py) on each host that runs homes. Python is all it needs. Each 30 seconds it runs `dockingbird --json fleet probe`. Each 60 seconds it runs `dockingbird --home NAME --json fleet scrape` for every home you name, so a slow home never holds up the others. From each envelope it keeps `id` and `fields`, and drops `lines`.

heading: Collect the metrics with Prometheus > Run it
summary: The first word is the port.
text:
```bash
python3 exporter.py 9105 --bind PRIVATE_ADDRESS --home NAME
```

The first word is the port. `--bind` is the address to listen on, and it defaults to loopback, so Prometheus on another computer needs the host's address on your private network. `--home NAME` names a home of this host and may repeat. With no `--home` the exporter reads the default home and labels it `default`. Run it as the user that owns the homes, with `dockingbird` on its `PATH`. To keep it running, start it from your service manager: a LaunchAgent on a Mac or a systemd user unit on Linux.

Check the page after the first reading, which takes up to a minute.

```bash
curl http://PRIVATE_ADDRESS:9105/metrics
```

The step worked when the page holds one `dockingbird_scrape_up` line per home with the value 1.

```text
dockingbird_scrape_up{home="NAME"} 1
```

heading: Collect the metrics with Prometheus > What the page holds
summary: A home that fails to read serves no agent figures, only `scrape_up` 0.
text:
| Series | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `dockingbird_host_*` | gauge | The probe's typed figures, such as `dockingbird_host_load_one`, `dockingbird_host_memory_free_bytes` and `dockingbird_host_docker_containers_running`, and `dockingbird_host_category_*{category}` per kind of process |
| `dockingbird_probe_up` | gauge | 1 when the last probe read worked and its schema is `dockingbird.fleet.probe/1`, else 0 |
| `dockingbird_agent_*` | gauge | Each home's own text, passed through with one added label, `home` |
| `dockingbird_scrape_up{home}` | gauge | 1 when the home's last read worked, else 0 |

A home that fails to read serves no agent figures, only `scrape_up` 0. A home that is off, because it turned itself off after 30 minutes with no agent, reads as not ready and also shows 0. On a Linux host the probe cannot run, so `probe_up` is 0 and the agent figures still arrive. [The metrics reference](../reference/metrics.md) lists every family.

heading: Collect the metrics with Prometheus > Add the two jobs to Prometheus
summary: Copy the jobs from [prometheus.yml](../../examples/observability/prometheus.yml) into your own configuration and replace the placeholder targets.
text:
Copy the jobs from [prometheus.yml](../../examples/observability/prometheus.yml) into your own configuration and replace the placeholder targets. The [configuration reference](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/configuration/configuration/) explains every key.

| Job | Target | Interval | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `dockingbird_hosts` | `lab.example:9105`, one per host, with a `host` label | 30 s | The probe refreshes every 30 s |
| `dockingbird_fleet` | `control-plane.example:9107`, the admitter | 60 s | One admission pass at least every 30 s, so 60 s sees each change |

The admitter serves its families at the fleet database's host, on the port that `FLEET_SCHED_METRICS_PORT` names. Use that port in the target. Leave the job out when your organisation runs no fleet scheduler. Restart Prometheus, or send it SIGHUP, so it reads the file.

heading: Collect the metrics with Prometheus > Check the targets
summary: Open the Prometheus page at `/targets` on its own port.
text:
Open the Prometheus page at `/targets` on its own port. The step worked when both jobs show the state `UP`. Then run these queries in its expression browser.

```text
dockingbird_scrape_up
count by (state) (dockingbird_agent_info)
```

The first returns one series per home. The second counts agents by state. [The queries page](../../examples/observability/queries.md) holds fourteen queries. To draw them, go on to [the Grafana guide](grafana.md).

heading: Collect the metrics with Prometheus > When it fails
summary: - [`FLEET_PROBE_NOT_MACOS`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_probe_not_macos): the host is not a Mac, so `dockingbird_probe_up` is 0.
text:
- [`FLEET_PROBE_NOT_MACOS`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_probe_not_macos): the host is not a Mac, so `dockingbird_probe_up` is 0. The agent figures still arrive.
- [`FLEET_SCRAPE_NO_STATUS`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_scrape_no_status): the home's status failed or Dockingbird is not ready there. Its `scrape_up` is 0.
- [`FLEET_DB_UNREACHABLE`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_db_unreachable): the admitter's database did not answer, so the fleet job has no target. Ends 69.
- [`FLEET_DB_REFUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_db_refused): the database turned the admitter's login down. Ends 78. Run `dockingbird org status`.

heading: Draw the metrics in Grafana
summary: This page loads a ready dashboard into your Grafana and sets the three alerts most worth having.
text: This page loads a ready dashboard into your Grafana and sets the three alerts most worth having. Grafana is yours to install. The [official install page](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/setup-grafana/installation/) covers every platform. The dashboard reads from the Prometheus that [the Prometheus guide](prometheus.md) sets up.

heading: Draw the metrics in Grafana > Before you start
summary: - Prometheus collects the exporter and, for the fleet row, the admitter.
text:
- Prometheus collects the exporter and, for the fleet row, the admitter. Check that `dockingbird_scrape_up` returns a series in the Prometheus expression browser.
- Grafana runs and you can sign in as an editor or an admin. Check by opening its address in a browser.
- Grafana has a Prometheus data source that points at your Prometheus. The [data source page](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/datasources/prometheus/configure/) shows how. Check that its Save and test button says it works.

heading: Draw the metrics in Grafana > Import the dashboard
summary: Open Dashboards, then New, then Import.
text:
Open Dashboards, then New, then Import. Upload [dashboard.json](../../examples/observability/dashboard.json) and press Import. The [import page](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/dashboards/build-dashboards/import-dashboards/) shows the same screen. The step worked when a dashboard titled `Dockingbird fleet` opens with five rows.

The file holds no data source of its own. At the top of the dashboard, the variable `Datasource` picks your Prometheus. Pick it once. The variables `Host` and `Home` list every value of the `host` and `home` labels, and both default to all.

heading: Draw the metrics in Grafana > The five rows
summary: The Fleet row stays empty when your organisation runs no fleet scheduler.
text:
| Row | Panels | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Fleet | Queue depth by priority, headroom per host in millicores and in MiB, holds by reason, mean queue wait per host, idle share per role | The admitter |
| Hosts | Load against the load line, free memory, containers running | The probe |
| Agents | A table of every agent with state, model, context fill, age of the last turn and cost, agents by state, context fill, agents near the compact point, turns in the last hour | The agents |
| Cost | Cost so far per model, the change over the last hour, token throughput by type | The agents |
| Health | Sign-in retries and token failures, bus losses, API retries, agents silent for over an hour, homes the exporter could not read | The agents and the exporter |

The Fleet row stays empty when your organisation runs no fleet scheduler. The Hosts row is empty for a Linux host, because the probe reads macOS only. [The queries page](../../examples/observability/queries.md) states each query and what it answers.

heading: Draw the metrics in Grafana > Read the dashboard
summary: The `Every agent` table in the Agents row is the quickest check.
text:
The `Every agent` table in the Agents row is the quickest check. Each row is one agent, with its host, home, state, model, effort, context fill, the seconds since its last turn, and its cost so far. Sort it by context fill to see which agent compacts next. The cost is Claude Code's own estimate, so a Codex agent shows none.

Cost panels read gauges that fall to zero when an agent restarts. The panel for the last hour uses `delta()`, so a restart appears as a dip. The queue panels read counters, so they use `rate()` over an hour.

The refresh is 30 seconds and the time range is the last 6 hours. Both are the dashboard's defaults. Change them in the dashboard settings.

heading: Draw the metrics in Grafana > The variables
summary: The fleet panels use none of them.
text:
| Variable | Type | Values | Used by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Datasource` (`DS`) | data source | Every Prometheus data source | Every panel |
| `Host` (`host`) | query | `label_values(dockingbird_scrape_up, host)`, from the job's `host` label | The agent, host and health panels |
| `Home` (`home`) | query | `label_values(dockingbird_scrape_up{host=~"$host"}, home)`, from the exporter's `home` label | The agent and health panels |

The fleet panels use none of them. The admitter serves its own `host` label for each pool host, and those names come from the pool, not from your Prometheus jobs.

heading: Draw the metrics in Grafana > Keep your changes
summary: Edits you make in Grafana stay in Grafana.
text: Edits you make in Grafana stay in Grafana. To keep a copy next to your own configuration, open the dashboard's settings, choose JSON Model, and save the text to a file. Importing the shipped file again asks before it overwrites, because the dashboard keeps the uid `dockingbird-fleet`.

heading: Draw the metrics in Grafana > Add a host
summary: Add its exporter to the `dockingbird_hosts` job in your Prometheus configuration, with its own `host` label, and restart Prometheus.
text: Add its exporter to the `dockingbird_hosts` job in your Prometheus configuration, with its own `host` label, and restart Prometheus. The step worked when the `Host` variable lists the new name after the next refresh of the page. No panel changes, because every panel filters on the variable.

heading: Draw the metrics in Grafana > Alert on three signals
summary: Grafana's [alerting pages](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/alerting/alerting-rules/create-grafana-managed-rule/) show how to create a rule.
text:
Grafana's [alerting pages](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/alerting/alerting-rules/create-grafana-managed-rule/) show how to create a rule. Open Alerting, then Alert rules, then New alert rule, choose your Prometheus data source, paste a query below and set the condition. The thresholds are examples. Choose your own.

| Signal | Query | Example condition |
|---|---|---|
| An agent's context is near its compact point | `max by (home, agent) (dockingbird_agent_context_used_tokens / dockingbird_agent_compact_at_tokens)` | Above 0.9 for 5 minutes |
| A host is over its load line | `dockingbird_host_load_one / dockingbird_host_load_line` | Above 1 for 10 minutes |
| The queue is waiting long | `rate(fleet_queue_wait_seconds_total[1h]) / rate(fleet_admissions_total[1h])` | Above 900 seconds for 15 minutes |

No family holds the oldest wait itself. The mean wait per host, from two counters, is the nearest figure. The probe's load line is 130% of the Mac's cores, and the compact point is the context size at which an agent compacts.

heading: Draw the metrics in Grafana > When it fails
summary: - [`FLEET_PROBE_NOT_MACOS`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_probe_not_macos): a Linux host cannot run the probe.
text:
- [`FLEET_PROBE_NOT_MACOS`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_probe_not_macos): a Linux host cannot run the probe. Its row in Hosts stays blank.
- [`FLEET_SCRAPE_NO_STATUS`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_scrape_no_status): one home would not answer. Its agents vanish from the panels, and Health names the home.
- [`FLEET_DB_UNREACHABLE`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_db_unreachable): the database behind the admitter is down or asleep, exit 69. Fleet shows nothing.
- [`FLEET_DB_REFUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#fleet_db_refused): the database rejected the admitter's login, exit 78. Fleet shows nothing.

heading: Harbor benchmark tasks
summary: The place of this page in the customer docs is pending a decision.
text:
The place of this page in the customer docs is pending a decision.

A Harbor benchmark task is a folder with a `task.toml`, an `instruction.md`, an `environment/` folder and a `tests/test.sh`. Each branch of a task repository holds one task. The `dockingbird harbor` commands run a task on this computer with the Harbor commit that the repository's CI pins, which Dockingbird installs under its own folder the first time it is needed. A finished job leaves only its folder of results.

heading: Harbor benchmark tasks > Before you start
summary: - Docker Desktop is running.
text:
- Docker Desktop is running. `docker version` answers.
- You stand in the task's folder, or you name it with `-p DIR`. Without a `task.toml` there, the command stops with `HARBOR_NOT_A_TASK`.
- For a real trial with Claude Code, a saved token or key. Run `claude setup-token`, then `pbpaste | dockingbird login claude --oauth-token -`, or use `dockingbird login claude --api-key`. See [sign-in and API keys](sign-in-and-api-keys.md).

heading: Harbor benchmark tasks > 1. Run the two baselines
summary: This runs an `oracle` job, whose `solution/solve.sh` must score 1, then a `nop` job, an agent that does nothing, which must score 0.
text:
```bash
dockingbird harbor baseline
```

This runs an `oracle` job, whose `solution/solve.sh` must score 1, then a `nop` job, an agent that does nothing, which must score 0. `-k 3` runs each three times. The first run installs Harbor at the pinned commit, with one live line for the step. Done when the line prints.

```text
Both baselines pass: oracle scored 1 and nop scored 0 on every attempt.
```

Message id `HARBOR_BASELINE_OK`. A failure names each failing trial and the last lines its verifier printed (`HARBOR_BASELINE_FAILED`). Fix the task and run it again.

heading: Harbor benchmark tasks > 2. Run one real trial
summary: This runs one trial with Claude Code and your own login.
text:
```bash
dockingbird harbor run -a claude-code
```

This runs one trial with Claude Code and your own login. Dockingbird lends the credential to the task's container for the whole trial: a saved token or key first, else your computer's own login when its expiry covers the trial. Any other word goes to Harbor's own `run` as Harbor reads it, such as `-k 3` or `--timeout-multiplier 2`. `--keep-images` keeps the images a job built, for a faster next run. Run `claude-code` only on a task whose `environment/` you trust: the task's image owns its container and can read the credential. Done when the job ends.

```text
Job {job} ran {count} trials:
{trials}
Results: {folder}
```

Message id `HARBOR_JOB_DONE`. With no saved credential and no usable login, nothing runs: `No Claude sign-in or saved key is stored, so a claude-code trial can't run.` (`HARBOR_NO_SIGNIN`).

heading: Harbor benchmark tasks > 3. List, read and clean jobs
summary: `jobs` lists what ran, newest first, in `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/harbor/jobs/`.
text:
```bash
dockingbird harbor jobs
dockingbird harbor results JOB
dockingbird harbor clean
dockingbird harbor version
```

`jobs` lists what ran, newest first, in `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/harbor/jobs/`. `results JOB` shows each trial's reward.

```text
Job {job} ({state}), {count} trials:
{trials}
Folder: {folder}
```

Message id `HARBOR_JOB_RESULTS`. A job is `running` while its command runs, `done` once Harbor wrote its result, else `stopped`. `clean` asks once, then removes the job folders and the leftovers of earlier jobs.

```text
These Harbor jobs go:
{jobs}
Remove them? [y/N]
```

Message id `HARBOR_CLEAN_QUESTION`. `--yes` asks nothing, and `--all` removes Harbor's install too, which the next run installs again. `version` says whether the pinned commit is installed (`HARBOR_VERSION`). When a job ends, its containers, networks, volumes and the images it built are removed, unless `--keep-images`. Docker's build cache stays; `docker builder prune` removes it.

`dockingbird harbor check`, which would hand a bundle to Harbor's `check` so a model reads it at your cost, is not yet available and says so.

heading: Harbor benchmark tasks > When it fails
summary: - Run `harbor run` or `harbor baseline` in a folder with no `task.toml` and you get [`HARBOR_NOT_A_TASK`](../troubleshooting.md#harbor_not_a_task).
text:
- Run `harbor run` or `harbor baseline` in a folder with no `task.toml` and you get [`HARBOR_NOT_A_TASK`](../troubleshooting.md#harbor_not_a_task). Change folder, or pass `-p DIR`.
- A baseline trial that scores other than what its job wants, or hits an error, gives [`HARBOR_BASELINE_FAILED`](../troubleshooting.md#harbor_baseline_failed) with the last lines its verifier printed. Fix the task, then run it again.
- A `claude-code` trial needs a credential. With no saved token or key and no usable login, nothing runs, and [`HARBOR_NO_SIGNIN`](../troubleshooting.md#harbor_no_signin) says how to save one.
- When your computer's login would expire before the trial ends, [`HARBOR_SIGNIN_TOO_SHORT`](../troubleshooting.md#harbor_signin_too_short) shows what it has and what the trial needs. A token from `claude setup-token` lasts much longer.
- A task with several steps, or one that sets Windows, gives [`HARBOR_TASK_UNSUPPORTED`](../troubleshooting.md#harbor_task_unsupported). Run that task with Harbor itself.
- An option that would mount a folder of this computer into the task is refused with [`HARBOR_OPTION_REFUSED`](../troubleshooting.md#harbor_option_refused).
- On a computer where no job has run, `harbor jobs` prints [`HARBOR_NO_JOBS`](../troubleshooting.md#harbor_no_jobs).

heading: The GUI
summary: The Dockingbird GUI is a terminal program that shows every agent of this computer in one window, one tab per agent, with your inbox in a sidebar.
text: The Dockingbird GUI is a terminal program that shows every agent of this computer in one window, one tab per agent, with your inbox in a sidebar. Its install is not yet available to customers, so no customer can open it today. This page says what the GUI does, and what `dockingbird ui` prints when no GUI is installed, which is the case on your computer.

heading: The GUI > What the GUI is
summary: Run `dockingbird ui` and the program `dockingbird-gui` opens in your terminal.
text: Run `dockingbird ui` and the program `dockingbird-gui` opens in your terminal. You drive it with the mouse. Each agent that runs at a terminal gets its own tab, named after the agent. A sidebar on the left lists your inbox and your agents, and a bar under the panes shows the selected agent with its buttons. Every action prints the `dockingbird` command it runs, so you can learn the commands by using it. Press `ctrl+b`, then `q`, to leave; the agents keep working. The GUI has no key for changing an agent's settings or for sending a message. `dockingbird set` and `dockingbird send` do those, as [delegating tasks](delegating-tasks.md) shows.

heading: The GUI > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird --version` prints a version.
- You can do all of the daily work without the GUI. `dockingbird claude --as NAME` shows any agent's screen, and `dockingbird status` lists them all.

heading: The GUI > What `ui` prints today
summary: With no GUI installed, `ui` stops and exits 1.
text:
```bash
dockingbird ui
```

With no GUI installed, `ui` stops and exits 1.

```text
The Dockingbird GUI isn't installed.
Install it: dockingbird ui --install
```

Message id `GUI_MISSING`. The install step the second line names is not yet available to customers. Until it is, use `dockingbird status`, `dockingbird claude --as NAME` and the other commands in [the daily loop](daily-loop.md). `dockingbird ui` also needs a terminal: in a pipe or a script it prints `dockingbird ui needs a terminal: run it in Terminal, not in a pipe or a script.` and exits 1.

heading: The GUI > When it fails
summary: Only one message belongs to this page.
text: Only one message belongs to this page. [`GUI_MISSING`](../troubleshooting.md#gui_missing) appears whenever no GUI is installed on this computer, which today is every customer's computer.

heading: One Mac, day one
summary: This cookbook takes one Apple silicon Mac from the install to an agent's commit on your branch.
text:
This cookbook takes one Apple silicon Mac from the install to an agent's commit on your branch. It needs Docker
Desktop, uv and a git repo of yours, `~/code/myapp` below, and you edit no file by hand. Each step shows the line
Dockingbird prints when the step is done. The [troubleshooting](../../docs/troubleshooting.md) catalogue holds every
such line under its message id.

heading: One Mac, day one > Before you start
summary: - An Apple silicon Mac.
text:
- An Apple silicon Mac. `uname -m` prints `arm64`.
- Docker Desktop, running. `docker info` prints the server section without an error.
- uv. `uv --version` prints a version.
- A git repo of yours with a branch checked out. `git -C ~/code/myapp status` prints the branch name.
- The license key from your purchase email, copied to the clipboard.

heading: One Mac, day one > 1. Install
summary: Copy the license key from your purchase email.
text:
Copy the license key from your purchase email. The first line passes it to uv in two environment variables, so the
key shows up neither on screen nor in your shell history.

```bash
UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_USERNAME=license UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD="$(pbpaste)" uv tool install dockingbird --index zeusfyi=https://license.zeus.fyi/simple/
dockingbird license activate
dockingbird completion --install
```

`dockingbird license activate` asks for the key again at a hidden prompt and links this Mac to your seat. It is done
when it prints the plan, the seats and the term.

```text
This computer is activated: {plan}, {seats}, {term}.
You use Dockingbird under its terms: {link}
```

The activation saves a download token, so `dockingbird update` needs no key after this. `dockingbird license status`
prints the same plan, seats and term on its first line. Tab completion starts working in the next terminal you open.
A shell that answers `command not found: dockingbird` needs `uv tool update-shell` and a new terminal.

heading: One Mac, day one > 2. `dockingbird status`
summary: Before the first run it sets nothing up and says so.
text:
```bash
cd ~/code/myapp
dockingbird status
```

Before the first run it sets nothing up and says so.

```text
Dockingbird isn't set up yet. Start here: dockingbird claude
```

The first run, `dockingbird claude`, sets it up: it checks your branch, builds the image (about 5 minutes, once),
starts Dockingbird, copies the branch for the agents and starts Claude Code in its own container, in this terminal. It
uses the Claude Code login already on this Mac, or shows a sign-in link once. To leave the agent working, close the
window.

heading: One Mac, day one > 3. `dockingbird start`
summary: `dockingbird start` hands an agent a task with no terminal:
text:
`dockingbird start` hands an agent a task with no terminal:

```bash
dockingbird start "Fix the flaky test"
```

It copies your branch for the agent, starts it, and ends with (agents are numbered across the installation, so the
first run's agent is `claude-1` and this one `claude-2`):

```text
claude-2 started on myapp (main).
Thread <id>. Watch: dockingbird wait claude-2
```

`dockingbird wait claude-2` gives its next message as it comes, `dockingbird inbox` lists what waits for you,
`dockingbird read 1` reads one, `dockingbird send claude-2 "yes"` answers it, and `dockingbird results claude-2` saves
the files it attached. `dockingbird status` now shows who is working on what.

heading: One Mac, day one > 4. `dockingbird sync`
summary: The agents' work reaches your branch only as commits, through sync:
text:
The agents' work reaches your branch only as commits, through sync:

```bash
dockingbird sync
```

When an agent shared commits, it takes them and names each, with the command to review them:

```text
myapp (main): 1 new commit from the agents
...
Updated your main to <commit>. Review it: git log -p <commit>..<commit>
```

With nothing new either way, it prints this.

```text
myapp (main): up to date.
```

heading: One Mac, day one > 5. `dockingbird ui`
summary: The Dockingbird GUI is not yet available to customers.
text:
The Dockingbird GUI is not yet available to customers. Today `dockingbird ui` prints `The Dockingbird GUI isn't
installed.` and exits 1, and [the GUI](../../docs/guides/gui.md) says what that message means.

The [operator guide](../../docs/operator-guide.md) has the rest: sign-ins and API keys, update and clean, and what
lives where. `dockingbird stop` turns it all off, and nothing is lost.

heading: One Mac, day one > When it fails
text:
| Message id | What it means | Entry |
|---|---|---|
| `SIGNIN_NEEDED` | The tool is not signed in. Run `dockingbird login` for it, as the message says, or use an API key. | [catalogue](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#signin_needed) |
| `HOME_NOT_EMPTY` | The folder for Dockingbird's files holds files it did not make. Unset `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` or point it at an empty or new folder. | [catalogue](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#home_not_empty) |
| `GUI_MISSING` | `dockingbird ui` found no GUI on this computer. The GUI is not yet available to customers. | [catalogue](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#gui_missing) |

heading: Recover from a failed install
summary: This cookbook gets a computer from a failed install to a working `dockingbird` with an activated seat.
text: This cookbook gets a computer from a failed install to a working `dockingbird` with an activated seat. It covers the three failures a first install meets: no index, a wrong key and a wrong platform. Each step ends with the line that shows it worked.

heading: Recover from a failed install > Before you start
summary: - Your license key is in the purchase email.
text:
- Your license key is in the purchase email. The clipboard holds it on a Mac. Check with `pbpaste | wc -c`, which prints a number above zero.
- uv is installed. Check with `uv --version`. On a Mac, `brew install uv` adds it.
- git exists at `/usr/bin/git`. Check with `/usr/bin/git --version`.
- Docker Desktop, or Docker Engine with buildx on Linux, is installed. Check with `docker buildx version`.

heading: Recover from a failed install > 1. Check the platform
summary: Dockingbird runs on Apple silicon Macs and arm64 Linux.
text:
Dockingbird runs on Apple silicon Macs and arm64 Linux.

```bash
uname -m
```

The step is done when it prints `arm64` on a Mac or `aarch64` on Linux. On `x86_64`, stop here. An Intel Mac, an x86 Linux machine and Windows are not supported, and the first `dockingbird license` command on one prints this.

```text
Dockingbird's license program runs on Apple silicon Macs and arm64
Linux, not on {platform}.
```

That is [LICENSE_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_platform_unsupported), exit 1. The fix is another computer: an Apple silicon Mac, or an arm64 Linux machine or cloud VM.

heading: Recover from a failed install > 2. Remove a bare install
summary: A command without the index, `uv tool install dockingbird`, installs a package of that name that is not Dockingbird.
text:
A command without the index, `uv tool install dockingbird`, installs a package of that name that is not Dockingbird. Remove it.

```bash
uv tool uninstall dockingbird
```

The step is done when uv exits 0. If you never ran the bare command, skip it.

heading: Recover from a failed install > 3. Install with the key
summary: On a Mac, with the key on the clipboard, run this.
text:
On a Mac, with the key on the clipboard, run this.

```bash
UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_USERNAME=license UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD="$(pbpaste)" uv tool install dockingbird --index zeusfyi=https://license.zeus.fyi/simple/
```

On Linux, read the key without echo, run the command with it, then unset it.

```bash
read -rs UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD
UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_USERNAME=license UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD="$UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD" uv tool install dockingbird --index zeusfyi=https://license.zeus.fyi/simple/
unset UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD
```

The step is done when uv exits 0. A wrong, truncated or revoked key makes the index answer with an HTTP 401, and uv installs nothing. Dockingbird is not on the computer yet, so uv prints that failure and no message id exists for it. Copy the key from the email again and repeat the step. A trial cannot install from the index.

heading: Recover from a failed install > 4. Check the version
summary: The step is done when it prints the Dockingbird version.
text:
```bash
dockingbird --version
```

The step is done when it prints the Dockingbird version. If the shell says the command is not found, run this, then open a new terminal and repeat the check.

```bash
uv tool update-shell
```

heading: Recover from a failed install > 5. Activate the computer
summary: Paste the key when it asks.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license activate
```

Paste the key when it asks. The input is hidden. The step is done when the product prints this line, then the terms line and the count of linked computers.

```text
This computer is activated: {plan}, {seats:seat|seats}, {term}.
```

Typing the key after the command is refused with exit 2. The refusal is [LICENSE_KEY_IN_ARGV](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_key_in_argv). Run the command with no argument.

heading: Recover from a failed install > When it fails
summary: The longer story, with Docker and git, is on [install fails](../../docs/troubleshooting/install-fails.md).
text:
| Message id | What it means and the fix |
|---|---|
| [LICENSE_PLATFORM_UNSUPPORTED](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_platform_unsupported) | This computer is not Apple silicon or arm64 Linux. Use another one. |
| [LICENSE_KEY_IN_ARGV](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_key_in_argv) | Paste the key when asked. |
| [LICENSE_KEY_INVALID](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_key_invalid) | The server does not know the key. Copy it again. |
| [LICENSE_SEATS_FULL](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_seats_full) | Every computer the license admits is linked. See [move your seat](../move-your-seat/README.md). |
| [LICENSE_AUTHORITY_UNAVAILABLE](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_authority_unavailable) | The license server was out of reach. Get online and run the command again. |
| [DOCKER_NOT_INSTALLED](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#docker_not_installed) | Install Docker, then run `dockingbird claude` again. |

The longer story, with Docker and git, is on [install fails](../../docs/troubleshooting/install-fails.md).

heading: Move your seat to a new laptop
summary: This cookbook moves a seat from an old computer to a new laptop.
text: This cookbook moves a seat from an old computer to a new laptop. A seat is one person, who may link up to three computers, so you free one link and take it on the new laptop. Each step ends with the line it prints when it worked.

heading: Move your seat to a new laptop > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is installed on the new laptop.
text:
- Dockingbird is installed on the new laptop. Check with `dockingbird --version`. If it is not, follow [recover from a failed install](../recover-from-a-failed-install/README.md).
- You have the license key from the purchase email. Both `activate` and `activations` ask for it, hidden.
- You saved what you want from the old computer: results, configs and `hosts.toml`. The [backup guide](../../docs/guides/backup-and-restore.md) lists them.

heading: Move your seat to a new laptop > 1. Give the seat back from the old laptop
summary: Skip this step when the old laptop is lost or wiped, and go to step 2.
text:
Skip this step when the old laptop is lost or wiped, and go to step 2.

```bash
dockingbird license deactivate
```

The step is done when the product prints this line.

```text
This computer no longer uses a seat of the license.
```

`dockingbird clean --all` does the same and also removes everything Dockingbird made on that computer. When the license server does not answer, it prints [LICENSE_SEAT_STILL_HELD](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_seat_still_held) and exits 0. The seat is then still held. Free it in step 2 or step 3.

heading: Move your seat to a new laptop > 2. Activate the new laptop
summary: The `--label` value names this computer in the list.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license activate --label new-laptop
```

The `--label` value names this computer in the list. A label takes letters, digits, `-` and `.`. The step is done when the product prints the activation line.

```text
This computer is activated: {plan}, {seats:seat|seats}, {term}.
  Computers linked: 3 of 3 (1 seat, 3 computers each)
```

If the line appears, go to step 4. If every computer is linked, the command prints [LICENSE_SEATS_FULL](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_seats_full) and exits 1.

```text
Every computer this license admits is linked, so this one can't join.
Free one: dockingbird license activations --release ID
```

Under those lines it names each linked computer, the one seen longest ago first, with its id.

heading: Move your seat to a new laptop > 3. Free the old laptop
summary: Read the ids again when you need to.
text:
Read the ids again when you need to.

```bash
dockingbird license activations
```

The command asks for the key and prints one line for each linked computer.

```text
{label}: activated {activated}, last seen {seen}, id {id}
```

Pick the old laptop by its label and the day it was last seen. Then free its seat.

```bash
dockingbird license activations --release ID
```

The step is done when the product prints this line and lists the computers that remain.

```text
The seat of activation {id} is free again.
```

A seat that nobody frees stops counting by itself after 90 days. Run `dockingbird license activate --label new-laptop` again on the new laptop.

heading: Move your seat to a new laptop > 4. Check the status on the new laptop
summary: The `--refresh` flag checks in with the license server first.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license status --refresh
```

The `--refresh` flag checks in with the license server first. The step is done when the screen shows the license and this computer's label.

```text
Licensed: {plan}, {seats:seat|seats}, {term}.
  This computer: new-laptop
```

heading: Move your seat to a new laptop > 5. Check the old laptop, if it still runs
summary: On a computer whose seat was freed from another one, the screen shows this and exits 0.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license status --refresh
```

On a computer whose seat was freed from another one, the screen shows this and exits 0.

```text
This computer's seat was freed from another computer.
Activate it again: dockingbird license activate
```

No action is needed. To clear the old laptop for good, run `dockingbird clean --all` on it, which removes what Dockingbird made there.

heading: Move your seat to a new laptop > When it fails
summary: The whole license story is on the [licensing guide](../../docs/guides/licensing.md).
text:
| Message id | What it means and the fix |
|---|---|
| [LICENSE_KEY_IN_ARGV](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_key_in_argv) | The key was typed after the command. Run the command alone. |
| [LICENSE_KEY_INVALID](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_key_invalid) | The server does not know the key. Copy it again. |
| [LICENSE_SEATS_FULL](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_seats_full) | Free a computer, as in step 3. |
| [LICENSE_OPTION_INVALID](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_option_invalid) | A `--label` or `--release` value has a character it does not take. |
| [LICENSE_AUTHORITY_UNAVAILABLE](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_authority_unavailable) | The license server was out of reach. Nothing changed. |
| [LICENSE_SEAT_STILL_HELD](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_seat_still_held) | `clean --all` could not reach the server. Free the seat as in step 3. |

The whole license story is on the [licensing guide](../../docs/guides/licensing.md).

heading: Give agents a database without the password
summary: Goal: agents of a `grader` role read a `scores` database and write score rows, and no agent ever sees the address or a password.
text: Goal: agents of a `grader` role read a `scores` database and write score rows, and no agent ever sees the address or a password. You connect the database twice, once read-only and once for brokered writes. You add a program that inserts one score with arguments you bound. Then you take the access back and give it again. The guides behind each step are [databases.md](../../docs/guides/databases.md), [mcp-and-services.md](../../docs/guides/mcp-and-services.md) and [connections.md](../../docs/guides/connections.md).

heading: Give agents a database without the password > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird status` must not print "Dockingbird isn't set up yet."
- A PostgreSQL server answers at `db.example.net:5433` with a database named `scores`, and Docker can reach it. `psql -h db.example.net -p 5433 -U postgres scores -c 'select 1'` prints one row.
- The server allows no prepared transactions. `SHOW max_prepared_transactions;` prints 0.
- A table `scores` exists, owned by an administrator and not by the roles below.
- A program of yours inserts one score. It lives in a git checkout, and it reads the `PG*` variables for its connection. `git rev-parse HEAD` in that checkout prints the commit step 4 pins.
- A swarm role named `grader` lists `scores-db` in its `connections`. The swarm is described in [swarms.md](../../docs/guides/swarms.md). Steps 7 and 8 work with no running agent, and then they say so.

heading: Give agents a database without the password > Steps
text:
1. Make the two roles. `reader` cannot write. `scorer` may insert into `scores`. The revoke is the cost of Dockingbird's check of the read-only role, and it is needed once for the database. On PostgreSQL 16 and earlier, name the function's two forms without the fourth parameter.

   ```sql
   CREATE ROLE reader LOGIN PASSWORD 'a long password';
   GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE scores TO reader;
   GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO reader;
   GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO reader;
   CREATE ROLE scorer LOGIN PASSWORD 'another long password';
   GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE scores TO scorer;
   GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO scorer;
   GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON scores TO scorer;
   REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION
     pg_catalog.pg_logical_emit_message(boolean, text, text, boolean),
     pg_catalog.pg_logical_emit_message(boolean, text, bytea, boolean)
   FROM PUBLIC;
   ```

   The step is done when `psql` prints `CREATE ROLE` twice. If the database has the `dblink` extension, also run the `dblink` revoke on [databases.md](../../docs/guides/databases.md).

2. Connect the database read-only. Dockingbird asks for the password on your terminal, hidden, and keeps it. It then opens the database itself and checks that the role cannot write.

   ```bash
   dockingbird connect app-db --database postgres://reader@db.example.net:5433/scores --password
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints these lines.

   ```text
   Password for reader (hidden):
   Connected app-db: db.example.net:5433/scores as reader, read-only, checked from Dockingbird.
   Agents of a config that names it query it through Dockingbird;
   none sees the database.
   A config that names it: connections = ["app-db"]
   ```

3. Connect the same database for brokered writes, under its own name. Dockingbird checks the server alone, because this role is meant to write. An agent then sends `db.execute` with one statement, and the broker runs it in one read-write transaction.

   ```bash
   dockingbird connect scores-db --database postgres://scorer@db.example.net:5433/scores --password --writes
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints these lines.

   ```text
   Password for scorer (hidden):
   Connected scores-db: db.example.net:5433/scores as scorer, which may write, checked from Dockingbird.
   Agents of a config that names it query and change it through Dockingbird;
   none sees the database.
   A config that names it: connections = ["scores-db"]
   ```

heading: Give agents a database without the password > Steps
text:
4. Write the service file `insert-score.toml`. It names your program, the checkout and the commit, and it declares two arguments. The bound keys are `minimum` and `maximum`, and `max_chars` bounds a text. `uses` hands the run the credential of `scores-db`, as `PGHOST`, `PGPORT`, `PGDATABASE`, `PGUSER` and `PGPASSWORD`, so the agent needs no grant on the database for this service. The file must be yours alone, not a link, and not in Dockingbird's folder.

   ```toml
   # What dockingbird serve add-score runs when an agent asks.
   program = "/path/to/scores/bin/add-score"
   checkout = "/path/to/scores"
   commit = "0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef01234567"
   # The most seconds one run may take.
   timeout_s = 60
   # The database connection whose credential each run gets.
   uses = ["scores-db"]
   # Its words: {output} is the folder it writes its result to.
   argv = ["--score", "{score}", "--note", "{note}", "{output}"]

   # A whole number from 1 to 100.
   [arguments.score]
   type = "int"
   minimum = 1
   maximum = 100

   # Text of at most 200 characters, passed on as the agent typed it.
   [arguments.note]
   type = "text"
   max_chars = 200
   ```

   ```bash
   dockingbird connect add-score --service ./insert-score.toml
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints these lines. It runs nothing.

   ```text
   Connected add-score: agents of a config that names it run /path/to/scores/bin/add-score here, as you,
   with the arguments it declares, when you run dockingbird serve add-score.
   A config that names it: connections = ["add-score"]
   ```

5. Name the connections in a config you add. A repo's own config cannot name a connection.

   ```toml
   command = "grader"
   workspace = "scratch"
   connections = ["app-db", "scores-db", "add-score"]
   ```

   ```bash
   dockingbird config add grader.toml
   dockingbird grader "Score the three newest rows"
   ```

   The step is done when the first command prints a line that starts as follows and the second prints the start lines.

   ```text
   Registered grader: dockingbird grader "task"
   grader-1 started in a scratch folder.
   ```

6. Serve the program. The agent's request to `add-score` waits in `dockingbird status` until you run `serve` in a terminal. The run executes as you, one at a time, with five variables, and its output folder lands in the agent's log folder.

   ```bash
   dockingbird serve add-score
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints these lines.

   ```text
   Serving add-score: agents' requests to it run here, as you, one at a time.
   Ran add-score for grader-1: done in 3 s.
   ```

heading: Give agents a database without the password > Steps
text:
7. Take the database from the role. Every running agent of `grader` stops using `scores-db` at its next request, with no restart. A later start, replacement or added agent of the role is denied too. Add `--swarm KEY` to narrow it to one swarm.

   ```bash
   dockingbird connect scores-db --revoke --role grader
   dockingbird connections scores-db
   ```

   The step is done when the first command prints this line.

   ```text
   scores-db: denied to role grader
   ```

8. Give it back for a while. The command lifts the denial and grants the connection to the role's running agents until the time you give. The time is an ISO timestamp with a timezone, in the future.

   ```bash
   dockingbird connect scores-db --to-role grader --until 2026-12-01T00:00:00+00:00
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints one of these lines.

   ```text
   scores-db: granted to role grader until 2026-12-01T00:00:00+00:00, 2 running agents
   scores-db: no running agent of role grader
   ```

   With no running agent, nothing was granted, and an agent of the role that starts later gets the connection as its config names it. To remove a connection for everyone, and the password Dockingbird kept, run `dockingbird disconnect scores-db`.

heading: Give agents a database without the password > When it fails
summary: - [`CONNECT_DATABASE_REFUSED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#connect_database_refused) in step 2 means the check found a role that can write, or a server that allows prepared transactions, or a missing revoke.
text:
- [`CONNECT_DATABASE_REFUSED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#connect_database_refused) in step 2 means the check found a role that can write, or a server that allows prepared transactions, or a missing revoke. The connection was removed. Fix the role and run the step again.
- [`CONNECT_DATABASE_INVALID`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#connect_database_invalid) means the URL holds a password, a query or a fragment, or its parts do not match `postgres://ROLE@HOST:PORT/DATABASE`.
- [`CONNECT_SERVICE_INVALID`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#connect_service_invalid) names the key of `insert-score.toml` to fix, and never shows its value. A key Dockingbird does not know is one cause, so spell the bounds exactly as `minimum` and `maximum`. Paths start with `/` or `~`, and the checkout is the top folder of a git checkout that has a commit.
- [`CONNECT_SERVICE_CHECKOUT_MOVED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#connect_service_checkout_moved) means the checkout is not at the commit the file names. Check that commit out, or write the commit it is at.
- [`SERVE_CHECKOUT_MOVED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#serve_checkout_moved) means the checkout moved after step 4, and nothing ran. Connect the service again.
- [`CONNECTION_UNKNOWN_CONNECTION`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#connection_unknown_connection) stops the start in step 5 when a name in `connections` is not enabled. `dockingbird connections` lists them.
- [`CONNECTION_INVALID_UNTIL`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#connection_invalid_until) rejects the `--until` of step 8 when it is past or has no timezone.

heading: Your own review command
summary: Goal: add a `dockingbird review "task"` command that starts a Claude agent on the bus, hands it your review skill and role text, and returns a list of fixes.
text: Goal: add a `dockingbird review "task"` command that starts a Claude agent on the bus, hands it your review skill and role text, and returns a list of fixes. You write one config, run it in one repo, then register it for every repo. The guide behind it is [your-own-commands.md](../../docs/guides/your-own-commands.md), and every key is in [the app config reference](../../docs/reference/files/app-config.md). The file below grows from the template in [templates/.dockingbird/app.toml](../../templates/.dockingbird/app.toml), plus its `context` key.

heading: Your own review command > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird status` must not print "Dockingbird isn't set up yet."
- You stand in a git checkout of your repo, here called `myapp`. `git status` runs.
- No config of that name exists yet. `dockingbird config list` prints "No configs yet." or does not list `review`.

heading: Your own review command > Steps
text:
1. Write the config file `.dockingbird/review.toml`. Every key has a comment, and a key you drop takes its default. The skill and instructions paths are read from the folder that holds this file.

   ```toml

   # .dockingbird/review.toml: adds dockingbird review in this checkout. Every key is optional.

   # The command: dockingbird review "...", agents review-1, review-2. Default: the file's name.

   command = "review"

   # Its one line in dockingbird -h and config list, and for your own harness through dockingbird mcp. Default: none.

   summary = "Review this branch and list what to fix"

   # true: dockingbird start with no --command runs review in this checkout. Default: false.

   default = false

   # On the bus, this file's text, with $TASK replaced by the task, is the first turn. Default: none.

   skill = "skills/review.md"

   # Role text, given to the agent after Dockingbird's own rules. Default: none.

   instructions = "review-role.md"

   # claude or codex. Default: claude. Set here, it is fixed: a start's --harness can't change it.

   harness = "claude"

   # repo: a copy of this repo; scratch: an empty folder of its own, no git repo needed

   # (an added config's command then runs from any folder). Default: repo.

   workspace = "repo"

   # bus: in the background, through messages; terminal: at your terminal. Default: bus. Set, it is fixed.

   mode = "bus"

   # kept: one conversation for all its deliveries; fresh: every task delivery starts a new conversation,

   # under the same rules (bus only). Default: kept.

   context = "fresh"

   # true: load the repo's own Claude Code or Codex settings, hooks and MCP servers, once trusted. Default: false.

   repo_settings = false

   # Its tools: "bus" (messages and files), "default" (claims and commits) or "full" (both). Default: "bus".

   tools = "bus"

   # allowlist: through a proxy of its own, its tool's hosts and those of allow; models: its tool's hosts alone;

   # none: no network, not even its model's API; full: its own network, open to the internet.

   # Default: full, or what dockingbird egress set.

   egress = "allowlist"

   # With allowlist, what else it may reach: the presets registries (package registries) and github

   # (GitHub's content), or hosts such as "docs.python.org" and "*.corp.example".

   # Default: the list dockingbird egress set, else nothing beyond its tool's own hosts.

   allow = ["registries", "github"]

   # Fixed arguments for the tool, such as its model. Default: none.

   harness_args = ["--model", "claude-haiku-5-5"]

heading: Your own review command > Steps
summary: mise_env = "ci"
text:
# mise's environments for its agents, comma-separated: "ci" makes mise read mise.ci.toml over mise.toml

   # (MISE_ENV). Default: none.

   mise_env = "ci"

   # Variables the agent's tool sees: settings, never secrets. Default: none.

   [env]

   REVIEW_STYLE = "short"

   # Bounds on an agent that works on the bus.

   [limits]

   # A turn that runs longer is interrupted and reported; at least 1.

   # Default: no turn deadline (a stuck turn ends with the session).

   turn_minutes = 20

   # The agent stops itself after this many hours; at least 1, and at most

   # the installation's maximum (168 by default). Default: 12.

   session_hours = 4

   ```

   The bus tools mean the agent shares no commits, so it reports through messages and attached files. A fresh context means a new conversation for each review.

2. Write the skill file `.dockingbird/skills/review.md` as plain Markdown. On the bus the agent gets it as its first turn, with your task where `$TASK` stands.

   ```markdown
   Review the changes on this branch for this task:

   $TASK

   List what to fix, file by file, in a Markdown file you attach, then mark the task done.
   ```

3. Write the role file `.dockingbird/review-role.md`. Two or three lines are enough, and the agent reads them right after Dockingbird's own rules.

   ```markdown
   You review code; you never change it.
   ```

4. Ask Dockingbird to list its configs. This repo's come first, each with its summary beneath.

   ```bash
   dockingbird config list
   ```

   The step is done when a row shows review with the source "this repo" and the summary sits below it. The other cells hold the workspace, the mode, the connections and the start of the digest.

   ```text
     review  this repo  review  repo  bus  <connections>  <digest>
       Review this branch and list what to fix
   ```

5. Run the command. It accepts every option of `start` except `--command`, and your task lands in the skill.

   ```bash
   dockingbird review "Check the login flow"
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints these lines.

   ```text
   review-1 started on myapp (main).
   Thread <id>. Watch: dockingbird wait review-1
   ```

   Then `dockingbird wait review-1` returns the agent's messages, and `dockingbird results review-1` saves the Markdown file it attached.

heading: Your own review command > Steps
text:
6. Register the command for every repo. The copy of the config and the two files it names go into Dockingbird, and the command then works in any repo. Add it again after each change, because the copy is what runs. An added config's `harness_args` and `[env]` apply at once, since you chose to add it.

   ```bash
   dockingbird config add .dockingbird/review.toml
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints this line. It prints "Replaced review" with the old digest when you add it again.

   ```text
   Registered review: dockingbird review "task"
   ```

   In this checkout the repo's own command still wins over the added one, and `dockingbird -h` says so with a line that starts `configs/review/config.toml: commands.review is replaced here by this repo's own`. In every other repo the added command runs.

7. Remove the added copy when you no longer want it in every repo. The repo's own file is untouched.

   ```bash
   dockingbird config remove review
   ```

   The step is done when the command prints this line.

   ```text
   Removed review.
   ```

heading: Your own review command > When it fails
summary: - [`CONFIG_INVALID_FILE`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#config_invalid_file) refuses the file in step 4, 5 or 6.
text:
- [`CONFIG_INVALID_FILE`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#config_invalid_file) refuses the file in step 4, 5 or 6. The line names the key and the cause, such as "not an allowed value" or "a name Dockingbird keeps", and never shows the value.
- [`CONFIG_PROBLEM_ROW`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#config_problem_row) lists a key that does not apply yet. In a checkout you marked untrusted, it reads `harness_args applies after dockingbird trust`, and `[env]` and `repo_settings = true` are off the same way.
- [`START_COMMAND_UNKNOWN`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#start_command_unknown) in step 5 means no config here gives `review`. Run `dockingbird config list` from the checkout that holds the file.
- [`START_CONFIG_FIXED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#start_config_fixed) means a flag such as `--terminal` or `--harness codex` disagrees with the `mode` or `harness` the file fixes. Drop the flag, or edit the file.
- [`CONFIG_NOT_REGISTERED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#config_not_registered) in step 7 means no added config has that name. `dockingbird config list` shows the added ones.

heading: Two Macs, over ssh
summary: You work on one Mac, and another Mac, `lab`, runs agents of its own.
text: You work on one Mac, and another Mac, `lab`, runs agents of its own. Once this Mac knows how to reach `lab`, the fleet commands show `lab`'s homes and agents beside this Mac's own, `local`. The GUI that shows them in one window is not yet available. [Hosts](../../docs/guides/hosts.md) is the guide behind this example.

heading: Two Macs, over ssh > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is installed and set up on both Macs ([One Mac, day one](../one-mac/README.md)).
text:
- Dockingbird is installed and set up on both Macs ([One Mac, day one](../one-mac/README.md)).
- This Mac's ssh reaches `lab` with no question asked: `ssh lab.example true` returns at once. Dockingbird runs your own ssh, with your own configuration and keys, and never copies or forwards a key.
- `lab` has Remote Login on (System Settings, General, Sharing).

Try what Dockingbird will run first.

```bash
ssh lab.example docker version
```

Done: Docker's client and server versions.

heading: Two Macs, over ssh > Add `lab`
summary: `set` reaches `lab` and reads its Docker and its Dockingbird homes as `dockingbird fleet agents --host lab` does.
text:
```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts set lab --ssh lab.example
```

`set` reaches `lab` and reads its Docker and its Dockingbird homes as `dockingbird fleet agents --host lab` does. Once that read succeeded, it saves the host, then prints what it read and says so. The last line is the done line (`FLEET_HOSTS_SET`).

```text
lab: 2 agents running in 1 home
...
lab: ssh lab.example, saved in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml.
```

When it can't read `lab`, it saves nothing and says what to try. The usual cause on a Mac: a login over ssh has a shorter `PATH` than a terminal, without the folder of Docker Desktop's `docker`. Give the commands run there a `PATH` that holds it.

```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts set lab --ssh lab.example --path /Applications/Docker.app/Contents/Resources/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
```

Done: `lab: ssh lab.example, updated in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml.` when the first attempt had saved the host, else the `saved in` line. The command writes [this file's](hosts.toml) table.

```toml
[[host]]
name = "lab"
ssh = "lab.example"
path = "/Applications/Docker.app/Contents/Resources/bin:/usr/bin:/bin"
```

`path` names Docker Desktop's folder, then the system's. When `lab`'s Docker answers on a socket other than the default one, `--docker-host URL` sets the `docker_host` key: the `DOCKER_HOST` value the commands run with there, `unix://` followed by the socket's path. Docker Desktop keeps its socket inside the login's own home folder, under `.docker/run/`, unless its settings allow the default socket. `docker context inspect`, run on `lab`, prints the one it uses.

heading: Two Macs, over ssh > Every day
summary: The three commands print these first lines, in order, and the last two add a row for every home and every agent (`FLEET_HOSTS_ROW`, `FLEET_HOST_ROW`).
text:
```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts                # the hosts this Mac reaches
dockingbird fleet agents --host lab    # lab's homes and agents
dockingbird fleet agents               # this Mac's, local
```

The three commands print these first lines, in order, and the last two add a row for every home and every agent (`FLEET_HOSTS_ROW`, `FLEET_HOST_ROW`).

```text
lab: ssh lab.example
lab: 2 agents running in 1 home
local: 5 agents running in 3 homes
```

To open a terminal agent of `lab` on this Mac, take its full container id from the JSON listing and attach. The attach prints its done line, and Ctrl-] then Ctrl-\ leaves the agent running.

```bash
dockingbird --json fleet agents --host lab
dockingbird fleet attach --host lab --container ID
```

```text
Opening NAME on lab. Ctrl-] then Ctrl-\ leaves it running.
```

Rename the host, or remove it from the file, with the next two commands. The page on [the hosts file](../../docs/reference/files/hosts-file.md) lists every key and rule of the file.

```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts rename lab bench
dockingbird fleet hosts forget bench
```

heading: Two Macs, over ssh > When it fails
text:
| Message id | What happened |
|---|---|
| [`FLEET_HOSTS_NOT_REACHED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_not_reached) | `set` could not read `lab` and saved nothing; the message gives `ssh lab.example docker version` to try, and `--path` and `--docker-host` when Docker is there but the login does not find it |
| [`FLEET_HOST_NOT_READ`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_host_not_read) | `fleet agents --host lab` could not read `lab` |
| [`FLEET_HOST_UNKNOWN`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_host_unknown) | the `--host` name is not in the file; `fleet hosts` lists the names |
| [`FLEET_HOSTS_FILE_INVALID`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_file_invalid) | a value in `hosts.toml` breaks a rule |
| [`FLEET_HOSTS_IN_USE`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_in_use) | the host is in a fleet pool; drain and remove it there before `rename` or `forget` |
| [`FLEET_ATTACH_BAD_CONTAINER`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_attach_bad_container) | `--container` is not a full container id; exit 2 |
| [`FLEET_ATTACH_GONE`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_attach_gone) | the agent ended after the list was read |

heading: A Mac and a cloud VM, over gcloud
summary: Your Mac reaches a Compute Engine VM, `cloud-1` in the zone `europe-west1-b` of the project `example-project`, that runs Dockingbird on arm64 Linux with Docker Engine.
text: Your Mac reaches a Compute Engine VM, `cloud-1` in the zone `europe-west1-b` of the project `example-project`, that runs Dockingbird on arm64 Linux with Docker Engine. Under the name `cloud`, the fleet commands show its homes and agents beside your Mac's own, `local`. The GUI that shows them in one window is not yet available. [Cloud VMs](../../docs/guides/cloud-vms.md) is the guide behind this example.

heading: A Mac and a cloud VM, over gcloud > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is installed and set up on the VM, as on a Mac ([One Mac, day one](../one-mac/README.md)).
text:
- Dockingbird is installed and set up on the VM, as on a Mac ([One Mac, day one](../one-mac/README.md)).
- The Google Cloud SDK is on your Mac and signed in: `gcloud compute ssh` reaches the VM. Dockingbird runs your own `gcloud` (from your `PATH`, else the SDK's usual places), with your own configuration, and never copies a key.
- The VM is running. A stopped VM can't be read, so start it first.

```bash
gcloud compute instances start cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project
```

Try what Dockingbird will run first.

```bash
gcloud compute ssh cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project -- docker version
```

Done: Docker's client and server versions.

heading: A Mac and a cloud VM, over gcloud > Add `cloud`
summary: `set` reaches the VM and reads its Docker and its Dockingbird homes as `dockingbird fleet agents --host cloud` does.
text:
```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts set cloud --gcloud cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project
```

`set` reaches the VM and reads its Docker and its Dockingbird homes as `dockingbird fleet agents --host cloud` does. Once that read succeeded, it saves the host, then prints what it read and says so. The last line is the done line (`FLEET_HOSTS_SET`).

```text
cloud: 4 agents running in 2 homes
...
cloud: gcloud cloud-1, saved in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml.
```

The command writes [this file's](hosts.toml) table.

```toml
[[host]]
name = "cloud"
gcloud = "cloud-1"
zone = "europe-west1-b"
project = "example-project"
```

When it can't read the VM, it saves nothing and says what to try first. When your `gcloud` is neither on your `PATH` nor in the SDK's usual places, write its absolute path into the table by hand as `gcloud_program`. A later `set` of `cloud` over gcloud keeps it.

Any other cloud's VM, or a VM you reach by its address, is a host over ssh instead: `dockingbird fleet hosts set cloud --ssh cloud.example` ([Two Macs, over ssh](../two-macs-ssh/README.md)).

heading: A Mac and a cloud VM, over gcloud > Every day
summary: The command prints this first line, then a row for each home and each agent (`FLEET_HOST_ROW`).
text:
```bash
dockingbird fleet agents --host cloud    # the VM's homes and agents
```

The command prints this first line, then a row for each home and each agent (`FLEET_HOST_ROW`).

```text
cloud: 4 agents running in 2 homes
```

A VM that is stopped reads as `Couldn't read cloud: ...` until it runs again. If the VM also belongs to your team's fleet pool, it keeps the name `cloud` there too ([a team fleet](../team-fleet/README.md)). The pool's admitter starts a stopped VM when work waits for it, but only when the admitter's own hosts file names `cloud` with this gcloud route.

heading: A Mac and a cloud VM, over gcloud > When it fails
text:
| Message id | What happened |
|---|---|
| [`FLEET_HOSTS_NOT_REACHED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_not_reached) | `set` could not read the VM and saved nothing; the message gives `gcloud compute ssh cloud-1 -- docker version` to try, says a stopped VM must be started first, and says when this Mac has no `gcloud` |
| [`FLEET_HOST_NOT_READ`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_host_not_read) | `fleet agents --host cloud` could not read the VM; a stopped VM reads this way |
| [`FLEET_HOSTS_ROUTE_NEEDED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_route_needed) | `--gcloud VM` needs `--zone` and `--project`; exit 2 |
| [`FLEET_HOSTS_FILE_INVALID`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_file_invalid) | a value in `hosts.toml` breaks a rule |
| [`FLEET_HOSTS_IN_USE`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_in_use) | the VM is in a fleet pool; drain and remove it there before `rename` or `forget` |

heading: Lock the tools your agents run
summary: This cookbook pins Claude Code to version 2.1.285 so that every agent you start from now on runs it.
text: This cookbook pins Claude Code to version 2.1.285 so that every agent you start from now on runs it. It then moves a running agent onto the pin, shows that `update` leaves the pin alone, and lets Claude Code follow the latest release again. The same steps work for Codex. Each step ends with the line the product prints when the step worked.

heading: Lock the tools your agents run > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird --version` prints a version.
- You know the version you want. Claude Code versions look like `2.1.285` and Codex versions like `0.162.1`.
- You know which agents run now. `dockingbird status` lists them. A pin never changes an agent that already runs.

heading: Lock the tools your agents run > 1. Pin the version
summary: `pin` writes one line into `versions.toml` in the home.
text:
```bash
dockingbird pin claude 2.1.285
```

`pin` writes one line into `versions.toml` in the home. The step is done when the product prints this line.

```text
Claude Code will run 2.1.285 from its next start; agents already running keep theirs.
```

For Codex, use `dockingbird pin codex 0.162.1`.

heading: Lock the tools your agents run > 2. Check the pin
summary: The step is done when the line for the tool says it is pinned.
text:
```bash
dockingbird --version
```

The step is done when the line for the tool says it is pinned.

```text
Claude Code 2.1.285 (pinned)
```

The next start downloads the version if it is not there yet, and shows `Getting Claude Code 2.1.285 ...` while it does. If the vendor has no such version, the start says so (`TOOL_PIN_NOT_FOUND`).

heading: Lock the tools your agents run > 3. Move a running agent to the pin
summary: A running agent keeps the version it started with.
text:
A running agent keeps the version it started with. `dockingbird status claude-1` shows the version it runs. To move it, stop it and pick it up.

```bash
dockingbird stop claude-1
dockingbird claude --as claude-1
```

The pick-up resumes the agent's conversation. The step is done when `dockingbird status claude-1` shows the pinned version.

heading: Lock the tools your agents run > 4. Update without losing the pin
summary: `update` fetches the latest of each tool you used, except a tool you pinned.
text:
```bash
dockingbird update
```

`update` fetches the latest of each tool you used, except a tool you pinned. A start or an update never changes a pinned version. Check that the pin held.

```bash
dockingbird --version
```

The step is done when the line still reads `Claude Code 2.1.285 (pinned)`.

heading: Lock the tools your agents run > 5. Follow the latest again
summary: The step is done when the product prints this line.
text:
```bash
dockingbird pin --clear claude
```

The step is done when the product prints this line.

```text
Claude Code follows the latest release from its next start.
```

`dockingbird pin claude latest` does the same. `dockingbird pin claude stable` follows Claude Code's slower channel, and Codex has no stable channel. Then fetch the latest now.

```bash
dockingbird update
```

The step is done when `update` names the tool.

```text
Got Claude Code 2.1.296.
```

It says `Claude Code 2.1.296 is the latest.` when you already have it. You can also edit `versions.toml` by hand: a line is `claude = "2.1.285"`, `codex = "0.162.1"`, `"latest"` or `"stable"`, and removing the line follows the latest. See [updates](../../docs/guides/updates.md).

heading: Lock the tools your agents run > When it fails
summary: Four messages can stop the steps above.
text:
Four messages can stop the steps above. Each one changes nothing on disk, so you can correct the command and run it again.

- Typing `2.1` or `v2.1.285` gets you [`PIN_INVALID_VERSION`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#pin_invalid_version), because only a release number, `latest` or `stable` is accepted. `dockingbird pin codex stable` fails the same way, since Codex has no stable channel.
- Running `dockingbird pin` with a tool and no version prints [`PIN_ARGUMENTS_REQUIRED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#pin_arguments_required) and exits 2.
- A hand edit of `versions.toml` that leaves a line which is no version stops every command with [`TOOL_PIN_INVALID`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#tool_pin_invalid). Fix the line or delete it.
- A pin the vendor never published gives [`TOOL_PIN_NOT_FOUND`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#tool_pin_not_found). Correct the number, or delete the line to run the latest.

heading: Restrict what agents can reach
summary: By default an agent can reach any host on the internet.
text: By default an agent can reach any host on the internet. This cookbook sets the default for new agents to an allowlist: the tool's own hosts, the package registries and two hosts of your own, `docs.python.org` and `packages.lab.example`. It then shows what the agent sees when it asks for any other host. Each step ends with the line the product prints when the step worked.

heading: Restrict what agents can reach > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up. `dockingbird --version` prints a version.
- Docker Engine is version 28 or later. Docker Desktop updated to a current release has it. A proxy mode on an older Engine fails at the agent's start (`EGRESS_PROXY_FAILED`), or on Engine 26 and older leaves the agent's network with an address on the Docker host. `full` works on any.
- You know the hosts the agent needs. This cookbook uses `docs.python.org` and `packages.lab.example`.

heading: Restrict what agents can reach > 1. See what new agents get now
summary: The step is done when the product prints the mode.
text:
```bash
dockingbird egress
```

The step is done when the product prints the mode.

```text
Egress for new agents: full.
Nothing is set: this is Dockingbird's own default.
```

Message id `EGRESS_SHOWN`. `full` means no limit: a hijacked agent can send the repo it works on and its own sign-in to any host.

heading: Restrict what agents can reach > 2. Set the allowlist
summary: `registries` is a preset: the package registries of npm and Yarn, PyPI, crates.io, the Go module proxy, RubyGems, Maven Central, NuGet, Packagist, pub.dev and Hex.
text:
```bash
dockingbird egress allowlist --allow registries --allow docs.python.org --allow packages.lab.example
```

`registries` is a preset: the package registries of npm and Yarn, PyPI, crates.io, the Go module proxy, RubyGems, Maven Central, NuGet, Packagist, pub.dev and Hex. The other preset is `github`. The entries you name are the whole list, besides the tool's own hosts, so add `--allow github` if you want it too. A `*.lab.example` entry admits every name under that domain. The step is done when the product prints this line.

```text
Egress for new agents is now allowlist (registries, docs.python.org, packages.lab.example).
Agents already running keep theirs.
```

Message id `EGRESS_SET`. Agents already running keep what they started with.

heading: Restrict what agents can reach > 3. Start an agent
summary: The agent gets the default you set in step 2, through a proxy container of its own.
text:
```bash
dockingbird claude
```

The agent gets the default you set in step 2, through a proxy container of its own. To try one start with another mode, `dockingbird claude --egress models` reaches the tool's hosts alone, and `--egress none` has no network at all, the model API included. `dockingbird status` shows the mode when it differs from the default for new agents. The step is done when the agent starts as it usually does.

```text
To leave it working, close this window.
```

heading: Restrict what agents can reach > 4. See a blocked request
summary: Ask the agent to fetch `https://blocked.lab.example`, which is not on the list, with a tool of its choice.
text:
Ask the agent to fetch `https://blocked.lab.example`, which is not on the list, with a tool of its choice. The proxy answers 407 and a message that names Dockingbird. The tool then fails with its own proxy-refused error, quickly, and not with a timeout.

```text
Dockingbird's egress proxy refuses with 407 a host that is not in the allow list or whose address is not public, and a request that names an upstream proxy of its own: allow a public host with allow in the config, or start with --egress full.
```

The step is done when that message appears in the agent. Three details help when you read it. A listed host whose name does not resolve gets a 502, as the lookup would fail anywhere. A listed host is open on every port, and the agent can post to it, so list only hosts you would let it send the repo to. A name that resolves to a private address is refused even when listed, so `host.docker.internal`, your network and other agents stay out of reach. The proxy sees the host name and the port, never what is inside the TLS connection.

heading: Restrict what agents can reach > 5. Go back to the default
summary: The step is done when the product prints this line.
text:
```bash
dockingbird egress --reset
```

The step is done when the product prints this line.

```text
Egress for new agents is Dockingbird's own default: full.
Agents already running keep theirs.
```

Message id `EGRESS_RESET`. See [egress and network](../../docs/guides/egress-and-network.md) for a config's `egress` and `allow` keys and for a proxy.

heading: Restrict what agents can reach > When it fails
summary: - An `--allow` entry such as `https://docs.python.org` is a URL and no host name, so [`EGRESS_ENTRY_INVALID`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#egress_entry_invalid) names it by its position among your `--allow` options.
text:
