- An `--allow` entry such as `https://docs.python.org` is a URL and no host name, so [`EGRESS_ENTRY_INVALID`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#egress_entry_invalid) names it by its position among your `--allow` options. Write `docs.python.org`.
- A hand edit of `egress.toml` that breaks its grammar gives [`EGRESS_FILE_INVALID`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#egress_file_invalid), and no new agent starts. `dockingbird egress --reset` removes the file.
- A proxy that does not answer in time gives [`EGRESS_PROXY_FAILED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#egress_proxy_failed), with the proxy's last lines. Nothing was started, so run the command again.
- About 30 networks fit in Docker's default address pools. When they are used up, a start prints [`START_NETWORK_POOLS_FULL`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#start_network_pools_full) with `docker network ls` and `docker network prune`.

heading: Update with agents running
summary: This cookbook updates Dockingbird while `claude-1` and `codex-1` work on the bus and `claude-2` sits at a terminal.
text: This cookbook updates Dockingbird while `claude-1` and `codex-1` work on the bus and `claude-2` sits at a terminal. The agents on the bus switch in place at their next stopping point and keep their conversations. The agent at a terminal keeps its code until its terminal closes. Each step ends with the line it prints when it worked.

heading: Update with agents running > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird is set up and this computer is activated.
text:
- Dockingbird is set up and this computer is activated. `dockingbird license status` shows the license.
- Agents run. `dockingbird status` lists them, one row each.
- You know which agents are at a terminal. Those never switch by themselves, and `update` never asks them.
- Your running version is at least the first release that rolls in place. If it is older, step 5 applies.

heading: Update with agents running > 1. Check that a newer release is out
summary: The step is done when the product prints this line.
text:
```bash
dockingbird update --check
```

The step is done when the product prints this line.

```text
A newer Dockingbird is out. Get it: dockingbird update
```

heading: Update with agents running > 2. Update
summary: The new code goes into the home's code store and Dockingbird's coordinator is replaced in the background.
text:
```bash
dockingbird update
```

The new code goes into the home's code store and Dockingbird's coordinator is replaced in the background. Your agents keep working while it restarts. If the release changes Dockingbird's records, `update` first prints `This update changes Dockingbird's records.` and `Once it takes over, it can't go back to 0.15.2.` The step is done when the product names the agents that will take the release.

```text
Dockingbird 0.15.3 is installed and takes over now.
claude-1 and codex-1 take it at their next stopping point.
```

Message id `UPDATE_ROLLING`. A command you run meanwhile waits for the coordinator's switch with `Switching Dockingbird to 0.15.3 ...`, minutes at most, and never waits for the agents. On a Mac, `update` last tries to install the GUI, which is not yet available to customers. If that fails, Dockingbird is already updated, and `update` ends with the GUI message and exit 1.

heading: Update with agents running > 3. Watch the switch
summary: `status` says how far the roll got and what holds each agent back.
text:
```bash
dockingbird status
```

`status` says how far the roll got and what holds each agent back. The step is done when each agent is accounted for.

```text
Dockingbird 0.15.3 is taking over: claude-1 and codex-1 take it at their next stopping point.
claude-1 takes 0.15.3 at the end of its turn (asked 2 min ago).
codex-1 was asked to take 0.15.3 2 min ago and hasn't answered yet.
claude-2 on 0.15.2 keeps its own until its terminal closes.
```

Message ids `STATUS_UPDATE_ROLLING` and `STATUS_UPDATE_STRAGGLERS`. An agent switches only between two turns, never inside a turn or a tool call, and no turn is ended for it. A Claude agent whose background work still runs waits up to 30 minutes for it. An idle agent that has not answered its ask in 10 minutes is left on its old code. When an agent switches, its tool is told before its next prompt.

```text
Dockingbird updated from 0.15.2 to 0.15.3 and resumed your conversation. Continue where you were.
```

heading: Update with agents running > 4. Finish the agent at a terminal
summary: An agent at a terminal never switches.
text:
An agent at a terminal never switches. Close its terminal, or stop it, then pick it up.

```bash
dockingbird stop claude-2
dockingbird claude --as claude-2
```

The pick-up starts `claude-2` on the new code with its conversation resumed. The step is done when `dockingbird status` no longer lists `claude-2` on `0.15.2`.

heading: Update with agents running > 5. Confirm that nothing waits
summary: Run again for the same version, `update` changes nothing.
text:
```bash
dockingbird update
```

Run again for the same version, `update` changes nothing. The step is done when it prints this line.

```text
Dockingbird 0.15.3 is in place, and no agent is waiting to take it.
```

Message id `UPDATE_ROLLING`. The roll waits for its stragglers up to 24 hours, then ends, and `status` names the ones still running. A later `dockingbird update` asks the bus stragglers again.

heading: Update with agents running > If the running version is too old to roll
summary: A home whose Dockingbird predates rolling updates waits once, until its agents end.
text:
A home whose Dockingbird predates rolling updates waits once, until its agents end.

```text
Dockingbird here is too old to take 0.15.3 while agents run,
so claude-1 on 0.15.2 keeps its own until it ends.
```

Message id `UPDATE_NO_ROLL_FLOOR`. `status` says `Dockingbird 0.15.3 is installed and takes over when claude-1 on 0.15.2 ends` (`STATUS_UPDATE_STAGED`). Once the last agent ends, Dockingbird switches by itself and stays off after a `dockingbird stop` until you next use it. Later updates reach working agents at their stopping points. See [updates](../../docs/guides/updates.md).

heading: Update with agents running > When it fails
summary: - A second `dockingbird update` while the first installs gives [`UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#update_in_progress).
text:
- A second `dockingbird update` while the first installs gives [`UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#update_in_progress). Run it again when the first ends.
- A coordinator that does not come up gives [`UPDATE_SWITCH_FAILED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#update_switch_failed). The old version still runs, and `dockingbird update` shows why.
- A Dockingbird from before rolling updates prints [`UPDATE_NO_ROLL_FLOOR`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#update_no_roll_floor) and waits for the agents to end.
- A release that changes the records prints [`UPDATE_MIGRATES`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#update_migrates) first. After it takes over, the old version cannot run on them.
- Agents still on old code show in `status` as [`STATUS_UPDATE_STRAGGLERS`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#status_update_stragglers), each named with its version.

heading: Before you replace a computer
summary: This cookbook saves what you want from a computer you are about to replace, gives its seat back, and starts fresh on the new one.
text: This cookbook saves what you want from a computer you are about to replace, gives its seat back, and starts fresh on the new one. Agents' copies live in a Docker volume and do not move, so you take their work first. A restore of a copied home waits for a run that proves it, and this cookbook does not do one. Each step ends with the line it prints when it worked.

heading: Before you replace a computer > Before you start
summary: - The old computer still runs Dockingbird.
text:
- The old computer still runs Dockingbird. `dockingbird --version` prints a version.
- You have a folder outside the Dockingbird home to save into. This cookbook uses `../save`. `dockingbird results --to` refuses a folder inside the home.
- The new computer has Docker Desktop, uv and git, and you have the license key from your purchase email. See [install](../../docs/getting-started/install.md).

heading: Before you replace a computer > 1. Take the agents' work and stop them
summary: Run `sync` in each repo where an agent worked.
text:
```bash
dockingbird sync
dockingbird stop
```

Run `sync` in each repo where an agent worked. A repo is clear when `sync` prints `myapp (main): up to date.` or an `Updated your main` line. `stop` then turns Dockingbird off, and it prints this line when it is done.

```text
Stopped claude-1. Dockingbird is off until you next use it.
```

Agent copies live in a Docker volume, so work they did not share is lost with the volume. `dockingbird status` lists each kept copy under "Needs your attention" with its pick-up command. Run that command, let the agent finish, and sync again.

heading: Before you replace a computer > 2. Save the results
summary: Run it once per agent.
text:
```bash
dockingbird results claude-1 --to ../save/claude-1
```

Run it once per agent. The step is done when each file prints its type and path, then this line.

```text
The copy in {where} is yours, outside dockingbird clean.
```

Message id `RESULTS_COPY_OWN`. `{where}` is the folder you gave. An agent with no files prints `claude-1's task thread has no artifacts yet.`

heading: Before you replace a computer > 3. Save your configs
summary: The step is done when each config you added has a row.
text:
```bash
dockingbird config list
```

The step is done when each config you added has a row.

```text
  {name}  {scope}  {commands}  {workspace}  {mode}  {connections}  {digest}
```

Message id `CONFIG_LIST_ROW`. Keep the TOML files you added each config from, because `config add` copied them into the home. A repo's own `.dockingbird/` folder is in git.

heading: Before you replace a computer > 4. Save hosts.toml and your own files
summary: `homes` lists every Dockingbird home on this computer, so you know which folders to copy.
text:
```bash
dockingbird homes
```

`homes` lists every Dockingbird home on this computer, so you know which folders to copy.

```text
default (default): Dockingbird stopped, version 0.15.3, this home
```

Message id `HOMES_ROW`. Copy these from each home's folder into `../save`: `hosts.toml`, `fleet.toml`, `versions.toml`, `config.toml`, the `instructions/` folder and any `vaults/`. The step is done when the files are in the save folder. `hosts.toml` names the other computers you reach, so the new computer reads them the same way. Sign-ins live in Docker volumes and are not in these files: you sign in again.

heading: Before you replace a computer > 5. Give the seat back
summary: The step is done when the product prints this line.
text:
```bash
dockingbird license deactivate
```

The step is done when the product prints this line.

```text
This computer no longer uses a seat of the license.
```

Message id `LICENSE_RELEASED`. A seat is one person with up to three computers, so you can skip this step and have both computers linked for a while. `dockingbird clean --all` gives the seat back first too. If you wipe the old computer without doing either, free it from another computer: [move your seat to a new laptop](../move-your-seat/README.md).

heading: Before you replace a computer > 6. Start fresh on the new computer
summary: Install Dockingbird.
text:
Install Dockingbird. Then take a seat.

```bash
dockingbird license activate
```

The step is done when the product prints the activation line.

```text
This computer is activated: {plan}, {seats:seat|seats}, {term}.
```

Message id `LICENSE_ACTIVATED`. Create the home folder, copy the saved `hosts.toml`, `fleet.toml`, `versions.toml`, `config.toml` and `instructions/` into it before the first start, then add each saved config.

```bash
dockingbird config add ./agents/triage.toml
```

Then start in a repo as the first day does. The first start sets up the rest and signs in. See [one Mac, day one](../one-mac/README.md). Restoring a whole copied home, folder and volumes together, is not documented yet.

heading: Before you replace a computer > When it fails
summary: - A `--to` folder that is missing, or lies inside the Dockingbird home, gives [`RESULTS_TO_INVALID`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#results_to_invalid).
text:
- A `--to` folder that is missing, or lies inside the Dockingbird home, gives [`RESULTS_TO_INVALID`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#results_to_invalid).
- A file name in the save folder that holds something else gives [`RESULTS_TAKEN`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#results_taken). Save into a new folder.
- `license deactivate` or `clean --all` with no answer from the license server leaves the seat held: [`LICENSE_SEAT_STILL_HELD`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_seat_still_held). Free it from the new computer.
- A license whose seats are all linked refuses the new computer with [`LICENSE_SEATS_FULL`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_seats_full). `dockingbird license activations --release ID` frees one.
- A new home folder that holds files other than your own and no marker gives [`HOME_NOT_EMPTY`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#home_not_empty).

heading: A team fleet: a pool of two hosts
summary: A team shares a fleet pool: a PostgreSQL database that the fleet scheduler queues swarms in, and the hosts it places them on.
text: A team shares a fleet pool: a PostgreSQL database that the fleet scheduler queues swarms in, and the hosts it places them on. Here the pool holds two hosts, `lab`, a Mac, and `cloud`, a Compute Engine VM. Each member submits [a swarm definition](swarm.toml) that the scheduler admits where it fits. [The team fleet guide](../../docs/guides/team-fleet.md) installs the store and its roles, and [the fleet scheduler guide](../../docs/guides/fleet-scheduler.md) runs the pool. This cookbook walks one small pool from the first login to an update.

heading: A team fleet: a pool of two hosts > Before you start
summary: - The store exists on PostgreSQL 18, and its admin has run `dockingbird org create`.
text:
- The store exists on PostgreSQL 18, and its admin has run `dockingbird org create`. The team fleet guide does this in its steps 1 to 3.
- Your login role exists, with a password the admin gave you, and you are a member of the project `example`.
- Both hosts have Docker and Dockingbird set up. Check each with `dockingbird --version`.
- This computer reaches both hosts, as [Two Macs, over ssh](../two-macs-ssh/README.md) and [a cloud VM](../cloud-vm-gcloud/README.md) show.

heading: A team fleet: a pool of two hosts > 1. One name
summary: A host has one name: the `name` of its `[[host]]` table in a member's `hosts.toml`.
text:
A host has one name: the `name` of its `[[host]]` table in a member's `hosts.toml`. That is also its name in the pool, the name its worker runs under (`dockingbird fleet worker --host lab`) and the name a swarm definition places work on. Set each host in your `hosts.toml` under its pool name.

```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts set lab --ssh lab.example
dockingbird fleet hosts set cloud --gcloud cloud-1 --zone europe-west1-b --project example-project
```

Each command prints this line when the host answered and was saved.

```text
{host}: {route} {target}, saved in {path}.
```

`fleet hosts rename` and `fleet hosts forget` of a host the pool holds are refused while it is there. Drain and remove it from the pool first, then rename it in your file, then enrol it again under its new name. A rename never changes a swarm definition, which names pool hosts.

heading: A team fleet: a pool of two hosts > 2. Log in to the store
summary: Every fleet scheduler command reads this computer's org login first.
text:
Every fleet scheduler command reads this computer's org login first. The login names the store, and the role each kind of command connects as. It never holds a password. Each role's password is a line of `~/.pgpass`, the file PostgreSQL's own tools read, which must be yours alone (`chmod 600`).

```bash
dockingbird org login db.example.net:5433 --as user --role alice
dockingbird org status
```

The command asks for the password without echo, or reads it from standard input with `--password-stdin`. The step is done when you see these lines.

```text
Saved: user logs in to db.example.net:5433, database dockingbird_fleet, as alice.
Connected as alice.
```

The admin logs in as `fleet_admin`, and adds `--project example` where the admin's own leases run. A host's worker logs in with `--as worker --role fleet_worker_lab`, and the admitter's machine with `--as admitter --role fleet_admin`. A command whose kind has no login ends 78 and names the login to run. An older home may still hold a `fleet.toml` with a `password`. This release refuses it, so run `dockingbird org login --from-fleet-toml --as KIND` once to move the login to the org pointer and `~/.pgpass`.

heading: A team fleet: a pool of two hosts > 3. The pool
summary: The admin enrols each host once, with its reservable share and the gate lines its OS requires.
text:
The admin enrols each host once, with its reservable share and the gate lines its OS requires. The first step of the fleet scheduler guide names them and explains each line.

```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts add cloud --os linux --cores 60 --memory 230g --line idle_millicores=4000,8000 --line free_mib=16384,32768 --line psi_io_full=1500,1200 --power gcloud
```

`--power gcloud` lets the pool's admitter start the stopped VM when work waits on it. The step is done when `fleet queue` lists the host.

```text
cloud: {liveness}, {policy}, no sample yet
```

heading: A team fleet: a pool of two hosts > 4. Services
summary: Each host runs its worker, `dockingbird fleet worker --host cloud`.
text:
Each host runs its worker, `dockingbird fleet worker --host cloud`. One machine of the pool that stays awake runs the admitter, `dockingbird fleet admitter`. Each runs until stopped, under the machine's own service manager: a LaunchAgent on a Mac, or a systemd user unit on Linux with `loginctl enable-linger`. Dockingbird prints no unit for these two commands, so you write each one for your service manager. It starts `installs/current/bin/dockingbird` with the command's arguments.

The step is done when the host's line in `fleet queue` stops saying `no sample yet`, because a worker publishes a sample every 30 seconds. A worker or admitter started against a store that lacks a migration refuses with `FLEET_STORE_BEHIND`. Run `dockingbird org create` as the admin first, then start it again.

heading: A team fleet: a pool of two hosts > 5. A swarm
summary: [swarm.toml](swarm.toml) places a reviewer, a tester and two builders on `lab` first, else `cloud`, in each host's home `/opt/dockingbird/homes/team-1`, on the branch `feature/example` of `example-org/example-app`.
text:
[swarm.toml](swarm.toml) places a reviewer, a tester and two builders on `lab` first, else `cloud`, in each host's home `/opt/dockingbird/homes/team-1`, on the branch `feature/example` of `example-org/example-app`. A home of the placement must already link a checkout of that repository on that branch, in a folder named `example-app`. `fleet submit` refuses a definition whose source no home of its placement has checked out. Write a brief for each role beside it, as `briefs/reviewer.md`, `briefs/tester.md` and `briefs/builder.md`.

No role of the definition names a model or an effort. The reviewer looks them up as `reviewer`, the tester as `tester` and each builder as `implementer`: first in `[roles.NAME]` of the project's `.dockingbird/project.toml`, then in the store. The admin records each kind's row once, with the model and effort words of your choice in place of `MODEL` and `EFFORT`. [The swarms guide](../../docs/guides/swarms.md#choose-each-roles-model-and-effort) recommends a kind of model and an effort for each role.

```bash
dockingbird org roles set implementer --harness claude --model MODEL --effort EFFORT
dockingbird org roles set reviewer --harness claude --model MODEL --effort EFFORT
dockingbird org roles set tester --harness claude --model MODEL --effort EFFORT
```

Each prints its row.

```text
implementer with claude now runs MODEL at effort EFFORT.
```

Then submit the definition.

```bash
dockingbird fleet submit swarm.toml
dockingbird fleet queue
```

`fleet submit` checks the definition against the pool and queues it. `fleet queue` shows each host and each workload, and `dockingbird fleet why ID` shows what holds one that waits.

```text
{id} pending, position {position}
```

heading: A team fleet: a pool of two hosts > 6. Update the pool
summary: A new release reaches a host's engine in this order: install it, update each home the worker serves, move `installs/current` to the release, then restart the host's services.
text:
A new release reaches a host's engine in this order: install it, update each home the worker serves, move `installs/current` to the release, then restart the host's services. `fleet update` runs that order on every pool host in rank order, or on the one host `--host` names. It is the admin's alone, and any other login ends 77.

Each pool host needs a `repoint` line in its `[[host]]` table in the `hosts.toml` of the computer you run it on. The line restarts that host's services and must return without waiting for them to stop.

```text
repoint = "launchctl kickstart -k gui/$UID/<label>"
repoint = "systemctl --user restart --no-block <unit>"
```

The first line is for a Mac and the second for Linux, so each host's table holds one of them. Before a release changes the store, the admin runs `dockingbird org create` at the new build, then `fleet update` moves the pool.

```bash
dockingbird fleet update --release V
```

The step is done when the last line prints. A step that fails stops the command with exit 1 and leaves the hosts after it as they are, so fix the cause and run the same command again.

```text
Dockingbird {release} runs on {names:and}.
```

heading: A team fleet: a pool of two hosts > When it fails
summary: Eight ids cover this cookbook.
text:
Eight ids cover this cookbook. Read the one your command printed.

- [`ORG_ROLE_MISSING`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#org_role_missing) shows that this computer has no login for the kind the command needs. Run the `org login` the message names.
- [`FLEET_DB_UNREACHABLE`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_db_unreachable) appears when the store does not answer. The command ends 69, and a service restarts itself until the store returns.
- [`FLEET_DB_REFUSED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_db_refused) appears when the store turns the login down. The command ends 78, so check the role and its password.
- [`FLEET_CONFIG_PASSWORD_REFUSED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_config_password_refused) comes from an older `fleet.toml` that still holds a password. Run `org login --from-fleet-toml --as KIND`.
- [`FLEET_STORE_BEHIND`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_store_behind) stops a worker or admitter whose build needs a migration the store lacks. The admin runs `org create`.
- [`FLEET_NOT_A_MEMBER`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_not_a_member) answers a submit for a project you are not a member of. An admin runs `org members add`.
- [`FLEET_UPDATE_NO_REPOINT`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_update_no_repoint) shows that a host has no `repoint` line, so nothing was updated.
- [`FLEET_UPDATE_NO_WORKER`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_update_no_worker) shows that a host's worker has not reported in time. Start it, then run the update again.

heading: A swarm from a role library
summary: This cookbook queues a swarm that takes its roles from a library and its sizes, models and efforts from each submit.
text:
This cookbook queues a swarm that takes its roles from a library and its sizes, models and efforts from each submit. A coordinator comes from Dockingbird's shipped roles. Four graders come from the project's own `grader` role. Each grader takes ideas from a database, researches each one on the web with an MCP server and its own `helper` subagents, scores it, and writes the score back through the broker. The agents never hold the database password.

It shows five things.

- A role written once as a library file with its texts, `.dockingbird/roles/grader.toml`, and used by name with `use = "grader"`. The coordinator is the shipped library's, `use = "dockingbird/coordinator"`.
- Declared parameters, `[params]`: `N`, `x`, `y`, `batch`, `effort` and `model`. They bind to roles' fields and to the words of the grader's brief.
- Values per role and per subagent at submit, as `--set` lines or as a values document, [graders.json](graders.json).
- Who may message whom with `send_to`. A grader reaches the coordinator and its parent, never another grader.
- Connections a role names: an MCP server, a database the broker writes through, and two Python functions the broker runs with the database's credential in their environment.

heading: A swarm from a role library > Before you start
summary: - The pool and your org login work, as [the team fleet guide](../../docs/guides/team-fleet.md) sets up.
text:
- The pool and your org login work, as [the team fleet guide](../../docs/guides/team-fleet.md) sets up. `dockingbird org status` ends with `Connected as {role}.`
- A home of the pool links a checkout of your repository. [The swarms guide](../../docs/guides/swarms.md) lists this as a prerequisite.
- A PostgreSQL database named `ideas` with the tables the brief names, and a role `grader` for it.
- The two functions, `insert_score` and `next_ideas`, exist in a checkout at the commit the connection files name.

`project = "example"` and the source `example-org/example-app` in the definition are placeholders. Copy the `.dockingbird/` folder into your repository's own, and write your project and repository in their place.

heading: A swarm from a role library > The files
summary: [The role and connection reference](../../docs/reference/files/roles-and-connections.md) lists every key of the role and connection files.
text:
| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `.dockingbird/swarms/graders/swarm.toml` | the definition: the parameters, the `coord` role and the `grader` role |
| `.dockingbird/roles/grader.toml` | the grader role: harness, texts, tools, connections and the `helper` subagent |
| `.dockingbird/roles/grader/brief.md` | the grader's first task, the loop; `N`, `x`, `y` and `batch` expand in it |
| `.dockingbird/roles/grader/rules.md` | the grader's rules, added after Dockingbird's own and the project's |
| `.dockingbird/roles/grader/helper.md` | the helper's prompt; its first line is its description |
| `.dockingbird/connections/insert-score.toml` | the brokered write: the `insert_score` function and its arguments |
| `.dockingbird/connections/next-ideas.toml` | the brokered read: the `next_ideas` function and its argument |
| `graders.json` | a values document for `--values` |

[The role and connection reference](../../docs/reference/files/roles-and-connections.md) lists every key of the role and connection files. Both connection files give each argument its bounds with `minimum` and `maximum`.

heading: A swarm from a role library > 1. Register the connections
summary: Register the four connections once for each pool home.
text:
Register the four connections once for each pool home. No file holds a secret. The database's password is asked for without echo and kept by the broker.

```bash
dockingbird connect search --mcp https://search.example/mcp
dockingbird connect scores --database postgres://grader@db.example.net:5433/ideas --password --writes
dockingbird connect insert-score --service .dockingbird/connections/insert-score.toml
dockingbird connect next-ideas --service .dockingbird/connections/next-ideas.toml
```

`--writes` lets a grader write through the broker with `db.execute`, a statement the broker runs on its own connection. The two services are the same write and read as your own code. The two forms are alternatives granted together to show both. For least privilege, leave `scores` off the role and keep the two services. The step is done when each command prints its connected line. The database one reads as the first line below, and each service as the second.

```text
Connected scores: {target} as {value}, which may write, checked from Dockingbird.
Connected insert-score: agents of a config that names it run {path} here, as you,
with the arguments it declares, when you run dockingbird serve insert-score.
```

heading: A swarm from a role library > 2. Serve the two services
summary: A service runs only while `serve` runs.
text:
A service runs only while `serve` runs. `serve --all` serves every service and browser connection of the home in one process. `serve --unit` prints the unit that keeps it running under the machine's service manager, a launchd property list on a Mac and a systemd user unit on Linux. It installs nothing, so a swarm's brokered commands run with no terminal open once you install the unit.

```bash
dockingbird serve --all
dockingbird serve --unit
```

The step is done when `serve` for a service prints its ready line. `serve --all` with no service or browser connection ends 1 and says `Nothing to serve: this home has no service or browser connection.`

```text
Serving insert-score: agents' requests to it run here, as you, one at a time.
Ctrl-C stops it.
```

heading: A swarm from a role library > 3. Describe what a submit takes
summary: It prints, as JSON, every parameter and every role's settable field with its type, its bounds or words, its default and where the default comes from.
text:
```bash
dockingbird fleet describe graders
```

It prints, as JSON, every parameter and every role's settable field with its type, its bounds or words, its default and where the default comes from. It connects to nothing, and its defaults alone are a values document that `--values` takes. The step is done when the document prints.

heading: A swarm from a role library > 4. Submit the swarm
summary: The first submit gives values per role and per subagent as `--set` lines.
text:
The first submit gives values per role and per subagent as `--set` lines.

```bash
dockingbird fleet submit graders \
  --set coord.model=MODEL --set coord.effort=xhigh \
  --set grader.count=4 --set grader.model=MODEL --set grader.effort=xhigh \
  --set grader.helper.model=MODEL --set grader.helper.effort=xhigh --set grader.helper.max=4
```

Write a model word of the role's tool in place of each `MODEL`. [Claude Code and Codex](../../docs/concepts/claude-code-and-codex.md#model-and-effort-per-role) names a model for each kind of role, and `xhigh` is the coordinator's recommended effort.

The second reads the counts, the efforts and the helpers' cap from a file. It names no model, so each role takes its model from `[roles.NAME]` of the project file, else from your organisation's store: `coord` by its name, then `coordinator`, the shipped role it uses.

```bash
dockingbird fleet submit graders --values graders.json
```

The third takes the definition's defaults through its own parameters, `N` graders, `y` helpers each, `effort` and `model`.

```bash
dockingbird fleet submit graders
```

`--set N=4 --set y=4 --set effort=xhigh --set model=MODEL` sets the parameters in place of the roles' fields. A `--set` beats the file's value for the same key. The definition has no `key`, so each submit queues a new swarm named `graders-` and the UTC time. `--key K` names one, and a repeated `--key K` answers the swarm it queued first. Each submit is done when it prints this line.

```text
{id} pending, position {position}
```

heading: A swarm from a role library > 5. Scale it while it runs
summary: Add two graders, then retire one.
text:
Add two graders, then retire one. Each stays within the role's `min` and `max`, and a retire waits for the agent's running turn to end.

```bash
dockingbird fleet add ID grader --count 2
dockingbird fleet retire ID NAME
```

To start larger, set `--set grader.count=6 --set grader.max=12` at the submit. Both commands print their result line.

```text
{id} running: added {names}; each starts once its host has room
{id} running: {name} retires once its running turn ends
```

heading: A swarm from a role library > 6. Revoke and give back a connection
summary: This stops every grader's next call to `insert-score` at once, with no restart.
text:
This stops every grader's next call to `insert-score` at once, with no restart. It keeps the connection from graders that start later until you lift it.

```bash
dockingbird connect insert-score --revoke --role grader
dockingbird connect insert-score --to-role grader --until ISO
```

```text
insert-score: denied to role grader
insert-score: granted to role grader until {until}, {count} running agents
```

heading: A swarm from a role library > The note on x
summary: Dockingbird runs one harness session per container, so `x`, the main agents in one grader's container, can only be 1.
text: Dockingbird runs one harness session per container, so `x`, the main agents in one grader's container, can only be 1. The definition pins it with its own bounds. More graders is `N`.

heading: A swarm from a role library > When it fails
summary: These ids come from the submit, the connections and `serve`.
text:
These ids come from the submit, the connections and `serve`. Each line says what the id means and what to do.

- [`FLEET_REFUSED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_refused) names a field of the definition and the rule it breaks, one line for each rule. Fix them all, then submit again.
- [`FLEET_NO_CONNECTION`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_no_connection) holds the swarm because its home lacks a connection a role lists. Connect it there, then run `fleet release ID`.
- [`CONNECT_SERVICE_INVALID`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#connect_service_invalid) means a service file has a key or a value that Dockingbird refuses. Nothing was saved.
- [`CONNECT_SERVICE_CHECKOUT_MOVED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#connect_service_checkout_moved) means the checkout is not at the commit the file names. Check that commit out, or name the commit it is at.
- [`CONNECT_MCP_INVALID`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#connect_mcp_invalid) means the MCP address is not an `https` address of the allowed form. The command ends 2.
- [`SERVE_CHECKOUT_MOVED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#serve_checkout_moved) means the checkout moved after the connection was made, so nothing ran.
- [`FLEET_RETIRE_REFUSED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_retire_refused) means the swarm is not running, the agent is unknown, or the role is at its `min`.

heading: Join a second computer to a control plane
summary: This cookbook joins a computer named `lab` to a control plane, so agents started on `lab` get a fleet inbox beside their own.
text: This cookbook joins a computer named `lab` to a control plane, so agents started on `lab` get a fleet inbox beside their own. It then removes `lab` and joins it again with a new bundle, as you would after a lost home. [The control plane concept page](../../docs/concepts/control-plane.md) explains the parts, and [the team fleet guide](../../docs/guides/team-fleet.md) covers the whole install.

heading: Join a second computer to a control plane > Before you start
summary: - Two computers with the same Dockingbird release.
text:
- Two computers with the same Dockingbird release. Check each with `dockingbird --version`.
- A private network between them, and the control plane computer's IPv4 address on it. This cookbook uses the placeholder `100.64.0.1`.
- No agents running in the two homes. `cp init` and `node join` are refused while agents run (`MODE_CHANGE_AGENTS_RUNNING`). Stop them with `dockingbird stop`.
- A second computer you can open a terminal on. The commands below say which home runs each one.

heading: Join a second computer to a control plane > 1. Make the control plane
summary: On the control plane's home, run `cp init` with the address the other computers reach it at.
text:
On the control plane's home, run `cp init` with the address the other computers reach it at. Then serve the hub's port to your network. The hub listens on port 4222 of that computer, published on loopback only, until you serve it.

```bash
dockingbird cp init --hub-address 100.64.0.1
tailscale serve --bg --tcp 4222 tcp://127.0.0.1:4222
```

The second line is for a tailnet, the network the product is built against. [Other networks](../../docs/guides/other-networks.md) covers the rest. The step is done when `cp init` prints this.

```text
This home is now the fleet's control plane, at {host}:{port}.
Make a bundle for each computer that joins.
dockingbird cp token --host LABEL --platform PLATFORM
```

A home that already is the control plane prints `CP_ALREADY_INITIALIZED` and changes nothing.

heading: Join a second computer to a control plane > 2. Make a bundle for lab
summary: Each computer needs a bundle of its own, and you make it on the control plane's home.
text:
Each computer needs a bundle of its own, and you make it on the control plane's home. Give the computer a label of one to eight lowercase letters or digits, starting with a letter. Give its platform too, macos or linux. The control plane prints the bundle as one line and keeps no copy of it, so copy it before you clear the screen.

```bash
dockingbird cp token --host lab --platform macos
dockingbird cp status
```

The step is done when `cp token` prints the three lines below and the bundle follows. Until the computer joins, `cp status` lists it as waiting to join.

```text
lab is enrolled as node {node_id} (macos).
Its bundle is the next line, shown once and not kept here.
paste it into dockingbird node join on that computer.
```

heading: Join a second computer to a control plane > 3. Join
summary: Now go to the home of the computer you named lab.
text:
Now go to the home of the computer you named lab. Run `node join`, paste the bundle and press Control-D. The command reads the bundle from standard input, because a bundle never goes on a command line. A bundle joins one computer once.

```bash
dockingbird node join
```

The step is done when it prints this.

```text
This computer joined the fleet as lab (node {node_id}).
Each agent started here from now on gets a fleet inbox.
```

heading: Join a second computer to a control plane > 4. Read the status
summary: On the control plane's home, `cp status` lists each computer on one line: its label and node id, its platform, whether it joined, waits to join or was removed, its version, how many of its agents have a fleet inbox and how long ago the control plane last heard from one.
text:
On the control plane's home, `cp status` lists each computer on one line: its label and node id, its platform, whether it joined, waits to join or was removed, its version, how many of its agents have a fleet inbox and how long ago the control plane last heard from one. With `--json`, each line also carries when the computer joined and when it was removed.

```bash
dockingbird cp status
```

The step is done when `lab` shows as joined.

```text
  lab  {node_id}  macos  joined  {version}  0 fleet inboxes
```

Start an agent on `lab` and `dockingbird status` there shows its fleet session under it. The fleet name is the label, a dash and the agent's name.

```text
fleet: lab-notes-1, heartbeat {age}, asks {n}
```

heading: Join a second computer to a control plane > 5. Remove lab
summary: `cp remove` takes the computer out at once, with no precondition.
text:
`cp remove` takes the computer out at once, with no precondition. It revokes its token, closes its agents' fleet inboxes and drops the computer from the hub. The agents on `lab` keep running there without the fleet.

```bash
dockingbird cp remove lab
```

The step is done when it prints this.

```text
lab (node {node_id}) is out of the fleet;
{count} fleet inboxes of its agents closed.
Its own agents keep running there without the fleet.
```

heading: Join a second computer to a control plane > 6. Join again after a lost home
summary: A computer whose home was lost, or that was removed, joins again with a new bundle.
text:
A computer whose home was lost, or that was removed, joins again with a new bundle. Remove it, make a new bundle, leave on the computer and join with the new bundle. Run the first two commands on the control plane's home and the last two on `lab`'s home.

```bash
dockingbird cp remove lab
dockingbird cp token --host lab --platform macos
dockingbird node leave
dockingbird node join
```

On a fresh home that never joined, `node leave` prints the second line below and changes nothing. A home that is still in the fleet prints the first, and then it must have no agent that uses the fleet (`NODE_SESSIONS_LIVE`). The final `node join` prints its joined line again.

```text
This computer left the fleet.
This computer isn't a fleet member; nothing changed.
```

heading: Join a second computer to a control plane > 7. Turn the control plane off
summary: `cp off` turns the control plane back into a plain home once every computer is removed.
text:
`cp off` turns the control plane back into a plain home once every computer is removed. While one is in the fleet it is refused.

```bash
dockingbird cp remove lab
dockingbird cp off
```

```text
This home is a plain home again; the fleet's control plane is off.
```

After the control plane's computer restarts, the first `dockingbird cp status` on its home starts the control plane again. The members reconnect by themselves.

heading: Join a second computer to a control plane > When it fails
summary: Eight ids cover these steps.
text:
Eight ids cover these steps. Read the one your command printed.

- [`CP_ALREADY_INITIALIZED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#cp_already_initialized) comes from a second `cp init` on the same home. Nothing changed, and `cp status` lists the computers.
- [`MODE_CHANGE_AGENTS_RUNNING`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#mode_change_agents_running) appears when `cp init`, `cp off`, `node join` or `node leave` meets agents that still run in the home. Run `dockingbird stop` first.
- [`NODE_ALREADY_ENROLLED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#node_already_enrolled) appears when a bundle joined once already. Remove the label on the control plane's home and make a new bundle.
- [`NODE_ALREADY_JOINED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#node_already_joined) appears on a home that is in the fleet. Leave it, then join with the new bundle.
- [`NODE_SESSIONS_LIVE`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#node_sessions_live) blocks `node leave` while an agent on this computer still holds a fleet inbox. Stop that agent, then leave.
- [`RPC_PEER_HOST_MISMATCH`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#rpc_peer_host_mismatch) shows that a bundle made for one computer was used on another. Leave and join again with a bundle made for this computer.
- [`NODE_VERSION_MISMATCH`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#node_version_mismatch) shows that the computer and the control plane run different releases. Fleet messages wait until you update the one that is behind.
- [`CP_HOSTS_ENABLED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#cp_hosts_enabled) answers a `cp off` while a computer remains in the fleet. Run `cp remove` for each, then try again.

heading: Uninstall completely
summary: This cookbook removes Dockingbird from a computer: every agent, copy, volume and image it made, the license seat, the command itself and Docker's cached build layers.
text: This cookbook removes Dockingbird from a computer: every agent, copy, volume and image it made, the license seat, the command itself and Docker's cached build layers. Your code is never touched. The order matters: remove what Dockingbird made first, then the command. Each step ends with the line it prints when it worked.

heading: Uninstall completely > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird still runs.
text:
- Dockingbird still runs. `dockingbird --version` prints a version.
- Docker Desktop is running. `docker version` answers.
- Work you want is saved. Run `dockingbird sync` in each repo and `dockingbird results NAME --to DIR` for each agent. [Clean and uninstall](../../docs/guides/clean-and-uninstall.md) says what each removal takes with it.

heading: Uninstall completely > 1. Stop every agent
summary: `stop` asks before stopping working agents.
text:
```bash
dockingbird stop
```

`stop` asks before stopping working agents. `--yes` skips the question. The step is done when the product prints this line.

```text
Stopped claude-1. Dockingbird is off until you next use it.
```

Message id `STOPPED`. With nothing running, the line is `Nothing is running. Dockingbird is off.` (`NOTHING_RUNNING`).

heading: Uninstall completely > 2. Clean everything
summary: `clean --all` lists what is lost: each agent still working, each stopped agent with its copy kept, and commits the agents shared that you have not synced, each with the step that keeps them.
text:
```bash
dockingbird clean --all
```

`clean --all` lists what is lost: each agent still working, each stopped agent with its copy kept, and commits the agents shared that you have not synced, each with the step that keeps them. Take those commits before you go on. It then says `Your code is untouched.` and asks you to type `delete`.

```text
claude-1 is working now: it will be stopped and its copy removed.
myapp (main): 2 commits the agents shared that you haven't synced.
To keep them: git switch main, then dockingbird sync
Your code is untouched. Type delete to go on:
```

Type `delete`. Any other answer prints `Nothing removed.` and exits 1. `--yes` accepts the loss, and without a terminal it is required. The step is done when the product prints these lines.

```text
Removed everything Dockingbird made ({freed}). Your code is untouched.
To remove the command too: uv tool uninstall dockingbird
```

Message id `CLEAN_ALL_DONE`. `{freed}` is the size. `clean --all` removes this installation's containers, its five volumes, every agent's dependency cache, its images, the links in your checkouts' `.git/config` and its files in the home. It keeps your code, your `config.toml` when it holds anything of yours, your `vaults/` folder when anything is in it, and one empty `logs/` folder so a later start works while Docker Desktop still shares it.

heading: Uninstall completely > 3. Check that the seat is back
summary: `clean --all` gives this computer's seat back before it removes anything.
text:
`clean --all` gives this computer's seat back before it removes anything. When the license server does not answer, it says so.

```text
Dockingbird couldn't reach the license server, so this computer
still uses a seat.
Free it from another computer: dockingbird license activations
```

Message id `LICENSE_SEAT_STILL_HELD`. The step is done when `clean --all` did not print it. If you saw it, run `dockingbird license activations --release ID` from another computer, as [move your seat to a new laptop](../move-your-seat/README.md) shows.

heading: Uninstall completely > 4. Remove the command
summary: uv prints its own confirmation.
text:
```bash
uv tool uninstall dockingbird
```

uv prints its own confirmation. Check that the command is gone.

```bash
command -v dockingbird
```

The step is done when that command prints nothing. Uninstalling before step 2 would leave Dockingbird's containers, volumes and image behind.

heading: Uninstall completely > 5. Prune the build cache
summary: Docker keeps the build cache of Dockingbird's image.
text:
```bash
docker builder prune
```

Docker keeps the build cache of Dockingbird's image. Every project's builds share it, and it carries no labels, so `clean --all` leaves it alone and its freed figure does not count it. `docker builder prune` removes the unused build cache of every project on this Docker, not only Dockingbird's. Run it only if that is what you want. The step is done when Docker prints its own total reclaimed.

heading: Uninstall completely > 6. Leftovers you may remove by hand
summary: - The empty `logs/` folder in the home.
text:
- The empty `logs/` folder in the home. Delete it once Docker Desktop has restarted.
- Two lines in your shell's startup file that `dockingbird completion --install` added. `clean --all` removes the completion script but not those lines.
- Your `vaults/` folder, if it kept the stores of your vault connections (`CLEAN_ALL_VAULTS_KEPT`).

heading: Uninstall completely > When it fails
summary: - `dockingbird stop` with no terminal while agents work prints [`STOP_REFUSED_NO_TTY`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#stop_refused_no_tty).
text:
- `dockingbird stop` with no terminal while agents work prints [`STOP_REFUSED_NO_TTY`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#stop_refused_no_tty). Add `--yes`.
- `dockingbird clean --all` with no terminal prints [`CLEAN_ALL_NEEDS_TERMINAL`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#clean_all_needs_terminal). Add `--yes`.
- Any answer except `delete` ends with [`CLEAN_ALL_DECLINED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#clean_all_declined), and nothing is removed.
- A removal that could not finish prints [`CLEAN_ALL_INCOMPLETE`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#clean_all_incomplete). Run `dockingbird clean --all` again.
- An image that something else in Docker uses stays: [`CLEAN_ALL_IMAGE_LEFT`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#clean_all_image_left). Remove that first, then run the command again.
- A license server that does not answer leaves the seat held: [`LICENSE_SEAT_STILL_HELD`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#license_seat_still_held). Free it from another computer.

heading: A fleet on a tailnet
summary: You end with a control plane on one computer and a second computer joined to it over your tailnet, so that an agent on the second computer has a fleet inbox.
text: You end with a control plane on one computer and a second computer joined to it over your tailnet, so that an agent on the second computer has a fleet inbox. The example joins a Linux VM labelled `lab`, tagged `tag:lab`, to a control plane on the computer that your policy calls `control-plane.example`. The [Tailscale guide](../../docs/guides/tailscale.md) explains each step in more depth.

heading: A fleet on a tailnet > Before you start
text:
| You need | Check |
|---|---|
| Dockingbird on both computers | `dockingbird --version` prints a version on each |
| both computers on your tailnet | `tailscale ip -4` prints one IPv4 address on each |
| no agent running in the control plane's home or the joining home | `dockingbird stop` prints `Nothing is running. Dockingbird is off.` |
| edit rights on your tailnet's policy, with `tag:lab` in its `tagOwners` section | the policy file opens and saves |

heading: A fleet on a tailnet > Steps > 1. Read the control plane's tailnet address
summary: Run this on the control plane's computer.
text:
Run this on the control plane's computer. It prints one IPv4 address, which the steps below call `<ipv4>`.

```bash
tailscale ip -4
```

heading: A fleet on a tailnet > Steps > 2. Make the home the control plane
summary: On the control plane's home, run `cp init` with that address.
text:
On the control plane's home, run `cp init` with that address. It is done when it prints these lines.

```bash
dockingbird cp init --hub-address <ipv4>
```

```text
This home is now the fleet's control plane, at <ipv4>:4222.
Make a bundle for each computer that joins.
dockingbird cp token --host LABEL --platform PLATFORM
```

heading: A fleet on a tailnet > Steps > 3. Serve the hub's port to the tailnet
summary: Docker publishes the hub's port on the control plane's loopback only.
text:
Docker publishes the hub's port on the control plane's loopback only. On that computer, forward the tailnet's port 4222 to it. The command is done when it returns with no error. Tailscale's page quotes no output line for it, so the join in step 6 is the real proof.

```bash
tailscale serve --bg --tcp 4222 tcp://127.0.0.1:4222
```

heading: A fleet on a tailnet > Steps > 4. Grant the tag access
summary: Your own devices on the tailnet need no grant, but a VM under a tag does.
text:
Your own devices on the tailnet need no grant, but a VM under a tag does. Add this line to your tailnet's policy, and the step is done when the policy saves.

```json
{"src": ["tag:lab"], "dst": ["control-plane.example"], "ip": ["tcp:4222"]}
```

heading: A fleet on a tailnet > Steps > 5. Make a bundle for the VM
summary: On the control plane's home, pick a label for the VM: one to eight lowercase letters and digits, starting with a letter.
text:
On the control plane's home, pick a label for the VM: one to eight lowercase letters and digits, starting with a letter. The command prints three lines and then the bundle on a line of its own. Copy the bundle now, since it is shown once and kept nowhere on the control plane.

```bash
dockingbird cp token --host lab --platform linux
```

```text
lab is enrolled as node NODE_ID (linux).
Its bundle is the next line, shown once and not kept here.
paste it into dockingbird node join on that computer.
```

heading: A fleet on a tailnet > Steps > 6. Join from the VM
summary: On the VM's home, run node join and paste the bundle from step 5.
text:
On the VM's home, run node join and paste the bundle from step 5. Joining has worked when two lines come back. They name the label `lab` and the node id the control plane gave the VM. They also say that each agent started from now on gets a fleet inbox.

```bash
dockingbird node join
```

```text
This computer joined the fleet as lab (node NODE_ID).
Each agent started here from now on gets a fleet inbox.
```

heading: A fleet on a tailnet > Steps > 7. List the computers
summary: Back on the control plane's home, read the fleet.
text:
Back on the control plane's home, read the fleet. The step is done when the VM has a row with its node id, its platform, its state, its version and its fleet inboxes. If the output says that no computer has joined the fleet yet, no bundle was made or every computer was removed.

```bash
dockingbird cp status
```

heading: A fleet on a tailnet > Steps > 8. Start an agent on the VM
summary: Start an agent on the VM with claude inside any repository, then run status.
text:
Start an agent on the VM with claude inside any repository, then run status. The agent's entry gains a fleet line. It holds the label `lab`, a dash, the agent's name, a heartbeat age and a count of open questions. The words `fleet: not open` instead mean the control plane has not opened the session yet.

```bash
dockingbird status
```

```text
fleet: lab-NAME, heartbeat AGE, asks N
```

heading: A fleet on a tailnet > Take a computer out and bring it back
summary: On the control plane's home, `cp remove` disables the computer, revokes its token and ends its agents' fleet sessions.
text:
On the control plane's home, `cp remove` disables the computer, revokes its token and ends its agents' fleet sessions. On the computer, `node leave` removes its credential. To join again, make a new bundle and join with it.

```bash
dockingbird cp remove lab
dockingbird cp token --host lab --platform linux
dockingbird node leave
dockingbird node join
```

The removal prints these lines.

```text
lab (node NODE_ID) is out of the fleet;
N fleet inboxes of its agents closed.
Its own agents keep running there without the fleet.
```

Leaving prints `This computer left the fleet.` and then says the agents keep running, with their fleet inboxes gone. When every computer is removed, `dockingbird cp off` prints that this home is a plain home again.

heading: A fleet on a tailnet > When it fails
text:
| Message id | What happened |
|---|---|
| [`MODE_CHANGE_AGENTS_RUNNING`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#mode_change_agents_running) | agents run in the home; run `dockingbird stop`, then the command again |
| [`CP_ALREADY_INITIALIZED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#cp_already_initialized) | the home is already the control plane; nothing changed |
| [`NATS_SERVER_UNAVAILABLE`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#nats_server_unavailable) | the hub did not answer in time; run the command again |
| [`NODE_ALREADY_ENROLLED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#node_already_enrolled) | the control plane already used that bundle; run `cp remove`, then `cp token` |
| [`NODE_ALREADY_JOINED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#node_already_joined) | the home is in the fleet; run `node leave` first |
| [`RPC_PEER_HOST_MISMATCH`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#rpc_peer_host_mismatch) | the bundle was made for another computer |
| [`FLEET_SESSION_NOT_OPENED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_session_not_opened) | the agent has no fleet inbox yet; check the serve line and the grant |
| [`NODE_VERSION_MISMATCH`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#node_version_mismatch) | the versions differ; update the control plane's home first, then each member |
| [`NODE_SESSIONS_LIVE`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#node_sessions_live) | `node leave` found agents that still use the fleet; stop them first |
| [`CP_HOSTS_ENABLED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#cp_hosts_enabled) | `cp off` found computers still in the fleet; remove each one first |

heading: A host behind a bastion
summary: You end with a host that only a bastion can reach, listed by `dockingbird fleet hosts` and read by `dockingbird fleet agents --host lab`.
text: You end with a host that only a bastion can reach, listed by `dockingbird fleet hosts` and read by `dockingbird fleet agents --host lab`. The example uses the bastion `bastion.lab.example` and the host `lab-1.internal.example`. The guide on [other networks](../../docs/guides/other-networks.md) explains the pieces.

heading: A host behind a bastion > Before you start
text:
| You need | Check |
|---|---|
| Dockingbird set up on the host, with Docker running | `ssh lab-1.internal.example docker version` works from the bastion |
| your ssh reaching the bastion with no question, so the key sits in your ssh agent | `ssh ops@bastion.lab.example true` returns at once |
| the bastion reaching the host's ssh | the same check, run from the bastion |

heading: A host behind a bastion > Steps > 1. Write the ssh entries
summary: Add two entries to `~/.ssh/config`.
text:
Add two entries to `~/.ssh/config`. OpenSSH reads `ProxyJump` as one or more jump hosts in the form `[user@]host[:port]`, visited in order. The step is done when the file saves.

```text
Host bastion
  HostName bastion.lab.example
  User ops

Host lab
  HostName lab-1.internal.example
  ProxyJump bastion
```

heading: A host behind a bastion > Steps > 2. Reach the host through the bastion
summary: This command succeeds when it returns at once and prints nothing.
text:
This command succeeds when it returns at once and prints nothing.

```bash
ssh lab true
```

heading: A host behind a bastion > Steps > 3. Run the command Dockingbird runs
summary: Dockingbird reads a host with this exact kind of call.
text:
Dockingbird reads a host with this exact kind of call. It prints Docker's client and server versions when the route and the login's `PATH` are right. If it says `docker` is missing, do step 5 first.

```bash
ssh lab docker version
```

heading: A host behind a bastion > Steps > 4. Add the host
summary: Give Dockingbird the entry's name as the destination.
text:
Give Dockingbird the entry's name as the destination. It saves nothing until a read of the host has worked, then prints the rows it read and the last line below.

```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts set lab --ssh lab
```

```text
lab: 2 agents running in 1 home
...
lab: ssh lab, saved in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml.
```

The command writes this table.

```toml
[[host]]
name = "lab"
ssh = "lab"
```

heading: A host behind a bastion > Steps > 5. Fix the PATH if the read fails
summary: A login over ssh sometimes has a shorter search path than a terminal, and `docker` is not on it.
text:
A login over ssh sometimes has a shorter search path than a terminal, and `docker` is not on it. Ask the host where `docker` lives, then pass those folders to `set` as the `path` key. The second command prints a last line that ends `updated in` followed by the file's path. `--docker-host URL` sets `DOCKER_HOST` the same way, for a socket that is not the default one.

```bash
ssh lab 'command -v docker'
dockingbird fleet hosts set lab --ssh lab --path /usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
```

heading: A host behind a bastion > Steps > 6. Read the host's agents
summary: The first command prints `lab: ssh lab`.
text:
The first command prints `lab: ssh lab`. The second prints `lab: 2 agents running in 1 home`, then a row for each home and each agent.

```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts
dockingbird fleet agents --host lab
```

heading: A host behind a bastion > Steps > 7. Attach to one agent
summary: Take the agent's container id from the JSON listing, then attach.
text:
Take the agent's container id from the JSON listing, then attach. The attach prints `Opening NAME on lab.` and tells you that Ctrl-] then Ctrl-\ leaves the agent running.

```bash
dockingbird --json fleet agents --host lab
dockingbird fleet attach --host lab --container ID
```

heading: A host behind a bastion > When it fails
text:
| Message id | What happened |
|---|---|
| [`FLEET_HOSTS_NOT_REACHED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_not_reached) | the read through the bastion failed and nothing was saved; the message gives `ssh lab docker version` to try, and `--path` when the login's `PATH` lacks `docker` |
| [`FLEET_HOST_NOT_READ`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_host_not_read) | the agents listing could not read the host |
| [`FLEET_HOST_UNKNOWN`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_host_unknown) | the `--host` name is not in the file; `fleet hosts` lists the names |
| [`FLEET_HOSTS_FILE_INVALID`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_hosts_file_invalid) | a value in `hosts.toml` breaks a rule, such as a space in `ssh` |
| [`FLEET_ATTACH_BAD_CONTAINER`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_attach_bad_container) | the value is not a full container id; exit 2 |
| [`FLEET_ATTACH_GONE`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_attach_gone) | the agent ended after the list was read |

heading: Prometheus and Grafana for a fleet
summary: Say a team has one Mac, `lab.example`, running a home with agents, and an admitter at `control-plane.example`.
text: Say a team has one Mac, `lab.example`, running a home with agents, and an admitter at `control-plane.example`. By the end of this page a Grafana shows their queue, load, context fill and cost, and one rule warns someone before an agent compacts. Each step ends with the thing to look for. Prometheus and Grafana are not part of Dockingbird, so install them from their own pages: [Prometheus](https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/installation/) and [Grafana](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/setup-grafana/installation/).

heading: Prometheus and Grafana for a fleet > The files
text:
| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [exporter.py](exporter.py) | The exporter. It reads `fleet probe` and `fleet scrape` and serves one page. |
| [prometheus.yml](prometheus.yml) | Two scrape jobs with placeholder targets. |
| [dashboard.json](dashboard.json) | The default Grafana dashboard. |
| [queries.md](queries.md) | Fourteen queries, each with one line on what it answers. |

heading: Prometheus and Grafana for a fleet > Before you start
summary: - Dockingbird on the host, with a home that has agents.
text:
- Dockingbird on the host, with a home that has agents. Check with `dockingbird status`.
- Python 3.12 on the host. Check with `python3 --version`.
- Prometheus and Grafana running somewhere that reaches the host. Check by opening each in a browser.
- For the fleet job, an admitter on a machine of your pool. [The fleet scheduler guide](../../docs/guides/fleet-scheduler.md) starts it.

heading: Prometheus and Grafana for a fleet > 1. Read the figures once by hand
summary: Run each one on its own.
text:
```bash
dockingbird fleet scrape
dockingbird --json fleet probe
dockingbird fleet queue --metrics
```

Run each one on its own. `fleet scrape` prints the agents' text and ends with a line reading `# EOF`. `fleet probe` prints one envelope with `id` `FLEET_PROBE`, and only on a Mac. `fleet queue --metrics` prints the scheduler's text, and only with an org login. None of them starts or changes anything. When one fails, its message id says what to fix: [`FLEET_SCRAPE_NO_STATUS`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_scrape_no_status), [`FLEET_PROBE_NOT_MACOS`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_probe_not_macos) or [`ORG_NOT_CONFIGURED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#org_not_configured).

heading: Prometheus and Grafana for a fleet > 2. Run the exporter on the host
summary: `PRIVATE_ADDRESS` is the host's address on your private network, and `NAME` is a home from `dockingbird homes`.
text:
```bash
python3 exporter.py 9105 --bind PRIVATE_ADDRESS --home NAME
```

`PRIVATE_ADDRESS` is the host's address on your private network, and `NAME` is a home from `dockingbird homes`. Wait up to a minute for the first reading, then fetch the page.

```bash
curl http://PRIVATE_ADDRESS:9105/metrics
```

The step worked when the page holds `dockingbird_scrape_up{home="NAME"} 1`. A 0 means the home could not be read, so run `dockingbird --home NAME fleet scrape` and read its message id. Start the exporter from a LaunchAgent on a Mac or a systemd user unit on Linux so it survives a restart.

heading: Prometheus and Grafana for a fleet > 3. Point Prometheus at it
summary: Copy the two jobs of [prometheus.yml](prometheus.yml) into your Prometheus configuration.
text:
Copy the two jobs of [prometheus.yml](prometheus.yml) into your Prometheus configuration. Replace `lab.example:9105` with the exporter's address, and `control-plane.example:9107` with the admitter's address and the port that `FLEET_SCHED_METRICS_PORT` names. Restart Prometheus. Open `/targets` on its port. The step worked when both jobs show `UP`.

The host job runs every 30 seconds, as the probe refreshes. The fleet job runs every 60 seconds, as the admitter updates at least every 30. [The Prometheus guide](../../docs/guides/prometheus.md) explains each choice.

heading: Prometheus and Grafana for a fleet > 4. Import the dashboard
summary: In Grafana, add your Prometheus as a data source.
text: In Grafana, add your Prometheus as a data source. Then open Dashboards, New, Import, and upload [dashboard.json](dashboard.json). The step worked when `Dockingbird fleet` opens with five rows: Fleet, Hosts, Agents, Cost and Health. Pick your Prometheus in the `Datasource` variable at the top. [The Grafana guide](../../docs/guides/grafana.md) describes each row.

heading: Prometheus and Grafana for a fleet > 5. Set one alert
summary: Open Alerting, Alert rules, New alert rule.
text:
Open Alerting, Alert rules, New alert rule. Choose your Prometheus data source and paste this query.

```text
max by (home, agent) (dockingbird_agent_context_used_tokens / dockingbird_agent_compact_at_tokens)
```

Set the condition to above 0.9 for 5 minutes and pick your own contact point. The rule reads Normal while every agent is under 90% of its compact point, and Firing when one passes it. The [alert rule page](https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/alerting/alerting-rules/create-grafana-managed-rule/) describes each field.

heading: Prometheus and Grafana for a fleet > When it fails
summary: - [`FLEET_PROBE_NOT_MACOS`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_probe_not_macos): the host is not a Mac.
text:
- [`FLEET_PROBE_NOT_MACOS`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_probe_not_macos): the host is not a Mac. `dockingbird_probe_up` is 0 and the Hosts row is empty.
- [`FLEET_SCRAPE_NO_STATUS`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_scrape_no_status): the home's status failed or the home is off. Its `dockingbird_scrape_up` is 0.
- [`ORG_NOT_CONFIGURED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#org_not_configured): no org login on this computer, so `fleet queue --metrics` has nothing to read.
- [`FLEET_DB_UNREACHABLE`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_db_unreachable): the fleet database did not answer. Ends 69.
- [`FLEET_DB_REFUSED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_db_refused): the database turned a login down. Ends 78.

heading: Run a test suite under a lease
summary: This cookbook runs `make test` under a lease, so several people's test runs share a host without starving each other.
text: This cookbook runs `make test` under a lease, so several people's test runs share a host without starving each other. A lease reserves cores and memory on a pool host for one command and ends with it. [The fleet scheduler guide](../../docs/guides/fleet-scheduler.md) runs the pool, and [the scheduler concept page](../../docs/concepts/fleet-scheduler.md) explains how a lease is admitted.

heading: Run a test suite under a lease > Before you start
summary: - The pool works and this computer is one of its hosts.
text:
- The pool works and this computer is one of its hosts. `dockingbird fleet queue` lists it. [The team fleet guide](../../docs/guides/team-fleet.md) sets the pool up.
- Your org login names a project for leases. The owner's login needs `--project` on `dockingbird org login`, or the command ends with `FLEET_LEASE_NO_PROJECT`.
- Your role is a member of that project, or the admin. A project's role runs and controls its own workloads only.
- A command that uses what the lease gives it. Here that is `make test`, with its parallelism read from the environment.

heading: Run a test suite under a lease > 1. Run the suite under a lease
summary: Give the lease its cores, its memory and a bound, then the command after `--`.
text:
Give the lease its cores, its memory and a bound, then the command after `--`. The command runs on the computer where you typed `fleet run`, so name this computer's pool host with `--hosts` if the pool has several. `fleet run` records the lease, waits for a host to take it, reads the host's row every 30 seconds, and runs the command in a process group of its own.

```bash
dockingbird fleet run --cores 4 --memory 8g --bound 30m --hosts lab -- make test
```

The command finds its lease in two environment variables, `FLEET_LEASE_CORES` and `FLEET_LEASE_HOST`. Use them to size the test runner.

```bash
dockingbird fleet run --cores 4 --memory 8g --bound 30m --hosts lab -- sh -c 'pytest -n "$FLEET_LEASE_CORES"'
```

The step is done when the command ends. `fleet run` then ends with the command's own exit status, and the lease ends with it. A suite that passed ends 0, and a failing suite ends with its own non-zero status.

heading: Run a test suite under a lease > 2. Watch the lease wait
summary: Until a host takes the lease, your command has not started, and the terminal shows nothing.
text:
Until a host takes the lease, your command has not started, and the terminal shows nothing. Open a second terminal. There, `fleet queue` lists the lease among the workloads with its kind, its state and the command it will run, and `fleet why ID` names the first thing that keeps the lease off each host.

```bash
dockingbird fleet queue
dockingbird fleet why ID
```

```text
{id} {project} {kind} {priority} {state}, {age} old, needs {need_millicores} millicores, {need_mib} MiB, {agents} agents
{host}: {hold}, has {have} millicores, needs {need}
```

heading: Run a test suite under a lease > 3. Bound the run
summary: At its `--bound` the command is interrupted, then stopped 15 seconds later if it has not ended, and `fleet run` ends 124.
text:
At its `--bound` the command is interrupted, then stopped 15 seconds later if it has not ended, and `fleet run` ends 124. The step is done when you see this line and the exit status.

```text
lease bound reached; CMD interrupted
```

Durations name their unit, such as `90s`, `20m` or `2h`, and are at most a day.

heading: Run a test suite under a lease > 4. Limit the wait
summary: A lease that no host takes within `--wait` is given up, the command never runs and `fleet run` ends 1.
text:
A lease that no host takes within `--wait` is given up, the command never runs and `fleet run` ends 1. The wait is 30 minutes unless you set it.

```bash
dockingbird fleet run --cores 4 --memory 8g --bound 30m --hosts lab --wait 10m -- make test
```

```text
lease not admitted within {wait}: {blocked_by}
```

`--kind picker --exclusive` also keeps a second lease of that kind off the host, so two runs of the same suite never share it.

heading: Run a test suite under a lease > 5. Cancel a lease
summary: A lease takes `cancel` and no other control.
text:
A lease takes `cancel` and no other control. Cancelling a running lease interrupts its command the same way a bound does. Stopping `fleet run` with Control-C, or a SIGTERM from a service manager, interrupts the command's process group too, and the lease ends with it.

```bash
dockingbird fleet cancel ID
```

```text
{id} {state}
```

heading: Run a test suite under a lease > What the lease bounds
summary: When the store does not answer, `fleet run` says so on one line and runs the command without a lease, as checks ran before the scheduler existed.
text:
| Computer | What the lease limits |
|---|---|
| Linux | the command runs inside a transient scope of your own systemd user manager whose `CPUQuota` and `MemoryMax` are the lease's; a kill at `MemoryMax` is the command's own status, 137 |
| Mac | nothing bounds the command, and a lease counts cores only |

When the store does not answer, `fleet run` says so on one line and runs the command without a lease, as checks ran before the scheduler existed. When the store turns the login down, `fleet run` ends 78 with `FLEET_DB_REFUSED` and never runs the command. A store that is down prints this line first.

```text
fleet: no answer from the database at {host} for {role} within {seconds} s: {error}; running without a lease
```

heading: Run a test suite under a lease > When it fails
summary: Seven ids belong to this page.
text:
Seven ids belong to this page. Read the one your command printed.

- [`FLEET_RUN_NOT_ADMITTED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_run_not_admitted) appears when no host took the lease within `--wait`. The line names what held each host off, and the command never ran.
- [`FLEET_RUN_ENDED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_run_ended) appears when the lease ended before a host took it, cancelled or past its wait.
- [`FLEET_RUN_BOUND`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_run_bound) shows that the command was still running at `--bound`, so `fleet run` ended 124.
- [`FLEET_RUN_CANCELLED`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_run_cancelled) shows a cancel during the run. `fleet run` ends with the command's own exit status.
- [`FLEET_RUN_NO_LEASE`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_run_no_lease) shows that the store did not answer, so the command ran with no reservation.
- [`FLEET_RUN_NO_SCOPE`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_run_no_scope) comes up on Linux when `systemd-run` is missing. The command runs under its lease with no ceiling.
- [`FLEET_LEASE_NO_PROJECT`](../../docs/troubleshooting.md#fleet_lease_no_project) comes from the owner's login when it names no project. Log in again with `--project`.

heading: Change a running swarm
summary: This cookbook resizes a swarm that is already running.
text: This cookbook resizes a swarm that is already running. You add two builders, retire one, and delete the agents' kept copies once the work is merged. Each change waits for an agent's running turn to end and never interrupts it. [The swarms guide](../../docs/guides/swarms.md) explains each command, and [the swarm definition reference](../../docs/reference/files/swarm-definition.md) names the `min` and `max` that bound them.

heading: Change a running swarm > Before you start
summary: - A swarm is running.
text:
- A swarm is running. `dockingbird fleet queue` lists it as `running`, with its id, which the steps below call `ID`.
- Your role queues and controls the swarm's project, or you are the admin.
- The role you add to has room under its `max`, and the role you retire from stays at or above its `min`. A role that names neither keeps its `count` for both.

heading: Change a running swarm > 1. Find the swarm and its agents
summary: `fleet queue` lists each workload not yet ended.
text:
`fleet queue` lists each workload not yet ended. Under a swarm it names the agents still working and the agents waiting to start. Note the id of the swarm and the name of the agent you will retire.

```bash
dockingbird fleet queue
```

The step is done when you can read the swarm's line and its agents. The first line below is the swarm's.

```text
{id} {project} {kind} {priority} running on {host}, {age} old, needs {need_millicores} millicores, {need_mib} MiB, {agents} agents
```

heading: Change a running swarm > 2. Add two agents of a role
summary: `fleet add` starts more agents of a role, up to its `max`, under the role's next names.
text:
`fleet add` starts more agents of a role, up to its `max`, under the role's next names. The reason stays with the change. Each new agent starts once its host has room for it, is briefed with the roster, and every other agent is told the new roster.

```bash
dockingbird fleet add ID builder --count 2 --reason "two more tasks arrived"
```

The step is done when this line prints. The new agents appear in `fleet queue` as waiting to start, then as working.

```text
{id} running: added {names}; each starts once its host has room
```

An agent that waits shows what holds it, and `fleet why ID` names it host by host.

heading: Change a running swarm > 3. Retire one agent
summary: `fleet retire` takes one agent out once its running turn ends and gives its share back to the pool.
text:
`fleet retire` takes one agent out once its running turn ends and gives its share back to the pool. An agent that never started retires at once. The host's worker refuses while the agent is working, asking or waiting, or has a question or a request open. It records the refusal and sends the agent nothing.

```bash
dockingbird fleet retire ID build-3 --reason "its task is merged"
```

The step is done when this line prints. A `still working` form names the agents that have not stopped.

```text
{id} running: {name} retires once its running turn ends
```

Retire is refused before anything changes when the swarm is not running, has no such agent, or the role is at its `min`. A role with `min = 0` can be emptied if it neither reviews nor tests.

heading: Change a running swarm > 4. Finish and find the tested head
summary: When the work is merged, end the swarm.
text:
When the work is merged, end the swarm. `fleet done` stops each agent after its running turn. `fleet ledger` lists the commits, newest first, with who approved each and its test result. Take the sha of the head that was tested.

```bash
dockingbird fleet done ID
dockingbird fleet ledger ID
```

```text
{id} {state}
{sha} by {author}: approved by {reviewer} at {approved_at}; tested {result} by {tester} at {tested_at}
```

heading: Change a running swarm > 5. Prune after the merge
summary: Prune deletes the agents' kept copies.
text:
Prune deletes the agents' kept copies. It applies to a swarm that is done or cancelled. Prove the head is merged in your own checkout first, because the scheduler never checks it.

```bash
git merge-base --is-ancestor SHA origin/main
dockingbird fleet prune ID --merged SHA
```

The first command ends 0 when the sha is in `origin/main`. The step is done when the prune is queued.

```text
Queued the prune of {id} as job {job_id}.
Its host's worker deletes each of its agents whose container has stopped.
```

The host's worker deletes only agents whose container has stopped, never a running one. A commit an agent made and never published goes with its copy.
