heading: The `--json` envelope
summary: Give `--json` before any command and Dockingbird prints each message as a single line of JSON, which this page calls an envelope.
text:
Give `--json` before any command and Dockingbird prints each message as a single line of JSON, which this page calls an envelope.
Six keys make up an envelope.
A script that reads three of them, the id, the fields and the exit code, keeps working when a release rewords a message.

heading: The `--json` envelope > The keys
text:
| Key | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `ok` | `true` when `exit_code` is 0, else `false` |
| `exit_code` | the status the message ends the command with ([exit codes](exit-codes.md)) |
| `id` | the message's id, such as `FLEET_HOSTS_SET`; [the catalogue](../../troubleshooting.md) lists every id under a heading of its own, with when it comes and its next step |
| `lines` | the words a person sees, one string per line, never wrapped |
| `next_step` | the command the message suggests, when it suggests one; absent otherwise |
| `fields` | the values the lines were filled with, by name: counts are numbers, sizes are bytes, durations are seconds and lists are arrays |

heading: The `--json` envelope > Other envelopes
text:
| Envelope | What it holds |
|---|---|
| a help screen (`dockingbird --json -h`, `dockingbird --json help status`) | `id` is `HELP`, `lines` holds the screen, and `fields.command` names the command it explains, null for the top screen |
| an extra key | some envelopes carry a key of Dockingbird's own beyond these, such as `detail`; a script leaves a key it does not know alone |
| a row of `dockingbird --json status` | an envelope of its own, with the keys in the next table |

heading: The `--json` envelope > Keys a status row adds
text:
| Row | Keys it adds |
|---|---|
| an agent | `name`, `tool`, `repo`, `branch`, `state` (`working`, `idle`, `waiting`, `preparing`, `stopped` or `crashed`), `terminal`, `next_step`, `next_argv`, `screen`, `container`, `attach_argv` |
| a `preparing` agent | `step` (`environment` or `dependencies`), `since`, `last_output_at` |
| a repo heading | `behind`, `both_moved`, `head` |
| `today` | `count`, `names` |
| a kept copy under "Needs your attention" | `state` (`stopped` or `crashed`), `terminal`, `next_step`, `next_argv`, `mode`, `command` |
| the first line | `claude` and `codex`, each `api-key`, `signed-in` or `none` |

heading: The `--json` envelope > What a script reads
text:
| Read | Why |
|---|---|
| `id`, `fields` and `exit_code` | the compatibility promise covers them; see [compatibility.md](compatibility.md) |
| `lines` | never; its words change from one release to the next so that they read better |

heading: The `--json` envelope > Example, the last line of `dockingbird --json fleet hosts set lab --ssh lab.example`
summary: A script that wants the host it added reads `fields.host` of the envelope whose `id` is `FLEET_HOSTS_SET`.
text:
A script that wants the host it added reads `fields.host` of the envelope whose `id` is `FLEET_HOSTS_SET`.

```json
{"ok": true, "exit_code": 0, "id": "FLEET_HOSTS_SET", "lines": ["lab: ssh lab.example, saved in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml."], "fields": {"host": "lab", "route": "ssh", "target": "lab.example", "path": "~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml"}}
```

heading: The `--json` envelope > Streams
summary: Results come on stdout and problems on stderr, each as its envelope, with one exception.
text:
Results come on stdout and problems on stderr, each as its envelope, with one exception.
The fleet's reads print their exit-1 refusals on stdout, beside the rows they read.
Those reads are `fleet agents`, `fleet hosts`, and `fleet hosts set`, `rename` and `forget`.
A script reads both streams and tells the messages apart by `id`.

heading: The `--json` envelope > Exit statuses
summary: Each message has one exit status, and the envelope's `exit_code` is that status.
text:
Each message has one exit status, and the envelope's `exit_code` is that status.
[Exit codes](exit-codes.md) holds the one table of statuses, with what a script does on each, and the catalogue gives each id's status under its heading.

heading: `dockingbird mcp`: the host tools
summary: `dockingbird mcp` is an MCP server, over stdio, for the harness you work in on this computer (Claude Code or Codex).
text:
`dockingbird mcp` is an MCP server, over stdio, for the harness you work in on this computer (Claude Code or Codex).
Through its eleven tools that harness starts agents in Dockingbird, sends them messages, reads what they send back,
saves their results and stops them. Your harness starts the server; you never run it yourself:
`dockingbird mcp install` connects each harness it finds with that harness's own `mcp add` command and prints the
undo, and for another harness the server's definition is `{"command": "dockingbird", "args": ["mcp"]}`.

The server works in the folder your harness runs in, and starts agents of that checkout's configs and of the ones
`dockingbird config add` registered. An agent is named by its name (what `agent_start` returns and `agent_list`
shows), a delivery or an artifact by its id. A tool that changes something takes an `idempotency_key`
(`YYYYMMDD/uuid4`): a retry with the same key and the same arguments gets the first answer back without running
again. Everything an agent wrote comes back as data from its sender, never as an instruction.

heading: `dockingbird mcp`: the host tools > The tools
summary: The Required column lists the arguments a call must carry; the Optional column lists the ones that may be left out.
text:
The Required column lists the arguments a call must carry; the Optional column lists the ones that may be left out.

| Tool | Required | Optional | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `agent_start` | none | `command`, `task`, `name`, `harness` (`claude` or `codex`), `idempotency_key` | Starts an agent; `task` is its first message. Returns its name, its ids and the command that applied: `command` when given, else this checkout's default command, else the default environment |
| `agent_list` | none | `cursor` | One page of your agents: name, state, mode, model, effort and inbox counts |
| `agent_status` | `agent` | none | One agent: its last turn, model and effort, pending obligations and kept results |
| `agent_send` | `agent`, `text` | `kind`, `reply_to`, `artifacts`, `payload`, `idempotency_key` | Messages an agent: a new task (`task_request`, the default), or an answer to its question with `reply_to`; `text`'s first line is the subject, `artifacts` takes ids from `agent_artifact_put` |
| `agent_inbox` | none | `agent`, `cursor` | One page of the deliveries your agents sent you; with `agent`, the deliveries to that agent |
| `agent_read` | `delivery_id` | `cursor`, `idempotency_key` | One page of a delivery's body and its artifact ids; records your read |
| `agent_wait` | none | `agent`, `timeout_s` (1 to 45) | Waits for the next delivery from `agent`, or from any agent; a timeout cancels nothing |
| `agent_results` | `agent` | `cursor` | One page of an agent's results: its artifacts saved under `results/<agent>/` in Dockingbird's folder, small text inline |
| `agent_stop` | `agent` | `idempotency_key` | Stops one of your agents; its results are kept |
| `agent_set` | `agent` | `model`, `effort`, `idempotency_key` | Changes a running agent's model or effort, from its next turn |
| `agent_artifact_put` | `agent`, `name`, `content` | `media_type`, `idempotency_key` | Stores a document as an artifact and returns the id `agent_send`'s `artifacts` takes |

heading: `dockingbird mcp`: the host tools > How the tools relate to the commands
summary: The tools, their names and their arguments are covered by [the compatibility promise](compatibility.md).
text:
| Tool | Shares rows with | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `agent_inbox` | `dockingbird inbox` | a delivery one of them has shown, the other does not show again as new |
| `agent_wait` | `dockingbird wait` | a delivery one of them has shown, the other does not show again as new |

The tools, their names and their arguments are covered by [the compatibility promise](compatibility.md).

heading: Compatibility: what you can build on
summary: The surfaces a customer may build on are:
text:
The surfaces a customer may build on are:

1. `--json`: the envelope's keys and each message's `id`, `fields` and `exit_code` as the troubleshooting page
   ([the catalogue](../../troubleshooting.md)) lists the messages ([the envelope](json.md));
2. `dockingbird mcp`'s host tools, `agent_start`, `agent_list`, `agent_status`, `agent_send`, `agent_inbox`,
   `agent_read`, `agent_wait`, `agent_results`, `agent_stop`, `agent_set` and `agent_artifact_put`, by name and
   argument ([the tools](mcp.md));
3. the exit statuses 0, 1, 2, 69, 77 and 78 and the tools' own ([exit codes](exit-codes.md));
4. the files a customer writes: `.dockingbird/*.toml` configs ([the app config](../files/app-config.md)), `hosts.toml`
   ([its format](../files/hosts-file.md)), `org.toml` ([the org file](../files/org-file.md)), `fleet.toml` and a swarm
   definition at `schema = 1` ([its keys](../files/swarm-definition.md)).

The promise: a surface listed here changes only with a line in the release notes; an `id`, a field, a tool, an argument
or a file key is never removed or renamed in the release that announces it, only in a later one, so a script has one
release to follow; additions need no notice; a message's `lines` text and the GUI's drawing are never a surface.

heading: `hosts.toml`: the other computers you reach
summary: The hosts file lists the other computers you reach from this one, so the fleet commands that take a host name can read their agents and open their screens.
text:
The hosts file lists the other computers you reach from this one, so the fleet commands that take a host name can read their agents and open their screens.
With no file there are no other hosts, which is not an error, and a command that writes the file makes it.

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| path | `~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml`, or `hosts.toml` in the folder `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` names |
| commands that read it | `fleet agents --host NAME` reads the agents on a listed computer, and `fleet attach --host NAME` opens one of their screens |
| this computer | never an entry, because it is `local` in every fleet line and `fleet agents` always reads it; a pool host is the one exception, written with `local = true` |

heading: `hosts.toml`: the other computers you reach > The three commands that write it
summary: - `set` reaches the host over its route and reads its Docker and its Dockingbird homes exactly as
text:
```bash
dockingbird fleet hosts set NAME --ssh DEST [--path PATH] [--docker-host URL]
dockingbird fleet hosts set NAME --gcloud VM --zone ZONE --project PROJECT
dockingbird fleet hosts rename OLD NEW
dockingbird fleet hosts forget NAME
```

- `set` reaches the host over its route and reads its Docker and its Dockingbird homes exactly as
  `dockingbird fleet agents --host NAME` does; only once that read succeeded does it write the host's `[[host]]`
  table, then it prints the host's rows and says so:
  `lab: ssh lab.example, saved in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml.` (`FLEET_HOSTS_SET`). For a name the file
  already has it says `updated in` (`FLEET_HOSTS_UPDATED`): the route keys are replaced, and the host's
  `[[host.home]]` tables and its place in the file are kept. When the host can't be read, nothing is saved, and the
  message says what to try first: `ssh DEST docker version`, or `gcloud compute ssh VM -- docker version`.
- `rename OLD NEW` renames a host, its `[[host.home]]` tables kept. Swarm definitions and pool records that name
  `OLD` are not changed.
- `forget NAME` removes a host and its `[[host.home]]` tables.

`set` and `rename` refuse a name that is not a host name and the name `local`, this computer's own; `rename` and
`forget` refuse a name the file lacks, and `rename` a new name the file already has. A command that writes the file
holds its lock, so two at once never lose each other's change; while another one is writing, it says so and changes
nothing. With `--json`, each line is an envelope ([the envelope](../integration/json.md)).

You may still write the file by hand. A write by Dockingbird keeps every table and their order, and leaves the file
readable by you alone (0600), but loses a hand-written file's comments and the order of keys inside a table.

heading: `hosts.toml`: the other computers you reach > One name
text:
| Rule | What it means |
|---|---|
| a host has one name | its `name` here is what `--host` takes and the rows say, its name in the fleet pool when it is in one, and the name a swarm definition places work on |
| renaming a pooled host | on a computer whose Dockingbird home holds a `fleet.toml`, `rename` and `forget` of a host the pool holds are refused (`FLEET_HOSTS_IN_USE`); drain and remove it from the pool first, then rename it here, then enrol it again under its new name |

heading: `hosts.toml`: the other computers you reach > `[[host]]`: one per computer
summary: Each `[[host]]` has a `name` and one route: `ssh`, or `gcloud` with `zone` and `project`; this computer as a pool host has `local = true` instead.
text:
Each `[[host]]` has a `name` and one route: `ssh`, or `gcloud` with `zone` and `project`; this computer as a pool host has `local = true` instead.

| Key | Route | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | both | the host's name: lowercase letters, digits and dashes, at most 56 characters, one per file, never `local` |
| `ssh` | ssh | a destination your own ssh reaches: `lab.example`, `user@lab.example`, or a `Host` of your ssh configuration |
| `path` | ssh | the `PATH` the commands run with there, for a login whose own `PATH` lacks Docker's `docker` |
| `docker_host` | ssh | the `DOCKER_HOST` the commands run with there, for a Docker whose socket is not the default one |
| `gcloud` | gcloud | a Compute Engine VM's instance name, reached through your own `gcloud compute ssh` |
| `zone` | gcloud | the instance's zone |
| `project` | gcloud | the instance's project |
| `gcloud_program` | gcloud | this computer's `gcloud`, as an absolute path, when it is neither on your `PATH` nor in the Google Cloud SDK's usual places; written by hand, and kept by a `set` that keeps the gcloud route |
| `repoint` | any | your own command that restarts the host's Dockingbird services, its worker and the admitter where it runs; `dockingbird fleet update` runs it over the host's route after it moves the host to a release |
| `local` | none | `true` for this computer when it is a pool host, written with neither `ssh` nor `gcloud`; its lines run here under `sh`, and `fleet hosts` shows it as `this computer` |

heading: `hosts.toml`: the other computers you reach > `[[host.home]]` and `[[home]]`: a home's own program
summary: You write both by hand, and `set` keeps them.
text:
| Table | Names |
|---|---|
| `[[host.home]]`, after a host's keys | one of that host's Dockingbird homes |
| `[[home]]`, at the top level | a home of this computer |

You write both by hand, and `set` keeps them.
A table names its home by `path` or by `name`, and `program` is the home's own `dockingbird`, which a send to one of its agents with no screen runs there.

| Key | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `path` | the home's folder, an absolute path; the worker identifies the home by its real path |
| `name` | a home `homes/NAME` of the worker's user, in place of `path`; its `program` is that home's own program file unless the table names one |
| `program` | the home's own `dockingbird`, an absolute path |
| `clones` | optional, an absolute folder where a fleet worker keeps one clone per repository and branch it starts swarms from |

```toml
[[host]]
name = "lab"
ssh = "lab.example"

[[host.home]]
path = "/opt/dockingbird/homes/team-1"
program = "/opt/dockingbird/bin/dockingbird"
```

heading: `hosts.toml`: the other computers you reach > `repoint`: the restart line `fleet update` runs
summary: `dockingbird fleet update` needs a `repoint` line in each pool host's `[[host]]` table.
text:
`dockingbird fleet update` needs a `repoint` line in each pool host's `[[host]]` table.
Dockingbird runs the line exactly as you wrote it, over the host's route, and composes no restart command of its own.
It must return without waiting for the services to stop, because a restart that takes longer than the call's 40 seconds reads as failed.

```toml
[[host]]
name = "lab"
ssh = "lab.example"
repoint = "systemctl --user restart --no-block UNIT"
```

On Linux `UNIT` is the systemd user unit of the worker. On a Mac the line is `launchctl kickstart -k gui/$UID/LABEL`, with the label of the worker's launchd unit in place of `LABEL`.
A Dockingbird older than the release that reads `repoint` and `local` refuses the whole file with `FLEET_HOSTS_FILE_INVALID` until it is updated, so write both keys on a computer that runs the newer release.

heading: `hosts.toml`: the other computers you reach > The rules
summary: Dockingbird reads the file before every fleet command that uses it and refuses one that breaks a rule.
text:
Dockingbird reads the file before every fleet command that uses it and refuses one that breaks a rule.
The refusal names the rule's place, such as `host[2].ssh` numbered from 1, and never a value (`FLEET_HOSTS_FILE_INVALID`).
Every value reaches a command as one word, so the rules refuse a value that could be read as an option or split in two.

| Applies to | Rule |
|---|---|
| the file | TOML of at most 1 MiB, a regular file of yours (not a link), holding `[[host]]` and `[[home]]` tables alone, each with no key but its own |
| a `[[host]]` | a `name` and exactly one of `ssh` and `gcloud`, or `local = true` with neither; `gcloud` with both `zone` and `project`; `ssh` with none of `zone`, `project` and `gcloud_program`; every value text |
| `ssh` | not empty, no leading `-`, no whitespace |
| `gcloud`, `zone`, `project` | not empty, no leading `-`, lowercase letters, digits, `-`, `.` and `:` alone |
| `path` | not empty |
| `docker_host` | not empty, no whitespace |
| `gcloud_program`, and each home's `path`, `program` and `clones` | an absolute path |
| every value | no character that is not printable |

heading: org.toml and the password file
summary: `org.toml` names the organisation's store, a PostgreSQL database, and the role each kind of command connects as.
text:
`org.toml` names the organisation's store, a PostgreSQL database, and the role each kind of command connects as.
It holds no secret: each role's password is a line of `~/.pgpass`, PostgreSQL's own password file, which `psql` reads too.

heading: org.toml and the password file > Where the files are
text:
| File | Path | Written by | Rules |
|---|---|---|---|
| `org.toml` | `~/.config/dockingbird/org.toml`, or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/dockingbird/org.toml` when `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is a path from `/` | `dockingbird org login` and `dockingbird org logout` only | a regular file of yours, mode 0600, in a folder of mode 0700; never read through a link |
| `~/.pgpass` | your home folder, or the file `PGPASSFILE` names | `dockingbird org login`, or by hand | a file of yours that no one else can read (`chmod 600`); a file anyone else can read is refused, and no refusal shows a password |

heading: org.toml and the password file > Keys of org.toml
summary: Any other key, a missing required key, a value of the wrong type or another `version` is refused, and the refusal names the key and never a value.
text:
```toml
version = 1

[org]
host = "db.example.net"
port = 5433
database = "dockingbird_fleet"
project = "example-app"

[org.roles]
user = "fleet_admin"
worker = "fleet_worker_lab"
admitter = "fleet_admin"
```

| Key | Values | Default | What it holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `version` | `1` | required | the file's format; any other number is refused |
| `[org] host` | text | required | the address the hosts reach the fleet database at |
| `[org] port` | 1 to 65535 | PostgreSQL's default | the database's port |
| `[org] database` | text | `dockingbird_fleet` | the database's name |
| `[org] project` | project slug | none | the project the owner's own leases count against |
| `[org.roles] user` | PostgreSQL role | none | the role for your own commands: `fleet_admin` for the owner, your own login role for every other person, their coordinators and runners included |
| `[org.roles] worker` | PostgreSQL role | none | the role for `dockingbird fleet worker` |
| `[org.roles] admitter` | PostgreSQL role | none | the role for `dockingbird fleet admitter` |

Any other key, a missing required key, a value of the wrong type or another `version` is refused, and the refusal names the key and never a value.

heading: org.toml and the password file > The password line
summary: `~/.pgpass` holds one line for each role, in PostgreSQL's own format, and `psql` reads the same line.
text:
`~/.pgpass` holds one line for each role, in PostgreSQL's own format, and `psql` reads the same line.

```text
db.example.net:5433:dockingbird_fleet:fleet_admin:PASSWORD
```

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `HOST:PORT:DATABASE:ROLE:PASSWORD` | the order of the five fields, with the role's password in place of `PASSWORD` |
| `dockingbird org login` | asks for the password without echo, or reads it whole from standard input with `--password-stdin`; a password is never a word of the command line |

heading: org.toml and the password file > What the files decide
text:
| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| no org login on this computer | the command ends 78 and names `dockingbird org login HOST --as user --role ROLE` |
| a kind of command with no role in `org.toml`, or a role with no line in `~/.pgpass` | the command ends 78 and names the login to run |
| the database does not answer within 5 seconds, or ends the work for a passing reason (restarting, too many connections) | the command names the database's host, the role tried and the connection's own words, and ends 69 |
| the database turns the login down (wrong password, a role or database it lacks) or answers with an error code once connected | the command is refused with that role and the words or the code, and ends 78 |
| an access rule that does not list this computer | the refusal comes before the password is asked, so it reads as no answer, with the database's own words on the line |
| one login | one login serves every Dockingbird home of that user on the computer |

heading: org.toml and the password file > The older fleet.toml
summary: Before `org.toml`, a fleet database login lived in a `fleet.toml` in your Dockingbird home.
text:
Before `org.toml`, a fleet database login lived in a `fleet.toml` in your Dockingbird home.

| Case | Result |
|---|---|
| no `org.toml`, and a `fleet.toml` without a `password` | the command still reads `fleet.toml` |
| a `fleet.toml` that holds a `password` | the command connects nothing, names the file and the line that moves it, and ends 78 |
| `dockingbird org login --from-fleet-toml --as KIND` | moves the login into `org.toml` and `~/.pgpass`, then takes the password out of the file after a yes; `--yes` answers it where there is no terminal |
| both files | `org.toml` is read and a line says `fleet.toml` is not |

| Key | Default | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| `host` | required | where the fleet database answers |
| `role` | required | `fleet_submitter_PROJECT`, `fleet_worker_HOST` or `fleet_admin` |
| `port` | 5432 | the database's port |
| `database` | `dockingbird_fleet` | the database's name |
| `project` | none | in the admin's file only: the project the admin's leases count against |
| `password` | refused | a file that holds one stops the command with exit 78 |

heading: org.toml and the password file > Commands that write these files
text:
| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `dockingbird org login HOST[:PORT] --as user\|worker\|admitter --role ROLE` | writes both files; `--database NAME`, `--project SLUG`, `--password-stdin` and `--replace` (sign in to another store in place of this one) adjust it |
| `dockingbird org status` | shows the login and connects once as `user` |
| `dockingbird org logout [--as KIND]` | takes the login away, or one kind's |

heading: org.toml and the password file > Related
text:
| Page | What it holds |
|---|---|
| [commands.md](../commands.md) | every `org` action |
| [exit-codes.md](../integration/exit-codes.md) | the statuses 69, 77 and 78 |
| [team-fleet.md](../../guides/team-fleet.md) | the steps that build the store |

heading: Swarm definition file
summary: A swarm definition is a TOML file, `swarm.toml`, at `schema = 1`.
text: A swarm definition is a TOML file, `swarm.toml`, at `schema = 1`. Keep it at `.dockingbird/swarms/NAME/swarm.toml` and submit it by name with `dockingbird fleet submit NAME`, or give a folder or a file path. [The swarms guide](../../guides/swarms.md) writes and submits one. `fleet describe NAME` prints every parameter and settable field as JSON.

heading: Swarm definition file > Top-level keys
text:
| Key | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `schema` | integer | required, `1` | the definition's version |
| `project` | string | required, or given by `--project` | the project's slug |
| `key` | string | `NAME` and the UTC time as `YYYYMMDDhhmmss`, or `--key` | a repeat of a key answers the swarm queued first |
| `priority` | `P0`, `P1`, `P2` or `P3` | required | the queue priority |
| `[source]` `repository` | string | required unless every role has `workspace = "scratch"` | the repository the agents work on, such as `example-org/example-app` |
| `[source]` `branch` | string | required with `repository` | the branch they work on |
| `[placement]` `hosts` | list of host names | every pool host that takes swarms, in pool rank order | the hosts to try, in order of preference |
| `[placement]` `home.<host>` | string | a home that fixes nothing: one with a checkout of the repository first, then the fewest running agents, then by path | the host's home, by the name its worker publishes or by its folder path |
| `[placement]` `spread` | `true` or `false` | `false` | `true` lets the fleet place the swarm's roles on more than one host; `fleet where ID` names where each agent runs |
| `[params]` | table of parameters | none | declared parameters, at most 32, each written `{{name}}` in values and in role texts; [Parameters](#parameters) has their keys |
| `[[attachments]]` | tables with `path` and `name` | none | files attached to the swarm, sent as they are, with no placeholder expanded |

heading: Swarm definition file > Parameters
summary: Each entry of `[params]` is one parameter, a table with a `type` and the keys of its type.
text:
Each entry of `[params]` is one parameter, a table with a `type` and the keys of its type. A parameter with no `default` must get a value at every submit.

```toml
[params]
N = { type = "int", default = 2, min = 1, max = 8 }
effort = { type = "choice", default = "high", choice = ["medium", "high", "xhigh"] }
focus = { type = "text", default = "the login flow", max_chars = 80 }
```

| Type | Its keys | A value given at submit |
|---|---|---|
| `int` | `default`, `min`, `max`; each a whole number of 0 or more | a whole number within `min` and `max` |
| `choice` | `choice`, the list of words, each once; `default`, one of them | one of the words |
| `text` | `default`; `max_chars`, 1 to 120, 120 when left out | one printable line of at most `max_chars` characters, with no `"`, no `\`, no `{{` and no `}}` |

A parameter's name is at most 32 characters of letters, digits and `-`, and its letters may be upper case, as in `N`. It is never a built-in's name. A parameter may narrow the field it fills, such as a `choice` of three efforts, and never widen it: a word or a bound the field refuses is refused at the declaration (`wider`).

heading: Swarm definition file > Parameters > Where a placeholder expands
summary: A string that is one placeholder of an `int` parameter and nothing else becomes that number, so `count = "{{N}}"` is `count = 4` for `--set N=4`.
text:
| Place | `{{name}}` expands |
|---|---|
| a string value of a `[[role]]` entry | when the definition declares `[params]`; without `[params]`, `{{` stays as written |
| a role's `brief`, its `instructions` and its subagent's `instructions` | when the definition declares `[params]` |
| a library role's string values and texts | always |
| an attachment, a `harness_config` file | never |

A string that is one placeholder of an `int` parameter and nothing else becomes that number, so `count = "{{N}}"` is `count = 4` for `--set N=4`. A placeholder in a key is refused (`placeholder-key`). A placeholder that names no declared parameter and no built-in is refused (`undeclared`).

heading: Swarm definition file > Parameters > Built-in parameters
summary: The submit supplies these.
text:
The submit supplies these. A definition never declares them.

| Placeholder | Its value | Where it expands |
|---|---|---|
| `{{swarm}}` | the swarm's key | everywhere a placeholder expands |
| `{{project}}` | the project's slug | everywhere a placeholder expands |
| `{{repository}}` | `[source]` `repository`; empty for a swarm with no `[source]` | everywhere a placeholder expands |
| `{{branch}}` | `[source]` `branch`; empty for a swarm with no `[source]` | everywhere a placeholder expands |
| `{{roles}}` | one line per role: its name, its count, and its model and effort as resolved, each with its source | in a text alone, such as a brief |
| `{{params}}` | one line per declared parameter and its value | in a text alone |

In a definition that declares `[params]`, names a new role key such as `use`, or gets values at submit, no role may be named `parent`, `repo`, `scratch`, a built-in or a declared parameter (`reserved`).

heading: Swarm definition file > Role keys
summary: Each `[[role]]` is one kind of agent.
text:
Each `[[role]]` is one kind of agent.

| Key | Type | Default | Meaning |

|---|---|---|---|

| `name` | slug | required | the role's name |

| `harness` | `claude` or `codex` | required, or from the library role or project file | the tool the agents run |

| `model`, `effort` | string | [where they come from](#where-a-roles-model-and-effort-come-from) | override only; a role none of the sources gives one is refused |

| `count` | integer or `"{{N}}"` | required | agents of the role at the start; at most 24 per home |

| `min` | integer | the role's `count` | the fewest agents a retire leaves; the fleet admits a swarm once every role's `min` fits; a role that reviews or tests keeps at least 1 |

| `max` | integer | the role's `count` | the most agents an add reaches |

| `brief` | path | required, or from the library role | the Markdown file of the first task, read under the definition's folder |

| `reviews`, `tests` | list of role names | none | whose commits this role reviews or tests |

| `kind` | slug | `reviewer` or `tester` by `reviews` or `tests`, else `implementer`, as the role library's `index.toml` names them | a name the model and effort are looked up by |

| `use` | string | none | `"NAME"` names `.dockingbird/roles/NAME.toml`; `"dockingbird/NAME"` names a shipped role |

| `instructions` | path | none | text the agents get after Dockingbird's rules and the project's |

| `connections` | list of names | none | the home's connections the agents are granted at start; each must name an enabled connection at submit |

| `[role.subagents.<name>]` | table | none | one helper kind, at most one table per role: `instructions` (required), `model`, `effort`, `max` and `tools`, as [the subagent block](roles-and-connections.md#subagent-block) gives them |

| `send_to` | list of role names | any agent of the project | the roles the agents may message beside their parent; `[]` allows the parent alone |

| `workspace`, `egress`, `allow`, `env` | as in a config | as in a config | session settings, as [`app.toml`](app-config.md) takes them |

| `context` | `kept` or `fresh` | `kept` | as a config's `context`: one conversation for every delivery, or a new one for each task delivery |

heading: Swarm definition file > Role keys
text:
| `tools` | `bus`, `full` or a list | as in a config | A config takes `bus` (messages and files, the default), `default` (claims and commits) or `full` (both); a swarm role takes `bus`, `full` or a list that keeps every bus tool; a list that drops a bus tool gives `refused: role[N].tools: drops a tool of the bus set` |

| `harness_config` | a path, or a table by harness | none | the harness's own settings file, the base under Dockingbird's own keys, read under the definition's folder or the library role's; never expanded |

| `compact_at` | `500000`, `500k` or `auto` | `500000` for a fleet-started agent | the point at which the agent's context compacts |

| `session_hours` | integer, 1 to 168 | 48 for a fleet-started agent | how long each agent may run |

| `needs` | cpus, memory and pids, each with `request` and `limit` | measured | the role's resource reservation |

| `args` | list from a closed set of start words | none | extra words a start takes |

| `hosts` | list of host names | the placement's hosts | the hosts of `[placement]` its agents may take, in order; the roles that publish commits (each role that reviews, and each role another reviews or tests) share one host, and in a swarm without `spread = true` every role does, else `hosts-apart` |

| `skills` | table of `path` and `into` | none | skills its agents' tool lists as its own, as a config's `[skills]` takes them: `path`, one skill or skills folder or a list of them, each a path from the top of the swarm's source; `into`, `both`, `claude` or `agents`; every start reads them from the swarm's clone, and a path the clone lacks holds the swarm (`skills_refused`) until you push the fix and run `fleet release ID`; `--set` cannot set it; see [skills.md](../../guides/skills.md) |

| `[role.fallback]`, `[role.fallback.on]` | tables | none | the tool its agents move to after a failed turn, and each error class's rule; see [A role's fallback](#a-roles-fallback) |

heading: Swarm definition file > Library roles
summary: The shipped roles are `coordinator`, `implementer`, `reviewer`, `tester`, `reader` and `hands`.
text:
The shipped roles are `coordinator`, `implementer`, `reviewer`, `tester`, `reader` and `hands`. Each names its `harness`, `brief`, `instructions`, `workspace` and `tools`, and none names a model or an effort. `hands` carries out a coordinator's host requests with no clone of its own: `workspace = "scratch"`, a list of tools and `compact_at = "300k"`.

`dockingbird init` copies them into `.dockingbird/roles/` with the library's `index.toml`, and a copy you edited survives a later `init`. A key the entry gives replaces the library role's whole value. Two tables merge field by field instead, the entry's field winning: `needs` and each `subagents.<name>`. A `skills` or a `fallback` table the entry gives replaces the library role's whole. [The roles and connections reference](roles-and-connections.md) lists the library file's keys and `index.toml`.

heading: Swarm definition file > Where a role's model and effort come from
summary: The first source that gives a value wins, separately for `model` and for `effort`.
text:
The first source that gives a value wins, separately for `model` and for `effort`.

1. A value given at submit: `--set ROLE.model=M`, `--set ROLE.effort=E`, or the role's entry in `--values FILE`.
2. The `[[role]]` entry.
3. The library role it names with `use`.
4. `[roles.<lookup name>]` of `.dockingbird/project.toml`, read only when its `harness` is the role's. An empty value there falls through.
5. Your organisation's store, the row of the lookup name and the role's harness, set by `dockingbird org roles set NAME --harness H --model M --effort E`.

A role none of them gives is refused, as `refused: role[N].model: missing`. The lookup name is the role's `kind`, else the name `index.toml` `[defaults]` gives for what the role does: `reviewer` for a role that reviews, `tester` for one that tests, `implementer` otherwise. A role that names a new key, such as `use`, `instructions`, `skills` or `send_to`, tries its own name first, then its library role's name, then those two. The first name with a row in the project file or the store gives the values.

A Claude effort is checked against `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max` at submit. A Codex effort and every model word reach the tool as given, so a word the tool does not take fails at the agent's first request. [Claude Code and Codex](../../concepts/claude-code-and-codex.md#model-and-effort-per-role) recommends a model and an effort for each kind of role.

heading: Swarm definition file > A role's fallback
summary: `[role.fallback]` under a `[[role]]`, or `[fallback]` in a library role file, takes the keys of a config's `[fallback]` table: `harness`, `model`, `effort`, `placement`, `retry_wait`, `retry_max` and `[role.fallback.on]`.
text:
`[role.fallback]` under a `[[role]]`, or `[fallback]` in a library role file, takes the keys of a config's `[fallback]` table: `harness`, `model`, `effort`, `placement`, `retry_wait`, `retry_max` and `[role.fallback.on]`. [The app.toml reference](app-config.md#keys-of-fallback) lists each key, the error classes and the defaults.

```toml
[[role]]
name = "builder"
harness = "claude"
count = 1
brief = "briefs/builder.md"

[role.fallback]
harness = "codex"

[role.fallback.on]
refusal = "fallback"
```

This table names no `model` or `effort`, so the submit takes them from the `codex` row of the role's lookup names. Name both in the table when no row gives them.

| Rule | Refusal |
|---|---|
| each key is checked as a config's | at `role[N].fallback.<key>` |
| `harness` names the role's own tool | `fallback-same` |
| `model` or `effort` left out takes the fallback tool's row by the role's lookup names: `[roles.<name>]` of the project file when its `harness` is the fallback's, else the store's row of the name and that tool | `fallback-model` when no row gives one |
| `placement = "require-login"` and the role's `hosts` pin a host whose home is not signed in to both tools, as of its last sample | `no-login-host` at `role[N].fallback.placement` |

With `placement = "require-login"`, the fleet also holds the swarm off a host whose home is not signed in to both tools, and `fleet why ID` names the hold `no_fallback_login`. Sign in there with `dockingbird login claude` or `dockingbird login codex`. The role's config carries the table to each of its agents, which follow its rules as an agent started with that config does.

heading: Swarm definition file > Values at submit
summary: A value's field is `set.<key>` for a `--set` and `values.<path>` for the document, such as `values.roles.grader.count`, and a parameter that gets no value is refused at `params.<name>`.
text:
| Form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--set KEY=VALUE` | repeatable; a parameter (`N=4`), a role's setting (`grader.count=6`), a subagent's (`grader.helper.max=4`) or a role's fallback key (`grader.fallback.harness=codex`) |
| `--values FILE` | JSON of the shape `{"params": {...}, "roles": {"ROLE": {...}}}`, a role's subagents under `subagents` and its fallback keys under `fallback` |
| precedence | a `--set` beats the file for the same key; a role's setting given at submit beats the value its entry got from a parameter |
| settable for a role | `count`, `min`, `max`, `model`, `effort`, `compact_at`, `session_hours` |
| settable for a subagent | `model`, `effort`, `max` |
| settable for a role's fallback | `harness`, `model`, `effort`, `placement`; each laid over the role's own table, or making one for a role that names none; a role whose subagent is named `fallback` keeps that subagent's meaning |
| where the values show | `fleet queue` and `fleet why` print the values a submit gave as `values: {values}`; the defaults are not shown |
| a refusal | one `refused: <field>: <rule>` line each, in a fixed order, then exit 1 |

A value's field is `set.<key>` for a `--set` and `values.<path>` for the document, such as `values.roles.grader.count`, and a parameter that gets no value is refused at `params.<name>`. These rules apply to the values themselves.

| Rule | Its words after the field |
|---|---|
| `undeclared` | names no declared parameter, built-in, role or subagent |
| `not-a-setting` | not a setting an invocation may set |
| `not-a-subagent` | names no subagent of that role |
| `twice` | named twice |
| `values-shape` | not the values document's shape: params and roles |
| `not-json` | not a JSON document |
| `range` | outside the parameter's own bounds or words |
| `missing` | missing, for a parameter with no default and no value |

heading: app.toml, the keys of a config
summary: Each TOML file in the `.dockingbird` folder at the top of a checkout is a config, and the commands it adds exist in that checkout only.
text:
Each TOML file in the `.dockingbird` folder at the top of a checkout is a config, and the commands it adds exist in that checkout only.
A config you add with `config add` works in every repo instead.
Every key is optional, and a key you leave out takes the default in the tables below.

heading: app.toml, the keys of a config > Where a config lives
text:
| Place | What it is |
|---|---|
| `.dockingbird/*.toml` at the top of a checkout | this repo's own configs; their commands exist in that checkout only, and each file is read again at every start |
| `dockingbird config add PATH` | an added config, copied into your Dockingbird home so its commands work in every repo; add it again after a change |
| `[commands.NAME]` tables | several commands in one file, in place of `command`, `default` and `skill` at the top |

heading: app.toml, the keys of a config > Keys of a command
text:
| Key | Values | Default | What it does |

|---|---|---|---|

| `command` | text | the file's name, `app` | the command's name, as in `dockingbird review`; a name Dockingbird keeps (`status`, `start`, `claude`) refuses the whole config |

| `summary` | text | none | one line shown by `dockingbird -h`, `config list` and, for your own harness, `dockingbird mcp` |

| `default` | `true` or `false` | `false` | `dockingbird start` with no `--command` runs this command in this checkout; `claude` and `codex` never use it |

| `skill` | path to a Markdown file | none | on the bus, the file's text with `$TASK` replaced by the task is the first turn |

| `[skills]` | table of `path` and `into` | none | skills the agent's tool lists as its own (Claude Code's Skill tool and `/` menu, Codex's `$` mention); [its keys](#keys-of-skills) are below, and [skills.md](../../guides/skills.md) gives them step by step |

| `instructions` | path | none | role text given to the agent after Dockingbird's own rules |

| `harness` | `claude` or `codex` | `claude` | the tool; once set it is fixed, and `--harness` on a start cannot change it |

| `workspace` | `repo` or `scratch` | `repo` | a copy of this repo, or an empty folder of its own that needs no git repo |

| `mode` | `bus` or `terminal` | `bus` | in the background through messages, or at your terminal; once set it is fixed, and `--terminal` cannot change it |

| `context` | `kept` or `fresh` | `kept` | bus only: one conversation for every delivery, or a new conversation for each task delivery under the same rules |

| `repo_settings` | `true` or `false` | `false` | load the repo's own Claude Code or Codex settings, hooks and MCP servers, once the checkout is trusted |

| `tools` | `bus`, `default` or `full` | `bus` | A config takes `bus` (messages and files, the default), `default` (claims and commits) or `full` (both); a swarm role takes `bus`, `full` or a list that keeps every bus tool. Commits made under `default` or `full` reach you through `dockingbird sync` |

| `egress` | `allowlist`, `models`, `none` or `full` | `full`, or what `dockingbird egress` set | what the agent may reach on the network |

heading: app.toml, the keys of a config > Keys of a command
text:
| `allow` | list of hosts and presets | the list `dockingbird egress` set, else nothing beyond the tool's own hosts | with `allowlist`, the presets `registries` and `github`, or hosts such as `docs.python.org` and `*.corp.example` |

| `harness_args` | list of words | none | fixed arguments for the tool: Claude takes `--model`, `--fallback-model`, `--max-turns` and `--effort` (`low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` or `max`); Codex takes `--model`, `-m` and `-c model_reasoning_effort=LEVEL`; anything else is refused |

| `harness_config` | a path, or a table by tool such as `{ claude = "claude-settings.json" }` | none | the tool's own settings file, a path beside this file, which the agent's tool takes as its base under Dockingbird's own keys |

| `mise_env` | text | none | mise's environments for the agent's toolchain, comma separated; `ci` makes mise read `mise.ci.toml` over `mise.toml` |

| `[env]` | table of text | none | variables the agent's tool sees; settings, never secrets, because the agent can read and send them |

| `[fallback]` | table | none, so every failed turn is reported | what a failed turn on the bus does: a retry, a report or a move to the other tool; [its keys](#keys-of-fallback) are below |

heading: app.toml, the keys of a config > Keys of `[skills]`
text:
| Key | Values | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `path` | a folder, or a list of folders | none | one skills folder, each of whose folders holding a `SKILL.md` is one skill (`".agents/skills"`), or a list of folders, each one skill or a skills folder (`[".agents/skills/review", "tools/skills"]`); a repo's own config names paths from the checkout's top, an added config's are relative to its file's folder, and `config add` copies them with it |
| `into` | `both`, `claude` or `agents` | `both` | where they go in the agent's home: `both` writes each skill to `~/.claude/skills`, where Claude Code finds personal skills, and to `~/.agents/skills`, where Codex finds a user's; `claude` or `agents` writes only that one |

heading: app.toml, the keys of a config > Keys of `[limits]`
text:
| Key | Values | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `turn_minutes` | whole number, at least 1 | none, so no turn deadline | a turn that runs longer is interrupted and reported |
| `session_hours` | whole number from 1 to the installation's maximum, 168 | 12 | the agent stops itself after this many hours |
| `cpus` | text such as `"2"` | none | the agent container's CPU limit |
| `memory` | text such as `"4g"` | none | the agent container's memory limit |
| any key named here | as above | as above | fixed for the config's agents: `--session-hours`, `--cpus` and `--memory` with another value are refused, the same value is not |

heading: app.toml, the keys of a config > Keys of `[fallback]`
summary: The table sets what a failed turn of an agent on the bus does: try it again, report it, or move the agent to the other tool with its conversation.
text:
The table sets what a failed turn of an agent on the bus does: try it again, report it, or move the agent to the other tool with its conversation. A command's `[commands.NAME]` table may hold its own `[fallback]`, which replaces the config's whole.

```toml
[fallback]
harness = "codex"
retry_wait = "5m"
retry_max = 3

[fallback.on]
refusal = "fallback"
server = "retry"
```

| Key | Values | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `harness` | `claude` or `codex`, never the config's own tool | none: no move, and the rules still retry and report | the tool the agent moves to |
| `model` | that tool's model word | that tool's own | the fallback tool's model; given only beside `harness` |
| `effort` | that tool's effort word | that tool's own | the fallback tool's effort; given only beside `harness` |
| `placement` | `any` or `require-login` | `any` | `any` starts the agent where the fallback tool is not signed in, with its move off; `require-login` starts it only where that tool is signed in |
| `retry_wait` | a time in seconds, minutes or hours, such as `30s`, `5m` or `1h`, from 1 second to 24 hours | `5m` | the wait before a retry |
| `retry_max` | whole number, 1 to 100 | `3` | the retries in a row of one delivery |
| `[fallback.on]` | a table of error class and action | each class's default, below | each class's rule; a class left out takes its default |

An action is `retry` (the turn again after `retry_wait`, at most `retry_max` times in a row), `retry-then-fallback` (those retries, then the move), `fallback` (the move at once) or `report` (the failure reported and left, as with no table). Each failed turn has one class.

heading: app.toml, the keys of a config > Keys of `[fallback]`
summary: With a `harness`, `refusal` is the one class that moves the agent by default, since a retry sends the same conversation to the same safety system.
text:
| Class | What ended the turn | Default with `harness` | Default without |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rate_limit` | a 429 against the request quota | `retry` | `retry` |
| `usage_limit` | the plan's usage window, used up | `retry` | `retry` |
| `auth` | a sign-in refused or expired | `retry`, after Claude's sign-in retries | `report` |
| `billing` | payment, credits or the plan's quota | `retry` | `report` |
| `server` | the provider's side failed | `retry` | `report` |
| `network` | the request got no answer | `retry` | `retry` |
| `invalid_request` | the request itself was refused | `report` | `report` |
| `context` | the conversation no longer fits the model's window | `report` | `report` |
| `cap` | the tool's own cap ended the turn | `retry` | `retry` |
| `refusal` | a safety system refused the model's response or the request | `fallback`, at once with no retry | `report` |
| `exited` | the tool's process ended with no result; it takes `report` alone | `report` | `report` |
| `other` | none of the above | `report` | `report` |

With a `harness`, `refusal` is the one class that moves the agent by default, since a retry sends the same conversation to the same safety system. Every transient class retries on the agent's own tool, because a move changes the model in the middle of a task. A table that wants a move for another class names it, as in `server = "fallback"`. The column without a `harness` also applies to an agent that has already moved as often as it may, and to one whose fallback is off on this computer.

A `usage_limit` retry takes neither `retry_wait` nor `retry_max`. It waits 1, 5 and 15 minutes, then every 30 minutes, until 24 hours after the first failure, and is then reported, or under `retry-then-fallback` the agent moves. A retry that completes starts the waits over.

heading: app.toml, the keys of a config > Keys of an added config only, refused in a repo's own config
text:
| Key | Values | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `connections` | list of connection names | connections you recorded with `dockingbird connect`, granted to each agent of the command for at most its `session_hours`; never a credential as a value |
| `browser` | `chrome` | a Google Chrome of Dockingbird's own in a container beside the agent, which `dockingbird watch` shows; the browser tools come with it whatever `tools` says |
| `browser_extensions` | list | with a browser: each entry a Chrome Web Store link, a 32-letter extension id, or an absolute folder (`/` or `~/` first) that holds a `manifest.json` |
| `[browser_policy]` | table | with a browser: Chrome policies by Google's names; policies that would cut Dockingbird's control of the browser are refused |
| `local_model` | model tag | a tag as `docker model ls` lists it, run on this Mac by Docker Desktop's Model Runner; used with `egress = "models"` |
| `version` | a tool version such as `"2.1.285"` | pins this config's tool version, at the top level or in one command |

heading: app.toml, the keys of a config > What a checkout you marked untrusted turns off
text:
| Key | Effect while the checkout is untrusted |
|---|---|
| `harness_args` | not applied until `dockingbird trust` marks the checkout trusted |
| `[env]` | not applied until `dockingbird trust` marks the checkout trusted |
| `harness_config` | not applied until `dockingbird trust` marks the checkout trusted; `dockingbird -h` and `config list` say `.dockingbird/app.toml: harness_config applies after dockingbird trust` |
| `[skills]` | not applied until `dockingbird trust` marks the checkout trusted; `dockingbird -h` and `config list` say `.dockingbird/app.toml: skills applies after dockingbird trust`; an added config's `[skills]` apply everywhere |
| `repo_settings = true` | the repo's own settings, hooks and MCP servers do not load |
| an added config's `harness_args`, `[env]`, `[skills]` and `harness_config` | still apply everywhere, because you chose to add the config |

heading: app.toml, the keys of a config > Smallest useful files
text:
```toml
# .dockingbird/app.toml
command = "review"
summary = "Review this branch and list what to fix"
skill = "skills/review.md"
```

```toml
# an added config: dockingbird config add agents/triage.toml
command = "triage"
harness = "codex"
connections = ["github-issues"]
```
