heading: Operator guide > Install
summary: You need:

heading: Operator guide > Install
summary: `dockingbird completion --install` adds tab completion; open a new terminal: it writes the completion script for the shell `$SHELL` names (or the one you name, `zsh`, `bash` or `fish`) to `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/completion/` and adds two lines to `~/.zshrc` or `~/.bashrc`, a comment and one that loads the script when it is there (for fish, the file `~/.config/fish/conf.d/dockingbird.fish` holds them), once however often you run it; the zsh script loads `compinit` itself when your `~/.zshrc` never did, and `dockingbird update` keeps the script current.
text: `dockingbird completion --install` adds tab completion; open a new terminal: it writes the completion script for the shell `$SHELL` names (or the one you name, `zsh`, `bash` or `fish`) to `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/completion/` and adds two lines to `~/.zshrc` or `~/.bashrc`, a comment and one that loads the script when it is there (for fish, the file `~/.config/fish/conf.d/dockingbird.fish` holds them), once however often you run it; the zsh script loads `compinit` itself when your `~/.zshrc` never did, and `dockingbird update` keeps the script current. `dockingbird clean --all` removes the script but not those two lines, which then load nothing; delete them yourself if you like. Never use a bare `uv tool install dockingbird`: that PyPI name is not ours. If `dockingbird` is not found afterwards, run `uv tool update-shell` and open a new terminal. The first `dockingbird claude` downloads about 1 GB, once, and takes about 5 minutes; the first start of each tool then fetches that tool's latest release into the program store and waits for it, `dockingbird start` too, with or without `--json` (see "Tool versions"). To uninstall: `dockingbird clean --all`, then `uv tool uninstall dockingbird`. Uninstalling first would leave Dockingbird's containers, volumes and image behind. Docker keeps the build cache of Dockingbird's image, shared with every other project's; `docker builder prune` frees all of it. The image's Ubuntu packages come from Dockingbird's apt pool, a folder under `~/.local/share/dockingbird/apt-pool/` that holds a copy of the pinned Ubuntu snapshot's files the image installs, one for every Dockingbird home of your user on that computer. Every build checks the folder against the list Dockingbird ships, each file's size and sha256, and reads it alone, with or without Docker's build cache, so it builds while Ubuntu's snapshot service is down. The first build on a computer without the folder (the first `dockingbird claude`, or the first `dockingbird update` after this change) fills it from that service, 441 MB once per snapshot, and says so in one line; when the service cannot be reached then, the build stops and `--verbose` names the folder and the first file it could not get. A copy of the folder from another computer (`rsync`) does as well: a build fetches only the files the folder lacks or holds with other bytes.

heading: Operator guide > The commands
text:
| Command | What it does |

|---|---|

| `dockingbird claude`, `dockingbird codex` | Start Claude Code or Codex on the repo you are in, each in its own container. The first run sets everything up |

| `dockingbird status`, `dockingbird status claude-1` | Who is working on what, what was shared today, and what needs you; with a name, one agent in detail. An agent that reported on its task and has nothing waiting for it shows idle until `dockingbird stop NAME`, one whose tool says its turn ended, or that it waits at its prompt, shows idle too, and one that asks you something shows "asks you" with how many questions it waits for and `dockingbird questions` (an agent that asked without waiting, `blocking` false, shows working or idle as its hooks say, and its question stays listed under what needs you); `status NAME` lists each of its shares that was not published, with why. It only looks: it never starts anything |

| `dockingbird homes` | Every Dockingbird home on this computer, one line each: each `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`, the default one included, read back from its coordinator's own `logs` folder, with its folder, its coordinator (running or stopped) and version (a home under `homes/` of the default home is listed by its name, the default home as `default`; a home of that folder with no coordinator yet reads "no Dockingbird started here yet"), and whether its commands would leave its coordinator as it is; a home whose commands would not says whether `dockingbird inspect swarm` reads it ("readable for inspection") and what a command from here would do (see [Reading across versions](#reading-across-versions)); a home whose folder is gone, or whose `logs` folder is not its own, shows no folder. `--json` gives each home's `home` (its folder, or null), `profile`, `version`, `coordinator`, `readable`, `agents_running`, `this`, `default`, `gone`, `name` (its name, or null for a home outside the default home's folder), `inspectable` and `inspect_from`, which the GUI reads. It only reads: it starts, builds and changes nothing, in any home |

heading: Operator guide > The commands
text:
| `dockingbird ui` | The Dockingbird GUI, whose install is not yet available to customers (see "The GUI"), built from herdr, mouse first: a tab for each running agent at a terminal, a sidebar row for each agent and one for the inbox, and a command bar for the agent you select; `ctrl+b`, then `d`, then a letter acts on an agent (`n` starts one, `x` stops a working agent and deletes a stopped one after a y, `a` opens its screen, where you answer it), each action showing the `dockingbird` command it runs, and `i` opens the inbox in a tab. It reads Dockingbird again every 2 minutes, and at once on `r`. It has no key that changes an agent's settings or sends it a message: `dockingbird set NAME` and `dockingbird send NAME TEXT` do. `ctrl+b q` detaches and every pane keeps running. `dockingbird ui stop` stops its server, and `dockingbird ui --install` installs or updates it |

| `dockingbird sync` | Take the agents' commits on the branch you are on, and send them yours |

| `dockingbird login claude`, `dockingbird login codex` | Sign in again, or as someone else; `--api-key` uses an API key instead |

| `dockingbird logout claude`, `dockingbird logout codex` | Sign out in Docker and remove the saved API key |

| `dockingbird update` | Get the latest Dockingbird, Claude Code and Codex, and on a Mac keep an installed Dockingbird GUI at the version Dockingbird pins; `--check` only says whether one is out. With agents running, it gets and builds the new version now, keeps the one they run for your commands, and switches by itself when the last one ends. |

| `dockingbird clean`, `dockingbird clean codex-1` | Free disk space; with names, delete those stopped agents (each one's kept copy, results and history), so `status` no longer lists them; `--all` removes everything Dockingbird made |

| `dockingbird stop`, `dockingbird stop claude-1`, `dockingbird stop claude-1 codex-1` | Stop every agent and turn Dockingbird off, or stop each named agent in turn. Nothing is lost |

| `dockingbird serve convert` | Run, here and as you, what agents ask of a program you connected as a service (see "Folders, databases and services"), one request at a time until Ctrl-C or you close its terminal; `--once` returns after one. The program runs only while this runs |

heading: Operator guide > The commands
text:
| `dockingbird watch claude-1` | Watch, or take over, the browser of an agent whose config asks for one (`browser = "chrome"`, see "Delegated agents"): it prints `vnc://127.0.0.1:<port>`, opens it in your VNC viewer (`--no-open` prints the address alone) and prints the VNC password once the viewer connected; the port takes your viewer's connections, from this Mac alone, one at a time, for the life of the watch (macOS Screen Sharing connects once to ask for the password and again to sign in), and no container port is published. Anything you type or paste into that browser is visible to the agent, which reads the page: sign in to nothing you would not hand it. Your Mac's clipboard does not cross: text copied on this Mac does not paste into that browser, and nothing copied there reaches your Mac. Closing the viewer ends the watch a moment later (it waits `WATCH_RECONNECT_WAIT_S` for the viewer to connect again), and so does Ctrl-C; the browser runs on |

| `dockingbird completion zsh` | Print a completion script (zsh, bash or fish); `dockingbird completion --install` installs it for your shell, and `dockingbird update` keeps it current |

| `dockingbird mcp` | The MCP server your own Claude Code or Codex starts, to start and steer agents from it (below); you never run it yourself |

| `dockingbird harbor baseline`, `dockingbird harbor run -a claude-code` | Run a Harbor benchmark task's two baselines (oracle must score 1, nop 0), or one real trial with your own login; `dockingbird harbor jobs`, `dockingbird harbor results JOB`, `dockingbird harbor clean` and `dockingbird harbor version` show, remove and name what ran (see "Harbor benchmark tasks") |

| `dockingbird cp ...` | The fleet's control plane, on the home made for it: `cp init` turns this home into it, given the hub's address, `cp token` makes the bundle a computer joins with, given its label and platform (printed once), `cp status` lists the computers in the fleet and their fleet inboxes, `cp remove LABEL` takes a computer out at once, and `cp off` turns the control plane off once no computer is in it |

heading: Operator guide > The commands
summary: On `claude` and `codex`, `--as NAME` picks the agent's name and `--new` always starts a new one; a name has lowercase letters, digits and `-`, and one that doesn't is a usage error (exit 2) with the name to try instead ("Try: dockingbird claude --as my-agent").
text:
| `dockingbird node ...` | This computer's place in the fleet: `node join` reads a bundle from standard input and joins, so each agent started here gets a fleet inbox beside its own; `node leave` leaves once no agent here still uses the fleet. Neither touches a running agent |

| `dockingbird org login HOST --as user --role ROLE`, `dockingbird org status` | This computer's login to your organisation's store, one PostgreSQL role for each kind of command (see "The fleet scheduler"); for an admin, the store itself: `org create` makes it or brings it to this release, and `org projects`, `org roles`, `org people` and `org members` list and change its projects, the model and effort of each kind of role, its persons and their projects |

| `dockingbird license activate`, `dockingbird license status` | This computer's seat (see "Licensing"): `activate` takes one with your license key, asked for and never on the command line, and `trial` starts a trial instead; `status` shows the plan, the seats and the term; `activations` lists the computers that hold the seats and `--release ID` frees one; `deactivate` gives this computer's seat back |

On `claude` and `codex`, `--as NAME` picks the agent's name and `--new` always starts a new one; a name has lowercase letters, digits and `-`, and one that doesn't is a usage error (exit 2) with the name to try instead ("Try: dockingbird claude --as my-agent"). Everything else after the tool's name goes to the tool, as in `dockingbird claude -p "Summarize the open TODOs"` or `dockingbird codex exec "Fix the tests"`; a `--` right after Dockingbird's options is dropped, so `dockingbird claude -- --help` shows Claude Code's own help (no agent starts). `--verbose` adds ids, codes, paths and timings, and `--json` prints JSON for scripts; for `claude` and `codex` they go before the tool's name (`dockingbird --verbose claude`), since everything after it is the tool's. `dockingbird -h` shows the help, as does `-h` after any command (`dockingbird sync -h`), and `dockingbird --version` (or `-v`) the versions. No command needs a state folder, an id or a path.

heading: Operator guide > The commands
summary: `--agent-md PATH` and `--claude-md PATH` (also `--agent-md=PATH`), on `claude`, `codex`, `start` and every config's command, give the agent your file as the root `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` of its copy: the copy's own file is replaced, or made when the branch has none, before the tool starts, so the tool reads yours and not the repo's, as in `dockingbird claude --agent-md RESEARCH-AGENTS.md`.
text: `--agent-md PATH` and `--claude-md PATH` (also `--agent-md=PATH`), on `claude`, `codex`, `start` and every config's command, give the agent your file as the root `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md` of its copy: the copy's own file is replaced, or made when the branch has none, before the tool starts, so the tool reads yours and not the repo's, as in `dockingbird claude --agent-md RESEARCH-AGENTS.md`. Your checkout is never touched and the file never reaches a commit: in the copy, git hides it (a replaced file is marked skip-worktree, a new one is listed in `.git/info/exclude`), so `git status` there stays clean and `dockingbird sync` never brings it to you. The file is read on this Mac first and must be a regular UTF-8 text file of at most 1 MB with no Dockingbird credential in it, else nothing starts. Codex doesn't read `CLAUDE.md` at startup, so `dockingbird codex --claude-md PATH` is refused. In a checkout that isn't trusted, `claude` gets your files as its own user memory, so it reads them and not the repo's; a config's command whose repo settings don't load (its `repo_settings` is off, or the checkout isn't trusted) is refused, because Claude reads no instruction file there. In a trusted checkout, Codex is refused a branch that holds `AGENTS.override.md`, which it reads instead of `AGENTS.md`. With `--agent-md`, Claude reads `AGENTS.md` beside a `CLAUDE.md`, and it still reads a `.claude/CLAUDE.md` beside yours. With `--claude-md` alone, Claude reads your `CLAUDE.md` and no longer the repo's `AGENTS.md`, as it does in any repo that has a `CLAUDE.md`; a `.claude/AGENTS.md` is read beside your `AGENTS.md`. An agent keeps the files it started with for its whole life: `--as NAME` picks it up or reconnects with the same files, and another file is refused (start a new agent with `--new` for that). A new agent without the options uses the repo's own files; on a kept copy it puts them back, and a copy of the given file that the earlier agent changed is first saved to Dockingbird's agent logs folder, and the start says where. A commit that adds, changes or deletes the given file is never published, so it never reaches your branch, `dockingbird sync` or a push.

heading: Operator guide > The commands
summary: `--skills PATHS`, on `claude`, `codex`, `start` and every config's command, gives the agent skills its tool lists as its own, as a config's `[skills]` does (see **Skills** under [Your own commands (configs)](#your-own-commands-configs)): skill folders, comma-separated, or a skills folder, each path relative to the folder you run the command in, or absolute.
text:
`--skills PATHS`, on `claude`, `codex`, `start` and every config's command, gives the agent skills its tool lists as its own, as a config's `[skills]` does (see **Skills** under [Your own commands (configs)](#your-own-commands-configs)): skill folders, comma-separated, or a skills folder, each path relative to the folder you run the command in, or absolute. `dockingbird claude --skills .agents/skills` gives every skill of that folder, and `--skills .agents/skills/a,.agents/skills/b` those two. A skill it names replaces a config's skill of the same name. A running agent takes more through `dockingbird set NAME --skills PATHS` (see [Delegated agents](#delegated-agents)).

Streams and exit codes: for `claude` and `codex`, Dockingbird's own lines go to stderr and stdout is the tool's, so a redirected one-shot holds only its answer.

The other commands print results on stdout and problems on stderr.

They exit 0 when done, 1 for a problem Dockingbird printed with its next step, and 2 for a usage error.

`claude` and `codex` exit with the tool's own status once it has started, 0 when the agent keeps working without a terminal, and 1 if Dockingbird stopped before starting it.

Only `claude`, `codex` and `login` set Dockingbird up (a first `login claude --api-key` sets it up, then saves the key, and the first start after it is an ordinary start, with no set-up line): before the first run, `sync`, `stop`, `clean`, `logout`, the exchange commands (`send`, `inbox`, `read`, `wait`, `results` and `search`), `connect`, `connections`, `revoke` and `disconnect` print status's "Dockingbird isn't set up yet." line, which ends "Start here: dockingbird claude" inside a repo and "cd into a repo, then: dockingbird claude; or, with no repo, sign in first: dockingbird login claude" anywhere else, and set nothing up (`sync`, the exchange commands, `connect`, `connections`, `revoke` and `disconnect` exit 1, as they could not do what was asked; `stop`, `clean` and `logout` exit 0, with nothing to do), while `update` upgrades only the command and says the first `dockingbird claude` will set it up, and `dockingbird clean --all` still removes whatever a failed setup left.

heading: Operator guide > The commands
summary: Lines wrap to the terminal's width, down to 50 columns for a half-width pane (and at 80 in a pipe or a file), and never inside a command, a size, a duration or a count and its noun: "Get it: dockingbird sync" moves to a line of its own rather than break, as "(1 MB)" and "1 commit" do, an end line too narrow for the pane breaks after its sentence first, "...
text:
Lines wrap to the terminal's width, down to 50 columns for a half-width pane (and at 80 in a pipe or a file), and never inside a command, a size, a duration or a count and its noun: "Get it: dockingbird sync" moves to a line of its own rather than break, as "(1 MB)" and "1 commit" do, an end line too narrow for the pane breaks after its sentence first, "... done" keeps its dots ("Setting up Dockingbird, first time only" over "... done (2 s)"), a command or a path too long for the pane stays whole on its own line, and a message never ends on a fragment of one or two words.

When the output is not a terminal (a pipe or a file: a script, an agent, or `dockingbird claude` piped to `tee`), nothing is drawn live: the first setup, an update's uv step and its rebuild, and a tool's download print their heading at once ("Setting up Dockingbird, first time only (about 5 min):", "Getting the latest Dockingbird ...", "Getting the latest Claude Code ..."), then a progress line at most once a minute (`SETUP_PROGRESS_INTERVAL_S`, 60 s) while they run ("still setting up: step 12 of 41, 3 min so far", "still setting up: step 12 of 41, no output for 2 min", "still getting the latest Dockingbird, 2 min so far", "still getting Claude Code 2.1.296: 45 MB of 89 MB, 1 min so far"), then their done line, so a caller can tell a slow setup from a hang; on a terminal the same work is one line redrawn in place.

Before the build's first step there is no step to name, so a build Docker never starts gets no progress line until the stall check below stops it.

With `--json`, only the final envelope comes.

With `--verbose`, each message also shows its ID in brackets on a line of its own, such as `[NOTHING_NEEDS_YOU]`.

The ID is the message's heading in [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md).

With `--json`, every message is one line of JSON: `ok`, `exit_code`, `id`, `lines` (never wrapped), `next_step` when it has one, and `fields`, the values its lines were filled with, so a script never parses a sentence.

A help screen is one too (`dockingbird --json -h`, `dockingbird --json help status`): `id` `HELP`, the screen's `lines`, and `fields.command`, null for the top screen.

heading: Operator guide > The commands
summary: Text is sanitized as on the screen, counts are numbers, sizes are bytes, durations are seconds and lists are arrays.
text:
Text is sanitized as on the screen, counts are numbers, sizes are bytes, durations are seconds and lists are arrays.

Each `status` row is an envelope of its own: an agent's row adds `name`, `tool`, `repo`, `branch`, `state` (`working`, `idle`, `waiting`, `preparing`, `stopped` or `crashed`), `terminal` (whether a terminal shows it), `next_step` (its reconnect or pick-up command, or null) and `next_argv` (that command's words as an array, such as `["dockingbird", "claude", "--as", "claude-1"]`, when that step is one plain command ending `--as NAME`, which a program can run without a shell; else null: a step that switches branch or changes folder first, a stop, a send with its text still to write, a step in words, or none), `screen` (`tty` when the agent has a screen that `dockingbird claude --as NAME` or `dockingbird codex --as NAME` shows: a running agent at a terminal, and a running agent on the bus that has a screen of its own, see "Its screen." under "Delegated agents"; `none` for any other running agent; null when it has no running container), `container` (its running container's name, or null) and `attach_argv` (the words that show its screen, such as `["dockingbird", "claude", "--as", "notes-1"]`, with the agent's own tool, a config's agent's too, whenever `screen` is `tty`, even while a terminal shows it; else null); a `preparing` row adds `step` (`environment` or `dependencies`), `since` and `last_output_at` (when that step began and when its command last printed, as the agent's own summary wrote them, or null); a repo's heading adds `behind` (the commits you lack; 0 when the heading says nothing, null when behind by an unknown count), `both_moved` (true when you have new commits too, so `sync` merges, false when it fast-forwards, and null when Dockingbird can't tell, as its heading says) and `head` (the agents' published head, the full commit id to compare with `git rev-parse origin/BRANCH`, or null when Dockingbird has no record of the repository); `today`'s row has its `count` and `names`, for example `{"count": 1, "names": ["claude-1"]}`; a kept copy under "Needs your attention" has its row's `state` (`stopped` or `crashed`), `terminal` (false), its pick-up as `next_step` and `next_argv`, and `mode` (`bus` or `terminal`) and `command` (its config's command), as the cache recorded how the agent ran, each null when no record says; and the first line, with the sign-ins, has `claude` and `codex`, each `api-key`, `signed-in` or `none`.

heading: Operator guide > The commands
summary: Agent names, in `names` too, come in the order the agents started.
text:
Agent names, in `names` too, come in the order the agents started.

An agent's end line carries the run's own status: when the tool exits 3, its envelope has `"ok": false` and `"exit_code": 3`, as the process does.

heading: Operator guide > Your first run and a normal day
summary: `cd myapp && dockingbird claude` does everything once: it first checks the branch you are on, so a branch holding files the agents don't take is refused in seconds, every one of them named, with nothing set up (no image, no Dockingbird, no sign-in; see "Sending yours" below); then it checks the platform and starts Docker Desktop if needed, builds the image (progress lines, live on a terminal; about 5 minutes), starts Dockingbird, and copies the branch you are on for the agents ("Copying myapp (main) for the agents").
text:
`cd myapp && dockingbird claude` does everything once: it first checks the branch you are on, so a branch holding files the agents don't take is refused in seconds, every one of them named, with nothing set up (no image, no Dockingbird, no sign-in; see "Sending yours" below); then it checks the platform and starts Docker Desktop if needed, builds the image (progress lines, live on a terminal; about 5 minutes), starts Dockingbird, and copies the branch you are on for the agents ("Copying myapp (main) for the agents").

The first time, it also downloads Claude Code's latest release into the program store and waits for it ("Getting Claude Code 2.1.296 ..." while it downloads, then its done line; in a pipe, the progress lines described above), as the first start of each tool does, `dockingbird start` with or without `--json` included; `dockingbird --version` names the version once that start has finished.

Then it starts `claude-1` in its container.

When Claude has no sign-in yet, the start line says so ("Starting claude-1 on myapp (main).

Claude will show a sign-in link: open it on this Mac, sign in, then paste the code here.

Only this once."; in a pane too narrow for its lines, each sentence starts a line of its own, for Codex too), and its own `claude auth login` runs first, inside the container: open its link on this Mac, sign in and paste the code.

Quit the sign-in and the agent ends with "Claude isn't signed in yet.

Run dockingbird claude again to sign in." and the API key route, "Or use an API key: dockingbird login claude --api-key": its empty copy is removed, never called work kept, and the next start shows the sign-in again.

Codex's first start runs `codex login --device-auth`: open the link and enter the one-time code; quit it and Codex's end line has the same first sentence, then "(If device code login is off, turn it on in ChatGPT's security settings.)" and the API key route.

Until a build has been timed, the setup line shows no countdown, only "first time: about 5 min"; later builds count down from the last one's time.

heading: Operator guide > Your first run and a normal day
summary: When Docker Desktop's Resource Saver has stopped its VM, the setup line says "waking Docker" until Docker answers `docker version` in time (within `DOCKER_WAKE_CALL_S`, 5 s, or, after slower answers on a busy Mac, the slowest recent one plus `DOCKER_WAKE_MARGIN_S`, at most `DOCKER_WAKE_CALL_CAP_S`, 30 s); after `DOCKER_WAKE_TOTAL_S`, 2 minutes, it ends with "Docker is answering slowly." when Docker kept answering too late, and "Docker isn't running." when it gave errors.
text:
When Docker Desktop's Resource Saver has stopped its VM, the setup line says "waking Docker" until Docker answers `docker version` in time (within `DOCKER_WAKE_CALL_S`, 5 s, or, after slower answers on a busy Mac, the slowest recent one plus `DOCKER_WAKE_MARGIN_S`, at most `DOCKER_WAKE_CALL_CAP_S`, 30 s); after `DOCKER_WAKE_TOTAL_S`, 2 minutes, it ends with "Docker is answering slowly." when Docker kept answering too late, and "Docker isn't running." when it gave errors.

A build Docker takes but never starts (no output and no context taken for `BUILD_STALL_S`, 2 minutes, before its first step) is stopped and sent once more after that check; a second one ends with "Docker didn't start the build." (Docker Desktop paused or still starting, or a base system that couldn't be downloaded) and the step to check Docker Desktop and the network.

A build step that prints nothing for `BUILD_QUIET_S` (1 minute; a download waiting on the network) is named above the setup line by what it downloads ("Downloading Claude Code is quiet (1 min).

Still waiting."), the setup line says how long it has waited ("no progress for 3 min"), and after `BUILD_QUIET_CHECK_S` (3 minutes) the note adds "Check your connection or Docker Desktop."; both go once the step moves, and the build goes on.

In a pane too narrow for the whole setup line (under about 70 columns), its words show once on a line of their own ("Setting up Dockingbird, first time only (about 5 min):"), with the same estimate the countdown under it starts from, and only the bar stays live; no live line ever reaches a pane's last column.

Ctrl-C during the setup ends it with "Set-up didn't finish.

Nothing changed.

Run this again." If Docker refuses Dockingbird's own `logs` folder ("bind source path does not exist", which Docker Desktop's file sharing says of a folder deleted and made again while it ran), the start says "Docker Desktop can't see ~/.local/share/dockingbird/logs, so Dockingbird couldn't start." and to restart Docker Desktop; when Dockingbird never got as far as writing its log, its refusal shows what Docker said instead of naming a log.

heading: Operator guide > Your first run and a normal day
summary: Before anything else, a command needs Docker to answer `docker version`: when Docker takes that request and gives no answer within `STATUS_DOCKER_TIMEOUT_S` (10 s), as a Docker Desktop waking from Resource Saver can, "Waking Docker ..." shows while it asks again for as long once more; one that still answers nothing gets "Docker isn't answering.
text:
Before anything else, a command needs Docker to answer `docker version`: when Docker takes that request and gives no answer within `STATUS_DOCKER_TIMEOUT_S` (10 s), as a Docker Desktop waking from Resource Saver can, "Waking Docker ..." shows while it asks again for as long once more; one that still answers nothing gets "Docker isn't answering.

Restart Docker Desktop, then run this again." On a terminal, the last start line is "To leave it working, close this window.", except for a Codex start that waits for Enter (see Trust below), where "Press Enter to open Codex." follows it.

- **Its copy.** Each agent works in its own copy of your branch, from your last commit, mounted at `/work/<repo-name>` in its container (a safe form of the folder's name: `My App` runs at `/work/My-App`). A second checkout whose folder has the same name gets a suffix, and its first start says so before it copies: "Another checkout is already called My App, so this one is My App-2." It never sees your uncommitted edits, and it runs without permission prompts, because the container is its sandbox.

- **Claude's first screens.** Claude starts without its onboarding screens, the theme choice among them: Dockingbird gives it the `auto` theme, which follows your terminal's light or dark background. A theme you pick with `/theme` lasts until the agent's container ends. Your own `~/.claude.json` on this Mac is never read for it.

- **Trust.** Every checkout is trusted unless you mark it untrusted on this Mac with `dockingbird trust --off` (`dockingbird trust` marks it trusted again; `--forget` is `--off` under its older name), or make untrusted the default: a `trust` line at the top of `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/config.toml`, `trust = "untrusted"` or `trust = "trusted"`, sets what a checkout with no mark is (no line is `"trusted"`); you edit it by hand, there is no command or flag for it.

Trust covers the repo's mise config too: its `[env]` and `[settings]` load only in a trusted checkout (see "Toolchains").

A mark decides over the default: a checkout you marked with `dockingbird trust` is trusted and one you marked with `trust --off` is untrusted whatever the line says (the marks are files under `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/trust/` and `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/untrusted/`, and a record Dockingbird 0.2.0 wrote in `trust/` for a checkout you trusted counts as its trusted mark).

heading: Operator guide > Your first run and a normal day
summary: Any other `trust` value, or a `config.toml` that isn't TOML, is refused by every command that reads trust and never read as either default: a start stops before anything runs, `dockingbird -h` and `config list` say it and go on without the repo's own configs.
text:
Any other `trust` value, or a `config.toml` that isn't TOML, is refused by every command that reads trust and never read as either default: a start stops before anything runs, `dockingbird -h` and `config list` say it and go on without the repo's own configs.

Dockingbird changes nothing in that file but its own build-timer line, `last_build_seconds`, and leaves every other byte as you wrote it; a `config.toml` holding anything of yours stays through `dockingbird clean --all` too (one holding only that line goes), and a fresh or cleaned `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` holding only your `config.toml` is Dockingbird's to use, so you can set the default before the first start.

Where the repo's own settings load (a trusted checkout, for the default environment or a command whose config asks for them), neither tool asks: Dockingbird answers Claude's question whether to trust `/work/<repo-name>` for you, and Codex's entry for that folder is trusted, so the start prints nothing about trust.

In a checkout you marked untrusted, and for a command whose config leaves `repo_settings` off, Claude may ask once per repo, and Codex shows its folder-access notice each time it opens its screen (one Enter opens its copy restricted; nothing is saved or loaded; a one-shot `codex exec` shows none); Dockingbird never answers either, and whatever you answer there turns nothing on.

Codex shows the notice as it opens, before or just after its prompt box, and its screen hides every line printed before it, so at a terminal Dockingbird prints its note before each such Codex start, a pick-up included, and waits for Enter ("Press Enter to open Codex.") before Codex runs; ctrl-C there ends the start before Codex runs, and a new agent ended so leaves nothing behind: `status` lists none of it, and a later start under its name starts a new agent (a pick-up stays as it was).

Meanwhile another terminal's start under that name is refused: "NAME is still starting in another dockingbird command, so it can't start again." and "Use it in the terminal where it is starting." At Codex's notice, press Enter before you type: `n`, `q`, `2` or Esc there close Codex and end the agent.

Claude's note stays on the first start of each repo.

heading: Operator guide > Your first run and a normal day
summary: A start whose stdin or stdout is no terminal (a pipe) prints Codex's note on the first start only and never waits; a `--json` start at a terminal prints it on every start and never waits.
text:
A start whose stdin or stdout is no terminal (a pipe) prints Codex's note on the first start only and never waits; a `--json` start at a terminal prints it on every start and never waits.

In a checkout you marked untrusted, Codex still reads the copy's `AGENTS.md`: Codex skips an untrusted project's own `AGENTS.md`, so Dockingbird links Codex's global instructions file (`CODEX_HOME/AGENTS.md`) to it, while the copy's `.codex/config.toml`, hooks and exec policies stay off.

Claude's project `CLAUDE.md` and skills stay off there too, because Claude Code loads them in one bundle with the project's settings and hooks.

Claude remembers a yes in its own state, so after `dockingbird trust --off` it doesn't ask again for that repo, and that yes still turns nothing on.

The repo's own settings, hooks and MCP servers load in every checkout but one you marked untrusted on this Mac, or left unmarked under `trust = "untrusted"` (the fact reaches the agent as a file the coordinator writes on a read-only mount) and only for a tool whose credential routing pin has been proven on the real tool (both today), so in a checkout you trusted, Codex's entry for the folder is trusted and its `.codex/config.toml` loads, and Claude's repo settings, hooks and MCP servers load too, whether Claude is signed in, uses a token or has a saved API key.

The pin is a managed policy file the image carries only for a proven tool (`/etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json`, `/etc/codex/managed_config.toml`, root-owned, written at build), plus, for Claude, a settings file Dockingbird writes per session above the repo's: it names Dockingbird's key helper when you saved an API key and an empty one otherwise, so a repo's own `apiKeyHelper` can take over neither the key nor the sign-in; until a tool is proven the image carries no such file and nothing about your sessions changes.

heading: Operator guide > Your first run and a normal day
summary: - **A trusted repo's own Codex config.** Codex reads a trusted repo's `.codex/config.toml`, and its `developer_instructions` key is the one the agent's Dockingbird rules travel in.
text:
- **A trusted repo's own Codex config.** Codex reads a trusted repo's `.codex/config.toml`, and its `developer_instructions` key is the one the agent's Dockingbird rules travel in. Until Dockingbird has proven that its own copy outranks the repo's, a Codex start in a trusted repo (every repo, unless you marked it untrusted) whose `.codex/config.toml` sets that key is refused on this Mac before anything runs ("sets developer_instructions, which replaces the agent's Dockingbird rules", exit 2) and again in the container; so is one whose file can't be read (a link, over its bound, not TOML). Remove the key, or `dockingbird trust --off` the repo to run it with its own settings off. The same line answers a bare `dockingbird codex` typed to get back to an agent that is already running in that repo: the agent keeps the rules it started with and keeps running, and you reach its terminal again once the key is gone. Claude is not affected, and an untrusted repo's file is never read. A `start` of a command whose config leaves `repo_settings` off (every config's default) is not refused either: Codex loads no project layer for it. On this Mac the check folds case (APFS), so a file at `.Codex/Config.toml`, any case variant, is refused as well, although Codex in the container (Linux) reads only the lowercase name; the check errs toward refusing, never toward running.

- **Names.** Agents are numbered across the whole installation (`claude-1`, `codex-1`, `claude-2`), up to 9999 per tool or command; past that, a start without `--as` starts nothing, exit 1: name an agent yourself, or start again with `clean --all`.

A number is never used twice in an installation: an agent that ended keeps its name, and a start under it continues it or names the command that does; `--as NAME --new` starts afresh under it.

`--as reviewer` names one yourself.

Picking an agent that ended up again with `--as NAME` continues its conversation too: its tool starts where it stopped, with its own resume; when nothing of the conversation could be kept, one line says so ("The earlier conversation couldn't be restored, so this is a new one.") and the conversation starts fresh.

heading: Operator guide > Your first run and a normal day
summary: An agent is continued in its own environment, by its own command, the one every screen's pick-up names: "dockingbird review --terminal --as review-1" for a `review` agent that ran at a terminal, "dockingbird review --as review-1" for one that ran on the bus, `dockingbird claude --as claude-1` for an agent of the default environment at a terminal, and `dockingbird start --as claude-4` for one that worked on the bus (`dockingbird start --harness codex --as codex-4` for Codex).
text:
An agent is continued in its own environment, by its own command, the one every screen's pick-up names: "dockingbird review --terminal --as review-1" for a `review` agent that ran at a terminal, "dockingbird review --as review-1" for one that ran on the bus, `dockingbird claude --as claude-1` for an agent of the default environment at a terminal, and `dockingbird start --as claude-4` for one that worked on the bus (`dockingbird start --harness codex --as codex-4` for Codex).

It keeps the egress its last start ran, too, unless its config sets one or you give `--egress` on the pick-up; `status` shows the mode when it differs from the default for new agents.

`dockingbird claude --as NAME` (or `codex`) asks for that agent at this terminal, so it continues an agent that ended in its own setup there, with one line saying so: a config's agent as its config's terminal command would ("review-1 picks up where it left off, as a review agent at this terminal."; one whose command works in a scratch folder continues in that folder, its start line "Starting review-1 in a scratch folder.", with nothing linked or pushed first; on a linked branch the same holds for every pick-up that is refused: an agent that ended elsewhere, or one another command must continue, is refused before anything is sent), and an agent that worked on the bus with its messages readable at this terminal ("claude-4 picks up where it left off at this terminal;" then "the messages waiting for it reach it when you type.").

It starts nothing, exit 1, for an agent whose config runs it on the bus only ("review-1 runs on the bus only, as its config says.

Continue it: dockingbird review --as review-1") and for the other tool's agent ("rev is a Codex that ended.

Pick another name for this Claude, or continue it: dockingbird codex --as rev"), for one that ran as neither ("rev ran as neither a Claude nor a Codex, so nothing here continues it.

Pick another name for this Claude."), and a name that ended on another repository gets the step from where you stand ("rev ended in Other (main)." then "To continue it: cd ../other, then dockingbird claude --as rev").

heading: Operator guide > Your first run and a normal day
summary: A config's command names a setup of its own, so it starts nothing for another environment's agent and names the command that continues it, exit 1: "review-1 is a review agent.
text:
A config's command names a setup of its own, so it starts nothing for another environment's agent and names the command that continues it, exit 1: "review-1 is a review agent.

Continue it: dockingbird review --as review-1" for an agent of another command, and, for one of the default environment, "claude-1 is a claude agent of this checkout, not review's." then "Continue it: dockingbird claude --as claude-1".

Dockingbird refuses the same continuations itself, whatever asks for them.

An agent that stopped with work kept holds its name until its copy is picked up and ends empty, or `clean` removes it, so `--new` can't take that name: `dockingbird claude --as keep10 --new` while keep10's copy is kept starts nothing and says "keep10 has work kept, so --new can't take its name.", then "Pick it up: dockingbird claude --as keep10" (or, for a copy kept on another branch or checkout, where it is and the step from where you stand, as below) and "Or start a new Claude: dockingbird claude --new", exit 1.

A name whose copy is kept on another branch gets the step that picks it up from where you stand, before anything is copied or asked about the branch you are on: "keep7 has work kept in My App (feature/r7)." and "To pick it up: git switch feature/r7, then dockingbird claude --as keep7" (with `cd` to the other checkout first when it is kept there), exit 1.

A name belongs to the tool that first used it: `dockingbird codex --as keep7` for that Claude says where its copy is kept and gives the same step ("Pick another name for this Codex, or pick it up: git switch feature/r7, then dockingbird claude --as keep7"), exit 1; for a Claude that is running it gives the command that reconnects to it, and for one that works on the bus, which has no terminal to reconnect to, the send that reaches it ("keep7 is a Claude that works on the bus.

Pick another name for this Codex, or send it a task: dockingbird send keep7 TEXT").

heading: Operator guide > Your first run and a normal day
summary: - **Your newest commits first.** When you have commits the agents don't, the start sends them first ("Sent your 1 new commit to the agents first.").
text:
- **Your newest commits first.** When you have commits the agents don't, the start sends them first ("Sent your 1 new commit to the agents first."). When both sides have new commits, it offers sync's merge on a terminal, and starts nothing without it. A paused branch, an unfinished merge, a tree the agents can't hold, a head that changed twice or a repository that stayed busy (an agent sharing a commit, or another Dockingbird command) also start nothing, with sync's own message. An agent in a scratch folder uses no branch, so a pause stops neither its start nor its pick-up.

- **Reconnecting.** Close the terminal and the agent keeps working; the start line says so ("To leave it working, close this window.").

A bare `dockingbird claude` reconnects to the one Claude on this repo that has no terminal (with two, it lists them).

`dockingbird claude --as NAME` reconnects to NAME from any branch or checkout, as status's row says; while another terminal shows NAME, it takes the agent over, and nothing asks: that terminal lets go of it (the agent keeps working, never stopped), leaves the agent's screen, says "claude-2 is now shown in another terminal.

It keeps working." then "To show it here again: dockingbird claude --as claude-2" and returns to its shell (exit 0), and this terminal shows the agent with its conversation.

When it can't (that terminal is another user's, or did not let go when asked, which the line names with its process), it says "claude-2 is open in another terminal" and nothing changes.

heading: Operator guide > Your first run and a normal day
summary: An agent working on the bus with a screen of its own (see "Its screen." under "Delegated agents") is shown by a bare `dockingbird claude --as NAME` the same way, takeover included, and when you leave it, it says "notes-1 keeps working on the bus, with or without its screen shown." then "To show its screen again: dockingbird claude --as notes-1"; with arguments, `--egress`, a limit or `--new`, and for an agent on the bus with no screen of its own, `--as NAME` says it is already running and how to reach it ("claude-2 is already running, so it can't start again." then "Send it a task: dockingbird send claude-2 TEXT"); a bare start with no name never shows an agent on the bus, which belongs to whoever sent its task; an agent that has ended is continued in its own setup at this terminal instead (see Names).
text:
An agent working on the bus with a screen of its own (see "Its screen." under "Delegated agents") is shown by a bare `dockingbird claude --as NAME` the same way, takeover included, and when you leave it, it says "notes-1 keeps working on the bus, with or without its screen shown." then "To show its screen again: dockingbird claude --as notes-1"; with arguments, `--egress`, a limit or `--new`, and for an agent on the bus with no screen of its own, `--as NAME` says it is already running and how to reach it ("claude-2 is already running, so it can't start again." then "Send it a task: dockingbird send claude-2 TEXT"); a bare start with no name never shows an agent on the bus, which belongs to whoever sent its task; an agent that has ended is continued in its own setup at this terminal instead (see Names).

A bare start resumes only a copy of its own environment and mode: a copy kept by an agent that worked on the bus, or by a config's command, keeps its name and its pick-up, and the start takes the next number.

The copy it resumes brings its conversation along, as `--as NAME` does.

A start with arguments for the tool, or with `--egress`, never reconnects (an agent's egress is fixed at its start), and neither `--new`, arguments nor `--egress` take the name of an agent that works: "claude-2 is already running, so --new can't take its name." (with arguments, "so it can't take these arguments."), then the way to reconnect and, for `--new`, "Or start a new Claude: dockingbird claude --new".

Docker's detach keys are set as well (`ctrl-]` then `ctrl-\`).

The chord leaves an agent working as closing the window does, though the start line names only the window.

Codex binds `ctrl-]` alone to its Skip Question action.

In `dockingbird ui` an agent's pane takes every key but `ctrl+b`, the GUI's prefix; pressing it twice sends the agent a plain `ctrl+b`.

heading: Operator guide > Your first run and a normal day
summary: - **One-shots.** `dockingbird claude -p "..."` and `dockingbird codex exec "..."` resume or start an agent that takes exactly those arguments, and print only the tool's answer on stdout.
text:
- **One-shots.** `dockingbird claude -p "..."` and `dockingbird codex exec "..."` resume or start an agent that takes exactly those arguments, and print only the tool's answer on stdout. A one-shot `--as NAME` pick-up continues the agent's conversation: Claude's `-p` runs after `--resume <id>`, and Codex's `exec` runs as `exec resume <id>`. Without a terminal and without a sign-in, they refuse and point at `dockingbird login claude`. Input you pipe or redirect into one reaches the tool, as `echo "the failing test's log" | dockingbird codex exec "Fix it"` does; when only the output is redirected or piped (`dockingbird codex exec "..." > answer.txt`, `| tee log`) and you are at a terminal, the tool reads nothing from your keyboard, so it never waits for Ctrl-D. A script that pipes nothing into a one-shot closes its input (`< /dev/null`), or Codex waits for input that never ends.

- **The end.** When the tool ends, Dockingbird prints what was shared ("claude-1 is done: 2 commits shared on main.

Get them: dockingbird sync") or what was kept; when its copy was empty, so nothing is kept, the last line names the command that continues its conversation ("claude-1 is done.

Nothing new to share." then "To continue it: dockingbird claude --as claude-1"), which picks the conversation up where it stopped, in the agent's own environment ("To continue it: dockingbird review --terminal --as review-1" for a `review` agent at a terminal); a tool that exits with an error having shared nothing ends with its status ("claude-1 ended with status 3.

Nothing new to share."), never "done", and one that shared first and then failed says both ("claude-1 ended with status 3 after sharing 1 commit on main.

Get it: dockingbird sync"); a failed tool whose copy is kept is named the same way ("claude-1 ended with status 3.

Its copy is kept: dockingbird claude --as claude-1").

When another agent shared on the branch since the copy started, Dockingbird can't count the copy's own commits yet, so the line never names only its files: "claude-1 ended with status 3.

heading: Operator guide > Your first run and a normal day
summary: Its copy is kept and may hold work:", and the same "may" shows in `status`, `status claude-1` ("kept; it may also hold commits not shared yet" under its files), `clean`'s question ("..., and may have left commits not shared yet."), `clean --all`'s list and the line that picks it up again ("Resuming claude-1: 1 file not committed; it may also hold commits not shared yet.").
text:
Its copy is kept and may hold work:", and the same "may" shows in `status`, `status claude-1` ("kept; it may also hold commits not shared yet" under its files), `clean`'s question ("..., and may have left commits not shared yet."), `clean --all`'s list and the line that picks it up again ("Resuming claude-1: 1 file not committed; it may also hold commits not shared yet.").

Each step runs from where you stand when it ends: after a reconnect from another branch, or when you switched the checkout's branch while the agent ran, it switches first ("Get it: git switch feature/r7, then dockingbird sync"; a kept copy's "Pick it up:" the same, and `cd` first for another checkout).

An empty copy is removed at once; the agent keeps its name, which `--as NAME` continues (see Names).

Empty means by the count Dockingbird takes once the tool and everything it started have ended, and by a second count of its own once the agent's container is gone, so a file written in between keeps the copy: after a crash (the out-of-memory killer, `docker kill`) or a restart, the last count may be older than the tool's last change, so the copy is always kept and the line says so ("claude-1 crashed, ...

Its copy is kept and may hold work:").

When Dockingbird refused to start the tool (its sign-in check failed, say), the line says why in plain words and names the copied log ("claude-1 stopped before it started: Claude's sign-in check failed."), never "done", and the command exits 1; `--verbose` adds the refusal's code.

Dockingbird turns itself off after 30 minutes with no agent (`COORDINATOR_IDLE_STOP_S`), and the next command turns it back on. At most once a day (`REPO_MAINTAIN_INTERVAL_S`, 86400 s), the sweep of a start, `sync`, `stop` or `clean` also tidies each repository the agents share: Dockingbird packs its refs and repacks and prunes what nothing reaches, such as a refused import's leftovers, under the repository's lock (`repo maintain`), and leaves a repository alone while a share of it is unsettled or paused.

heading: Operator guide > Making a repository ready: `dockingbird init`
summary: Run `dockingbird init` anywhere in a repository.
text: Run `dockingbird init` anywhere in a repository. It writes `.dockingbird/project.toml`, the project's file: its `slug` (the project's name in your organisation's store: `--project SLUG`, else the name of the repository's `origin` remote, else its folder's; lowercase letters, digits and `-`), the release that wrote it, its rules file, each shipped role's harness, model and effort, and `[lint] forbidden`; `.dockingbird/rules.md`, the lines every agent of the project gets after Dockingbird's own rules; an example swarm in `.dockingbird/swarms/example/` (fill its `[placement] hosts` from `dockingbird fleet hosts`, then `dockingbird fleet submit .dockingbird/swarms/example`); this release's skills in `.agents/skills/`, with the link `.claude/skills` to them, its agent definitions in `.claude/agents/`, and `.dockingbird/skills.lock`, which lists every file it installed with its digest. Keep them in git: `git add .dockingbird .agents .claude && git commit`. A later run changes only what a new release changed: an installed file you edited is kept and named, and `--force` replaces it; `project.toml`, `rules.md` and the swarms are never rewritten. `dockingbird init --check` writes nothing and exits 1 when an installed file is not the running release's, so a repository's own checks can run it; the lock's `release` line only records which release last wrote it and is never judged. `init` writes nothing through a link: a `.dockingbird`, `.agents` or `.claude` that is a link, or a `.claude/skills` that links anywhere but `../.agents/skills`, stops it before anything is written. Last, with an org login on this computer, `init` adds the project to your organisation's store as your `user` role: its slug, the `origin` remote's address, the default branch and this release, once (a later run says the store has it). Only an admin adds a project: a login that is not one, a store that isn't made yet (an admin runs `dockingbird org create`) or a store that doesn't answer is named on that line, and `init` still ends 0. With no org login the line says to log in first (`dockingbird org login HOST --as user --role ROLE`), and `dockingbird init --no-register` skips the step.

heading: Operator guide > Sync
summary: `dockingbird sync` works on the branch you are on, in the checkout you run it in, and its one-line results name that branch ("My App (feature/notes): up to date.").
text:
`dockingbird sync` works on the branch you are on, in the checkout you run it in, and its one-line results name that branch ("My App (feature/notes): up to date."). After a sync that ends well, each other linked branch of the same checkout that lacks the agents' commits gets one more line with the step that takes them: "My App (main) is behind too: git switch main, then dockingbird sync" (or "My App (main) has new commits from the agents too: ...", when you have new commits there as well, or Dockingbird can't tell). It says "too" only when this sync took the agents' commits; after "up to date." or "sent your 1 commit", the line is the same without it ("My App (main) is behind: git switch main, then dockingbird sync"). A branch you made under a deleted branch's name is never called behind there: its line says what `status` says, with the sync that asks first ("My App (feature/x) has a deleted branch's name, so sync asks first: git switch feature/x, then dockingbird sync"). On a branch no agent has worked on yet, sync says so and names those branches the same way, without "too" ("No agent has worked on feature/notes yet." and "My App (main) is behind: git switch main, then dockingbird sync", or "has new commits from the agents"), and says "Start one: dockingbird claude" only when nothing of the checkout waits; it exits 1 either way.

- **Taking the agents' commits.** Their branch arrives as a git bundle, read with `index-pack --strict` into the named ref `dockingbird/<branch>`. When you are behind, sync takes the agents' commits at once: it fast-forwards your branch and names each commit with the agent that shared it, from Dockingbird's own record, never the author field. When you both have new commits, it stops so you can look first: `git log -p main..dockingbird/main` shows theirs. It sends only what this checkout lacks when it can, and the whole history once when that is refused.

heading: Operator guide > Sync
summary: - **Turning a commit down.** Don't want an agent's commit? Undo it with a commit of your own: `git revert COMMIT`, then `dockingbird sync`, which sends your revert to the agents.
text:
- **Turning a commit down.** Don't want an agent's commit? Undo it with a commit of your own: `git revert COMMIT`, then `dockingbird sync`, which sends your revert to the agents. Resetting or deleting your branch doesn't remove it: the agents' copy keeps it, so the next sync brings it back. Made the branch again under its old name and said no to the agents' commits? `dockingbird sync --let-go` asks once, names what goes, and makes yours the branch; the agents' copies keep their work, but a copy built on the commits let go can't share until it syncs onto yours.

- **Your open edits.** Edits you haven't committed stay as they are. Only when the agents changed a file you are editing, ignored files included, does sync change nothing and name the files: commit or stash those, then run it again.

- **Both sides moved.** On a terminal, sync offers to merge theirs into yours ("Merge theirs into yours now? [Y/n]"). Yes runs your own `git merge` with sync's protections and then sends the merge to the agents. A conflict leaves the merge for you to finish, and a merge still in progress stops every later sync and start until you commit it. Without a terminal it shows the same "you and the agents both have new commits" heading and rows, then the look-first command and "When you are ready: git merge dockingbird/main, then dockingbird sync". Ctrl-C at the question merges nothing, prints those two lines and exits 130.

heading: Operator guide > Sync
summary: - **Sending yours.** Your commits go to the agents as a bundle (`repo advance` in Dockingbird), only what they lack.
text:
- **Sending yours.** Your commits go to the agents as a bundle (`repo advance` in Dockingbird), only what they lack. A symlink whose relative target stays inside the repo goes to the agents as it is. A branch that would bring in a symlink to an absolute path, one leaving the repo or pointing into `.git`, a chain of symlinks too long or looping, a symlink with an unusable target or in place of a git file, a submodule or a Git LFS file is refused before anything is bundled (and, on a start, before anything is set up), naming each such file with its kind and, for a symlink, where it points ("b-link -> ../../outside (symlink leaving the repo)"): at most 100, the rest counted, and the next ones listed once these are fixed. When the commits sync takes from the agents add a symlink or change where one points, sync notes each one with its target ("Note: the agents added or changed a symlink:"), for you to look at before you build or run anything.

- **Protections on your Mac.** Every git call sync makes in your checkout runs `/usr/bin/git` with a scrubbed environment, hooks off (`core.hooksPath=/dev/null`), fsmonitor off, submodule recursion off, git's automatic gc and maintenance off (so no background repack keeps running in your checkout after sync ends), no transport and `GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1`, so no LFS download or hook an agent chose runs here. Like your own `git pull`, sync follows the agents' `.gitattributes`: a filter or merge driver your own git config defines runs when they name it. When your hooks folder is inside the work tree and the incoming commits change it, sync merges nothing and names the files. When the agents changed `.gitattributes`, `.gitmodules` or `.lfsconfig`, sync shows the new lines: your own later git commands will follow them. Review the agents' commits before you build or run them.

- **Paused.** When the agents' copy of a branch was changed outside Dockingbird, sharing pauses and nothing is lost. `dockingbird status --verbose` shows what changed, and `dockingbird sync --accept 5555555` (the commit sync names) goes on from there.

heading: Operator guide > Sync
summary: - **When it can't finish.** A sync that Dockingbird or git could not finish says why and what to do (your checkout moved to another branch while it ran, your branch and the agents' copy share no history, a step took too long or got no answer, the agents' commits are over what Dockingbird takes at once, or your checkout has too many changed or untracked files for it to check), and only an error with no step of yours to take says an unexpected error stopped it (a git that fails is one, never "moved to another branch" or "share no history"); `--verbose` adds the code of either.
text: - **When it can't finish.** A sync that Dockingbird or git could not finish says why and what to do (your checkout moved to another branch while it ran, your branch and the agents' copy share no history, a step took too long or got no answer, the agents' commits are over what Dockingbird takes at once, or your checkout has too many changed or untracked files for it to check), and only an error with no step of yours to take says an unexpected error stopped it (a git that fails is one, never "moved to another branch" or "share no history"); `--verbose` adds the code of either. Such a stop that left your checkout as it was says "Nothing changed."; once sync has merged the agents' commits into your branch (you said yes, and sending the merge was refused as a move), a stop of its next attempt leaves that sentence out and its last line says the merge stays ("The merge of their commits stays. Review: git log -p c91f6c7..main", a command that names the branch, so it shows the merge wherever your checkout is by then). A `dockingbird sync --accept 5555555` that took too long may or may not have gone through: it says so, with `dockingbird status` as the step that finds out, then run it again.

heading: Operator guide > Status and stop
summary: `dockingbird status` shows every repo and branch, each agent's paths and how long it has been working, who waits for whom, today's shares, how far behind you are (or "you and the agents both have new commits", never "behind", when sync would merge, and "the agents have new commits" when Dockingbird can't tell whether you have new commits too), with a step that runs from where you stand (in a pane too narrow for the whole line, on the next line, two columns in like the rows): `dockingbird sync` for the branch you are on, "git switch main, then dockingbird sync" for another branch of the checkout you run it in, and `cd` to another checkout first, its path quoted as a shell needs, with `git switch` too when that checkout is on another branch (`--json` marks the heading you stand on with `here` and gives the whole step as its `next_step`), and "Needs your attention" for what it can't repair: each agent that stopped with its copy kept, with its pick-up command (the config's command it ran, for an agent that ran one on the bus, else its tool's, as in `dockingbird claude --as claude-1`), which runs from where you stand as a heading's step does ("Pick it up: git switch feature/r7, then dockingbird claude --as keep7" on main; `--json` gives the same `next_step`), a merge left in progress in your checkout, a crash, and a branch whose last start stopped because Dockingbird couldn't make the agents' copy of it, with why and the command that starts it again ("My App (main)   the last start failed 3 min ago: the clone of the agents' copy failed or ran out of time.

Try again: dockingbird claude"; a start you named carries its name in that command, `dockingbird codex --as reviewer`, so the same agent starts and not the next numbered one; the off screen shows it too), until a start on that branch gets going.

It ends with "Nothing needs your attention." whenever there is none of these, on the empty screen too.

With no agent working it says how to start one, "Start one here: dockingbird claude" when you run it in a repo `dockingbird claude` starts in, linked or not.

A repo where no agent works still shows its block when something was shared there today or your checkout is behind.

heading: Operator guide > Status and stop
summary: A branch you deleted with `git branch -d` is named "(feature/x, no longer in your checkout)" on its heading, on `status NAME`'s first line and on the off screen; when the agents shared commits there that you haven't synced, its heading says so, outside "Needs your attention", with the step that makes the branch again first ("the agents have new commits: git switch -c feature/x dockingbird/feature/x, then dockingbird sync"; counted, as "you are 2 commits behind", when your checkout has their head), and a branch you deleted after syncing it gets no step.
text:
A branch you deleted with `git branch -d` is named "(feature/x, no longer in your checkout)" on its heading, on `status NAME`'s first line and on the off screen; when the agents shared commits there that you haven't synced, its heading says so, outside "Needs your attention", with the step that makes the branch again first ("the agents have new commits: git switch -c feature/x dockingbird/feature/x, then dockingbird sync"; counted, as "you are 2 commits behind", when your checkout has their head), and a branch you deleted after syncing it gets no step.

A new branch you made under a deleted branch's name, while that branch's agents' commits wait, says so instead of how far behind you are, and ends on the sync that asks first: "My App (feature/x)   has a deleted branch's name, so sync asks first: dockingbird sync".

A copy kept on the branch you deleted is never shown as the new branch's own: its note says "keep9 stopped in My App (the feature/x you deleted)" and "To pick it up, say yes when it asks:", and `status keep9`'s first line marks it the same way.

The off screen can't tell, so it shows the place as it is: it reads no agents' head, and only that head tells a new branch from one that already has everything the agents shared, which links without a question.

`dockingbird status claude-1` shows that one agent: what it works on or waits for (or how it stopped), its commits not shared and files not committed by name (at most 5 of each, then "and N more"; Dockingbird reads them from the agent's copy itself, inside Docker), how to reconnect or pick it up (the pick-up from where you stand, as its note gives it), and where Dockingbird's log of it is (`logs/agents/claude-1-*.log`, once the agent ends).

It only looks: it reads `state.json`, `docker ps` and the coordinator's state, never starts Docker or Dockingbird, and never waits longer than `STATUS_DOCKER_TIMEOUT_S` (10 s).

Before the first run it says "Dockingbird isn't set up yet.

heading: Operator guide > Status and stop
summary: Start here: dockingbird claude" inside a repo, and how to get to one anywhere else (as `sync`, `stop`, `clean` and `logout` do then, setting nothing up), and while Docker or Dockingbird is off it shows the sign-ins and the kept work from its cache, each copy's pick-up from where you stand (a scratch agent's kept folder is listed once Dockingbird runs); with nothing linked yet (after a first `dockingbird login claude --api-key`, say) it ends with "Nothing is linked yet.
text:
Start here: dockingbird claude" inside a repo, and how to get to one anywhere else (as `sync`, `stop`, `clean` and `logout` do then, setting nothing up), and while Docker or Dockingbird is off it shows the sign-ins and the kept work from its cache, each copy's pick-up from where you stand (a scratch agent's kept folder is listed once Dockingbird runs); with nothing linked yet (after a first `dockingbird login claude --api-key`, say) it ends with "Nothing is linked yet.

Start here: dockingbird claude" inside a repo and "Nothing is linked yet. cd into a repo, then: dockingbird claude" anywhere else, and in a repo with no work kept, with "Start one here: dockingbird claude".

In a repo whose branch isn't linked yet and holds files the agents don't take, each of these start steps gives way to "myapp (main) can't be linked yet: it has 3 files the agents don't take.

See them: dockingbird claude" (after the first sentence alone: "Dockingbird isn't set up yet.", "Nothing is linked yet." or "No agents are working."): status checks the branch once, read only, within `STATUS_TREE_CHECK_BUDGET_MS` (2 s), and claims nothing when git is slower.

heading: Operator guide > Status and stop
summary: An agent whose container runs and whose tool hasn't started yet is `preparing` until the tool's first sign of life, with the step and how long it has taken: "claude-1   preparing: setting up the environment, {elapsed}" while its container sets up the versions its repo names, and ", no output for {quiet}" after it once the step's command has printed nothing for `BUILD_QUIET_S` (60 s) (`{elapsed}` and `{quiet}` stand for the times it shows, which depend on the repo and the network); an agent started before 0.5.0, or with the image's versions, says "setting up the environment" with the time since its start.
text: An agent whose container runs and whose tool hasn't started yet is `preparing` until the tool's first sign of life, with the step and how long it has taken: "claude-1   preparing: setting up the environment, {elapsed}" while its container sets up the versions its repo names, and ", no output for {quiet}" after it once the step's command has printed nothing for `BUILD_QUIET_S` (60 s) (`{elapsed}` and `{quiet}` stand for the times it shows, which depend on the repo and the network); an agent started before 0.5.0, or with the image's versions, says "setting up the environment" with the time since its start. `dockingbird status claude-1` adds a `toolchain` row after the model rows: the versions it started with ("Python 3.12.7 and Node 20.18.1", with "(locked)" when the checkout's `mise.lock` names every one of them), or "the image's versions". Under "Needs your attention", a running agent whose repo now asks for another version than it runs says so, with the restart that gives it the new one: "claude-1 runs Node 20.18.1; the repo now asks for 22.11.0. To restart it: dockingbird stop claude-1, then dockingbird claude --as claude-1" (`status` reads this from the agent's record and the repo's last look, which every start and every `dockingbird env` rewrites, and runs nothing); and an agent whose container couldn't set up its environment says that in place of a crash, with mise's last lines and its pick-up ("claude-1's environment couldn't be set up. Its last lines:"; when the checkout is untrusted and its mise config needs trust, it says so and offers `dockingbird trust`).

heading: Operator guide > Status and stop
summary: Under `--json`, every running agent's row (a preparing or retrying one too), and the line of `dockingbird status claude-1`, also carries the figures its supervisor writes in the agent's `summary.json`, after its model, effort and context: `phase`, `turns`, `turn_running`, `last_turn_at`, `last_turn`, `context_window`, `compact_at_asked`, `changed`, `untracked`, `screen_held`, `token_failed`, `sign_in_retry`, `bus_losses`, and the harness's last result, `result_input_tokens`, `result_cache_creation_tokens`, `result_cache_read_tokens`, `result_output_tokens`, `result_cost_usd` (in US dollars; Claude only), `result_turns`, `result_duration_ms` (in milliseconds) and `result_reasoning_output_tokens` (Codex only), each as the tool reported it and never summed (a Codex agent's token figures are its thread's running totals, from its last `turn.completed`, and its `result_turns` and `result_duration_ms`, which Codex names neither of, are the requests its last turn made, read from its rollout, and that turn's wall time), and the cumulative figures of its process (Claude) or thread (Codex): `model_usage`, a list of one object per model it sent requests to (`model`, `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `cache_read_tokens`, `cache_creation_tokens` and `cost_usd`, each null when it is no figure; a Claude agent's totals count its subagents' and its compaction requests' too, and the cost is Claude Code's own estimate; a Codex agent's are the sums of the requests its rollout records, a request's `input_tokens` being its whole prompt, cached tokens included, where Claude's are the uncached part, with no cost), `compactions`, the compaction events its stream wrote since its process started (Claude) or the compactions its thread's rollout records (Codex), and `api_retries` (Claude only), the API retry events its stream wrote since its process started.

Under `--json`, every running agent's row (a preparing or retrying one too), and the line of `dockingbird status claude-1`, also carries the figures its supervisor writes in the agent's `summary.json`, after its model, effort and context: `phase`, `turns`, `turn_running`, `last_turn_at`, `last_turn`, `context_window`, `compact_at_asked`, `changed`, `untracked`, `screen_held`, `token_failed`, `sign_in_retry`, `bus_losses`, and the harness's last result, `result_input_tokens`, `result_cache_creation_tokens`, `result_cache_read_tokens`, `result_output_tokens`, `result_cost_usd` (in US dollars; Claude only), `result_turns`, `result_duration_ms` (in milliseconds) and `result_reasoning_output_tokens` (Codex only), each as the tool reported it and never summed (a Codex agent's token figures are its thread's running totals, from its last `turn.completed`, and its `result_turns` and `result_duration_ms`, which Codex names neither of, are the requests its last turn made, read from its rollout, and that turn's wall time), and the cumulative figures of its process (Claude) or thread (Codex): `model_usage`, a list of one object per model it sent requests to (`model`, `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `cache_read_tokens`, `cache_creation_tokens` and `cost_usd`, each null when it is no figure; a Claude agent's totals count its subagents' and its compaction requests' too, and the cost is Claude Code's own estimate; a Codex agent's are the sums of the requests its rollout records, a request's `input_tokens` being its whole prompt, cached tokens included, where Claude's are the uncached part, with no cost), `compactions`, the compaction events its stream wrote since its process started (Claude) or the compactions its thread's rollout records (Codex), and `api_retries` (Claude only), the API retry events its stream wrote since its process started.

A Codex agent's `model_usage` and `compactions` are null until its rollout was read, and its `result_cost_usd` and `api_retries` stay null: Codex names no cost and no API retry in its stream or its rollout.

`phase` is the supervisor's word (`starting`, `running`, `exited` or `refused`), never the row's state; `compact_at_asked` is the compact point asked, beside `compact_at`, the point that applies.

Each is null, or false for a yes-or-no figure, when the summary holds none (`model_usage` is also null for a list of more than `MODEL_USAGE_MODELS_MAX` models, or one that names a model twice), and the screen shows none of them.

heading: Operator guide > Status and stop
summary: Under `--json`, the row of a running agent on the bus (not one at a terminal) also carries four figures for the requests other agents sent it that wait in its inbox, read from the first page of it: `pending`, how many review requests and tasks from other agents are open (pending or accepted; a status note or an alert is no wait, nor anything the host sent, the fleet scheduler's briefs among them; at most `PAGE_MAX_ITEMS`), and, for the oldest of them, `oldest_pending_s` (its age in whole seconds), `oldest_pending_from` (the sender's name) and `oldest_pending_subject` (printable, at most 120 characters); the three of the oldest are null when none waits, and all four are null when the inbox could not be read in time.
text:
Under `--json`, the row of a running agent on the bus (not one at a terminal) also carries four figures for the requests other agents sent it that wait in its inbox, read from the first page of it: `pending`, how many review requests and tasks from other agents are open (pending or accepted; a status note or an alert is no wait, nor anything the host sent, the fleet scheduler's briefs among them; at most `PAGE_MAX_ITEMS`), and, for the oldest of them, `oldest_pending_s` (its age in whole seconds), `oldest_pending_from` (the sender's name) and `oldest_pending_subject` (printable, at most 120 characters); the three of the oldest are null when none waits, and all four are null when the inbox could not be read in time.

That row also carries `resume`, how the agent picked up when it continued an earlier session: `native` (its own conversation), `stale` (an older one, since its last session saved nothing) or `packet` (a summary of it, since its conversation could not be restored), else null; the fleet scheduler briefs a `packet` agent again.

The screen shows none of them; `dockingbird status NAME` of a bus agent has one row for them, "inbox", such as "2 deliveries waiting, the oldest 6 min from review-1".

heading: Operator guide > Status and stop
summary: `dockingbird stop` asks before stopping working agents (`--yes` skips the question; without a terminal it refuses; any answer but yes prints "Nothing stopped." and exits 1, and Ctrl-C at the question prints it too and exits 130), then turns Dockingbird off and says what it stopped: "Stopped claude-1.
text: `dockingbird stop` asks before stopping working agents (`--yes` skips the question; without a terminal it refuses; any answer but yes prints "Nothing stopped." and exits 1, and Ctrl-C at the question prints it too and exits 130), then turns Dockingbird off and says what it stopped: "Stopped claude-1. Dockingbird is off until you next use it.", or with no agent running, "Stopped Dockingbird. It's off until you next use it." ("Nothing is running. Dockingbird is off." when it was off already). `dockingbird stop claude-1` stops one agent. Its work is kept, and the next `dockingbird claude --as claude-1` picks it up; when its copy is kept on another branch or in another checkout, the line says where and gives the step from where you stand ("keep9 isn't running. Its work is kept in My App (feature/r9)." and "To pick it up: git switch feature/r9, then dockingbird claude --as keep9"), as the restart line and status's notes of an agent that stopped unexpectedly do; after `git branch -m`, each names the branch as it is now, as status does. Every screen that names several agents (status, stop, update, login, logout, clean, the reconnect list) names them in the order they started.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet probe
summary: `dockingbird fleet probe` reads this Mac and its Docker once and prints what it found, a line per figure: its cores, memory and load against the load line (`FLEET_LOAD_LINE_PERCENT`, 130% of its cores), how busy its CPU is and how many cores are idle, its free and compressed memory and its swap, how busy its GPU is, Docker's CPUs and memory and what Docker's VM holds resident, the containers running and in all, the networks, then each kind of process (agents, coordinators, sidecars, other containers, Docker's VM, the harness host, tests, the system, PostgreSQL, the rest) with its CPU, memory and count.
