text: `dockingbird fleet probe` reads this Mac and its Docker once and prints what it found, a line per figure: its cores, memory and load against the load line (`FLEET_LOAD_LINE_PERCENT`, 130% of its cores), how busy its CPU is and how many cores are idle, its free and compressed memory and its swap, how busy its GPU is, Docker's CPUs and memory and what Docker's VM holds resident, the containers running and in all, the networks, then each kind of process (agents, coordinators, sidecars, other containers, Docker's VM, the harness host, tests, the system, PostgreSQL, the rest) with its CPU, memory and count. It shows numbers and those kinds only, never a name a program printed. With `--json` it prints one line, whose `fields` hold the whole reading: every container of every home by its id, with its labels and figures, the heaviest process names (`FLEET_PROBE_PROCESS_NAMES_MAX`, 200), the disk Docker's data is on, and `unread`, each part it couldn't read with why (a timeout, an output too large, a shape it doesn't know, no GPU, no Docker, or a failed command), whose figures are `null` there and "unread" on the screen, which then ends with "Not read:" and the same parts. `dockingbird fleet probe --disk` also reads Docker's disk use, which can take a while on a large image store. It only looks, as `dockingbird status` does: it starts, stops and changes nothing, Docker included, gives each read at most `FLEET_PROBE_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_S` (20 s) and stops after `FLEET_PROBE_TIMEOUT_S` (60 s) in all, and ends 0 with whatever it read. It runs on a Mac only, and `dockingbird -h` doesn't list it.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet probe
summary: `dockingbird fleet read-home` reads the Dockingbird home it runs under (the default one, or the one `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` names) once and prints what it found, a line per figure: the home's folder, this CLI's version and whether Dockingbird is ready there ("ready", "not ready" or "not set up"), how many agents the home has and how many are in each state, how many rows wait in its inbox, and its open questions with the oldest one's age.
text: `dockingbird fleet read-home` reads the Dockingbird home it runs under (the default one, or the one `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` names) once and prints what it found, a line per figure: the home's folder, this CLI's version and whether Dockingbird is ready there ("ready", "not ready" or "not set up"), how many agents the home has and how many are in each state, how many rows wait in its inbox, and its open questions with the oldest one's age. It reads them with the home's own commands, run by the program the home records (as `dockingbird fleet scrape` runs them), for that home in its own folder with nothing else of your environment, so what it reports is the same wherever you run it: `dockingbird status --json`, then, only while Dockingbird is ready there, `dockingbird inbox --all --json` (reading the inbox can start Docker or Dockingbird, so a home that isn't ready gets no inbox read, and its inbox is "unread"), each given at most `FLEET_HOME_READ_TIMEOUT_S` (30 s). It shows the home's folder, numbers and fixed words only, never a name, subject or other text the two commands printed. With `--json` it prints one line, whose `fields` hold the whole read: every agent by name with its tool, state, session, model and effort (asked and reported), context, claims, questions, last error and kept copy, the counts by state of all its agents, listed or not, the open questions, every open inbox row, at most `FLEET_HOME_ROWS_MAX` (200) agents and rows each with the rest counted, and `unread`, the inbox when it couldn't read it, with why (Dockingbird not ready there, a timeout, an output too large, a shape it doesn't know, or a failed command); the screen then ends with "Not read from this home:" and the same part. A home whose folder doesn't exist yet is "not set up", and nothing runs for it. Without the home's status there is nothing to report: it says why and ends 1; otherwise it ends 0 with whatever it read. It starts, stops and changes nothing itself, `dockingbird fleet read-home --disk` is refused (`--disk` is the probe's), and `dockingbird -h` doesn't list it. The fleet's collector will run it for each home.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet probe
summary: `dockingbird fleet scrape` prints the figures of each running agent of the home it runs under in the Prometheus text format: the same lines, with the same values, that the agent's container serves at `/metrics` on its port `METRICS_PORT` (9464) inside its own network, which no port of this Mac reaches, under the home's labels: `profile`, then the agent's name (`agent`), its session (`session`) and its tool (`tool`).
text: `dockingbird fleet scrape` prints the figures of each running agent of the home it runs under in the Prometheus text format: the same lines, with the same values, that the agent's container serves at `/metrics` on its port `METRICS_PORT` (9464) inside its own network, which no port of this Mac reaches, under the home's labels: `profile`, then the agent's name (`agent`), its session (`session`) and its tool (`tool`). It reads them from the home's `dockingbird status --json`, run as `dockingbird fleet read-home` runs it (in the home's own folder, with nothing else of your environment, at most `FLEET_HOME_READ_TIMEOUT_S`, 30 s), by the program the home records, the `program` file in the home, which each `dockingbird start` and `dockingbird update` writes (one line: the absolute path of the `dockingbird` script that ran, its links resolved), so one exporter reads every home of a host whatever version each runs, and a home moved to another build is read right after its first start or update there; a home with no such file is read by this command's own script, and a record that is no executable file of yours that nobody else can write is `program-invalid`: the read says so and runs nothing. It writes the text itself, so it connects to no container, and an agent's figures are as fresh as the last ones its container wrote: its last turn's end, its last renewal or its last change, seconds to a minute behind. The page holds each family's `# HELP` and `# TYPE` lines once, then one sample line per agent in the order status lists them, and one `# EOF` line ends it. A kept copy, a stopped or crashed agent and an agent with no session yet print nothing. With `dockingbird fleet scrape --json` it prints one line, whose `fields` hold when it read the status (`read_at`), the home's folder and profile, every agent by name with its session, tool, state and labels (`null` for one that prints nothing), at most `FLEET_HOME_ROWS_MAX` (200) agents with the rest counted, and the text as its lines (`exposition`). A home whose status it can't read, or where Dockingbird isn't ready, has no figures to print: it says why and ends 1. It starts, stops and changes nothing itself, `dockingbird fleet scrape --disk` is refused (`--disk` is the probe's), and `dockingbird -h` doesn't list it.

heading: Operator guide > Every agent on every host
summary: `dockingbird fleet agents` lists every Dockingbird agent running on this computer, in every home and on every version, with its home, version, mode and whether it has a screen, read from Docker alone: it runs no Dockingbird command in those homes and changes nothing.
text:
`dockingbird fleet agents` lists every Dockingbird agent running on this computer, in every home and on every version, with its home, version, mode and whether it has a screen, read from Docker alone: it runs no Dockingbird command in those homes and changes nothing. This computer is `local` in every fleet line, as in the GUI ("local: 5 agents running in 3 homes"; with `--json`, its rows' `host` is `null`), and a fresh install shows `local`, its homes and its agents, from nothing you wrote. `dockingbird fleet agents --host NAME` does the same on another host your `hosts.toml` names, in one call given at most `FLEET_PROBE_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_S` (20 s); one that can't be read says why and ends 1, and a NAME the file lacks is refused with the command that adds it. `dockingbird fleet hosts` lists the file's hosts, or says that none is set and how to add one.

These commands add, rename and forget the hosts of the file:

```
dockingbird [--json] fleet hosts set NAME --ssh DEST [--path PATH] [--docker-host URL] [--home HOME]
dockingbird [--json] fleet hosts set NAME --gcloud VM --zone ZONE --project PROJECT
dockingbird [--json] fleet hosts rename OLD NEW
dockingbird [--json] fleet hosts forget NAME
```

`dockingbird fleet hosts set NAME --ssh DEST` adds a host. It first reaches the host over your own ssh and reads its Docker and its Dockingbird homes exactly as `dockingbird fleet agents --host NAME` reads them, the same call under the same bound, which starts and changes nothing there; only once that read succeeded does it write the host into `hosts.toml`, then it prints the host's rows, as `fleet agents` and the GUI will show them, and says so ("lab: ssh lab.example, saved in ~/.local/share/dockingbird/hosts.toml."). A NAME the file already has is updated the same way ("updated in"): its route is replaced, and its home tables and its place in the file are kept. When the host can't be read, nothing is saved: the command ends 1 with what went wrong and what to try yourself first (`ssh DEST docker version` for a host over ssh), and you run `set` again once that works. NAME is lowercase letters, digits and dashes, at most `TEXT_FIELD_MAX_CHARS` (56) characters, and never `local`, this computer's own name.

heading: Operator guide > Every agent on every host
summary: DEST is any destination your own ssh reaches without asking, with your own configuration and agent; a host that doesn't answer within `FLEET_SSH_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_S` (15 s) is not reached.
text:
DEST is any destination your own ssh reaches without asking, with your own configuration and agent; a host that doesn't answer within `FLEET_SSH_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_S` (15 s) is not reached. For a Mac whose login there doesn't find Docker Desktop's `docker` on its `PATH`, `--path PATH` sets the `PATH` the commands there run with (folders that hold that `docker`), and `--docker-host URL` sets their `DOCKER_HOST`, for Docker Desktop's socket; the ssh refusal says when to add them. `--home HOME` adds a `[[host.home]]` table that names a home of the host by its name (`dockingbird homes` lists them there), without checking that it exists: a home is made by the first command that runs in it, and a second `set` with the same name changes nothing. A Linux host is added the same way, with Docker Engine there.

A Compute Engine VM is added with `dockingbird fleet hosts set NAME --gcloud VM --zone ZONE --project PROJECT` and reached through your own `gcloud compute ssh`; another cloud's VM is a host over ssh. A stopped VM must be started first: `set` can't read it, and its refusal says so, with `gcloud compute ssh VM -- docker version` to try. The `gcloud` it runs is the one on your `PATH`, else one where the Google Cloud SDK installs it; when yours is elsewhere, name it by hand as the host's `gcloud_program` in the file, which a later `set` of that host keeps while the host stays on `--gcloud` and drops, with the other gcloud keys, when it moves to `--ssh`.

heading: Operator guide > Every agent on every host
summary: `dockingbird fleet hosts rename OLD NEW` gives a host a new name in the file, its home tables kept, and `dockingbird fleet hosts forget NAME` removes its entry and its home tables.
text:
`dockingbird fleet hosts rename OLD NEW` gives a host a new name in the file, its home tables kept, and `dockingbird fleet hosts forget NAME` removes its entry and its home tables. They change the file alone: never the fleet pool's records or a swarm definition that names the host (the rename's second line says so); the GUI keeps a host's group folded or open under its new name after a rename it runs. With a `fleet.toml` in your home, each reads the pool before it changes the file and refuses a host the pool holds, since the pool's row keeps the name: drain and remove it there (`dockingbird fleet hosts drain NAME`, then `dockingbird fleet hosts remove NAME`), rename it in the file, then enrol it under the new name; a fleet database that doesn't answer, or turns the login down, ends the command as it ends every fleet scheduler command (69 or 78), the file unchanged. Without a `fleet.toml`, nothing but the file is read.

`hosts.toml` in your Dockingbird home is the record: one `[[host]]` per host, its `name` and one route, `ssh` (with `path` and `docker_host`) or `gcloud`, `zone` and `project` (with `gcloud_program`). It may still be edited by hand. The three commands write it whole (0600) under the lock `locks/hosts.lock`, so a second command meanwhile says another is changing the file and changes nothing; a write keeps every table in its order, but loses the file's comments and the order of the keys inside a table. A home's own program is named by hand: a `[[host.home]]` table under its host (`path`, the home's folder there, and `program`, its `dockingbird`), or a top-level `[[home]]` table for a home of this computer; `set` and `rename` keep them with their host, and the send line below and the fleet worker read them.

A host has one name across your file, the fleet pool and swarm definitions. A pool host is reached under its pool name, its worker's `--host`, so `set` it under that name; and the admitter's home names a gcloud pool host under that same name, since the admitter finds the VM to start by the pool's name in its own `hosts.toml`. A pool host your file doesn't name is in `fleet queue` and not in `fleet hosts` or `fleet agents`, where `--host NAME` of it gives the `set` command that adds it.

heading: Operator guide > Every agent on every host
summary: The Dockingbird GUI's sidebar runs the same three commands: "add a host…" on its DOCKINGBIRD heading asks for the route, the destination and the name, and for a host over ssh also "PATH for docker there (or empty)" and "docker host URL there (or empty)", its `--path` and `--docker-host`, each optional (an empty answer leaves it out); "rename…" on a host's heading asks "rename OLD: its new name" in a popup that offers the old name (the first key you type replaces it), and "forget…" forgets it once you type `y`; `local` has neither.
text:
The Dockingbird GUI's sidebar runs the same three commands: "add a host…" on its DOCKINGBIRD heading asks for the route, the destination and the name, and for a host over ssh also "PATH for docker there (or empty)" and "docker host URL there (or empty)", its `--path` and `--docker-host`, each optional (an empty answer leaves it out); "rename…" on a host's heading asks "rename OLD: its new name" in a popup that offers the old name (the first key you type replaces it), and "forget…" forgets it once you type `y`; `local` has neither.

`dockingbird fleet attach --container ID` opens one of the agents `fleet agents` lists in your terminal (with `--host NAME`, one on that host): its screen, which you leave with Ctrl-] then Ctrl-\ while it keeps running, or, for an agent with no screen, its log as it grows and a line to send it a message, which runs that home's own `dockingbird send -- NAME TEXT` when `hosts.toml` names that program (`[[host.home]]` with `path` and `program`, or `[[home]]` on this computer). When the log of an agent on another host ends, ssh's own line may follow it: "Connection to NAME closed." The Dockingbird GUI on your Mac reads them too and lists every agent under its host and home; a click opens it the same way. `dockingbird -h` doesn't list `fleet`.

Each agent also shows its state, read from its home's coordinator in the same call: `working`, `idle`, `asks` with how many questions it waits for (a question an agent asked without waiting is not counted), or `unknown` with the reason (`no-coordinator`, `timeout`, `refused`, `unexpected-shape`, `not-read`, `no-session`). The read runs only in the coordinators of homes whose agents run, and changes nothing there.

heading: Operator guide > Joining a computer to the fleet
summary: A fleet is one control plane and the computers that join it.
text:
A fleet is one control plane and the computers that join it. The control plane is a Dockingbird home of its own, made for the fleet; every other computer joins it from one of its homes with a bundle the control plane makes for that computer, and leaves it the same way. The commands below run on each computer's own host, as every other command does. The word names two things here: the fleet scheduler (`dockingbird fleet ...`, the pool of hosts that places swarms, each host under the name `fleet hosts set NAME` gave it) and the control plane's fleet (the computers that joined with `node join`, each under the label `cp token --host LABEL` gave it); a computer carries both names, chosen apart, so a host the scheduler calls `lab-1` may be `lab` to the control plane, and its agents' fleet sessions carry the label.

```bash
# On the control plane's home, once, with its IPv4 address on your tailnet:
dockingbird cp init --hub-address <ipv4>
# For each computer: the first line on the control plane's home, the second on that computer's home:
dockingbird cp token --host <label> --platform macos|linux
dockingbird node join
# On the control plane's home, at any time:
dockingbird cp status
# To join a computer again (a lost home, a removed computer):
dockingbird cp remove <label>
dockingbird cp token --host <label> --platform macos|linux
dockingbird node leave
dockingbird node join
# Once every computer is removed:
dockingbird cp off
```

`cp init` turns the control plane's home into it, given the hub's address: the IPv4 address on your tailnet at which the other computers reach it. It makes the control plane's key, keeps it on that home's state volume beside the hub's address and configuration, and records its public key; a home already initialized refuses it.

heading: Operator guide > Joining a computer to the fleet
summary: `cp token` adds one computer, given its label and its platform (`macos` or `linux`).
text:
`cp token` adds one computer, given its label and its platform (`macos` or `linux`). The label names the computer in every fleet agent's name it holds: one to eight lowercase letters and digits, starting with a letter. A label a computer in the fleet already holds, or one an agent of the project is named under, is refused. It prints one line, the bundle: the computer's hub, node id, label, key and token, shown this once and stored nowhere on the control plane, which keeps only the computer's public key and its token's digest. Paste it into `node join` on that computer's home, which reads it from standard input.

`cp status` lists each computer on one line: its label, node id and platform, whether it joined, is waiting to join or was removed, its fleet version, how many of its agents have a fleet inbox, and how long ago the control plane last heard from one of them, by the control plane's clock. With `--json`, each computer's line also carries when it joined and when it was removed.

`cp remove` takes a computer out at once, with no precondition: it disables the computer, revokes its token, ends its fleet agents' sessions and names them, and drops the computer from the hub. A computer whose home was lost, or that was removed, joins again with a new bundle: `cp remove`, then `cp token` once more, and on that computer `node leave`, then `node join` with the new bundle. `cp off` turns the control plane back into a plain home once every computer is removed; while one is in the fleet it is refused.

**Before the first computer joins.** The hub listens on the control plane's computer on `NATS_PORT` (4222), which Docker publishes on that computer's loopback only. On that computer, serve the port to your tailnet with the first line below. A member that is not a device of yours on the tailnet, such as a computer in a cloud under a tag, also needs the grant on the second line in your tailnet's policy, with its tag and the control plane's device in place of the placeholders. Frames between computers are as private as the tailnet.

```text
tailscale serve --bg --tcp 4222 tcp://127.0.0.1:4222
{"src": ["tag:<the member's tag>"], "dst": ["<the control plane's device>"], "ip": ["tcp:4222"]}
```

heading: Operator guide > Joining a computer to the fleet
summary: **After the control plane's computer restarts.** The first `dockingbird cp status` on the control plane's home starts the control plane and its hub again, as the first command after a restart starts any home, then lists the computers; the fleet sessions survive as rows, and every member's fleet-link reconnects by itself.
text:
**After the control plane's computer restarts.** The first `dockingbird cp status` on the control plane's home starts the control plane and its hub again, as the first command after a restart starts any home, then lists the computers; the fleet sessions survive as rows, and every member's fleet-link reconnects by itself.

**Updating a fleet.** Update the control plane's home first, then each member, each with `dockingbird update` as "Update" says. Until a member updates, every fleet frame of it is refused with `NODE_VERSION_MISMATCH` ("This computer runs Dockingbird 0.15.2 and the control plane runs 0.15.3, so fleet messages wait until they match."), and its agents keep working on their home, without the fleet.

**What a member's agents get.** On a joined home, `dockingbird start` opens each agent's fleet session on the control plane after the agent's own session and before its container, and the agent gets a fleet inbox there beside its own; its fleet name is the computer's label, a dash and its name. An agent whose tools include `bus_send` gets ten more: `fleet_send`, `fleet_inbox`, `fleet_read`, `fleet_ack`, `fleet_wait`, `fleet_thread`, `fleet_withdraw`, `fleet_artifact_put`, `fleet_artifact_get` and `fleet_whoami`. `fleet_send` reaches a fleet agent by its fleet name, an agent of the control plane's home by its name, or, with no `to`, `parent`, the operator on the control plane's home, where `dockingbird questions` lists a `question` sent to it and `dockingbird answer ROW` answers it. The agent reads both inboxes, the more urgent delivery first, and a choice its tool puts up or a plan to approve is asked on the control plane first and on its own home when the control plane does not take it. When the control plane does not answer at the start, the agent starts all the same and the start says so ("notes-1 has no fleet inbox yet: the control plane didn't answer. It works here as usual and gets one once the control plane answers."). On the member, `dockingbird status` shows under each running agent `fleet: <label>-<name>, heartbeat <age>, asks <n>` (the open questions of its fleet session), `fleet: not open` while its fleet session is not open yet, or `fleet: none`. What does not cross: a home's work, runs, claims and publication stay the home's, a fleet thread and a home thread are two threads, a message sent on one store is never seen on the other, and a home's own `questions` lists none of the fleet's.

heading: Operator guide > Joining a computer to the fleet
summary: **Limits.** A computer's label is at most `HOST_LABEL_MAX_CHARS` (8) characters.
text:
**Limits.** A computer's label is at most `HOST_LABEL_MAX_CHARS` (8) characters. An agent's name on a joined home is at most `SLUG_MAX_CHARS` (63) less the label's length and its dash; a start of a longer one is refused with `FLEET_NAME_TOO_LONG`. The control plane's overview lists at most `STATUS_LIST_MAX_ROWS` (100) fleet sessions and says `truncated` past it, in the `Fleet` section of `dockingbird status` on the control plane's home and in `dockingbird cp status`, and a fleet agent it does not list is unknown to a command that names it. A bundle decodes to at most `NODE_BUNDLE_MAX_BYTES` (4096 bytes). A fleet call waits at most `NATS_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_S` (30 s) for its answer, and an agent's own fleet inbox reads and heartbeats at most `AGENT_PERIODIC_RPC_TIMEOUT_S` (10 s). A member's fleet-link finds a silent control plane within (`NATS_PING_MAX` + 1) times `NATS_PING_INTERVAL_S`, 40 s, then reconnects by itself, and fleet calls are refused at once meanwhile. A message to a fleet agent whose home is asleep or offline waits on the control plane's store until that home reads it, at most `PENDING_DELIVERIES_MAX` (200) for one agent. The hub takes at most `NATS_MAX_CONNECTIONS` (1024) connections, one for each member's fleet-link and one for the control plane. A fleet attachment is at most `ARTIFACT_MAX_BYTES` (1048576 bytes).

**A computer in a cloud.** A computer in a cloud that the fleet scheduler places swarms on may join like any other, on four conditions: its credential acts for its own home only, opening fleet sessions under its own label and reading the replies to its own inbox; the credential lives only in `<home>/fleet/container/` and the fleet-link's read-only bind, never in an agent's container, a log or a command line; `dockingbird cp remove <label>` cuts it off at once with no precondition, and `dockingbird node leave` on it removes the credential; and its fleet sessions expire with their hours. A compromised member can send instructions to any agent of the fleet, including ones whose grants reach repositories, and read what is addressed to its own agents, attachments included; it cannot read another computer's inboxes, the harness's sign-in or either database. `dockingbird cp remove <label>` ends it.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: The fleet scheduler queues swarms on the fleet's hosts and admits each where its reservation fits and the host's live gate is green, by priority, then age.
text:
The fleet scheduler queues swarms on the fleet's hosts and admits each where its reservation fits and the host's live gate is green, by priority, then age.

Every fleet scheduler command reads this computer's org login first: the org pointer, `~/.config/dockingbird/org.toml` (under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME` when that names a folder from `/`), which names the fleet database's `host` (the address the hosts reach it at), its `port` and `database` (`dockingbird_fleet` by default), the `project` that the leases of `fleet_admin` count against, and the role each kind of command connects as: `user` for your own commands (`fleet_admin`, the role that owns the fleet database, for its admin, your own login role for every other person, their coordinators and runners included), `worker` for a machine's worker and `admitter` for the admitter.

It never holds a password: each role's password is its line of `~/.pgpass` (or of the file `PGPASSFILE` names), PostgreSQL's own password file, which `psql` reads too; that file must be yours and readable by you alone (`chmod 600`), a file anyone else can read is refused, and no refusal ever shows a password.

`dockingbird org login db.example.net:5433 --as user --role fleet_admin` writes both, asking for the password without echo, or reading it whole from standard input with `--password-stdin` (a password is never a word of the command line); `dockingbird org status` shows the login and connects once as `user`, and `dockingbird org logout` takes it away (`--as worker` takes one kind's).

A command with no org login ends 78, naming `dockingbird org login HOST --as user --role ROLE`; one whose kind has no role in the pointer, or whose role has no line in `~/.pgpass`, ends 78 naming the login to run.

Without an org pointer, a command falls back to the `fleet.toml` of your Dockingbird home.

If that file holds a `password`, the command refuses it.

It connects nothing (`fleet run` runs no command).

It names the file and prints the line that moves the login: `dockingbird org login --from-fleet-toml --as worker`.

Use `--as user` or `--as admitter` for the other kinds, whichever kind that home's commands connect as.

The command ends 78.

Running that line reads the file, moves its login into the pointer and `~/.pgpass`, and removes the password from the file after you answer yes (`--yes` where there is no terminal).

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: When both files exist, the command reads the pointer and prints a line saying it ignored the file.
text:
When both files exist, the command reads the pointer and prints a line saying it ignored the file.

Every command opens its own connection and waits at most `FLEET_DB_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_S` (5 s) for the database.

Two cases end 69: the database does not answer, or it ends the work for a passing reason such as a restart or too many connections.

The command then names the database's host and the role it tried, and quotes the connection's own words for the failure.

A database that answers no is a different case: the login or the database's roles are wrong, and the database is up.

A wrong password, or a role or database it doesn't have, is refused with that role and the database's words.

So is an error code once connected.

Both end 78.

A refusal sent before the password is asked, because the database's access rules don't list this computer, reads as no answer, with the database's own words on the line.

Install the fleet in the order below, before you run the first fleet command. Step one is the fleet database, on PostgreSQL 18, and its admin role. Run these three statements as the cluster's superuser: `CREATE ROLE fleet_admin LOGIN CREATEROLE;`, `CREATE DATABASE dockingbird_fleet OWNER fleet_admin;` and `\password fleet_admin`. The superuser does nothing else in this install. PostgreSQL 16 and later give a role with `CREATEROLE` the `ADMIN OPTION` on every role it creates, so `fleet_admin` makes, grants, revokes and drops the fleet's groups itself. The fleet's roles log in over TCP with passwords, so the cluster needs two settings. `listen_addresses` in `postgresql.conf` names the loopback address and the address the hosts connect to, on the private network they share. PostgreSQL reads it at its restart. `pg_hba.conf` gets `host` lines for `dockingbird_fleet`, from the loopback address and the hosts' addresses on that network, with the method `scram-sha-256`, PostgreSQL 18's default for the passwords it stores. PostgreSQL reads that file at its reload.

Then its schemas, once per database, as `fleet_admin`: log in as it on the computer you run it from (`dockingbird org login db.example.net:5433 --as user --role fleet_admin`, below), then run `dockingbird org create`.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: It makes, in one transaction, the `fleet` schema with its row-level security, the `org` schema (the organisation's projects, the model and effort of each kind of role, its persons and their projects), the `work` schema (the organisation's work queue, see "The work queue") and the group roles `fleet_submitter` and `fleet_worker` where the cluster has none yet, none able to log in, and says the store's version, the last migration it carries; run again, it says the store is current, and a role that is no member of `fleet_admin` is refused (exit 77).
text:
It makes, in one transaction, the `fleet` schema with its row-level security, the `org` schema (the organisation's projects, the model and effort of each kind of role, its persons and their projects), the `work` schema (the organisation's work queue, see "The work queue") and the group roles `fleet_submitter` and `fleet_worker` where the cluster has none yet, none able to log in, and says the store's version, the last migration it carries; run again, it says the store is current, and a role that is no member of `fleet_admin` is refused (exit 77).

A fleet database made by an earlier build is upgraded instead, once, after the update, by the role that owns the `fleet` schema's tables (`SELECT DISTINCT tableowner FROM pg_tables WHERE schemaname = 'fleet'` names it): `dockingbird org create` as `fleet_admin` where `fleet_admin` owns them, which applies each migration the database lacks, each in one transaction, and names the version it reached; else the role that owns them applies the migrations, and no customer command does that yet; afterwards `dockingbird org create` says the store is current.

A worker or the admitter at a build whose migrations the store lacks refuses to start, naming a migration the store lacks and `dockingbird org create` (`FLEET_STORE_BEHIND`); under its service manager's restart loop such a worker publishes no sample, so after `HOST_STALE_S` (180 seconds) its host is stale and its swarms are interrupted until `org create` migrates the store and the sample returns: run `org create` at the new build before any worker or the admitter restarts at it.

A worker or an admitter of an earlier build keeps running against a store a later build migrated, unless that migration's row in [Migrations and older workers](#migrations-and-older-workers), below, says it restarts first.

Then restart every machine's worker that runs swarms and the admitter at the new build, and only then use `fleet retire`, `add`, `replace` or `prune`: a worker still at the earlier build reads a retired, retiring, picked-up or held agent as gone and interrupts its swarm.

Move the workers first, each publishing one sample at the new build, then the admitter and the submitters: a `fleet submit` at the new build refuses every swarm whose hosts' workers have not yet published their homes' checkouts.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: Then the login roles, in `psql -d dockingbird_fleet` as `fleet_admin`: one admin, one login for each machine's worker and one for each person; no project has a login of its own.
text:
Then the login roles, in `psql -d dockingbird_fleet` as `fleet_admin`: one admin, one login for each machine's worker and one for each person; no project has a login of its own.

The admin connects as `fleet_admin` itself, the one login the admin's machines and the admitter share.

Each machine of the pool gets its own: `CREATE ROLE "fleet_worker_<host>" LOGIN;`, `GRANT fleet_worker TO "fleet_worker_<host>";` and `INSERT INTO fleet.role_host (role_name, host) VALUES ('fleet_worker_<host>', '<host>');`, `<host>` its name in the pool (its worker's `--host`).

Each person gets their own: `CREATE ROLE "<person>" LOGIN;`, then `dockingbird org people add <person> --account <account>` records the person in the store, and `dockingbird org members add <person> --project <slug>` makes them a member of each project they act for.

The projects' groups are `fleet_admin`'s to make and to grant: it may grant, revoke and drop `fleet_submitter`, `fleet_worker` and each project's group `fleet_submitter_<project>` it makes.

A fleet database made before this release, whose groups the superuser made, needs these lines once, as the cluster's superuser: `ALTER ROLE fleet_admin CREATEROLE;`, `GRANT fleet_submitter TO fleet_admin WITH ADMIN TRUE, INHERIT FALSE, SET FALSE;` and, for each project group it holds, `GRANT "fleet_submitter_<project>" TO fleet_admin WITH ADMIN TRUE, INHERIT FALSE, SET FALSE;`: a group the superuser made gives `fleet_admin` no right to grant it by itself.

Give each login its password with psql's `\password` (`\password fleet_admin`, `\password "fleet_worker_<host>"`, `\password "<person>"`), which asks for it and sends only its hash, so the password itself reaches no statement and no server log: paste it from your own secret store, and give it to `dockingbird org login HOST --as user --role ROLE` (or the kind its commands connect as) on each computer that logs in as that role, which keeps it in that user's `~/.pgpass` alone: no TOML file holds it, and `psql` reads the same line.

A machine's worker connects as `fleet_worker_<host>`, whose `fleet.role_host` row names that same host.

A person acts for a project as a member of its group.

`fleet submit` and `fleet run` take the group of the project they act for, `fleet_submitter_<project>`, before they write anything; a person who is not its member, or a project with no group yet, is refused, nothing recorded, naming the person, the project and `dockingbird org members add <person> --project <slug>`, which makes the group when the project has none yet (a project `dockingbird init` registered), and the command ends 77.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: `fleet_admin` takes no group and acts for any project.
text:
`fleet_admin` takes no group and acts for any project.

Reading the queue and the controls take no group: a person sees and acts on the workloads of every project they are a member of, and of no other.

A host's or a project's name may hold `-`, so a role name holding one is written in double quotes.

Each machine and each person then logs in once, as each kind its commands connect as: `dockingbird org login db.example.net:5433 --as user --role fleet_admin --project myapp` on the admin's machines (`--project` where the admin's leases run), `--as admitter --role fleet_admin` on the admitter's machine, `--as worker --role fleet_worker_<host>` for a machine's worker, and `--as user --role <person>` on each person's computers, their coordinators' and runners' included, each with `--database` where the cluster's differs from `dockingbird_fleet` and the address's port where its port does; one login serves every Dockingbird home of that user on the computer, and `dockingbird org status` checks it. A machine's worker also reads `hosts.toml` in its home. The file holds one `[[home]]` table for each home the worker starts agents in. A table names its home in one of two ways. `name` points at the home `homes/<name>` of the worker's user, whose `program` is that home's own program file unless the table names one. The older way is `path`, that home's folder, with `program`, that home's own `dockingbird`. The worker runs that program's `start` there. A third key, `clones`, is optional: an absolute folder where the worker keeps one clone per repository and branch it starts swarms from. `path` may be spelled as the file system folds it. The worker identifies the home by its real path, as the home's own `dockingbird` does, and logs the real path at start when the spellings differ.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: Last comes the checkout a swarm starts in.
text: Last comes the checkout a swarm starts in. Each home the worker starts agents in links one checkout of the `[source]` repository, on any branch, in a folder whose last part is the repository's name (for `example-org/example-app`, a folder named `example-app`). Sign the home in first if it isn't yet: `dockingbird login claude --here`, with `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` naming it. Then, in the checkout, `dockingbird start --as fleet-link` links it. Given no task, that command starts an agent that waits and runs no turn. `dockingbird stop fleet-link --yes` stops that agent, and the link stays. From then on the worker starts a swarm in the first of three places that applies. First, a clone of its own of the swarm's branch, when the home's `[[home]]` in `hosts.toml` names `clones` and the clone is already under it (`<clones>/<branch, its slashes dashes>-<7 hex digits>/<repository name>`). Second, the home's linked checkout on the swarm's branch, when exactly one exists. When more than one checkout is on that branch, the swarm is held (`many`). Third, with `clones`, a new clone of its own there. It is made from the checkout the home links on any branch (its objects and `origin`) and fetched over `https` or `ssh` with your own git configuration and credentials (the worker's `HOME`, `PATH` and ssh agent). The swarm's first start links that clone. The pass never places a swarm on a host whose placed home has no checkout of the repository; `fleet why` names the home and `no_seed`. Four cases hold the swarm (`no_checkout`; `fleet why ID` names which): a start that finds no checkout to fetch from, a fetch git refuses (an unpushed branch, a remote your git cannot reach, an `origin` that is a local folder or a `git://` URL), a clone folder it cannot make (a read-only or full disk), and a clone of its own switched to another branch. Fix the cause, then run `dockingbird fleet release ID`. Every start attempt, the one `fleet release` makes included, first fetches and fast-forwards a clone of its own from its `origin`, so a fix you pushed reaches the start; a clone that cannot fast-forward (it holds commits not yet pushed) is used as it is, and the worker's log says so.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: `dockingbird fleet submit swarm.toml` checks a swarm definition (its project, key, priority, source, placement and roles, each brief read under the definition's folder) against the pool and queues it: `<id> pending, position <n>`.
text:
`dockingbird fleet submit swarm.toml` checks a swarm definition (its project, key, priority, source, placement and roles, each brief read under the definition's folder) against the pool and queues it: `<id> pending, position <n>`.

A definition your project sent before with the same key answers that first swarm instead.

A `[[role]]` names a `model` or an `effort` only to override them: `fleet submit` takes each from the role itself, else from the repository's `.dockingbird/project.toml` (`[roles.<kind>]`, when its `harness` is the role's), else from your organisation's store, whose rows `dockingbird org roles` lists and an admin sets with `dockingbird org roles set <kind> --harness claude --model <model>` (and `--effort`), and refuses a role that none of them gives one.

A role's kind is its `kind`, any slug, else `reviewer` for a role that reviews, `tester` for one that tests and `implementer` for any other, as the role library's `index.toml` names them; a role whose entry names any of `use`, `instructions`, `connections`, `subagents`, `send_to`, `workspace`, `tools`, `egress`, `allow`, `env` or `skills` (the next paragraph) looks its model and effort up under its own name, then its library role's, its kind and that default.

A `[[role]]` may also name `compact_at`, its agents' compact point in the forms a start takes (`500000`, `500k`, or `auto` for the tool's own), `session_hours`, how long each may run (1 to 168 hours), and `min` and `max`, the fewest of its agents a retire leaves and the most an add reaches, each the role's `count` when left out; every agent the fleet starts is started as `dockingbird start --compact-at 500000 --session-hours 48` unless its role names its own point or life, so a long-running agent compacts at half a 1M window instead of being replaced by hand, and lives two days.

The fleet admits a swarm once its roles' `min` agents fit its host and starts those; each agent above a role's `min` waits as a `fill` row and starts once its host has room for it, one at a time and before the fleet admits any new swarm, so a running swarm fills up ahead of a waiting one of any priority (a check run is not slowed: swarms never reserve its lease headroom).

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: `fleet submit` refuses a swarm when no home of its placement links a checkout of its `[source]` repository, on any branch, as of each host's last sample (`refused: source: no home of the placement links a checkout of the repository, as of its host's last sample`; a refusal's rule is said in its whole words, on the screen and under `--json`, up to 120 characters, never cut at the screen's text limit): each machine's worker publishes its homes' linked checkouts every `HOST_SAMPLE_INTERVAL_S` (30 seconds).
text:
`fleet submit` refuses a swarm when no home of its placement links a checkout of its `[source]` repository, on any branch, as of each host's last sample (`refused: source: no home of the placement links a checkout of the repository, as of its host's last sample`; a refusal's rule is said in its whole words, on the screen and under `--json`, up to 120 characters, never cut at the screen's text limit): each machine's worker publishes its homes' linked checkouts every `HOST_SAMPLE_INTERVAL_S` (30 seconds).

A `[placement]` names a host's home with `home.<host>`, by name as that host's worker publishes it, or by its folder's path.

A definition may leave `[placement]` out: its swarm then goes to every pool host that takes swarms, in the pool's order (`dockingbird fleet hosts add NAME --rank N` and `dockingbird fleet hosts policy NAME --rank N`, 1 first; unranked hosts after the ranked ones by name), each in a home of that host that fixes nothing (one with a checkout of the repository first, then the fewest running agents, then by path; a host whose placed home has none is held `no_seed` until it has one); the pass places a swarm on the first host of its placement's order with room, green lines and a seeded home, and only among hosts the placement does not rank on the fullest under `RESERVE_CAP_PERMILLE`.

While a swarm runs, the engine watches its reviewers' and testers' inboxes through the home's `status --json`: when a review request or an approved commit has waited `FLEET_WAIT_LINE_S` (five minutes) for one of them, it gives that implementer to another agent of the role that is idle with nothing waiting, telling all three, or else adds one agent of the role within the role's `max` and the host's room; it records each decision (`wait_passed`, `reassigned`, `agent_added`) and never stops, restarts or moves a working agent.

A home whose `status` carries no waiting figures is never judged: the engine records `figures absent`.

At the first start each implementer is given a reviewer and a tester, round-robin, and every brief's roster names them.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: `dockingbird fleet queue` shows the pool and the queue: each host's liveness and policy, its sample's age, its cores and memory reserved against what it may reserve with the load of everything the fleet didn't start, and its gate lines with their colours; then each workload not yet ended, in the order the fleet admits them, with its project, priority, state and age, the cores, memory and agents it needs (what its reservation holds), and where it is, why it is held, or what keeps it waiting first.
text:
`dockingbird fleet queue` shows the pool and the queue: each host's liveness and policy, its sample's age, its cores and memory reserved against what it may reserve with the load of everything the fleet didn't start, and its gate lines with their colours; then each workload not yet ended, in the order the fleet admits them, with its project, priority, state and age, the cores, memory and agents it needs (what its reservation holds), and where it is, why it is held, or what keeps it waiting first.

Under a swarm it names the agents still working, the agents waiting to start with the first thing that holds them (the hold's word and the host, from the fleet's latest `growth_blocked` record; "no pass has weighed them yet" before one), and the agents about to start.

`dockingbird fleet queue --host NAME` shows one host, and `dockingbird fleet queue --metrics` prints the fleet's metrics in the Prometheus text format instead (the queue's depth by priority, each host's reservations, headroom, red gate lines, staleness and interrupted workloads, and the holds by reason; counters of each host's admissions, starts and seconds of queue wait, and of each role's agent seconds and idle seconds on each host, which only grow, so Prometheus's `rate` gives their means; and each host's fullest home's agents against its agent cap; as the admitter serves them at `FLEET_SCHED_METRICS_PORT`), for the workloads your role can see; it takes neither `--json` nor `--host`.

`dockingbird fleet why ID` names, for a waiting workload, the first thing that keeps it off each host with its figures (a gate line's value and bound, what a host has against what the workload needs), and for any other its state and host, and for a running swarm with agents waiting to start, which they are and what holds them, with its figures.

A definition the checkout keeps in `.dockingbird/swarms/<name>/swarm.toml` is submitted by its name from anywhere in the checkout, `dockingbird fleet submit NAME` (a path is still a folder or a file).

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: A submit takes values for the definition: `--set KEY=VALUE`, repeatable, where `KEY` is a parameter the definition declares (`N=4`), a role's setting (`grader.count=6`) or its subagent's (`grader.helper.max=4`), and `--values FILE`, a JSON document of the same shape, `{"params": {...}, "roles": {"<role>": {...}}}`, a role's subagents under its `subagents`; a `--set` beats the file for the same key, and the settings a submit may give are a role's `count`, `min`, `max`, `model`, `effort`, `compact_at` and `session_hours`, its fallback's `harness`, `model`, `effort` and `placement` (`grader.fallback.harness=codex`, or the role's `fallback` object in the values document, each key laid over the role's own table, or making one for a role that names none; a role whose subagent is named `fallback` keeps that subagent's meaning) and a subagent's `model`, `effort` and `max`.
text:
A submit takes values for the definition: `--set KEY=VALUE`, repeatable, where `KEY` is a parameter the definition declares (`N=4`), a role's setting (`grader.count=6`) or its subagent's (`grader.helper.max=4`), and `--values FILE`, a JSON document of the same shape, `{"params": {...}, "roles": {"<role>": {...}}}`, a role's subagents under its `subagents`; a `--set` beats the file for the same key, and the settings a submit may give are a role's `count`, `min`, `max`, `model`, `effort`, `compact_at` and `session_hours`, its fallback's `harness`, `model`, `effort` and `placement` (`grader.fallback.harness=codex`, or the role's `fallback` object in the values document, each key laid over the role's own table, or making one for a role that names none; a role whose subagent is named `fallback` keeps that subagent's meaning) and a subagent's `model`, `effort` and `max`.

A definition may declare `[params]`, each an `int`, a `choice` or a `text` with its default and bounds, and write `{{<name>}}` in its values and in its roles' texts.

A definition without `key` queues a new swarm at each submit, keyed `<name>-<UTC time as YYYYMMDDhhmmss>`, unless `--key KEY` names one.

`fleet submit` runs every rule before it stores anything and prints every refusal, one `refused: <field>: <rule>` line each in a fixed order, then ends 1; `fleet queue` and `fleet why` show the values a swarm was given.

A role whose `fallback` table's `placement` is `require-login` needs its placement home signed in to the role's tool and to its fallback tool, as of the host's last sample (`signed` or `key`; `not-yet`, and a home whose words the sample did not read, are not): the fleet holds its swarm off a host whose home is not (`no_fallback_login`, judged again at each pass), and a role whose `hosts` pin such a host is refused at submit (`refused: role[N].fallback.placement: a host whose home is not signed in to the role's harness and its fallback's, as of its last sample`); sign in there with `dockingbird login claude` or `dockingbird login codex`.

A `[[role]]` may take its settings and texts from a role library: `use = "<name>"` names the project's `.dockingbird/roles/<name>.toml`, and `use = "dockingbird/<name>"` the role of that name Dockingbird ships (`coordinator`, `implementer`, `reviewer`, `tester`, `reader` and `hands`), which `dockingbird init` copies into `.dockingbird/roles/` with the library's `index.toml` (a copy you edited survives a later `init`, as a skill's does); each key the entry gives replaces the library role's, a subagent's table field by field.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: A role may also name `instructions`, a text its agents get after Dockingbird's own rules and the project's; `connections`, the home's connections its agents are granted at start (the delegated agents' connections), each refused at submit when no enabled connection of the home has that name; a `[subagents.<name>]` table for each helper its harness runs, with the helper's own `model`, `effort` and `instructions` and the `max` of them running at once; `workspace`, `egress`, `allow` and `env`, as a session config takes them, `context`, `kept` or `fresh`, a new conversation for every task delivery of the role's agents (as a config's `context`, "Your own commands (configs)"), and `tools`, `bus`, `full` or a list, which keeps every bus tool (`refused: role[N].tools: drops a tool of the bus set` otherwise); and `send_to`, the roles of the swarm its agents may message beside their parent (`[]` for the parent alone; left out, any agent of the project, as before).
text:
A role may also name `instructions`, a text its agents get after Dockingbird's own rules and the project's; `connections`, the home's connections its agents are granted at start (the delegated agents' connections), each refused at submit when no enabled connection of the home has that name; a `[subagents.<name>]` table for each helper its harness runs, with the helper's own `model`, `effort` and `instructions` and the `max` of them running at once; `workspace`, `egress`, `allow` and `env`, as a session config takes them, `context`, `kept` or `fresh`, a new conversation for every task delivery of the role's agents (as a config's `context`, "Your own commands (configs)"), and `tools`, `bus`, `full` or a list, which keeps every bus tool (`refused: role[N].tools: drops a tool of the bus set` otherwise); and `send_to`, the roles of the swarm its agents may message beside their parent (`[]` for the parent alone; left out, any agent of the project, as before).

A role may also name `skills`, a table as a session config's `[skills]` takes it (`path`, one skill or skills folder or a list of them, each a path from the top of the swarm's source, a library role's too; `into`, `both`, `claude` or `agents`), whose trees every start reads from the swarm's clone, where its agents run, and places as a config's skills are placed.

`fleet submit` reads the paths from the top of the checkout the definition is in by a config's rules (no link, no hidden entry, the skills' bounds) and refuses what it cannot read at its key (`refused: role[N].skills.path: not a skills table: path (skill or skills folders of the source checkout), into (both, claude or agents)`, or at `role[N].skills.<name>` for one skill and `role[N].skills` for the set's bounds), as it refuses `skills` in a swarm with no `[source]`, which has no clone; `fleet describe` reads no tree.

A start whose clone lacks a path (its branch moved after the submit) holds the swarm (`skills_refused`; the worker's log names the agent, its role, the key and the cause) until you push the fix and run `dockingbird fleet release ID`.

A Codex role whose `path` is the clone's own `.agents/skills` lists each skill twice, the placed copy and the repository's; name a folder outside it to list each once.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: A role may name a fallback too, the keys of a config's `[fallback]` table ("A fallback tool", below) as `[role.fallback]` and `[role.fallback.on]` under its `[[role]]`, or `[fallback]` in a library role's file, whose table an entry's own replaces whole: each key is checked as a config's and refused at `role[N].fallback.<key>`, a `harness` that is the role's own is refused (`fallback-same`), and a `model` or an `effort` the table leaves out comes from the project file's `[roles.<kind>]` when its `harness` is the fallback's, else from your organisation's row for the kind and the fallback tool (`dockingbird org roles set <kind> --harness codex --model <model>`), the role refused when neither gives one (`fallback-model`).
text:
A role may name a fallback too, the keys of a config's `[fallback]` table ("A fallback tool", below) as `[role.fallback]` and `[role.fallback.on]` under its `[[role]]`, or `[fallback]` in a library role's file, whose table an entry's own replaces whole: each key is checked as a config's and refused at `role[N].fallback.<key>`, a `harness` that is the role's own is refused (`fallback-same`), and a `model` or an `effort` the table leaves out comes from the project file's `[roles.<kind>]` when its `harness` is the fallback's, else from your organisation's row for the kind and the fallback tool (`dockingbird org roles set <kind> --harness codex --model <model>`), the role refused when neither gives one (`fallback-model`).

The role's config carries the table to each of its agents, which follow its rules as an agent started with that config does.

`dockingbird fleet describe NAME` prints, as JSON and connecting to nothing, every parameter and every role's settable field with its type and its bounds or words, and its default with where it comes from (`file`, `params.<name>`, `library` or `project`) when the checkout gives one (a model or an effort it does not give is `required`, from the org store or the submit); its defaults alone are a values document `--values` takes.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: A check run takes a lease rather than a swarm: `dockingbird fleet run --cores 4 --memory 8g --bound 30m -- make test` records a lease of 4 cores and 8 GiB, waits for a host to take it (reading its row every `HOST_SAMPLE_INTERVAL_S`, 30 s, and holding no connection between two reads), then runs `make test` here, in a process group of its own, with `FLEET_LEASE_CORES` and `FLEET_LEASE_HOST` in its environment, and ends with its exit status once it ends, the lease ended with it.
text: A check run takes a lease rather than a swarm: `dockingbird fleet run --cores 4 --memory 8g --bound 30m -- make test` records a lease of 4 cores and 8 GiB, waits for a host to take it (reading its row every `HOST_SAMPLE_INTERVAL_S`, 30 s, and holding no connection between two reads), then runs `make test` here, in a process group of its own, with `FLEET_LEASE_CORES` and `FLEET_LEASE_HOST` in its environment, and ends with its exit status once it ends, the lease ended with it. `--hosts H,...` names the hosts it may run on, `--wait 10m` how long it may wait (`LEASE_WAIT_S`, 30 minutes, by default; a lease not taken by then is given up, naming what kept it off each host, and ends 1), and `--kind picker --exclusive` keeps a second lease of that kind off the host. Durations name their unit (`90s`, `20m`, `2h`), at most `LEASE_DURATION_MAX_S` (a day). At its `--bound` the command is interrupted, then stopped after `LEASE_KILL_GRACE_S` (15 s), and `fleet run` ends 124; `dockingbird fleet cancel ID` of a running lease interrupts it the same way. On Linux the command runs inside a transient scope of your own systemd user manager (`systemd-run`) whose `CPUQuota` and `MemoryMax` are the lease's (a kill at `MemoryMax` is the command's own status, 137); on a Mac nothing bounds it, and a lease there counts cores only. When the fleet database doesn't answer, `fleet run` says so on one line, naming the database, the role and why, and runs the command without a lease, as checks ran before; when it answers no (a turned-down login, an error code), `fleet run` is refused, ends 78 and never runs the command. Stopping `fleet run` (Ctrl-C, or a SIGTERM from a service manager) interrupts the command's process group too, and the lease ends with it. `fleet_admin` maps to no project, so its leases count against the org pointer's `project`.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: The controls take a workload's id: `dockingbird fleet hold ID --reason TEXT` keeps a waiting one out of every pass and `dockingbird fleet release ID` puts it back; `dockingbird fleet pause ID`, `dockingbird fleet resume ID`, `dockingbird fleet cancel ID` and `dockingbird fleet done ID` act on a running team, each of whose agents stops after its running turn, never during it, and the answer names the state entered and the agents still working; `dockingbird fleet set ID --priority P0` changes a priority in any state but an ended one, the workload keeping its age.
text:
The controls take a workload's id: `dockingbird fleet hold ID --reason TEXT` keeps a waiting one out of every pass and `dockingbird fleet release ID` puts it back; `dockingbird fleet pause ID`, `dockingbird fleet resume ID`, `dockingbird fleet cancel ID` and `dockingbird fleet done ID` act on a running team, each of whose agents stops after its running turn, never during it, and the answer names the state entered and the agents still working; `dockingbird fleet set ID --priority P0` changes a priority in any state but an ended one, the workload keeping its age.

`fleet retire ID NAME [--reason TEXT]` retires one agent of a running swarm once its running turn ends, never during it (one that never started retires at once), and gives its share back to the pool.

The host's worker refuses it when the agent is working, asking, waiting or has a question or a request open, records `retire_refused` and sends the agent nothing.

It is refused before anything changes when the swarm is not running, has no such agent, or the role is at its `min` (a `min` of 0 lets you empty a role that neither reviews nor tests; a role that names no `min` keeps its `count`).

An agent that hands its parent back `status: done` (a `status` message whose first line is `status: done`) is retired the same way, on its own word: the worker reads each home's inbox once per sample, asks that agent's retire with the reason `handback done`, waits while it works or has a question or a request open, never takes its role below its `min` (it records `retire_refused` instead), keeps its copy and marks the message read; `status: partial` or `status: blocked` retires nothing, and the fleet sends nothing back.

`fleet ledger ID` prints a swarm's ledger, one line per commit, newest first: who approved it and when, and its test line's result, who sent it and when (`none` for a half not seen yet), from the `approved <sha> by <author>: <task>` and `tested <sha>: green|red <lines>` messages its reviewers and testers send their parent, which the worker records and marks read; a line whose sha isn't 40 or 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits, whose author isn't an agent of the swarm or whose result isn't `green` or `red` records nothing.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: `fleet add ID ROLE [--count N] [--reason TEXT]` adds agents of a role, up to its `max`, under the role's next names, the reason kept on its `agent_added` event; each starts once its host has room, is briefed with the roster, and every other agent is told the new roster.
text:
`fleet add ID ROLE [--count N] [--reason TEXT]` adds agents of a role, up to its `max`, under the role's next names, the reason kept on its `agent_added` event; each starts once its host has room, is briefed with the roster, and every other agent is told the new roster.

`fleet replace ID NAME` stops an agent at its turn boundary and starts it again by its name, its conversation kept, with a task naming its brief; with `--fresh`, a new agent of its role takes its place under the next name.

An agent whose last turn failed (its `status` row `failed`), or whose process crashed while its container still runs (`crashed`), runs no turn: `fleet replace ID NAME` is its recovery, the product's own (the worker stops it with `stop NAME` and the grow job picks it up by its name with its conversation and its inbox), taken whatever is open; `fleet retire` and `fleet replace --fresh` take it only with no question and no request open.

The engine recovers no failed turn by itself.

When a swarm is done or cancelled and its branch is merged, `dockingbird fleet prune ID --merged SHA` deletes its agents' kept copies: SHA is the tested head you proved merged in your own checkout (for example with `git merge-base --is-ancestor SHA origin/main`); the engine never checks it, and a commit an agent made but never published goes with its copy.

A project's role acts on its own project's workloads only (another project's read as unknown); `fleet_admin` acts on any.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: The pool belongs to `fleet_admin`: `dockingbird fleet hosts add NAME --os linux --cores 60 --memory 230g --line idle_millicores=4000,8000 --line free_mib=16384,32768 --line psi_io_full=1500,1200` enrols a host of `hosts.toml` with its reservable share and its gate lines (every line its OS requires), `--lease-headroom`, `--agent-cap`, `--rank N`, `--no-swarms` and `--power gcloud` beside them; `dockingbird fleet hosts policy NAME --takes-swarms no` changes its policy or lines, `--rank N` sets its place in the order, and `dockingbird fleet hosts policy NAME --line free_disk_mib=45056,90112` gives it a free-disk line (MiB: the least free disk over its homes and, on Linux, Docker's root; a line for a 60-core VM at an agent cap of 10), which no host must carry, given once the host's sample shows the figure, since a line on a figure its sample lacks is red; `dockingbird fleet hosts drain NAME`, `dockingbird fleet hosts undrain NAME` and `dockingbird fleet hosts remove NAME` take it out of new work, back in, or out of the pool (refused while a workload is reserved on or pinned to it).
text:
The pool belongs to `fleet_admin`: `dockingbird fleet hosts add NAME --os linux --cores 60 --memory 230g --line idle_millicores=4000,8000 --line free_mib=16384,32768 --line psi_io_full=1500,1200` enrols a host of `hosts.toml` with its reservable share and its gate lines (every line its OS requires), `--lease-headroom`, `--agent-cap`, `--rank N`, `--no-swarms` and `--power gcloud` beside them; `dockingbird fleet hosts policy NAME --takes-swarms no` changes its policy or lines, `--rank N` sets its place in the order, and `dockingbird fleet hosts policy NAME --line free_disk_mib=45056,90112` gives it a free-disk line (MiB: the least free disk over its homes and, on Linux, Docker's root; a line for a 60-core VM at an agent cap of 10), which no host must carry, given once the host's sample shows the figure, since a line on a figure its sample lacks is red; `dockingbird fleet hosts drain NAME`, `dockingbird fleet hosts undrain NAME` and `dockingbird fleet hosts remove NAME` take it out of new work, back in, or out of the pool (refused while a workload is reserved on or pinned to it).

`dockingbird fleet hosts` with no verb still lists `hosts.toml`.

`dockingbird -h` doesn't list `fleet`; `dockingbird fleet -h` shows every action.

Two long-running commands do the fleet's work, each started and restarted by the machine's own service manager and connected as its kind's role in the org pointer (`worker`, `admitter`).

`dockingbird fleet worker --host NAME` is one machine's worker, `NAME` its name in the pool: it publishes the machine's sample every `HOST_SAMPLE_INTERVAL_S` (30 s), runs the start jobs the admitter gives this machine, each agent through its home's own `dockingbird start` with the role's limits, then sets each agent's model and sends its brief once, and supervises what it started (the stop after the running turn that pause, cancel and done ask of every agent the home lists alive, whether or not its container is seen; an agent neither listed by Docker nor readable from the home's status waits, unjudged, until the status reads; a memory kill Docker reports; an agent gone).

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: An agent whose process a memory kill ended is picked up while its swarm runs, decided at the worker's next tick and started by a `grow` job, at most `FLEET_DEATH_PICKUPS_MAX` (2) times per agent and swarm: by its name, its conversation kept, while its last context was below its compact point or either figure is unknown, else by a fresh agent of its role under the next name, the share passing to it; at the bound it stays dead and the worker records `pickup_refused`, the swarm running on.
text:
An agent whose process a memory kill ended is picked up while its swarm runs, decided at the worker's next tick and started by a `grow` job, at most `FLEET_DEATH_PICKUPS_MAX` (2) times per agent and swarm: by its name, its conversation kept, while its last context was below its compact point or either figure is unknown, else by a fresh agent of its role under the next name, the share passing to it; at the bound it stays dead and the worker records `pickup_refused`, the swarm running on.

An agent that ends at its session life (its role's `session_hours`, else 48 hours) is picked up by its name every time, never read as lost.

The worker's homes are the `[[home]]` tables of `hosts.toml`; each home's program is the one its own `program` file names, else the table's `program` line.

On a Mac it runs under a LaunchAgent; on Linux under a systemd user unit, with `loginctl enable-linger` so it runs while nobody is logged in.

`dockingbird fleet admitter` runs once, on one machine of the pool that stays awake (a Mac under a LaunchAgent with its sleep disabled, or a Linux host under a systemd user unit).

It runs the admission pass after each change to the queue or the pool and at least every `HOST_SAMPLE_INTERVAL_S`, and the housekeeping every `HOUSEKEEP_INTERVAL_S` (30 s): stale hosts, stalled workers, expired leases, a stopped `gcloud` VM started when work waits for it.

It serves the fleet's metrics, the text `dockingbird fleet queue --metrics` prints, at the org pointer's database host on `FLEET_SCHED_METRICS_PORT`.

Both run until stopped.

When the database doesn't answer, each ends 69 and its service manager starts it again; when the database turns its login down, each ends 78, and its login needs fixing first (`dockingbird org status`).

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: A new Dockingbird release reaches a machine's engine in this order, which `dockingbird fleet update` (below) runs on every host of the pool: install it into `installs/<release>/`, run `<installs/release>/bin/dockingbird --home NAME update` from the new install for each home the worker runs, then move `installs/current` to the release and restart the machine's worker and admitter services, which name `installs/current/bin/dockingbird` (kickstart the LaunchAgent on a Mac, restart the systemd user unit on Linux).
text:
A new Dockingbird release reaches a machine's engine in this order, which `dockingbird fleet update` (below) runs on every host of the pool: install it into `installs/<release>/`, run `<installs/release>/bin/dockingbird --home NAME update` from the new install for each home the worker runs, then move `installs/current` to the release and restart the machine's worker and admitter services, which name `installs/current/bin/dockingbird` (kickstart the LaunchAgent on a Mac, restart the systemd user unit on Linux). That update writes the home's `program` file to the install and rolls the home's agents. The worker reads that file first, so it serves the rolled homes meanwhile, within one release of them, and its row reporting the release is the machine's last change: it marks the machine done, which a re-run reads. Restarting the services first would mark a machine done before its homes were updated; this order is safe because a container made before this release never switches, so the first move has no hand-over for an old worker to misread, and from this release on the worker honours a hand-over. The first move to the release that brings this layout points the services at `installs/current/bin/dockingbird` once, by hand (their `ProgramArguments` on a Mac, their `ExecStart` on Linux), with `installs/current` made beside the release folders; from then on `fleet update` moves the link. `dockingbird fleet hosts` says which worker is behind (a worker older than the newest release a home's agents run, or older than what the fleet now writes, which holds it until it is updated) and, per home, which source the worker used for the home's program: `file`, the home's own `program` file, or `table`, the `program` line of its `[[home]]` table, shown with the program, and with the reason the file was refused when the table's program was used instead. The worker reads a home's `program` file first, so editing a `[[home]]` table's `program` line by hand does nothing for a home whose `program` file names another install, until a `start` or an `update` of a newer program rewrites the file.

`dockingbird fleet update` runs that order on the pool's hosts, one after another, in the pool's order (by `--rank`, the unranked after by name), or on the one host `--host NAME` names.

It is the admin's alone: a login that is no member of `fleet_admin` ends 77.

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: The release is the one `--release V` names, else this program's own, and its commit is its release tag's, read once from the source by this computer's git ("There is no Dockingbird 0.15.3 to install.", exit 2, when the source lists no such tag).
text:
The release is the one `--release V` names, else this program's own, and its commit is its release tag's, read once from the source by this computer's git ("There is no Dockingbird 0.15.3 to install.", exit 2, when the source lists no such tag).

When git here can't read the source at all, it says "Dockingbird couldn't read versions from" the source, exit 1, before anything runs: check the network, and that git on this computer can read that repository, as for `dockingbird update`.

Before anything runs it reads each host's newest live worker row: a host whose worker already runs the release is skipped and said; every other needs a live worker row (one beat within `WORKER_STALLED_S`, 3 minutes) that says which homes it serves, waited for at most two samples (60 s) after a worker's start, and a `[[host]]` table in this computer's `hosts.toml` with a `repoint` line: your own command that restarts that host's Dockingbird services (its worker, and the admitter where it runs), run over the host's route as you wrote it, never composed by Dockingbird.

Any refusal runs nothing on any host, and ends 2.

The services name `installs/current/bin/dockingbird`, the link the command moves, so the line is the restart alone, and it must return without waiting for the services to stop, since a worker's stop can outlast the call's `REMOTE_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_S` (40 s) and a restart that worked would then read as failed: `repoint = "launchctl kickstart -k gui/$UID/<label>"` on a Mac, `repoint = "systemctl --user restart --no-block <unit>"` on Linux.

Then, host by host, over the host's route: the release is installed into `installs/<release>/` under the host's data root (`~/.local/share/dockingbird/installs/`), pinned to its release tag's commit, by the `uv` the `[[host]]` table's `path` finds, within `UV_UPDATE_TIMEOUT_S` (15 minutes), and a private source is read with the host's own git credential, since the route forwards no ssh agent; an install whose program already answers the release is kept, and a folder whose program doesn't answer is installed again.

Each home of the host's worker runs `update` from that install, in path order, each within `BUILD_TIMEOUT_S` (an hour) plus 330 s, the time a base rebuild and the coordinator's replacement may take; `installs/current` is moved to the release and the `repoint` line runs, each within 40 s; and the command waits for the host's worker to report the release, at most `FLEET_UPDATE_HOST_WAIT_S` (10 minutes).

heading: Operator guide > The fleet scheduler
summary: Each step is said as it starts.
text:
Each step is said as it starts.

A step that fails, or a worker that doesn't run the release in time, stops the command, ending 1, with the host and the route's own words; the hosts after it are left as they are and the hosts done stay done, so once it's fixed, run the same command again: it skips the hosts done and repeats the rest, each step safe to repeat.

A host's homes finish moving to the release on their own after its `DONE` line, and `dockingbird status` in each of them shows how far it got.

This computer, when it is a pool host, is a `[[host]]` with `local = true` and neither `ssh` nor `gcloud`: its lines run here under `sh`, for `fleet update` and for every command that takes `--host`, and `fleet hosts` shows it as `this computer`.

A Dockingbird older than this release refuses the whole `hosts.toml` once it holds a `repoint` or `local` key (`FLEET_HOSTS_FILE_INVALID`) until it is updated, so write the two keys on the computer that runs this release; the same `fleet update` restarts that computer's own worker.

heading: Operator guide > Migrations and older workers
summary: A fleet migration is one named change to the store, which `dockingbird org create` applies and the store records by name.
text:
A fleet migration is one named change to the store, which `dockingbird org create` applies and the store records by name. A worker or the admitter of a release refuses to start against a store that lacks one of its build's migrations, naming one it lacks (`FLEET_STORE_BEHIND`), until the admin runs `org create`; a store that names migrations its build does not know is allowed. Each migration's row says whether the workers and the admitter of the release before it keep running against a store it migrated, or restart at its build first, and why: a migration that needs the earlier workers restarted first says so here, and the start-up check then gains a floor.

| Migration | Earlier workers | Why |

|---|---|---|

| `0001_roster_operations` | `restart first` | It adds the roster's steps `retire_asked`, `retired`, `pickup` and `held`, which a worker of the earlier build reads as an agent gone, interrupting its swarm: every worker and the admitter restart at the new build before anyone uses `fleet retire`, `add`, `replace` or `prune` (`docs/operator-guide.md`, the fleet scheduler's install). |

| `0002_done_after_a_loss` | `keep running` | It adds the state grants of three moves a done makes after a loss and changes no move an earlier worker or admitter makes. |

| `0003_assignments_told` | `keep running` | It adds `reviewer_told` and `tester_told`, filled with each row's assignees, which an earlier worker neither reads nor writes; the submitter's insert policy refuses only a row naming them, which no earlier build writes. |

| `0004_efficiency` | `keep running` | Its tables, kinds and column are new to earlier builds, which write none of them; a `fleet submit` at the new build refuses a swarm whose hosts' workers have not published their homes' checkouts, so the workers move to the new build before the admitter and the submitters (`docs/operator-guide.md`). |

| `0005_host_rank` | `keep running` | It adds `host.rank`, null for every host enrolled before it and riding the table's grants; it was applied before any install moved. |

| `0006_org` | `keep running` | Workers and an admitter at the earlier build keep working through it; it is applied before any worker, admitter or submitter restarts at the new build. |

| `0007_membership` | `keep running` | As `0006_org`; a project's submitter login keeps working, since a role is a member of itself and its login is its `session_user`. |

heading: Operator guide > Migrations and older workers
text:
| `0008_sql_audit` | `keep running` | The policies admit the same rows, the index and the InitPlan change plans only, and the name check admits every engine-made row. A worker or the admitter of this build against a store without it refuses to start (`FLEET_STORE_BEHIND`), so `org create` runs before they restart. |
