| `0009_rolling_updates` | `keep running` | It adds each process's release, schema, kind and homes on `fleet.worker`, each roster row's release and code, and the vocabulary floor; a worker or the admitter of the build before beats with its three columns, the new ones left null, which the fleet's floor reads as older than every migration, so a write of the new words waits until every live process is updated. |

| `0010_role_config` | `keep running` | It adds each roster row's `config_digest` and the event kind `denied_by_role`; a worker or the admitter of the build before neither writes nor reads either, and a worker of this build writes them only once every live process is at this migration, the fleet's floor. A worker or the admitter of this build against a store without it refuses to start (`FLEET_STORE_BEHIND`), so `org create` runs before they restart. |

| `0011_work_queue` | `keep running` | It adds the schema `work`, the organisation's work queue, which no worker or admitter reads or writes, and changes nothing of `fleet` or `org`. A worker or the admitter of this build against a store without it refuses to start (`FLEET_STORE_BEHIND`), so `org create` runs before they restart. |

heading: Operator guide > The work queue
summary: The work queue is the organisation's board of what is being built, kept in the fleet database as one more schema, `work`, beside `fleet` and `org`, so that a person, a coordinator's hands and a script read and write the same rows from any computer that has the org login.
text: The work queue is the organisation's board of what is being built, kept in the fleet database as one more schema, `work`, beside `fleet` and `org`, so that a person, a coordinator's hands and a script read and write the same rows from any computer that has the org login. It holds three kinds of row. An item is one unit of work, a feature, a bug, a task, a decision or a program, with its title, its area, its status, its priority and its owner, its ETA and its deadline, the line it is at now and the step it takes next, the items it waits for and, when it waits for you, the ask; every change to an item and every thing that happens to it (a merge, a review, a hand-back, a note) is an event under it, and events are only ever added, so an item's log is its history. An agent's row records one session that works on an item: its task, its role, its model and effort, the item and the pull request it works on, its ETA and why the ETA moved, and, once it ends, its outcome and its result. A request is what an agent asks of the coordinator (a bug it found, a feature, a question or a hand-off, among others), kept with the answers it gets. An item names the fleet's workload that builds it by that workload's id alone. `work` is a command of the host CLI beside `fleet`, and like `fleet` it is not on the top screen: `dockingbird -h` doesn't list it, and `dockingbird work -h` shows every action.

heading: Operator guide > The work queue
summary: Each `work` action reads this computer's org login first, as every fleet command does (`dockingbird org login db.example.net:5433 --as user --role <role>`, above), connects as the kind `user` unless `--as KIND` names another, and ends 78 naming the login to run when there is none.
text: Each `work` action reads this computer's org login first, as every fleet command does (`dockingbird org login db.example.net:5433 --as user --role <role>`, above), connects as the kind `user` unless `--as KIND` names another, and ends 78 naming the login to run when there is none. The queue is read by the admin (`fleet_admin`), by each person's login, through its membership of a project's group (`fleet_submitter_<project>`), and by each machine's worker (`--as worker`). The admin and the people also write it, and so do the coordinators and runners that connect as a person, but a worker only reads, and a write it tries is refused by the database. Each event and each answer records the database login that wrote it, so who wrote a row is read from the row. The schema comes with the store: `dockingbird org create` makes it, with `fleet` and `org`, on a new database; run as the role that owns the `fleet` schema's tables, it applies the migration `0011_work_queue` to a database made before this release, once, after the update, as it applies every migration the database lacks (above), and names the version it reached. Every action takes `--json`, which prints each line as one envelope, and `--as KIND`. A command ends 0 when it did its work, 2 when its words or options are refused before any connection is made, 1 when the store refuses a write, names no such item, agent or request, or the database refuses the login's write (a worker's, `FLEET_NOT_PERMITTED`, as the fleet's commands say it), 69 when the database does not answer, and 78 when its login is missing or turned down.

heading: Operator guide > The work queue
summary: The commands that read are these.
text:
The commands that read are these. `dockingbird work status`, with `--area A`, `--status S`, `--priority P` and `--all` as options, prints the items in work, those not archived and not in the backlog (`--all` adds the backlog), by priority, then ETA, then id, one line for each with its priority, id, status, owner, ETA and the items it waits for, and under it the line it is at now when it has one, and ends with how many requests are open and how many agents are running (`--area`, `--status` and `--priority` each take one value). `dockingbird work show ID` prints one item's fields, then its events, newest first. `dockingbird work needs-you` prints the items whose status is `waiting-user`, by deadline and then priority, each with the ask it waits on. `dockingbird work check` prints what the schema cannot say by itself, a dependency cycle between items, an agent with no end whose item is archived, a request still open on an archived item, and ends 1 when it prints any. `dockingbird work search TEXT` prints the best 50 hits (`WORK_SEARCH_LIMIT`) over the items, events, agents, requests and answers whose words match `TEXT`, an item whose id or a request whose number is `TEXT` first. `dockingbird work agents` prints the agents that have not ended, each `working` while its ETA is ahead or not set and `past its ETA` after. `dockingbird work requests [--all]` prints the open requests, and with `--all` the answered ones too. `dockingbird work request show N` prints request `N` with its body and each answer it has. `dockingbird work stamp` prints this computer's local time as `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM ZONE`, the form in which the queue's lines carry a time.

The commands that write record the time of the computer they run on.

`dockingbird work new ID --title T --area A --priority P --owner K` makes an item, `ID` its name (a slug), in the backlog and as a feature unless `--status S` or `--kind K` says otherwise, with `--agent ID`, `--project SLUG`, `--observed-at SHA`, `--ask TEXT`, `--depends-on A,B`, `--links L,L`, `--deadline D` and `--now TEXT` to fill in the rest.

heading: Operator guide > The work queue
summary: `dockingbird work log ITEM --kind K --text T` adds one event to an item's log, `K` one of `log`, `merge`, `review`, `launch` and `handback`, with `--pr N[,N]`, `--agent ID`, `--stage S`, `--sha SHA`, `--usd X` and `--ago MIN` (an event noticed late, at most 1,440 minutes ago) beside it, and a `merge` needs `--pr` and `--sha`.
text:
`dockingbird work log ITEM --kind K --text T` adds one event to an item's log, `K` one of `log`, `merge`, `review`, `launch` and `handback`, with `--pr N[,N]`, `--agent ID`, `--stage S`, `--sha SHA`, `--usd X` and `--ago MIN` (an event noticed late, at most 1,440 minutes ago) beside it, and a `merge` needs `--pr` and `--sha`.

`dockingbird work set ITEM FIELD VALUE` changes one field of an item and records the change as an event: `title`, `area`, `status`, `priority`, `kind`, `owner`, `agent`, `project`, `workload`, `observed_at`, `deadline` (a date, a date with a time, or `none`), `depends_on` and `links` (each a comma list that replaces what was), `ask`, `now` (with `--count N --total N --unit U` for a counted step), `next`, and `eta`, which takes only `none` and clears it.

`dockingbird work eta ITEM --in 45m --kind estimate` sets an item's ETA that long from now (`45m`, `2h`, `1h30m` and `2d` are the forms), as an `estimate` or as `measured`.

`dockingbird work agent start NAME --task T --kind K --model M --effort E` records an agent that has started, with `--item ID`, `--pr N`, `--workload ID` and `--eta 45m` for the item and pull request it works on, the workload whose roster it is in and when it should be done.

`dockingbird work agent eta NAME --eta 45m` moves a running agent's ETA, with `--why T` keeping the reason.

`dockingbird work agent done NAME --outcome O` records its end, with `--result T` keeping its result.

`dockingbird work request new --from X --kind K --title T` files a request, with its body as `--text T` or `--file PATH` and `--to NAME`, `--item ID`, `--priority P` and `--observed-at SHA` beside it, and prints its number.

`dockingbird work request info N --text T` adds the requester's own word to a request that waits for more information.

`dockingbird work respond N --decision D` answers request `N`, with the answer as `--text T` or `--file PATH` and `--item ID` beside it.

A body read from a file, or given as text, is at most 65,536 bytes of UTF-8 (`WORK_BODY_MAX_OCTETS`); a title, an ask, a now line and a log line are one line of at most 1,000 characters (`WORK_LINE_MAX_CHARS`).

heading: Operator guide > The work queue
summary: The words of a fixed list are a code table of the database, each named after the column that uses it, so a word outside the list is refused by the column's name and the command prints the list.
text: The words of a fixed list are a code table of the database, each named after the column that uses it, so a word outside the list is refused by the column's name and the command prints the list. An item's status is `backlog`, `ready`, `in-progress`, `review`, `blocked`, `waiting-user` or `done`; its priority `P0` (now), `P1` (this week), `P2` (soon) or `P3` (when there is time); its kind `feature`, `bug`, `task`, `decision` or `program`; its owner `main` (the coordinating session), `user` (the operator), `agent` (the agent its `agent` field names) or `none`; and its ETA `measured`, `estimate` or `none`. An agent's kind is `coordinator`, `implementer`, `reviewer`, `tester`, `hands` or `reader`, the six roles Dockingbird ships, or `other`, and its outcome is `done`, `partial`, `blocked` or `stopped`. A request's kind is `bug`, `feature`, `question`, `handoff`, `claim`, `progress`, `finish` or `release`, and an answer's decision is `accepted`, `granted`, `refused`, `done`, `needs-info` or `answered`. The commands write an event's kind themselves (`created`, `status`, `eta`, `owner`, `field`, `now`, `archived`, `agent_start`, `agent_eta`, `agent_done`, `request_new`, `respond` and `request_info`), except for the five `work log` takes. An area, a model, an effort and a project are your organisation's own words, never Dockingbird's: an area is a slug (lowercase letters, digits and `-`, up to 63 characters, as a project's name is), a project is the slug of one of your organisation's projects, and a model and an effort are the text an agent was started with. The database keeps its own rules, so every writer meets them. No event is ever changed or deleted: a trigger refuses it, whatever the login, and the submitter role holds no right to either. A request stays open until an answer whose decision is not `needs-info` closes it, and one sender has at most one open request of a title (case ignored): a repeat is refused with the number of the one that is open. An item of kind `bug` names the commit it was seen at (`--observed-at`), as a request of kind `bug` does. An item whose status is `waiting-user` carries its ask. An item that is archived is `done`, and `dockingbird work set ITEM status done` archives it.

heading: Operator guide > The work queue
summary: A swarm is tracked in the queue from before it is submitted until it is merged, by the coordinator and its hands through the org login of the person they act for, and no commit is made for it.
text: A swarm is tracked in the queue from before it is submitted until it is merged, by the coordinator and its hands through the org login of the person they act for, and no commit is made for it. The item for the feature exists before the swarm is submitted (`work new`, or `work set` on one that exists), and when `fleet submit` answers with the workload's id the item takes it, `dockingbird work set ITEM workload ID`, by id alone. Each agent of the roster, whether the fleet or the coordinating session starts it, gets a row with `dockingbird work agent start NAME --task T --kind K --model M --effort E --item ITEM --pr N`, its role as the kind and an `--eta` when it has one, which `work agent eta` moves as the work does. Each merge of a pull request is logged on the item with the pull request's number and the merge commit's sha, `dockingbird work log ITEM --kind merge --pr N --sha SHA`. Each hand-back ends its agent's row: the word of its `status:` line, `done`, `partial` or `blocked`, is the outcome (`dockingbird work agent done NAME --outcome done`). The item's own line, `dockingbird work set ITEM now TEXT` (with `--count` and `--total` for a counted step), is set at each change of state, and its status moves with the work; `dockingbird work set ITEM status done` closes the item and archives it, and it leaves `dockingbird work status`. What is in work, and when each agent ends, is then read from the queue, with `dockingbird work status` and `dockingbird work agents` beside `dockingbird fleet queue`, and never from a folder of files.

heading: Operator guide > Settings
summary: Dockingbird's runtime settings (the runtime table of parameters: poll intervals, timeouts, page sizes and the like, each a whole number within its bounds) are set in the shell that runs `dockingbird`, as `DOCKINGBIRD_<NAME>`: `export DOCKINGBIRD_DB_QUERY_TIMEOUT_S=60` raises the bound of one database statement for `connect --database`'s check and for the agents' queries alike.
text: Dockingbird's runtime settings (the runtime table of parameters: poll intervals, timeouts, page sizes and the like, each a whole number within its bounds) are set in the shell that runs `dockingbird`, as `DOCKINGBIRD_<NAME>`: `export DOCKINGBIRD_DB_QUERY_TIMEOUT_S=60` raises the bound of one database statement for `connect --database`'s check and for the agents' queries alike. Every command passes the settings your shell exports into the containers that read them (Dockingbird itself and each agent), so they take effect there and are never left at their defaults in silence. A value outside its bounds, values that break a rule between settings, a name spelled in another case, or a setting of Dockingbird outside Docker (the database's address and roles, the developer's role switch, the host git's path) stops the command before it runs, naming the variable and never its value; unset it or fix it, then run the command again. A running Dockingbird keeps the settings it started with: after you change one, the next command says "Dockingbird is running with other settings than this terminal's." and names the step, `dockingbird stop`, after which the next command starts it with the new settings; `dockingbird status` shows the same lines under "Needs your attention" and restarts nothing. The settings reach the agents' harnesses too (their Dockingbird MCP server reads them); none is a secret, and `docker inspect` shows them.

heading: Operator guide > Signing in
summary: Dockingbird uses the Claude and Codex logins already on your Mac.
text:
Dockingbird uses the Claude and Codex logins already on your Mac.

The first start that needs one reads the login Claude Code or Codex uses here (Claude's default profile, the one a plain `claude` uses; Codex's `auth.json`), keeps a copy in the coordinator's store, and follows it from then on; `dockingbird login claude --here` does the same on demand.

Claude's login is looked for in three places, in the order Claude Code itself uses them: first a token in `~/.claude/settings.json` (its `env` block's `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, with the gateway in `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` beside it when there is one: a Mac whose Claude Code signs in through a gateway), then the Keychain item, then `~/.claude/.credentials.json`.

From the settings file only those two values are read, and only from a file of yours that others cannot write; every other setting is left unread.

The gateway must be an `https://` address, or an address of this Mac itself: Dockingbird sends a token only to an `https://` gateway, except when Claude Code here sends its requests to a gateway on this Mac (a loopback host, `127.0.0.1` or any `127.x` address, `localhost` or `[::1]`, with any port and path, such as a proxy of yours at `http://127.0.0.1:59471`), which may be plain `http://`: an agent's Claude then sends its requests to that same gateway with the same token, reaching it as `http://host.docker.internal:PORT` (Docker Desktop's name for the Mac seen from a container; the scheme, port and path are kept), whichever login Dockingbird follows, a settings token, the Keychain item or the login file.

Any other plain `http://` gateway is refused by name ("This computer's Claude login goes through http://..., and Dockingbird sends a token only to an https:// gateway.

Nothing changed."), and nothing is followed until Claude Code here points at the gateway's `https://` address.

A gateway on this Mac is reached only through Docker Desktop on a Mac: on Linux a settings token sent through it is refused by name ("This computer's Claude login goes through http://127.0.0.1:59471, this computer's own address, which agents reach only through Docker Desktop on a Mac.

heading: Operator guide > Signing in
summary: Nothing changed.") and nothing is followed, while a login file beside it is followed without the gateway, which `dockingbird status` names as one the agents don't use; and an agent in the `allowlist` or `models` egress mode cannot reach it either (its proxy admits no address of this computer), so such a start names the gateway and the mode and starts nothing: point Claude Code here at an `https://` address agents can reach, or start the agent in the `full` egress mode (`dockingbird start --egress full`).
text:
Nothing changed.") and nothing is followed, while a login file beside it is followed without the gateway, which `dockingbird status` names as one the agents don't use; and an agent in the `allowlist` or `models` egress mode cannot reach it either (its proxy admits no address of this computer), so such a start names the gateway and the mode and starts nothing: point Claude Code here at an `https://` address agents can reach, or start the agent in the `full` egress mode (`dockingbird start --egress full`).

Beside a Keychain or login-file sign-in, a gateway elsewhere is not followed, and `dockingbird status` says so ("Claude Code here sends its requests through https://..., which the agents don't use").

A changed gateway reaches the store the moment it lands and the next start uses it; an agent already running keeps the gateway it started with.

The copy of a Keychain login or a login file leaves out its refresh token; the copy of a settings token is the token and the gateway, which an agent's Claude then uses exactly as your own `claude` does (`dockingbird status` then says "Claude uses this computer's login through https://...", or, for a gateway on this Mac, "Claude uses this computer's login through http://127.0.0.1:59471 (agents reach it at http://host.docker.internal:59471).").

Nothing on your Mac is written, copied or mounted for it: nothing under `~/.claude` but that one read of `settings.json`, not `~/.claude.json`, not `~/.codex`, not the Keychain; the refresh token never leaves your Mac, so no agent can renew or sign out your login, and your own Claude Code and Codex stay the only programs that refresh it.

Each tool can also sign in separately, inside Docker, with its own command (`dockingbird login claude`), which then wins until `dockingbird logout claude`.

heading: Operator guide > Signing in
summary: - **Where the sign-in lives.** Each tool's volume (`dockingbird-home-claude`, `dockingbird-home-codex`) holds its credentials store, `creds/`, and the saved key; both volumes are mounted into the coordinator (`/dockingbird/home/<tool>`) and into the login, tool-help, put and seed containers Dockingbird itself runs, never into an agent.
text:
- **Where the sign-in lives.** Each tool's volume (`dockingbird-home-claude`, `dockingbird-home-codex`) holds its credentials store, `creds/`, and the saved key; both volumes are mounted into the coordinator (`/dockingbird/home/<tool>`) and into the login, tool-help, put and seed containers Dockingbird itself runs, never into an agent. Each agent's tool runs with a private HOME on its container's own volume (`/tmp/home`, on `/tmp`, which no other container mounts); at its start the agent asks the coordinator for its tool's sign-in, saved key and (Claude) its state record, which the coordinator issues under the session's grant, so nothing another agent writes reaches the HOME a tool loads its settings, hooks or plugins from, and no agent can read another tool's secret.

- **Refreshing.** For Claude, one live session at a time holds the sign-in's refresh lease (the coordinator's holder file): it receives the full credential and is the only one whose refreshed sign-in the coordinator accepts back. Every other Claude session gets a copy without the refresh token, so two copies of a rotating token never invalidate each other; a session started while the holder is still signing in waits for its sign-in however long that takes, and stops only if the holder ends without one. Each Codex session receives the whole `auth.json` and sends it back when it changes, and the last writer wins. A running session picks up a sign-in another session stored back (and a change of Dockingbird's copy of your Mac's login, below): an agent working without a terminal gets the new copy within one heartbeat (about 20 seconds), and Claude restarts between two tasks to use it, resuming its conversation, while Codex's next task reads it; an agent in a terminal gets the new copy within one heartbeat as well, and its Claude Code reads it at its next request. Picking up a copy never makes a session the refresh holder: once the holder ends, the next start holds the lease.

- **Your Mac's own login.** `dockingbird status` says when a tool uses it.

heading: Operator guide > Signing in
summary: It is renewed on your Mac by Claude Code or Codex themselves (or by a tool of yours that rewrites the default profile's login, which Dockingbird follows the same way); while Dockingbird is on, it copies the change the moment it lands: a background watcher that every command starting or using Dockingbird leaves running (one per Dockingbird folder, alive while Dockingbird runs, ended when it stops) waits on macOS's change notification for the login keychain's file (`~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db`), Claude Code's settings file (`~/.claude/settings.json`, for a changed token or gateway) and the login files (`~/.claude/.credentials.json`, `~/.codex/auth.json`), confirms a notification by the item's attributes (`security find-generic-password` without `-w`, never the secret) or the file's metadata, and copies the changed login into the store at once (well under a second), with no command and no polling.
text:
It is renewed on your Mac by Claude Code or Codex themselves (or by a tool of yours that rewrites the default profile's login, which Dockingbird follows the same way); while Dockingbird is on, it copies the change the moment it lands: a background watcher that every command starting or using Dockingbird leaves running (one per Dockingbird folder, alive while Dockingbird runs, ended when it stops) waits on macOS's change notification for the login keychain's file (`~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db`), Claude Code's settings file (`~/.claude/settings.json`, for a changed token or gateway) and the login files (`~/.claude/.credentials.json`, `~/.codex/auth.json`), confirms a notification by the item's attributes (`security find-generic-password` without `-w`, never the secret) or the file's metadata, and copies the changed login into the store at once (well under a second), with no command and no polling.

A login tool of yours is followed when it rewrites the Keychain item or replaces the login file by rename; a link left in its place is refused.

A changed settings token or gateway reaches the store the same way; an agent already running keeps the token and gateway it started with, and the next start uses the new ones.

A login folder that isn't there yet (`~/.codex` before Codex's first run) is watched for through the folder it goes in, so a first login is copied the moment it lands too.

The backstops stay: Dockingbird also picks the renewal up at its next command and every minute while an agent runs in a terminal or your own Claude Code's Dockingbird connection is open, and running agents take it up as described under Refreshing (one in a terminal too).

A change the watcher saw but couldn't copy shows in `dockingbird status` ("Dockingbird couldn't update its copy of Claude's login 3 min ago: the login here couldn't be read.

The agents keep the earlier copy.") and in `dockingbird.log`; on Linux there is no watcher and the interval reads alone apply.

If macOS asks whether security may read the login, choose Always Allow: otherwise it asks at every read, once a minute while an agent runs in a terminal.

`dockingbird logout claude` stops following it (Dockingbird then has no Claude login until `dockingbird login claude --here` or a separate sign-in).

heading: Operator guide > Signing in
summary: A Claude agent whose copy expired before Dockingbird's next command fails its turn and says so; the next command renews Dockingbird's copy, a new start uses it, and an agent working without a terminal takes it up before its next task; an agent in a terminal reads the renewed copy at its next request.
text:
A Claude agent whose copy expired before Dockingbird's next command fails its turn and says so; the next command renews Dockingbird's copy, a new start uses it, and an agent working without a terminal takes it up before its next task; an agent in a terminal reads the renewed copy at its next request.

A start on a login that expired here, or that you signed out of here, says so and starts nothing until the login is renewed on your Mac.

Dockingbird reads your login only from a shell whose `HOME` is your home folder; from any other it reads nothing and keeps the copy it has.

Dockingbird's copy stays valid exactly as long as your own login does: it carries no refresh token, so your own Claude Code or Codex renews it by being used.

An agent that must outlive your login signs in for Dockingbird only: `dockingbird login claude`.

- **Reusing a sign-in you made elsewhere.** Run `claude setup-token` in a terminal, copy the token it shows, then `pbpaste | dockingbird login claude --oauth-token -` (and `pbcopy < /dev/null` to clear the clipboard); `cat ~/.codex/auth.json | dockingbird login codex --auth-json -` keeps a Codex sign-in from a file. Both read the value from the pipe only, and the value never appears in a command line, a log or a file on your Mac. A Claude token is the subscription's credential, not an API key: `status` says "signed in", and in a trusted checkout the repo's own settings load for it as for a sign-in. The last login wins: either form removes that tool's saved API key. Both refuse while that tool's agents run, as a sign-in does.

- **Signing in again.** `dockingbird login claude` or `dockingbird login codex` runs the same sign-in in a login container, for an expired or revoked sign-in or another account. It refuses while that tool's agents run. A sign-in that does not finish changes nothing and names the API key route: "Or use an API key: dockingbird login claude --api-key". To quit a sign-in, press ctrl-C: the login container passes it to the tool and waits for it to end, so only those two lines follow, on a line of their own after the terminal's `^C`, never a traceback.

heading: Operator guide > Signing in
summary: - **Codex.** If Codex's device-code sign-in doesn't finish, turn on device code login in ChatGPT's security settings.
text:
- **Codex.** If Codex's device-code sign-in doesn't finish, turn on device code login in ChatGPT's security settings. If Codex asks you to sign in again while it runs, choose its device-code option, or quit and run `dockingbird login codex`.

- **Signing out.** `dockingbird logout claude` and `dockingbird logout codex` remove that tool's sign-in and saved API key from the coordinator's store (with neither there, "Claude wasn't signed in. Nothing to do.", exit 0); both refuse while that tool's agents run, and both need the coordinator (they start it if it is off). A sign-out revokes nothing at Anthropic or OpenAI (Claude's own `claude auth logout` is no longer run), so if an agent may have copied the sign-in, also sign out in your account.

heading: Operator guide > API keys
summary: `dockingbird login claude --api-key` asks for an Anthropic API key (hidden), or reads it from stdin without a terminal; Ctrl-C at the question says "No key was saved.
text:
`dockingbird login claude --api-key` asks for an Anthropic API key (hidden), or reads it from stdin without a terminal; Ctrl-C at the question says "No key was saved. Nothing changed." and exits 130. `dockingbird login codex --api-key` does the same for OpenAI. With `--api-key`, `--base-url URL` (an `https://` gateway) sends that tool's requests there, for either tool: Claude takes it as `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` in its managed settings, Codex as `openai_base_url` in its `config.toml`. It goes with Claude's token too: `pbpaste | dockingbird login claude --oauth-token - --base-url URL` saves the token and the gateway together, and an agent's Claude then sends its requests there with that token. Give Codex's URL in `OPENAI_BASE_URL`'s form, ending in `/v1`, after which Codex adds `/responses` and `/models`; Claude's is the origin, after which Claude adds `/v1/...`.

- The key goes from the prompt, through a put container's stdin (`--network none`), into the volume's `.dockingbird/keys`, 0600. It is never in an argv, a container environment, `docker inspect`, a log or a file on your Mac.
- Agents mount no tool volume: an agent asks the coordinator for its own tool's key at its start, and the coordinator issues it under the session's grant, so an agent can neither change the key nor read the other tool's.
- Claude reads it through its `apiKeyHelper`, `dockingbird-claude-key`, which asks the coordinator and prints the key and nothing else. Codex takes it with `codex login --with-api-key`, on stdin.
- The last login wins: a plain `login` after `--api-key` removes the key once the sign-in succeeds, and `--api-key` replaces the sign-in. While a key is saved, `status` says "Claude uses an API key".

heading: Operator guide > Your own rules
summary: Agents get Dockingbird's built-in rules for the coordination tools.
text:
Agents get Dockingbird's built-in rules for the coordination tools. To use your own, write `~/.local/share/dockingbird/instructions/claude.md` or `codex.md`. Dockingbird copies a changed file into Docker the same way as a key, read-only to agents, and never mounts it.

A repository's own rules reach every agent started in it: the file `[rules] file` in `.dockingbird/project.toml` names (`.dockingbird/rules.md` when the key is unset) is read from the checkout at each start and given to the agent after Dockingbird's rules and before a config's own instructions, Claude and Codex alike. A rules file the project names that is missing, a link, not UTF-8 text or holding a Dockingbird credential stops the start, and so does one that makes the agent's rules longer than `INSTRUCTIONS_MAX_BYTES` (64 KB). In a repository you marked untrusted (`dockingbird trust --off`) it is not read.

heading: Operator guide > Update
summary: `dockingbird update` runs `uv tool upgrade dockingbird` (uv found in an absolute `PATH` entry; the command you would type), then the upgraded script puts its code into the home's code store, builds the image only when the image's base changed (see "Rolling updates") and swaps the coordinator, rolling back to the old one if the new one doesn't become healthy, then fetches the latest release of each tool you have used into the program store and says so per tool ("Claude Code 2.1.296 is the latest." or "Got Claude Code 2.1.296."; a tool you never used is not fetched; see "Tool versions").
text:
`dockingbird update` runs `uv tool upgrade dockingbird` (uv found in an absolute `PATH` entry; the command you would type), then the upgraded script puts its code into the home's code store, builds the image only when the image's base changed (see "Rolling updates") and swaps the coordinator, rolling back to the old one if the new one doesn't become healthy, then fetches the latest release of each tool you have used into the program store and says so per tool ("Claude Code 2.1.296 is the latest." or "Got Claude Code 2.1.296."; a tool you never used is not fetched; see "Tool versions").

An install still on Python 3.14 (any made before Dockingbird moved to Python 3.12) is moved to Python 3.12 by its next `dockingbird update` with no agent running, which runs `uv tool upgrade --python 3.12 dockingbird` after the upgrade and before the rebuild ("Moving Dockingbird to Python 3.12 ..."), or, installed from a release tag, by uv's reinstall of the next release.

Run that first update with no agent running, because the agents' running commands keep only the parts of Dockingbird they had already loaded.

When it replaced Dockingbird, it ends with "Dockingbird 0.15.3 is installed and takes over now." and, after a rebuild, what it kept: your repos, their history, and only the sign-ins and saved API keys there are ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 is installed and takes over now.

Your repos, history and your saved Claude API key are kept."); with nothing to change, it says so ("Up to date.", or, installed from a release, "Dockingbird 0.15.3 is the latest.

Nothing to do.").

With agents running, the new version takes over at once and each agent takes it at its next stopping point, keeping its conversation: see "Rolling updates".

While another `update` is installing or switching, it is refused ("Another dockingbird update is under way here.").

Installed from a folder on this Mac, it rebuilds only when the image is out of date.

Before the first run there is nothing to rebuild: it upgrades only the command (installed from a folder, it says it stays at its version), then says "Dockingbird isn't set up yet; the first dockingbird claude will set it up." and exits 0, setting nothing up.

When uv fails, it names the exact command it ran, so you can run it yourself.

`dockingbird update --check` only says whether a newer version is out.

heading: Operator guide > Update
summary: On a Mac, `update` then installs the Dockingbird GUI the new Dockingbird pins, as `dockingbird ui --install` does, when none is installed (`DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/bin/dockingbird-gui`) and Dockingbird is set up, or puts it in place of one that is another version, gives no version or can't start.
text:
On a Mac, `update` then installs the Dockingbird GUI the new Dockingbird pins, as `dockingbird ui --install` does, when none is installed (`DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/bin/dockingbird-gui`) and Dockingbird is set up, or puts it in place of one that is another version, gives no version or can't start.

The GUI is not yet available to customers, so this step can fail; when it fails, Dockingbird itself is already updated and has said so, and `update` ends with the refusal and its next step, `dockingbird ui --install`, and exits 1 (see "The GUI").

On any other computer, such as a cloud VM, no GUI runs: `update` downloads none, says nothing of it and leaves one already there as it is, and `dockingbird claude --as NAME` there still shows each agent's screen.

Then each tab completion script `dockingbird completion --install` wrote in `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/completion/` becomes the new version's, and `update` says so for each one it rewrote ("Updated tab completion for zsh:" and its path); your shell's startup file is never touched.

heading: Operator guide > Update
summary: After a `uv tool upgrade dockingbird` of your own, the next command finishes the update: it switches Dockingbird and waits for that switch ("Switching Dockingbird to 0.9.1 ...
text: After a `uv tool upgrade dockingbird` of your own, the next command finishes the update: it switches Dockingbird and waits for that switch ("Switching Dockingbird to 0.9.1 ... done"), and a command that meets the new version in the middle of its work stops instead ("Dockingbird is switching to 0.9.1, so this command stopped."), to be run again once `dockingbird status` shows it; with agents running, the home rolls, as "Rolling updates" says. When the upgrade keeps the version (a newer commit of the same release), no command switches Dockingbird by itself: `status` says the code differs ("This program's code differs from the Dockingbird 0.9.1 running here. To switch to it: dockingbird update"), an agent you start runs the code installed here and says so once ("This agent runs the Dockingbird 0.9.1 installed here, not this program's code. To switch to this program's code: dockingbird update"), and `dockingbird update` from the upgraded program switches it. Two `dockingbird` programs with different code on one home (the one on your `PATH` and a checkout's, or the GUI's) never switch it back and forth: the last switch is noted in `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/update/`, and a program whose code that switch replaced won't switch the home back by itself ("Another dockingbird program with different code switched this home last, so this one (0.9.1) won't switch it back by itself."); a typed `dockingbird update` decides, and switches to the program you run it from.

heading: Operator guide > Rolling updates
summary: Dockingbird's own code no longer lives in its image: each release's code goes into the home's code store (a Docker volume), and every container runs the code it was started on, so an update builds the image only when the image's base changed: its operating system, its toolchains, its locked Python packages or its launcher.
text: Dockingbird's own code no longer lives in its image: each release's code goes into the home's code store (a Docker volume), and every container runs the code it was started on, so an update builds the image only when the image's base changed: its operating system, its toolchains, its locked Python packages or its launcher. With agents running, `dockingbird update` puts the new code in the store and starts a background process that replaces Dockingbird's coordinator at once, then asks each running bus or screen agent on other code to take the new code at its next stopping point. `update` names them ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 is installed and takes over now. claude-1 and codex-1 take it at their next stopping point."), after saying, when the new version changes Dockingbird's records, that there is no way back once it takes over ("This update changes Dockingbird's records. Once it takes over, it can't go back to 0.15.2."). An agent switches in place: the same container, the same session and the same conversation, which its tool resumes; its deliveries, held notices and open questions are kept, and before its next prompt, at no cost of a turn, its tool is told ("Dockingbird updated from 0.15.2 to 0.15.3 and resumed your conversation. Continue where you were."). Your agents keep working while the coordinator restarts: their calls are retried through the gap, the claims they hold don't expire because of it, and a question an agent asks meanwhile is retried for a few minutes before the agent is told to ask it again. A command you run meanwhile waits for the coordinator's switch ("Switching Dockingbird to 0.15.3 ..."), minutes at most, never for the agents. Any command of a newer `dockingbird` rolls a home the same way and says so ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 took over. The agents take it at their next stopping point."); a `dockingbird` of the same version with other code, such as a checkout with a local commit, rolls nothing until you run `dockingbird update` from it.

heading: Operator guide > Rolling updates
summary: An agent switches only at a stopping point, never inside a turn or a tool call, and no turn is ended for it.
text: An agent switches only at a stopping point, never inside a turn or a tool call, and no turn is ended for it. A Claude or Codex agent on the bus stops between two turns, when no turn runs; a screen agent at its open gate, once the person's turn has ended; an agent at a terminal never, since a person is at its screen: it keeps its code until its terminal closes, and `update` never asks it. A turn running when the ask comes ends on its own, or at its `turn_minutes` deadline when its command set one, and the agent switches after it. A Claude agent whose own background work (a background command, a subagent or a monitor) still runs when it goes idle waits for that work, up to `SWITCH_BACKGROUND_WAIT_MAX_S`; past it the switch ends the work, and the resumed agent is told that it may have been ended ("A background command of yours may have been ended by the update; check its effect before you run it again."). An agent asked to stop after its turn ends as asked and never switches.

heading: Operator guide > Rolling updates
summary: While a roll runs, `dockingbird status` says how far it got ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 is taking over: claude-1 and codex-1 take it at their next stopping point.") and, beneath, what holds an agent back: an ask an idle agent hasn't answered yet ("claude-1 was asked to take 0.15.3 12 min ago and hasn't answered yet."), a turn it is running, at whose end it switches ("claude-1 takes 0.15.3 at the end of its turn (asked 2 min ago)."), background work it waits for ("claude-1 takes 0.15.3 once the work it runs in the background ends (waiting 5 min; at 30 min at the latest)."), an agent at a terminal ("claude-2 on 0.15.2 keeps its own until its terminal closes."), an agent already on a newer Dockingbird, which is never asked to move ("claude-3 on 0.15.4 is newer and keeps its own until it ends."), and an agent that couldn't take it, with why ("codex-1 on 0.15.2 couldn't take 0.15.3 (its restart command was refused) and keeps its own until it ends.").
text: While a roll runs, `dockingbird status` says how far it got ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 is taking over: claude-1 and codex-1 take it at their next stopping point.") and, beneath, what holds an agent back: an ask an idle agent hasn't answered yet ("claude-1 was asked to take 0.15.3 12 min ago and hasn't answered yet."), a turn it is running, at whose end it switches ("claude-1 takes 0.15.3 at the end of its turn (asked 2 min ago)."), background work it waits for ("claude-1 takes 0.15.3 once the work it runs in the background ends (waiting 5 min; at 30 min at the latest)."), an agent at a terminal ("claude-2 on 0.15.2 keeps its own until its terminal closes."), an agent already on a newer Dockingbird, which is never asked to move ("claude-3 on 0.15.4 is newer and keeps its own until it ends."), and an agent that couldn't take it, with why ("codex-1 on 0.15.2 couldn't take 0.15.3 (its restart command was refused) and keeps its own until it ends."). An idle agent that leaves its ask unanswered for `SWITCH_ASK_ANSWER_MAX_S` is left on its code ("claude-1 on 0.15.2 didn't answer the ask for 0.15.3 in 10 min while idle and keeps its own until it ends or answers."). An agent Dockingbird couldn't ask for `SWITCH_ASK_ANSWER_MAX_S` is left on its code and asked again at every check ("claude-1 on 0.15.2 couldn't take 0.15.3 (Dockingbird couldn't ask it) and keeps its own until it ends."). Run again for the same version, `dockingbird update` changes nothing and says the same, or, once no agent is left to take it, "Dockingbird 0.15.3 is in place, and no agent is waiting to take it."

heading: Operator guide > Rolling updates
summary: The agents a roll leaves on their old code are its stragglers: an agent at a terminal, a screen agent whose gate stays closed, an agent that couldn't take the new code or never answered, and one whose turn runs on.
text:
The agents a roll leaves on their old code are its stragglers: an agent at a terminal, a screen agent whose gate stays closed, an agent that couldn't take the new code or never answered, and one whose turn runs on. The roll checks every `UPDATE_ROLL_POLL_S` and waits for them until each has switched or ended, or until `ROLL_STRAGGLER_WAIT_MAX_S` has passed since only stragglers were left; then it ends, and `status` names the stragglers still running, one line per kind ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 is in place. claude-2 on 0.15.2 keeps its own until its terminal closes."). An agent among them that was asked keeps its ask and switches by itself at its next stopping point ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 is in place. codex-1 on 0.15.2 takes it at its next stopping point, or keeps its own until it ends."), an agent Dockingbird couldn't ask keeps its code until a later `dockingbird update` asks it ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 is in place, but Dockingbird couldn't ask claude-1 on 0.15.2, which keeps its own until it ends. To try again: dockingbird update"), and the old code stays in the store while an agent runs it. A later `dockingbird update` asks the bus and screen stragglers again; an agent at a terminal is never asked, so stop it and start it again to move it to the new code.

| Bound | Default | Past it |
|---|---|---|
| `SWITCH_BACKGROUND_WAIT_MAX_S` | 30 minutes | an idle agent's background work is ended and the agent switches, told so |
| `SWITCH_ASK_ANSWER_MAX_S` | 10 minutes | an idle agent that hasn't answered its ask is left on its code, a straggler |
| `ROLL_READ_FAILED_MAX_S` | 30 minutes | the roll stops when Dockingbird here or its code can't be read for that long; once it is fixed, the next command here resumes the roll |
| `ROLL_STRAGGLER_WAIT_MAX_S` | 24 hours | the roll ends with its stragglers |

heading: Operator guide > Rolling updates
summary: A roll that fails stops, and `status` says so under "Needs your attention" with what fixes it: the new coordinator didn't come up, and the old one runs again ("Dockingbird didn't switch to 0.15.3, so 0.15.2 still runs.
text:
A roll that fails stops, and `status` says so under "Needs your attention" with what fixes it: the new coordinator didn't come up, and the old one runs again ("Dockingbird didn't switch to 0.15.3, so 0.15.2 still runs. See why and try again: dockingbird update"); the new version changed the records but didn't come up, and the old one can't run on them ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 changed the records but didn't come up, and 0.15.2 can't run on them. Fix and try again: dockingbird update"); Dockingbird here couldn't be read ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 is installed, but Dockingbird here or its code couldn't be read for 30 min, so the roll stopped. Fix it; the next command here resumes the roll."); the new code is gone from the store ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 is installed, but its code is gone from here, so the roll stopped. Run it again: dockingbird update"); or the Dockingbird running here was put on other code by hand twice during one update ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 is installed, but the Dockingbird running here was put on other code by hand twice during this update, so the roll stopped. Run it again: dockingbird update").

One case still waits for the agents to end, as every update with agents running did before.

A home whose running Dockingbird is older than `ROLL_FLOOR`, the oldest release a home rolls from in place (the release that brought rolling updates), waits once, for its first update to a release that rolls ("Dockingbird here is too old to take 0.15.3 while agents run, so claude-1 on 0.15.2 keeps its own until it ends.").

`update` judges that from the version label of the Dockingbird running here, before it reads anything through it, builds or stages anything: a label it can't read is refused, exit 1 ("Dockingbird can't tell which version runs here, so it can't take 0.15.3.

Fix the host, then: dockingbird update"), and so, whatever the floor, is a program older than the Dockingbird here while a bus or screen agent runs ("Dockingbird here is newer than this program, so it can't take over while claude-1 on 0.15.3 runs.

Once it has ended, run this again."); an agent at a terminal alone lets it through.

heading: Operator guide > Rolling updates
summary: Meanwhile `status` says what waits ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 is installed and takes over when claude-1 on 0.15.2 ends: Dockingbird here is too old to switch agents while they run."), and, installed from a release, your commands run an exact copy of the version the agents run, kept under `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/update/`.
text:
Meanwhile `status` says what waits ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 is installed and takes over when claude-1 on 0.15.2 ends: Dockingbird here is too old to switch agents while they run."), and, installed from a release, your commands run an exact copy of the version the agents run, kept under `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/update/`.

The switch then happens by itself: once the last agent ends, and the terminal that showed it or `dockingbird stop` has finished ending it, the background process `update` started stops the old Dockingbird and starts the new one, with no command typed, then puts in place the GUI `update` downloaded for it and rewrites the tab completion scripts; it fetches no tool, so the first start after it gets each tool's latest release, as any start does.

A switcher of the kept older copy that is still running when the new release stages is ended by the update.

A switcher of an older release that was loaded before an in-place upgrade ends on its own when it next reads the new record; until the next command run here, which starts the new switcher, the staged update has no switcher.

After a `dockingbird stop`, the switch still happens and Dockingbird stays off until you next use it (with no copy kept, `stop` says so: "Stopped Dockingbird.

It switches to 0.15.3 now and stays off until you next use it.").

A start that a base change overtook starts nothing and says so ("Dockingbird's engine changed while claude-1 started, so claude-1 didn't start.

Run the same command again.").

heading: Operator guide > Rolling updates
summary: An update that changes Dockingbird's engine, the image's base, rolls too: no running container can take a new image, so at its next stopping point each bus or screen agent on the old engine moves to a new container on the new one, keeping its name, its session and its conversation, which its tool resumes.
text:
An update that changes Dockingbird's engine, the image's base, rolls too: no running container can take a new image, so at its next stopping point each bus or screen agent on the old engine moves to a new container on the new one, keeping its name, its session and its conversation, which its tool resumes. `update` names those agents apart ("Dockingbird 0.15.3 is installed and takes over now. It changes Dockingbird's engine too, so claude-1 and codex-1 restart at their next stopping point and keep their conversation."). Each start keeps a record of how its agent was started, `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/agents/<name>/spec.json`, and the move starts the new container from it; `dockingbird clean` removes the record with the agent's copy. An agent started by an older Dockingbird has no record, so `dockingbird set NAME --switch-code KEY` with a key that changes the engine is refused for it, exit 2, and asks nothing ("claude-1 can't take Dockingbird 1a2b3c4d: it changes Dockingbird's engine, and claude-1 started before Dockingbird could restart an agent in place. It keeps 0.15.2 until it ends."); a key on the same engine is asked as before.

You can also move one agent by hand, with or without a roll: `dockingbird set claude-1 --switch-code 3f9a0c21` asks it to take the code with that key at its next stopping point ("claude-1 takes Dockingbird's code 3f9a0c21 at its next stopping point. See it: dockingbird status claude-1"), and `dockingbird set claude-1 --switch-code -` takes the ask back ("claude-1 keeps the Dockingbird code it runs: no switch is asked."). A key the store doesn't hold is refused, exit 2 ("Dockingbird has no code 3f9a0c21 here."), and so is an agent at a terminal ("claude-2 runs at a terminal, which keeps its Dockingbird until it closes. Stop it: dockingbird stop claude-2"). Each `set` is a new ask, so one an agent refused can be asked again.

heading: Operator guide > Reading across versions
summary: Your `PATH` may hold a different Dockingbird from the one a home runs.
text:
Your `PATH` may hold a different Dockingbird from the one a home runs. A home runs the version that last started or updated it. For each home, `dockingbird homes` says what this computer's Dockingbird can do there. It reports two separate things.

- **Readable:** the home's coordinator runs the image this Dockingbird would run there. A command from here leaves that coordinator as it is.

- **Readable for inspection:** the home's coordinator runs Dockingbird 0.6.2 or later, which its `com.dockingbird.version` label shows. Release 0.6.2 is the first whose coordinator answers `inspect`. Three readers can look at such a home: `dockingbird inspect swarm`, `dockingbird inspect config --agent NAME` and the GUI's Swarms tab. Each reads it as `status` reads a home, with one `docker ps` and one `docker exec` in its running coordinator. Each starts, updates and locks nothing.

The list that `inspect swarm` shows comes from the home's own coordinator. One that lists only the running agents shows those, whichever Dockingbird or GUI reads it. An older one lists every agent record, up to 64, until you update it. The GUI runs `dockingbird inspect swarm --roster`, which lists the agents alone, without the pairs. A coordinator of 0.11.1 or later reads only its roster. An older one is read as before and its pairs are left out. Either way the answer is the same: `roster_only` is true and there is no `permissions`. From 0.11.1, `dockingbird --json inspect capabilities` says `roster` and its `version`.

A `dockingbird` older than 0.6.2 on this computer has no `inspect` at all, so the GUI's Swarms tab shows "Inspection unavailable" for every home. A `dockingbird` from before `inspectable` lists no such field. A GUI that reads it falls back to `readable`, and a GUI older than the field reads only readable homes.

The GUI's Inbox tab reads only a readable home. In a home whose coordinator is older, an `inbox` or `questions` call would update that coordinator. Use `dockingbird --json homes` to get `readable`, `inspectable` and `inspect_from` for each home. `inspect_from` is the release that inspection exists from. Use `dockingbird --json inspect instances` to get each home's `inspectable`.

heading: Operator guide > Reading across versions
text:
| The home | `dockingbird homes` says | `inspect` and the Swarms tab | A command from here |
|---|---|---|---|
| Its coordinator runs the image this Dockingbird would run there | its line, readable | read it | runs as usual |
| Its coordinator runs 0.6.2 or later, an older image | "readable for inspection; a command from here would update it" | read it | updates its coordinator to this Dockingbird; its running agents follow (see "Rolling updates") |
| Its coordinator runs a newer Dockingbird whose answer this one reads | "readable for inspection; commands from here are refused: it is newer, update this computer's Dockingbird" | read it (the Swarms tab ignores members it doesn't know) | refused: update this computer's Dockingbird |
| Its coordinator runs a newer Dockingbird that answers in a newer form | the same | refused, exit 1, naming both Dockingbirds and both forms ("... answers inspection in a newer form (2) than this Dockingbird 0.9.1 reads (1): update this computer's Dockingbird."); the Swarms tab shows that line | refused: update this computer's Dockingbird |
| Its coordinator runs a Dockingbird older than 0.6.2, or one that names no version | "not readable from here: its Dockingbird 0.6.1 has no inspection (from 0.6.2)" | refused, exit 1, before anything runs in it, naming its version and 0.6.2 ("... runs Dockingbird 0.6.1, which has no inspection (from 0.6.2): nothing was read."); the Swarms tab says why | updates it; with agents running, it switches once they end |
| Its coordinator is stopped | "not readable from here: a command from here would start it" | nothing is read: `inspect` prints the line `status` prints for it, and the Swarms tab says the home's Dockingbird is stopped | starts it |
| A fleet host answers in a newer form (`--host`) | | refused, exit 1, naming the host, this Dockingbird and both forms | |
| Its `state.json` was written by a newer Dockingbird | its line, as before | read the record as before | the commands that use Docker, `update` and `mcp install` are refused (`STATE_NEWER`) |

heading: Operator guide > Reading across versions
summary: Three refusals say that a pair can't work, and each names both sides.
text: Three refusals say that a pair can't work, and each names both sides. For `INSPECT_NOT_SUPPORTED`, update the home's Dockingbird. Run `dockingbird --home lab update` for the home named `lab`, or `dockingbird update` with `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` set to its folder. With agents running, it waits until they end. For `STATE_NEWER` and `INSPECT_SCHEMA_NEWER`, update this computer's Dockingbird (`dockingbird update`).

heading: Operator guide > Clean
summary: `dockingbird clean` removes old images of this installation and the copies agents left behind, removing a copy that is provably empty at once and asking about each other one first (work not shared yet, changed files, a crash, or an agent that ended before its files were counted; default No).
text:
`dockingbird clean` removes old images of this installation and the copies agents left behind, removing a copy that is provably empty at once and asking about each other one first (work not shared yet, changed files, a crash, or an agent that ended before its files were counted; default No). `--yes` removes them without asking. Without a terminal to ask, or with `--json`, `clean` without `--yes` keeps each copy it would ask about, says so, and exits 1. It names what it removed, each copy with what it held, and how much it freed, in MB under a gigabyte ("Removed 2 copies (reviewer: 1 commit not shared; rev2: empty) and temporary files: 300 MB freed."), and "under 1 MB freed" below a megabyte. A copy you answered no for is named too: "Kept claude-1's copy. Nothing else to clean." Ctrl-C at a question is its no, and the no of every question after it: the rest goes on as answered, and `clean` then exits 130. Harbor's jobs and leftovers are `dockingbird harbor clean`'s (see "Harbor benchmark tasks").

`dockingbird clean codex-1` deletes one agent that stopped, or several (`dockingbird clean codex-1 claude-2`): its kept copy, its results folder and its history, so status and the GUI no longer list it and its name is free for a new agent. It asks first about a copy or results that may hold work, as `clean` does (default No; `--yes` deletes without asking), and it deletes an agent whole or not at all: an answer of no, or a copy it could not remove, keeps everything of that agent and says so. A working agent is refused ("codex-1 is running. To delete it, stop it first: dockingbird stop codex-1"), a name it knows nothing of is said as such, and one with nothing left says "Nothing to delete: codex-1 has no kept copy, results or history." It names what it deleted and what that freed ("Deleted codex-1: its copy (1 commit not shared), its results and its history; 300 MB freed."). Names and `--all` do not go together. On the coordinator's side the history is forgotten, not deleted: each ended session of the name is marked so, and its records stay.

heading: Operator guide > Clean
summary: `dockingbird clean --all` removes everything Docker mode made: this installation's containers, its five volumes (every agent's copy and history, the sign-ins and the saved key, the tools' store, and the toolchains agents get), every agent's dependency cache, its images, every link in your checkouts' `.git/config` (a renamed branch's too; one git can't change is named), and its files in `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` (a `config.toml` you wrote in stays), the marker last.
text:
`dockingbird clean --all` removes everything Docker mode made: this installation's containers, its five volumes (every agent's copy and history, the sign-ins and the saved key, the tools' store, and the toolchains agents get), every agent's dependency cache, its images, every link in your checkouts' `.git/config` (a renamed branch's too; one git can't change is named), and its files in `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` (a `config.toml` you wrote in stays), the marker last.

With `bin/` goes the link to the GUI beside `dockingbird` on your PATH (`~/.local/bin/dockingbird-gui` for a uv install) when it points at this home's GUI; a file or a link to anything else there stays, and the summary names it ("Kept ~/.local/bin/dockingbird-gui: it isn't the link to the GUI this Dockingbird installed."), as it names the link when its folder refuses the removal ("Dockingbird couldn't remove its link to the GUI, so it stays:"; `--verbose` adds why).

`harbor/` goes with them: Harbor's install, its jobs and every container, network, volume and `hb__` image of its jobs, a running job's included, and the list of what is lost names it ("Harbor's jobs and its install go too: ...").

It empties `logs/` but keeps that folder, and so `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` around it: `logs/` is the folder the coordinator writes its logs to through a mount, and Docker Desktop's file sharing can refuse a folder deleted and made again at the same path until Docker Desktop restarts, so the next start would fail.

The summary names it ("Kept the empty folder ~/.local/share/dockingbird/logs, so the next start works."); the next start uses a home holding only that empty folder as its own, and a second `dockingbird clean --all` finds nothing to clean.

To remove it after uninstalling, delete it once Docker Desktop has restarted.

heading: Operator guide > Clean
summary: First it lists what is lost, every item named however long the list, each starting two columns in and its later lines four, so the items never run together: each agent still working, one line each ("  claude-1 is working now: it will be stopped and its copy removed."), each agent that stopped with its copy kept, with what the copy holds when it was counted ("  keep8 stopped with 1 file not committed: its copy will be removed."), and commits the agents shared that you haven't synced, each with the step that keeps them from where you run it ("To keep them: git switch main, then dockingbird sync"; "the agents shared commits you haven't synced" when your checkout lacks their head, uncounted, and "may have shared" only when Dockingbird can't tell); for a branch no longer in your checkout, the commits that only Dockingbird keeps there, synced or not, with the step that makes the branch again ("My App (feature/redo, no longer in your checkout): 2 commits the agents shared are kept only by Dockingbird." and "To keep them: git switch -c feature/redo dockingbird/feature/redo"), and no line when no commit would be lost; for a branch you made under a deleted branch's name, the same count with sync's step, which asks first ("To keep them, say yes when sync asks: dockingbird sync"); then it says "Your code is untouched." and asks you to type `delete` (`--yes` accepts the loss and afterwards names the working agents it stopped; without a terminal and without `--yes` it refuses; any other answer prints "Nothing removed." and exits 1, and Ctrl-C prints it too and exits 130).
text:
First it lists what is lost, every item named however long the list, each starting two columns in and its later lines four, so the items never run together: each agent still working, one line each ("  claude-1 is working now: it will be stopped and its copy removed."), each agent that stopped with its copy kept, with what the copy holds when it was counted ("  keep8 stopped with 1 file not committed: its copy will be removed."), and commits the agents shared that you haven't synced, each with the step that keeps them from where you run it ("To keep them: git switch main, then dockingbird sync"; "the agents shared commits you haven't synced" when your checkout lacks their head, uncounted, and "may have shared" only when Dockingbird can't tell); for a branch no longer in your checkout, the commits that only Dockingbird keeps there, synced or not, with the step that makes the branch again ("My App (feature/redo, no longer in your checkout): 2 commits the agents shared are kept only by Dockingbird." and "To keep them: git switch -c feature/redo dockingbird/feature/redo"), and no line when no commit would be lost; for a branch you made under a deleted branch's name, the same count with sync's step, which asks first ("To keep them, say yes when sync asks: dockingbird sync"); then it says "Your code is untouched." and asks you to type `delete` (`--yes` accepts the loss and afterwards names the working agents it stopped; without a terminal and without `--yes` it refuses; any other answer prints "Nothing removed." and exits 1, and Ctrl-C prints it too and exits 130).

It also removes, in each linked checkout, the refs Dockingbird keeps the agents' head under, `refs/remotes/dockingbird/*`, each by its full name and no other ref; if git can't, it names the checkout and `git branch -dr dockingbird/<branch>`.

Under `--yes`, your own `instructions/` folder and your `versions.toml` are kept; without it, the list names `versions.toml` ("Your tool versions file goes too: ~/.local/share/dockingbird/versions.toml") and it goes.

Your `vaults/` folder, where the stores of your vault connections live, is kept whenever anything is in it, with or without `--yes`, and the summary says so ("Kept the stores of your vault connections: ~/.local/share/dockingbird/vaults"); only an empty one goes, and the next start uses a home holding your kept stores as its own.

heading: Operator guide > Clean
summary: It only ever removes objects carrying this installation's labels, by exact id, and never touches your code, `~/.claude` or `~/.codex`.
text:
It only ever removes objects carrying this installation's labels, by exact id, and never touches your code, `~/.claude` or `~/.codex`.

Docker keeps its build cache, which every project's builds share and which carries no labels, so Dockingbird leaves it alone, and the space it names as freed does not count it.

Dockingbird's own build keeps its downloads there too (apt's packages and lists, uv's cache and the pinned tools' archives), so a rebuild fetches only what changed, and Docker's own garbage collection bounds that cache.

To reclaim that space too, `docker builder prune` removes the unused build cache of every project on this Docker, not only Dockingbird's, so run it only if that is what you want.

heading: Operator guide > Licensing
summary: Dockingbird is licensed by seats: **a seat is one person, who may link up to three computers** (the license's computers per seat): a laptop, a desktop and a cloud VM (on arm64, the only platform Dockingbird runs on) are one seat; a second Dockingbird home on the same computer (another `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`) shares its computer; agents, containers and repos are never counted.
text:
Dockingbird is licensed by seats: **a seat is one person, who may link up to three computers** (the license's computers per seat): a laptop, a desktop and a cloud VM (on arm64, the only platform Dockingbird runs on) are one seat; a second Dockingbird home on the same computer (another `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`) shares its computer; agents, containers and repos are never counted. The terms are Zeusfyi's end-user licence agreement, published at `https://zeus.fyi/legal/dockingbird-eula`, and the privacy note lists what licensing sends to Zeusfyi: nothing from a repo or an agent.

- **Activate.** `dockingbird license activate` asks for your license key (hidden), or reads it from standard input without a terminal (`pbpaste | dockingbird license activate`), and never from the command line: a key given as a word is refused (exit 2), so it never reaches your shell's history or `ps`. This computer is then linked to the license, and it prints the plan, its seats and when the term ends, then the computers linked of the computers its seats admit ("  Computers linked: 4 of 30 (10 seats, 3 computers each)"), or, with a license client that reports no computers, the seats in use ("  Seats in use: 2 of 10"). A license whose computers are all linked refuses the activation (exit 1): "Every computer this license admits is linked, so this one can't join." and "Free one: dockingbird license activations --release ID", then one line per computer linked, seen longest ago first, each with its id; with `--json` that is one envelope whose fields carry those computers and both counts. `dockingbird license activate --label TEXT` names this computer in the list of computers (by default its hostname, at most `LICENSE_LABEL_MAX_CHARS` characters), and `--accept-terms VERSION` accepts the agreement's version for a scripted install. Activating again on a computer already linked keeps its link.

- **Trial.** `dockingbird license trial` starts a trial on this computer, with no key: one per computer.

heading: Operator guide > Licensing
summary: - **Status.** `dockingbird license status` shows the state, the plan, the seats and the term's end, then how many computers one seat may link ("  Computers per seat: 3", when the license client reports it), this computer's label, the lease's end and the last check-in, from the license file on this computer with no network; `dockingbird license status --refresh` checks in with Zeusfyi first.
text:
- **Status.** `dockingbird license status` shows the state, the plan, the seats and the term's end, then how many computers one seat may link ("  Computers per seat: 3", when the license client reports it), this computer's label, the lease's end and the last check-in, from the license file on this computer with no network; `dockingbird license status --refresh` checks in with Zeusfyi first. `dockingbird status` shows the state in one line once this computer has a license file and the license client is here; it never downloads the client. With `--json` they are fields.

- **Seats.** `dockingbird license activations` lists the computers linked to the license (it asks for the key as `activate` does) under the same count line as `activate`; the list holds at most 80 computers, the ones seen longest ago first, and when the license has more it says how many it shows ("  Showing the 80 seen longest ago of 90"). `dockingbird license activations --release ID` frees one, for a computer lost or wiped, then lists the rest. A computer rebuilt with a new identifier (a re-imaged VM, a cloud instance recreated on each deploy, a container or CI runner without a machine id) is a new computer each time. Before you destroy one, run `dockingbird license deactivate` (or `dockingbird clean --all`); otherwise free it with `dockingbird license activations --release ID`; an unreleased one stops counting by itself after 90 days. `dockingbird license deactivate` gives this computer's seat back. `dockingbird clean --all` gives it back first too; when Zeusfyi can't be reached it says the seat is still held, so you can free it from another computer.

- **Check-ins.** Once licensing is enforced, a start whose last check-in is older than `LICENSE_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_S` (a day) checks in with Zeusfyi first, within `LICENSE_HELPER_TIMEOUT_S`, and a failed check-in never stops the start. Without a check-in the license keeps working for its lease, so a computer offline, or an outage at Zeusfyi, interrupts nothing.

heading: Operator guide > Licensing
summary: - **What a refusal means.** Licensing only ever concerns a new agent's start (`claude`, `codex`, `start`, a config's command and `agent_start` of `dockingbird mcp`); reconnecting to a running agent is not a new start.
text: - **What a refusal means.** Licensing only ever concerns a new agent's start (`claude`, `codex`, `start`, a config's command and `agent_start` of `dockingbird mcp`); reconnecting to a running agent is not a new start. `sync`, `stop`, `clean`, `status`, `results`, `read`, `inbox`, `serve`, `update`, `login` and every running agent are never stopped by it, so you always get your work back. In this version licensing is not enforced (`LICENSE_GATE_ENFORCED` is 0): a start reaches no network and downloads nothing; it runs the license client only when one is already here (from an earlier `license` action, such as `dockingbird license activate`, or `DOCKINGBIRD_LICENSE_CLIENT_PATH`), reads its state with no check-in, prints one line for any state but a valid license or none ("agents start because licensing isn't enforced yet" for a reason that would refuse), and the agent starts; a client here that can't be used is noted in the error log, and the agent starts. Once licensing is enforced, from the release that sells the first plan: when the term nears its end, the computer has been offline a while, or the term or lease has ended and its grace period runs, a start prints one line saying so and the agent starts. Past the grace period, the start is refused before anything runs (exit 1), with the reason and its next step: `dockingbird license activate` (no license here, a seat freed from another computer, another computer's or an unreadable license file), `dockingbird license status --refresh` once the license is renewed or this computer is back online, or `dockingbird update` when the license needs a newer Dockingbird. A license client that couldn't be downloaded refuses the start too, saying why, with the next step `dockingbird license status`, which tries the download again at once; one that is here but broken or too slow to answer refuses it with the next step `dockingbird update`; never a silent pass.

heading: Operator guide > Licensing
summary: - **The license client.** Licensing runs Zeusfyi's license client, `zeusfyi-license`: Dockingbird hands it the key on its standard input, reads its answer and shows it, and decides nothing itself.
text:
- **The license client.** Licensing runs Zeusfyi's license client, `zeusfyi-license`: Dockingbird hands it the key on its standard input, reads its answer and shows it, and decides nothing itself. The first `license` action (`dockingbird license activate`, `dockingbird license trial`, and the others) downloads it from Zeusfyi into `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/bin/`, within `LICENSE_CLIENT_FETCH_TIMEOUT_S` and `LICENSE_CLIENT_MAX_BYTES`, checks it against the sha256 this Dockingbird pins before writing it, and keeps it; a wrong digest leaves nothing. Once licensing is enforced, a start downloads it too when it is missing, and after a failed download a start tries again only once `LICENSE_CLIENT_RETRY_S` (an hour) has passed (the failure's time is kept beside it); a `license` action always tries at once. `DOCKINGBIRD_LICENSE_CLIENT_PATH` names a client of your own instead (an absolute path; tests use it), and `DOCKINGBIRD_LICENSE_AUTHORITY_URL` another license server.

- **Updates from Zeusfyi's index.** Installed from Zeusfyi's package index, `dockingbird update` and `dockingbird update --check` use this computer's activation as the index's password (its download token, read from the license file and given to uv in its environment only, never in a command line or a log). The index serves releases to a current license only: after a term ends, the installed version keeps working, and new releases need the license renewed. Without an activation, `update` says to run `dockingbird license activate` first.

heading: Operator guide > Toolchains
summary: Each agent runs the language versions its repo names where production reads them: its `mise.toml`, its `.tool-versions`, and the version files its `mise.toml` enables under `[settings]` (`idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools = ["node", "python"]` makes mise read `.nvmrc` and `.python-version`), with `mise.lock` deciding over them, as mise decides.
text:
Each agent runs the language versions its repo names where production reads them: its `mise.toml`, its `.tool-versions`, and the version files its `mise.toml` enables under `[settings]` (`idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools = ["node", "python"]` makes mise read `.nvmrc` and `.python-version`), with `mise.lock` deciding over them, as mise decides. Dockingbird reads none of these files itself: [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev) does, in a container of Dockingbird's own, and installs each version once per Mac into a store every agent mounts read-only. A start says what the repo's agents get on its first line, "Toolchain for myapp: Python 3.12.7 (mise.toml) and Node 20.18.1 (.nvmrc).", and when a version isn't installed yet, installs it with a live line before anything else starts ("Installing Node 20.18.1 ... {elapsed}: <mise's latest line>", then "Installed Node 20.18.1 ({elapsed})."); a second agent on the same repo prints the first line alone. A repo that names nothing starts as before, with the image's versions: "Toolchain for myapp: nothing named; agents get the image's versions." An install that fails stops the start before anything is made, with mise's last lines; `dockingbird claude --no-toolchain` (also on `codex` and `start`) starts with the image's versions for that one start, and `--no-deps` keeps the toolchain and skips the repo's dependency install (below). Neither is remembered. Ctrl-C while a version installs ends the start (exit 130) and leaves the install going, so the next start uses it. A running agent keeps the versions it started with; `dockingbird status` says when its repo now asks for others.

`dockingbird env` shows the table for the repo you are in: each tool its files name, with the request and its file, beside the version agents get, "(locked)" when `mise.lock` names it, "(not installed yet)" when no start has installed it; then the image's Python, Node and Go that nothing names; then how many toolchains this Mac holds, and how to change one:

```text
myapp (main)   repo wants         agents get
  Python       3.12 (mise.toml)   3.12.7 (locked)
  Node         20 (.nvmrc)        20.18.1
  Go           nothing named      1.27.2 (the image's)
Dependencies: none preinstalled (no lock file).
Downloaded: 2 toolchains. Unused ones go with: dockingbird clean
Change one: dockingbird env use TOOL VERSION
```

heading: Operator guide > Toolchains
summary: It runs mise's look in a container, with your checkout mounted read-only, and writes nothing in it.
text: It runs mise's look in a container, with your checkout mounted read-only, and writes nothing in it.
