Before the store's line it names the dependency installs a start runs for a repo that names a toolchain, read from the lock files on your Mac ("Dependencies: uv sync --locked (uv.lock) and npm ci (package-lock.json)", or "Dependencies: none preinstalled (no lock file)."); for a repo that names none, whose agents get the image's versions and install nothing, it says "Dependencies: none preinstalled (the repo names no toolchain).". With Docker off it shows the heading, says the versions need Dockingbird running, and shows the store's line from its last record and the dependencies line from the lock files, which then can't tell whether the repo names a toolchain. Outside a repo it says so and exits 1. In a narrow pane each tool's two values stack under its name; with `--json` each line is one envelope, a tool's row adding `tool_word`, `locked` and `installed`. `dockingbird env install` installs those versions now, so the next start waits for none, and writes nothing in your checkout. `dockingbird env lock` writes each version, exact, into the repo's `mise.toml` and locks it in `mise.lock`, and says to commit both (`git add mise.toml mise.lock`): every Mac, and every agent, then gets the same. `dockingbird env use node 22` writes one version into the repo's `mise.toml`, making the file when there is none, and installs it: "Wrote mise.toml: node = "22" (was .nvmrc: 20; mise.toml wins now). Agents started from now get Node 22.11.0.", then the running agents that keep theirs until restarted. Its TOOL is one of python, node, go, java, rust, ruby, bun, deno, zig, pnpm, yarn and npm, and its VERSION a version number (`22`, `3.12`, `1.82.0`; Go's `prefix:1.20`; Java's `temurin-21`, or `21` for mise's default vendor), never `lts` or `latest`, which it refuses with an example; another tool mise knows goes into `mise.toml` by hand. `dockingbird clean` removes the versions no running agent and no repo's last look names, and clears mise's download cache; `dockingbird clean --all` removes the store with the other volumes.

heading: Operator guide > Toolchains
summary: **Dependencies.** Before its tool starts, an agent whose repo names a toolchain installs the repo's dependencies in its own copy (one with the image's versions installs none), from the lock files at the repo's top, with the toolchain's own package managers, as production would: `uv.lock` runs `uv sync --locked`, `package-lock.json` `npm ci`, `pnpm-lock.yaml` `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `yarn.lock` `yarn install --immutable` (Yarn 2 and later) or `yarn install --frozen-lockfile` (Yarn 1), `go.sum` `go mod download`, `Cargo.lock` `cargo fetch --locked` and `Gemfile.lock` `BUNDLE_FROZEN=true bundle install`.
text: **Dependencies.** Before its tool starts, an agent whose repo names a toolchain installs the repo's dependencies in its own copy (one with the image's versions installs none), from the lock files at the repo's top, with the toolchain's own package managers, as production would: `uv.lock` runs `uv sync --locked`, `package-lock.json` `npm ci`, `pnpm-lock.yaml` `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `yarn.lock` `yarn install --immutable` (Yarn 2 and later) or `yarn install --frozen-lockfile` (Yarn 1), `go.sum` `go mod download`, `Cargo.lock` `cargo fetch --locked` and `Gemfile.lock` `BUNDLE_FROZEN=true bundle install`. A lock file that doesn't match its manifest fails the install, as it would in production; a Maven or Gradle build and a `requirements.txt` without a lock file get nothing. Only a checkout you trust gets them, since install scripts are the repo's code: in one you marked untrusted the agent gets its toolchain alone and says "Dependencies: skipped (untrusted checkout; dockingbird trust allows them).". The agent shows "Installing myapp's dependencies: uv sync --locked (uv.lock)", the command's own lines as they come, then "Dependencies installed ({elapsed})." on its screen at a terminal, or in its log on the bus, where `dockingbird status` shows it as "preparing: installing dependencies". An install that fails ends the agent before its tool starts ("claude-1 stopped before it started: its dependencies couldn't be installed."). `dockingbird status` then names the command, its last lines and the way on without them: `dockingbird claude --as claude-1 --no-deps`. Downloads from npm, uv and Go go to a cache of the agent's own, the Docker volume `dockingbird-cache-<agent>` at `/dockingbird/cache`. A restart of the same agent keeps it. The other package managers keep their caches in the agent's own HOME. `dockingbird clean` removes an agent's cache with its kept copy. `dockingbird clean NAME` removes it with the agent, and `dockingbird clean --all` removes all of them. An agent whose egress is `none` or `models` reaches no registry. It runs each command's offline form (`uv sync --locked --offline`, `npm ci --offline`, and so on) from what is cached. When a package isn't cached, the agent ends ("its dependencies couldn't install offline"). `dockingbird status` then names two ways on. One is `dockingbird claude --as claude-1 --egress full`, whose egress reaches the registries. The other is `dockingbird claude --as claude-1 --no-deps`, which skips all of it ("Dependencies: skipped (--no-deps).").

heading: Operator guide > Toolchains
summary: A repo's mise config can do more than name versions.
text: A repo's mise config can do more than name versions. Its `[env]` sets variables and its `[settings]` change how mise installs. Both load only in a checkout you trust. Every checkout counts as trusted, unless you marked it with `dockingbird trust --off` or made untrusted the default (see "Trust"). In a checkout you marked untrusted, a config that needs trust stops the start, and `env` does the same, with mise's own words and two ways on. The first is `dockingbird trust`. The second is a start with the image's versions, `dockingbird claude --no-toolchain`. A `mise.toml` of plain versions, a `.tool-versions` and the version files need no trust. For an agent whose repo names a toolchain, a config's `[env]` (see "Your own commands (configs)") arrives through mise too, before the repo's own. The repo's `mise.toml` entry of a name therefore wins. A config's `mise_env` names mise's environments for its agents (`mise_env = "ci"` makes mise read `mise.ci.toml` over `mise.toml`), for their toolchain's install and for their environment.

heading: Operator guide > The GUI
summary: The GUI's install is not yet available to customers, so on your computer `dockingbird ui` prints `GUI_MISSING`, as [the GUI](guides/gui.md) shows.
text:
The GUI's install is not yet available to customers, so on your computer `dockingbird ui` prints `GUI_MISSING`, as [the GUI](guides/gui.md) shows.

`dockingbird ui` opens the Dockingbird GUI, `dockingbird-gui`, in the terminal you run it in: a terminal program built from [herdr](https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr) (Apache-2.0), with herdr's colours, layout and plugins, that shows every agent and runs Dockingbird's actions.

It is mouse first: click a pane, a tab, a workspace or a row to focus it, drag a border to resize a split, drag over text to copy it, and right-click for a menu; every action has a key too.

Its header shows a small bird beside "Dockingbird" and its version (one line and no bird on a terminal under 20 rows or 60 columns).

Each running agent at a terminal gets a tab of its own, named after it, whose one pane is the agent's screen, in a workspace for its repo and branch, named as status names them ("My App (main)"); a tab you close stays closed until you open it from the agent's row.

The pane runs `dockingbird claude --as NAME` (or `codex`, or its config's command), typed with the full path of the `dockingbird` the GUI reads with, in the agent's checkout when status names one, else in the folder you started `dockingbird ui` in, so it takes the agent over from a terminal that shows it, as that command does anywhere.

Under the workspaces, above herdr's own agents panel, the section "dockingbird" shows once Dockingbird has something to show (with no agent, no message and no question there is no section and no command bar, and `ctrl+b d` still works): first a row for the inbox, "Inbox (3)", then a row for each agent whose container runs, those on the bus too, each agent once: in each home the agents that ask first, then those `working`, `preparing`, `waiting`, `idle`, `failed`, `crashed`, `stopped`, `done` and `ended`, in status's order within one state.

An agent whose container is gone, the kept copy of a stopped or crashed agent or one that ended, has no row here; `dockingbird status` still lists it.

heading: Operator guide > The GUI
summary: A row has up to three lines: its name and its state as Dockingbird writes it (`working`, `idle`, `asks 1`, `stopped`, `failed`, `done`); its tool and the computer it runs on, then "no screen" for an agent without one (`claude · local-macbook-pro`); and its repo and branch (`my-app · feat/x`), a line only an agent with a branch has.
text:
A row has up to three lines: its name and its state as Dockingbird writes it (`working`, `idle`, `asks 1`, `stopped`, `failed`, `done`); its tool and the computer it runs on, then "no screen" for an agent without one (`claude · local-macbook-pro`); and its repo and branch (`my-app · feat/x`), a line only an agent with a branch has.

The computer is named after the Mac's model as macOS gives it, such as `local-macbook-pro` on a MacBook Pro; on Linux, or when macOS gives no model, it is `local-` and the first part of the hostname.

The row of the selected agent, the one the command bar shows, takes the active row's colour.

When a read fails, a line "status: ..." with the error follows the inbox row, and the rows of the last good read stay; rows that do not fit end in "+2 more".

A click on an agent's row, or Enter on it after `ctrl+b` and the arrows past the last workspace, opens the agent's screen: its tab comes forward, or opens and runs its command, and when the pane's shell is idle in front (after a detach or a takeover) the GUI types the command there again.

An agent on the bus has no screen with this Dockingbird: a click on its row only selects it, for the command bar, and `a` on it says "it has no screen to open".

A pane's state (working, blocked or idle) is Dockingbird's own record of the agent: the GUI reports it for the pane, and that report wins over what herdr reads on the agent's screen, so an agent that asks you something is blocked, "asks you 1 question(s)", and one that works is working whatever its screen shows.

The GUI reads `dockingbird --json status` and `dockingbird --json inbox`, and `dockingbird --json questions` while a question waits, when it starts and then 2 minutes after each read ends, and again at once for `r` and when a command's popup ends; a start here, a pick-up that starts an agent and a click that opens a tab wait for the next read, so a new agent's row can take up to 2 minutes unless you press `r`.

An agent that ends keeps its tab until you close it; while its container runs its row shows how it ended, and the command bar shows its next step.

heading: Operator guide > The GUI
summary: herdr's prefix is `ctrl+b`: press it, let go, then press a key, as `ctrl+b ?` lists every binding (Dockingbird's layer is one line there); pressing `ctrl+b` twice sends the pane a plain `ctrl+b`.
text:
herdr's prefix is `ctrl+b`: press it, let go, then press a key, as `ctrl+b ?` lists every binding (Dockingbird's layer is one line there); pressing `ctrl+b` twice sends the pane a plain `ctrl+b`.

Dockingbird's actions are a layer under the prefix, `ctrl+b`, then `d`, then a letter: `n` starts an agent (a form of four questions: here, in a tab of its own, or in the background on the bus; the tool, `claude`, `codex` or a config's command; its name; and, in the background, its task), `x` stops a working agent with `dockingbird stop NAME --yes` (the same as `dockingbird stop NAME`, which asks nothing, since its work is kept) or, after a y, deletes a stopped one, `R` saves its results, `y` syncs the folder you started the GUI in, `p` picks up an ended agent, `a` opens its screen, as a click on its row does, `i` opens the inbox tab and `r` reads everything again; `Esc` or any other key leaves the layer and runs nothing, `m` and `s` too: the GUI has no form that changes a model, effort or compact point or sends a message (`dockingbird set NAME` and `dockingbird send NAME TEXT` do, in a shell).

A right click on an agent's row opens a menu of the same actions for it: "Stop" ("Delete..." once it ended), "Results", "Pick up" (an ended agent with a command to pick it up), "Answer in its screen" (while it asks), "Start an agent...", "Sync", "Inbox" and "Read everything again".

A key that needs an agent acts on the agent of the focused pane, else on the only agent, else asks "which agent?".

Each action composes the exact `dockingbird` command: a stop, a delete, results, a sync, a start in the background and a pick-up that starts no agent show it on the first line of a popup and run it there, in a pane of its own, and the GUI reads Dockingbird's state again when it ends, while a start here and a pick-up that starts an agent type it in the agent's tab.

`x` on a stopped codex-1 asks "delete codex-1? its records go too; type y to delete" and runs `dockingbird clean codex-1 --yes` only after your y, and `n` in the background with `claude`, notes-2 and a task runs `dockingbird start --bus --as notes-2 --harness claude TASK`.

heading: Operator guide > The GUI
summary: Under the panes, one row is the command bar, for the selected agent, the one whose pane has the focus, else the row you clicked last: on its left its name, tool and state, its model, effort and context in status's short marks (`->` while a `set` change is on its way) and one note, the first that applies (that it asks you, its pane's trouble, what the GUI typed for it or waits for, or an ended agent's next step, "next: ..."); on its right its buttons, each the layer's key for that agent: `results`, `stop`, `answer` while it asks, `sync` when status names its checkout (a sync in that checkout), `inbox`, `start` and `refresh` for a working agent; `pick up` when it has a command, `delete`, `results`, `inbox`, `start` and `refresh` for one that ended; `start` and `refresh` with none selected.
text:
Under the panes, one row is the command bar, for the selected agent, the one whose pane has the focus, else the row you clicked last: on its left its name, tool and state, its model, effort and context in status's short marks (`->` while a `set` change is on its way) and one note, the first that applies (that it asks you, its pane's trouble, what the GUI typed for it or waits for, or an ended agent's next step, "next: ..."); on its right its buttons, each the layer's key for that agent: `results`, `stop`, `answer` while it asks, `sync` when status names its checkout (a sync in that checkout), `inbox`, `start` and `refresh` for a working agent; `pick up` when it has a command, `delete`, `results`, `inbox`, `start` and `refresh` for one that ended; `start` and `refresh` with none selected.

The inbox is a tab, "inbox", that `i`, the bar's `inbox`, a click on the inbox row or the menu's "Inbox" opens, or brings forward: the questions first, each with its options numbered under it, then the messages, or "Nothing waits for you."; the arrows (or `j` and `k`) and the wheel select a row, Enter or a click on a message runs `dockingbird read 3` and shows its output in the tab (`Esc` goes back), Enter or a click on a question opens the asking agent's screen, where you answer it, `r` reads again at once (else it reads every 2 minutes) and `q` closes the tab.

The inbox view over the panes is gone, with its reply, its digits that picked an option and its typed answer.

Nothing in the GUI answers a question or sends a message.

You answer in the agent's screen (see `answer` under "Delegated agents").

With an agent's tab open, the GUI types one thing Dockingbird holds for that agent, and never an answer: a change you made with `dockingbird set claude-1 --effort low` to a Claude agent at a terminal.

It types it at the agent's next idle prompt with nothing typed in it (see `set`).

`ctrl+b q` detaches.

The GUI's server keeps running in the background, with every pane and its agent, as it does when you close the terminal window.

`dockingbird ui` attaches to it again, with the panes as you left them.

heading: Operator guide > The GUI
summary: This computer has one GUI server, whichever `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` and whichever folder you start `dockingbird ui` from.
text:
This computer has one GUI server, whichever `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME` and whichever folder you start `dockingbird ui` from.

Its herdr session is `dockingbird`.

On a computer whose GUI ran before Dockingbird 0.4.4, it is the session the GUI had then, `dockingbird-` and the default home's profile id, for as long as its folder in `~/.config/dockingbird-gui/sessions` is there.

The first `dockingbird ui` starts the server.

Every later one, from any home and any folder, attaches to it.

It shows every Dockingbird home that `dockingbird homes` lists: the home you started it from, and every other home while its agents run.

The GUI runs in your home folder (`HOME`, else `/`), never in the folder you typed `dockingbird ui` in.

Its commands, popups and a start here outside a checkout run there.

When the session 0.4.4 started runs beside the one from before, `dockingbird ui` says so before the GUI opens, with the commands that open it and end it.

Nothing in either is ended.

`dockingbird ui stop` stops that server, and every attached view ends.

It needs no terminal, so it runs in a script too.

It runs the GUI `dockingbird ui` finds, with that session and herdr's `server stop`.

A `dockingbird-gui` you run bare from your `PATH` targets herdr's default session, not Dockingbird's, which is why `ui stop` exists.

Closing a pane leaves its agent working, as closing a terminal window does.

The GUI's own files are named `dockingbird-gui`, never `herdr` (its settings are `~/.config/dockingbird-gui/config.toml`), so a herdr of your own is untouched, and it makes no network call of its own: no update check, no announcements, no release notes.

The sidebar's borders move with a drag, and the one under the pointer is drawn in the theme's accent colour: the line between the sidebar and the panes, which you can grab in three columns (the sidebar's last column, the line itself and the pane's border beside it), sets the sidebar's width (18 to 36 columns; a second press within 350 ms puts back the default, 26), the rule under the workspaces sets their share, and the rule above herdr's agents panel, with the two title rows under it, sets the Dockingbird section's share (until you drag it, the section takes the rows its agents need).

Each is saved when you let go, under `~/.local/state/dockingbird-gui` (`$XDG_STATE_HOME/dockingbird-gui` when that is set), and read back next time.

heading: Operator guide > The GUI
summary: When the GUI is not connected to its server, the keys and clicks you send a pane are dropped, never sent later, and a yellow card at the top right says so once for that spell, for 8 seconds: "Input not sent", "Local is not ready, so your keys and clicks were not sent.
text:
When the GUI is not connected to its server, the keys and clicks you send a pane are dropped, never sent later, and a yellow card at the top right says so once for that spell, for 8 seconds: "Input not sent", "Local is not ready, so your keys and clicks were not sent.

Send them again once it is online."

`dockingbird ui --install` installs the GUI, or puts the version this Dockingbird pins in place of another: it fetches that version, checks the file's SHA-256 against the pinned one and puts it at `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/bin/dockingbird-gui`, and a link to it next to `dockingbird` on your PATH (`~/.local/bin/dockingbird-gui` for a uv install), so `dockingbird-gui` works as a command; run bare it opens herdr's default session, not Dockingbird's (herdr's session `dockingbird`): use `dockingbird ui`, and `dockingbird ui stop` to stop the server ("Installed dockingbird-gui 0.1.0:", its path, "On your PATH:" and the link's, then "Open it: dockingbird ui").

A link already there is replaced; a file of your own in its place is left as it is and named ("Dockingbird left this as it is, since it didn't make it:"), and a folder that refuses the link is named too ("Dockingbird couldn't put dockingbird-gui on your PATH here:"); the GUI is installed either way, and `dockingbird ui` runs it.

It needs no terminal, so it runs in a script and with `--json` too.

A download whose checksum differs installs nothing: it names both checksums and says "Nothing was installed, and the dockingbird-gui you had stays." When the fetch fails, it shows what git said, and a build with no pinned checksum yet is not installed at all ("Dockingbird installs nothing it can't check."); each of these exits 1.

The GUI is built for Apple silicon Macs and arm64 Linux, and anywhere else it says "dockingbird-gui has no build for" the platform.

On a Mac, `dockingbird update` installs the GUI and keeps it at the pin: when `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/bin/dockingbird-gui` is missing and Dockingbird is set up, or is another version, gives no version or can't start, it installs the pinned one after its own last line, and when it is at the pin but its link is missing or points elsewhere, it makes the link again ("dockingbird-gui 0.1.0 is on your PATH now:").

heading: Operator guide > The GUI
summary: On any other computer, such as a cloud VM, `update` gets no GUI and leaves one already there as it is; `dockingbird ui --install` still installs it there when you ask.
text:
On any other computer, such as a cloud VM, `update` gets no GUI and leaves one already there as it is; `dockingbird ui --install` still installs it there when you ask.

`dockingbird ui` runs the GUI that `DOCKINGBIRD_GUI` names (a path, for development; nowhere else then), else `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/bin/dockingbird-gui`, else the first `dockingbird-gui` on your `PATH`, and only the version this Dockingbird pins: without one it says "The Dockingbird GUI isn't installed.

Install it: dockingbird ui --install", for another version "The Dockingbird GUI at <its path> is 0.0.9, and this Dockingbird needs 0.1.0.

Install that one: dockingbird ui --install", for a file it can't run "The Dockingbird GUI at <its path> can't be run.

Install it again: dockingbird ui --install", and for a `DOCKINGBIRD_GUI` that names no file "There's no Dockingbird GUI at <its path>, which DOCKINGBIRD_GUI names.

Unset it to use the installed one: unset DOCKINGBIRD_GUI", each exit 1.

In the same way, for development and tests, `DOCKINGBIRD_GUI_SESSION` names another session for the GUI than the one every home shares (`dockingbird ui` and `dockingbird ui stop` then run in that one), and set but empty it is refused: "DOCKINGBIRD_GUI_SESSION is set but empty, so it names nothing to run the GUI in.

Unset it to use the GUI's own: unset DOCKINGBIRD_GUI_SESSION", exit 1.

It needs a terminal: in a pipe or a script, and with `--json` (`dockingbird --json ui`), it prints "dockingbird ui needs a terminal: run it in Terminal, not in a pipe or a script." (under `--json`, that message's envelope) and exits 1.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: Besides `dockingbird claude` and `dockingbird codex`, which you work in, Dockingbird runs agents you hand a task to and talk to through its message bus, each in its own container with its own copy, as today.
text:
Besides `dockingbird claude` and `dockingbird codex`, which you work in, Dockingbird runs agents you hand a task to and talk to through its message bus, each in its own container with its own copy, as today. Every exchange command acts as one client of yours on this Mac (the "host" client), so a question an agent asks you waits in one inbox, and every message you send names you as its sender, so the agent can answer you.

**Starting one.** `dockingbird start "Fix the failing test"` starts an agent on this repo, in its own container and without a terminal, and returns once the agent is running, which takes about half a minute; it prints a line for each step it waits on (preparing the agent's copy, starting its container, sending the task).

The task is the first message of the agent's own thread, and the command names the agent, the thread and the way to follow it: "claude-1 started on myapp (main)." then "Thread <id>.

Watch: dockingbird wait claude-1".

It runs Claude unless `--harness codex` says otherwise, and names its agents as the tool's own command does (`claude-1`, `claude-2`, and so on).

`--task -` reads the task from standard input, and `--file PATH` attaches a text file to it (repeatable).

Without a task the agent starts idle, and the command says how to send it its first one.

`--terminal` runs the agent attached to this terminal instead; `--bus` names the bus, the mode a start takes when no config fixes the terminal, and a config whose `mode` fixes the other one refuses either flag ("review runs with mode = terminal: .dockingbird/app.toml says so") instead of running the mode you didn't ask for; both flags at once are refused too.

`--cpus N` and `--memory SIZE` limit the agent's container (`--cpus 2`, `--cpus 1.5`, `--memory 4g`, `--memory 512m`; a memory limit leaves it no swap), on `claude` and `codex` too, and a config's `[limits]` table sets them as `cpus = "2"` and `memory = "4g"`, which a different flag can't override; without them the container has no limit of its own.

`status NAME` shows them, an `--as NAME` pick-up keeps them unless you give others, and `set` can't change them: they are fixed when the container starts.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: `--compact-at N` sets the context size at which the agent's tool compacts its conversation, in tokens or `auto` (`500000`, `500k` and `1M` are the forms `set` takes; Claude Code takes 100K to 1M, Codex any count of tokens); the start asks it of the agent's session as it opens and before its container is made, as `set NAME --compact-at` asks it of a running agent, so the tool applies it from the agent's next turn on (a Codex agent at a terminal, whose session takes no such ask, gets it as Codex's own word after the tool's arguments, `-c model_auto_compact_token_limit=N`, and `auto` adds none); an `--as NAME` pick-up of an agent whose last session had a point asked keeps it, by asking it again, unless you type another; a point outside the range is refused before anything starts.
text:
`--compact-at N` sets the context size at which the agent's tool compacts its conversation, in tokens or `auto` (`500000`, `500k` and `1M` are the forms `set` takes; Claude Code takes 100K to 1M, Codex any count of tokens); the start asks it of the agent's session as it opens and before its container is made, as `set NAME --compact-at` asks it of a running agent, so the tool applies it from the agent's next turn on (a Codex agent at a terminal, whose session takes no such ask, gets it as Codex's own word after the tool's arguments, `-c model_auto_compact_token_limit=N`, and `auto` adds none); an `--as NAME` pick-up of an agent whose last session had a point asked keeps it, by asking it again, unless you type another; a point outside the range is refused before anything starts.

`--session-hours N` sets how long the agent may run before it ends itself, a whole number from 1 to 168 hours (a config's `session_hours` may go as far as the installation's maximum); without it the agent gets its config's `[limits]` `session_hours`, 12 hours when the config names none; with no config a bus agent gets the installation's default of 12 hours, and an agent at a terminal runs with no session limit; the connections an added config grants it end with that life.

A config whose `[limits]` names a `session_hours` fixes it, as it fixes `cpus` and `memory`: a different `--session-hours` is refused and the same value is not.

An `--as NAME` pick-up of an agent started with `--session-hours` asks for the same life again unless you type another; a value outside the range is refused before anything starts.

`--as NAME` names the agent: a name whose agent has ended picks up where it left off and gets what waited for it, by that agent's own command or in the default environment it ran in, whatever the checkout's default, each such message marked as delivered again after the restart so that the agent acknowledges work it already finished instead of repeating it (`--new` starts it afresh), and a name still running is refused, with the step that sends it a task instead.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: `--command NAME` runs a config's command (below); with no command named, a checkout whose `.dockingbird/` marks one command `default = true` runs that one and says so first ("Using review from .dockingbird/app.toml for this checkout"), and any other checkout runs the default environment, the agent you get with no config.
text:
`--command NAME` runs a config's command (below); with no command named, a checkout whose `.dockingbird/` marks one command `default = true` runs that one and says so first ("Using review from .dockingbird/app.toml for this checkout"), and any other checkout runs the default environment, the agent you get with no config.

The words after `--` go to the tool as its own arguments, except the flags Dockingbird sets itself for an agent without a terminal and the hook-trust bypass, which are refused before anything runs.

An agent without a terminal can't sign in, so a start refuses a tool that has neither a sign-in nor a saved API key, with the step to sign in first.

| Command | What it does |

|---|---|

| `dockingbird inbox` | The messages waiting for you, one page, each priority's newest first; `--all` lists every row, each with its row number, its sender, its kind, its priority, its subject (whole, up to the bus's bound of 120 characters, on the screen and under `--json`, as in every row that carries a subject: the fleet engine reads a reviewer's `approved` line from it) and its age; "N more" with the `--all` that lists them when more wait than the page shows. `--priority P1` lists only the messages of that priority (`P0` to `P3`) and `--questions` only the questions, so you see what needs an answer; given together, a message must match both, and "N more" counts the matching ones and names the same options. `--page 2` shows the second page of 20 (of the matching messages, with a filter), and the line after its rows says how many more wait and names `--page 3`; a page past the last says it is empty and how many pages there are; `--page` with `--all` is refused. A message gets its number when you first see it, here or from `dockingbird wait`, and keeps it while it waits, so the numbers of the others never shift when one leaves; they start at 1 again once your inbox is empty. Only the messages a listing shows get numbers, so `dockingbird wait` still tells you one a filter hid |

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
text:
| `dockingbird inbox claude-2` | The messages waiting in that agent's inbox: what the other agents (and you) sent it, each with its sender, kind, priority, subject, age and the `dockingbird read <id>` that reads it; no row numbers, since those belong to your own inbox. This is how you read what your agents send each other (see "Between agents" below); nothing is copied into your inbox |

| `dockingbird inbox --clear` | Clears what agents that have stopped left in your inbox: each of their notices (a message that needs no answer) is marked read, as reading it with `dockingbird read <id>` marks it, and each of their open questions is closed with one fixed answer saying the agent had stopped, its inbox row too. Their tasks, review requests and handed-over work stay in your inbox, and the last line counts them; messages from Dockingbird itself and from running agents are left alone. It prints a row for each item it cleared: the agent, the kind, "read" or "closed", and the id. Nothing is deleted: every message still reads by its id, `dockingbird read <id>`. It takes no agent name and, of the inbox options, only `--swarm`, `--engine` and `--no-swarm` (the next row), with which it clears only the stopped agents they pick; on a home whose swarm record holds two or more swarms it needs them, and without them it is refused before anything is cleared, naming the command that clears them all, such as `dockingbird inbox --clear --swarm billing,onboarding --no-swarm` |

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
text:
| `dockingbird inbox --swarm billing` | Only the messages from that swarm's agents, by the home's swarm record (`dockingbird swarm list` shows it): on a home that several sessions share, such as a fleet engine home, each session lists its own agents' messages this way. `dockingbird inbox --engine <id>` lists those from the agents of a fleet workload, by the id `fleet submit` printed, and `--no-swarm` those from agents in no swarm and Dockingbird's own notices; `--swarm` and `--engine` take several, separated by commas (`--swarm billing,onboarding`), the options add up, and with `--priority` or `--questions` a message must match both. A swarm the record does not hold is no error: it lists nothing, as a swarm none of whose agents has started yet does. An agent the record does not hold, such as one started without `--swarm`, is in no swarm, whatever its name. Under `--json`, every row of `inbox`, `read` and `wait` names its sender's `swarm` and that swarm's `workload_id`, each null when there is none; `wait` takes none of these options, so a script that waits picks its messages by those. On a shared home, each session gives its own options on every `inbox`, `read` and `inbox --clear` it runs there, and `read` with them never marks another session's message (the `dockingbird read 3` row below) |

| `dockingbird search "closed issues"` | The newest messages in every thread of this repo's agents whose subject or body has every word, each with its sender, kind, subject and age; "More messages match" when a page is not all of them. It reads as the operator, so it sees the agents' own threads too, and shows no body: it finds, `read` reads what came to you |

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
text:
| `dockingbird read 3` | One message: its kind, sender and subject, then its whole body (every control character escaped), then the files it names. A row number prints what it resolved to first ("read 3 -> <id>"), and `read 1` after `read 2` still reads the message that was 1; the id from `dockingbird --json inbox` always works. Reading marks the message read, and a message that needs no answer (a status notice) then leaves your inbox; `dockingbird read 3 --keep` shows it and leaves it as it was, unread and in your inbox. With `--swarm`, `--engine` or `--no-swarm`, as `dockingbird inbox` takes them, read reads only the messages they pick: `dockingbird read 3 --swarm billing` refuses any other ("Message 3 is from build-2 of swarm onboarding, not of --swarm billing; it stays in your inbox for its reader."), reads and marks nothing, and names `dockingbird read 3 --keep`, which shows any message. A message's id is checked the same way while it waits in your inbox. Without them, `read` reads any message; a script that reads one session's messages on a shared home gives them on every read |

| `dockingbird send notes-1 "Yes, include the closed ones."` | A plain message answers the agent's one open question, or is a new task when it asked none, continuing the agent's thread; two open questions are refused: say which with `--reply-to ROW` (the question's inbox row, not its number in the questions list) or `--kind KIND`. A message sent with `--kind` to an agent that waits for your answer does not answer it and says so; to one that asked without waiting, the same line says the question stays listed. `--file PATH` attaches a text file (repeatable); an agent that has stopped gets the message when you continue it with the command the line names: its own command ("dockingbird notes --as notes-1"), or `dockingbird start --as NAME` for an agent of the default environment, whose own terminal can't read messages |

| `dockingbird send notes-1 --withdraw 3` | Takes a message back: deliveries no agent took yet are withdrawn, and one an agent accepted asks it to stop that work |

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
text:
| `dockingbird wait notes-1` | Returns at once with a message from the agent you haven't seen yet, in your inbox's listing or from an earlier wait, else waits for its next one (any agent's without a name), wherever it sorts in your inbox, past the first page too, for the whole `--seconds N` (default 25 s), and names its row ("Read it: dockingbird read 4"); each message is told once. When the time is up with nothing new, it says how many messages still wait in your inbox ("Nothing new in 45 s. 2 messages wait in your inbox: dockingbird inbox") |

| `dockingbird questions` | The questions your agents ask you, one page, oldest first, each with its row number, the agent, the kind (a choice its tool put up, a plan to approve, the end of a Codex turn at a terminal that takes your next words, or a question an agent on the bus asked you, `bus_send` with kind `question` to its parent), the question's first line, its choices or "any text", and its age (a question an agent asked without waiting for it says `not waiting`); `dockingbird questions 3` shows one whole: the question, its options numbered with their descriptions, and the answer that fits. These are the questions an agent's row in `dockingbird status` counts ("asks you 1 question") and lists under what needs you, by the same row numbers. A question keeps its row number while it is open, as inbox rows do |

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
text: | `dockingbird answer 3 --option 2`, `dockingbird answer 3 "Use Vue."` | Answers a question by one of its numbered options, or in words. An agent at a terminal sees its tool's own dialog on its screen, where you pick your answer with the arrow keys and Enter, or type your words and Enter; `answer` records it and says so ("notes-1's screen shows it: pick it there with the arrows and Enter.", then "dockingbird ui opens that screen from the agent's row."). In `dockingbird ui` ("The GUI"), a click on the agent's row, `a`, the bar's `answer` or Enter on its question in the inbox tab opens that screen; the GUI types no answer. A Codex agent at a terminal whose turn ended takes your words as its next input, typed at its prompt in that screen ("codex-1's prompt takes it: type it there, then Enter."). In the inbox tab, a question of an agent with no screen to open, such as an agent on the bus, says "it has no screen to answer in: dockingbird answer 3 in a terminal". A Claude agent on the bus gets the answer to its tool's question in its hook. A question an agent asked you over the bus is answered with a message that replies to it, the option's words or yours, which the agent reads as any reply; `dockingbird send NAME TEXT` answers it the same way, and so does `send --reply-to ROW` with the question's row in `dockingbird inbox`, an inbox row and not its number in `dockingbird questions` (question 3 may be inbox row 10). A reply to another agent's question is refused, naming that agent. An answer by id to a question that is answered or withdrawn is refused before it is sent, and a row number names an open question only; a follow-up to a withdrawn one is `dockingbird send NAME TEXT --reply-to ID` (the question's message id), which goes to the agent's live session, and to an answered one `dockingbird send NAME TEXT --reply-to ID --kind status --payload '{"phase":"..."}'`. A Codex agent on the bus asks you nothing when its turn ends: once it reported, it shows idle, and `dockingbird send NAME TEXT` gives it more work. A question a stopped agent asked is withdrawn |

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
text:
| `dockingbird results notes-1` | Saves the files the agent attached in its task thread under `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/results/notes-1/`, each named by the first 16 hex digits of its SHA-256 and its name, with no extension, readable only by you and never overwritten (one already there is "saved before"), and prints each path with its type; `--to DIR` also copies them into a folder of yours outside `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`, which `clean` never touches |

| `dockingbird stop notes-1` | Stops the agent and removes its egress proxy and its own network; its thread, its files and its results stay, and its log is copied to `logs/agents/notes-1-<stamp>.log`: Dockingbird's own events, never the tool's output |

| `dockingbird set notes-1 --model claude-opus-5-5 --effort xhigh --compact-at 600k` | Changes a running agent's model, effort or compact point (the context at which its tool compacts the conversation), as `/model` and `/effort` do in Claude Code and Codex, and `/autocompact` in Claude Code: the change applies from the agent's next turn, never one in flight (a running Claude gets the same commands as messages before its next turn, `/model`, `/effort` and `/autocompact`, and is asked for its settings again; a change of its model also types `/autocompact` with the point a set or the start asked again after `/model`, since Claude Code 2.1.288 and later keeps the compact window per model, but not a point only the agent's own `--autocompact` names, which governs whatever the model; Codex's next turn starts with the new words, its compact point as `-c model_auto_compact_token_limit=N`), and `dockingbird status notes-1` shows what was asked beside what the tool reports, with the context used of the compact point (the context used is the last request's: for Claude its input, cache creation and cache read tokens summed; for Codex its `total_tokens`, Codex's own count of the tokens in the context window, read from its rollout as its model and effort are, so a Codex agent's context is unknown, and its model and effort show the values asked, marked `(asked)`, until its rollout names them, for a bus agent after its first turn; with `--json`, the row's `model` and `effort` each carry `asked` beside `reported`, `context_used` and `compact_at` are token counts, and `compact_at_source` says whether the point is `reported`, `asked` or Claude Code's documented `default`, null with no point); until the tool reports the change, the agent's row says "changing to" the values asked.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: Claude's levels are `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max`; Codex takes the levels its model takes.
text:
Claude's levels are `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max`; Codex takes the levels its model takes.

The compact point takes the forms `/autocompact` takes: `auto` (the tool's own window), a token count, `600k` or `1M`, or `600` for 600 thousand; Claude takes 100K to 1M, Codex any count.

A bus agent keeps its task across a compaction: right after it, Claude Code's hook gives the agent its name and its task's delivery, subject and files again, the next delivery fed to it opens with a line saying its context was compacted, and Codex's compaction prompt asks the summary to keep them.

A Claude Code agent at a terminal takes the change too: its supervisor holds it, and `set` says it is "applied by dockingbird ui at its next idle prompt": while the agent has its tab in `dockingbird ui` ("The GUI"), once it is idle, no dialog is open and its prompt box is empty, the GUI types `/model`, `/effort` and `/autocompact` there, one at a time, each with its Enter, and the note on its command bar says what it typed ("typed /effort low"); while the box holds unsent text the change waits ("waits: unsent text at the prompt"), as it does while a dialog is open ("waits: a dialog is open") or the agent works ("waits: the agent is working"), and the GUI never types over or deletes that text; the bar shows `->` between the reported and the asked values, and the agent's row in `dockingbird status` says "changing to" until its status line names the asked model and effort and its own settings the compact point.

A Codex agent at a terminal takes no typed command for it, so `set` names the pick-up that applies the change, `dockingbird stop codex-1`, then `dockingbird codex --as codex-1 -- -m MODEL -c model_reasoning_effort=LEVEL -c model_auto_compact_token_limit=N` (`auto` alone is the plain pick-up), since a change does not outlive a stop; a stop and pick-up read the agent's config again |

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
text: | `dockingbird set notes-1 --skills .agents/skills/a` | Adds skills to a running agent, named as `--skills` names them at a start (skill folders, comma-separated, or a skills folder, each path relative to where you run the command, or absolute) and read on this Mac first, else nothing changes: a skill of a name the agent has is replaced, and none is removed. Its tool lists them from its next turn ("notes-1: skills added: a; its tool lists them from its next turn."): on the bus, Claude Code is told `/reload-skills` before that turn, and Codex reads them when its next turn starts; an agent whose screen runs lists them from its next idle prompt, where Claude Code is typed `/reload-skills` and Codex reads them again itself; an agent at a terminal lists them within seconds, through Claude Code's own watcher or Codex's own re-read. `--skills` goes alone: beside another change, such as `--model`, `set` refuses both and changes nothing. The skills do not outlive a stop: a pick-up has the skills its own start names. A Codex agent started with no skill lists the skills added later within Codex's own budget, 2% of its context window (see **Skills** under [Your own commands (configs)](#your-own-commands-configs)), since Dockingbird sets its `skills.max_context_tokens` only at a start with skills |

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: **Between agents.** An agent sends to another agent of the project by name: in its `bus_send` it sets `to=<name>` (the name `dockingbird status` shows, such as `claude-2` or `review-1`), and Dockingbird delivers the message to that agent's inbox; you do nothing for it to arrive, and a name no agent has, or an agent that has ended, is refused with the reason (`AGENT_UNKNOWN`, `AGENT_ENDED`).
text:
**Between agents.** An agent sends to another agent of the project by name: in its `bus_send` it sets `to=<name>` (the name `dockingbird status` shows, such as `claude-2` or `review-1`), and Dockingbird delivers the message to that agent's inbox; you do nothing for it to arrive, and a name no agent has, or an agent that has ended, is refused with the reason (`AGENT_UNKNOWN`, `AGENT_ENDED`). Dockingbird also tells each agent who works with it: when other agents are already on the same work (the same repository and branch, or the same starter for a scratch-folder agent) as it starts, its first delivery names them (an agent that starts alone gets no such delivery), and every agent on that work gets `Agent <name> joined your work` the moment one starts there and `Agent <name> left your work` the moment one ends or is stopped; an agent on the bus gets such a notice with its next delivery, as a line above it, never as a turn of its own (the notice waits in its inbox until that turn completes), and one in a terminal at its next prompt. An agent of a swarm role that names `send_to` reaches its parent and the agents of its own swarm whose role its `send_to` names alone: any other send is refused `FORBIDDEN` with the reason `NOT_IN_SEND_RULES`, its first delivery names only the others it may message, and it hears of an agent joining or leaving only when it may message that agent. To read what your agents sent each other, when you choose: `dockingbird inbox claude-2` lists the deliveries waiting in claude-2's inbox, and `dockingbird read 7c3d...` (the id a row shows) reads one; from your harness, `agent_inbox` with `agent: "claude-2"` lists them and `agent_read` with that `delivery_id` reads one. Reading another agent's delivery changes nothing: it stays pending for that agent.

**Results.** `dockingbird results notes-1` saves the files of the agent's task thread: the thread its start opened, which every later task you send continues, so a follow-up's files are saved too. A file attached to a message outside it (a question it opened on its own) is reached through the file rows `dockingbird read 3` prints.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: **Its screen.** An agent on the bus can run its tool's own screen, as an agent at a terminal does, while its messages keep arriving whether or not anyone looks: Dockingbird's supervisor types each message into the tool's prompt itself.
text:
**Its screen.** An agent on the bus can run its tool's own screen, as an agent at a terminal does, while its messages keep arriving whether or not anyone looks: Dockingbird's supervisor types each message into the tool's prompt itself.

A tool runs this way only once a probe of its version has passed: Claude Code and Codex do, and `dockingbird status` says which agents have one (`--json`'s `screen`, above).

A start that gives the tool words only a run without a screen takes, after `--` (Claude's `--max-turns`, for one) or in a config's tool arguments, runs without one and says so: "notes-1 runs without a screen: its arguments are for a run without one." So does a start where the tool would ask whether to trust the folder, which nobody at an agent's screen answers: a checkout marked untrusted, or a config that leaves its repository settings off (`repo_settings = true` in it turns them on): "notes-1 runs without a screen: its tool would ask whether to trust this folder." A start that works in a scratch folder (`workspace = "scratch"` in its config) takes the screen form: its container trusts the agent's own folder for Codex and answers Claude's question there, so neither tool asks.

`dockingbird claude --as notes-1` (or `dockingbird codex --as notes-1`) shows the screen of a running agent named `notes-1` and lets you work in it as in any terminal, `/model` and `/effort` included; closing the window, or Docker's detach keys, leaves it working, and the next look redraws the screen.

`dockingbird status notes-1` names both ways to reach it, the send and the screen.

Once you type in its screen, no message is typed there until you send a prompt of your own in it, the tool ends the turn it is working on, or Dockingbird clears what you left (below); a command such as `/model`, a menu you closed or a box you cleared yourself does not count.

While what you typed waits unsent, `dockingbird status` says "A message waits until you finish typing in notes-1's screen." under "Needs your attention"; it does not say so while the tool works on a prompt you sent.

Claude tells Dockingbird when such a turn begins.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: Codex does not, so with Codex your Enter on what you typed begins it, until Codex says the turn is done or its screen stays still for `TUI_STILL_MS` (2 s), as it does after an Enter that only picked from a list.
text:
Codex does not, so with Codex your Enter on what you typed begins it, until Codex says the turn is done or its screen stays still for `TUI_STILL_MS` (2 s), as it does after an Enter that only picked from a list.

A turn Codex starts by itself, from text you queued while it worked, shows as its screen still drawing.

A message that has waited five minutes is told once in its own thread, with how long it waited and why: someone is typing in the screen, the tool hasn't started yet or is still working, or its screen is still drawing.

Sending a prompt in that screen lets in a message your typing held.

If you leave it unsent instead, Dockingbird clears it for you: once that message's wait has been told and no key has come from you for five minutes (`TUI_HOLD_REPORT_S`), it empties the box once with the keys you would press, ctrl-K and then ctrl-U, says so in the message's thread ("Cleared unsent text left in notes-1's screen.

This message had waited 5 min."), and the message goes in once the screen is still.

A key you press puts that off, so a box you are still typing in is never cleared.

Two things the clear cannot reach, since Dockingbird does not read the screen: a box taller than the screen, and a menu or picker left open.

The message then joins what was left or goes into the menu, and its turn is told as failed instead of counted as delivered.

A question the agent's tool asks waits on the bus as before, so `dockingbird answer 3 "Use Vue."` still answers it, and shows in its screen as soon as you look at it there.

`dockingbird set notes-1 --model claude-sonnet-5-5` changes it as any agent on the bus, "applied at its next idle prompt": its supervisor types the tool's own commands there (Claude), types them again at a later pause between turns when the tool missed them, and after repeated misses starts the tool again between turns with the change; a Codex agent's tool is started again with the change.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: Words after `--` that are only the tool's model and effort flags, each followed by its value, keep the screen, at a start or a pick-up alike: for Claude `-- --model claude-opus-5-5 --effort max`, for Codex `-m MODEL` (or `--model MODEL`) and `-c` with its `KEY=VALUE`, such as `-c model_reasoning_effort=high`.
text:
Words after `--` that are only the tool's model and effort flags, each followed by its value, keep the screen, at a start or a pick-up alike: for Claude `-- --model claude-opus-5-5 --effort max`, for Codex `-m MODEL` (or `--model MODEL`) and `-c` with its `KEY=VALUE`, such as `-c model_reasoning_effort=high`.

**Turns and errors.** After each turn, an agent on the bus sends you a status message: `turn 3` with its final text, at `P3`, the lowest priority, so every question and task sorts before it.

An error comes at once, at `P1`, so it sorts before every summary, task and question in `dockingbird inbox` and `dockingbird wait` returns with it: `turn 3 failed` with its tool's own error text (a usage limit, a refused sign-in, any error its tool reports), `notes-1 stopped: its tool exited` when its tool exited or crashed (for Claude, with the exit status), and `notes-1 stopped: the bus refused its session` with the refusal's code.

The agent is each message's sender, and the last two come before its session ends.

If that message can't be sent, the agent's log names the refused send (`FEED_REFUSED` for `messages.send`, or `CRASH_STATUS_FAILED`), and `dockingbird status` still shows a failed turn with its error line, and a crash once Dockingbird's sweep has ended that session.

When Anthropic refuses a Claude agent's sign-in during a turn (as when the login changes on the Mac while agents still hold the old one), Dockingbird tries that turn again by itself once its `turn 3 failed` has reached you: at most `SIGN_IN_RETRY_MAX` (3) times, after 30 s, 60 s and 120 s, each try a `SIGN_IN_RETRY` line in the agent's log, with `dockingbird status` saying "retrying after a sign-in refusal (1 of 3)" meanwhile; a stop, or a message you send, during a wait ends the tries, and if the last one fails too, `status` shows the failed turn and its recovery.

When a Claude agent's turn ends because the model API could not be reached (Claude's `server_error`, such as a refused connection), Dockingbird tries that turn again by itself after 60 s, and again after each try that ends the same way, each try an `API_RETRY` line in the agent's log, with `dockingbird status` saying "retrying since <first failure's time> (retry 1)" meanwhile; a stop, or a message you send, ends the tries.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: A failed turn's subject also names the class Dockingbird read from its error, `turn 3 failed (rate_limit)`: one of `rate_limit`, `usage_limit`, `auth`, `billing`, `server`, `network`, `invalid_request`, `context`, `cap`, `refusal`, `exited` and `other`, which `dockingbird status` names after "failed" and `--json` carries as `last_turn_class` (null for an agent an older Dockingbird started).
text:
A failed turn's subject also names the class Dockingbird read from its error, `turn 3 failed (rate_limit)`: one of `rate_limit`, `usage_limit`, `auth`, `billing`, `server`, `network`, `invalid_request`, `context`, `cap`, `refusal`, `exited` and `other`, which `dockingbird status` names after "failed" and `--json` carries as `last_turn_class` (null for an agent an older Dockingbird started).

An agent with fallback rules (next) may retry the turn or move to its other tool first; an agent without them reports every failure as above.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: **A fallback tool.** An agent on the bus can follow rules for its failed turns and move to the other tool with its conversation.
text: **A fallback tool.** An agent on the bus can follow rules for its failed turns and move to the other tool with its conversation. A config's `[fallback]` table sets them (the example under [Your own commands (configs)](#your-own-commands-configs) shows each key), and `start`'s flags fill the keys a config leaves unset: `--fallback codex` (the tool to move to, never the agent's own), `--fallback-model M` and `--fallback-effort E` (that tool's model and effort; without them, its own defaults) and `--fallback-placement any` or `require-login` (below). A flag that differs from a value the config sets is refused, as `--cpus` is, and so are a model or an effort with no tool to move to and any of these flags at a terminal. Each class has a rule, the table's `[fallback.on]` or its default: `retry` (the turn again after `retry_wait`, 5 minutes unless the table says otherwise, at most `retry_max` times in a row for one delivery, 3 unless it says otherwise), `retry-then-fallback` (those retries, then the move), `fallback` (the move at once) or `report` (the failure reported and left, as with no table). With a tool to move to, `refusal` (a safety system refused the model's response or the request) is the one class that moves; `rate_limit`, `network`, `auth` (after the sign-in retries above), `billing`, `server`, `usage_limit` and `cap` retry, and the rest are reported. A move changes the model in the middle of a task, so a table that wants one for another class names it (`server = "fallback"`); without one (a table with no `harness`, an agent that has already moved as often as it may, or a fallback that is off here, below), `rate_limit`, `network`, `usage_limit` and `cap` retry and the rest, `refusal` among them, are reported. `exited` is always reported. A `usage_limit` retry takes neither `retry_wait` nor `retry_max`: it waits 1, 5 and 15 minutes, then every 30 minutes, until 24 hours after the first failure, and is then reported (or, under `retry-then-fallback`, the agent moves); a retry that completes starts it over, and a pick-up of the agent within those 24 hours carries it on. While a retry waits, `dockingbird status` says so under "Needs your attention" ("claude-1 is retrying after rate_limit (1 of 3), next in 5 min.", or for a usage limit "(attempt 5), next in 30 min, until" the end of its 24 hours), and `--json`'s `rule_retry` is the attempt.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: **The move.** The agent ends its turn and stops, its copy kept: you get `claude-1 stopped after server: moving to Codex` at `P1`, with its tool's error line, and Dockingbird's next sweep ends its session and keeps the copy.
text: **The move.** The agent ends its turn and stops, its copy kept: you get `claude-1 stopped after server: moving to Codex` at `P1`, with its tool's error line, and Dockingbird's next sweep ends its session and keeps the copy. `dockingbird start --as claude-1 --fallback` then continues it on the fallback tool, with its conversation and what waited for it, under the fallback's model and effort. A config's agent moves the same way by its own command (`dockingbird review --as review-1 --fallback`), and Dockingbird's fallback watcher on this computer runs that pickup for you, at most three times for one agent, then names the command under "Needs your attention". That pick-up is refused when the agent records no tool to move to (`FALLBACK_NONE`; `--fallback codex` names one), when it has already moved as often as an agent may, once by default (`FALLBACK_MAX`), and when this home can't sign that tool in (`FALLBACK_NO_LOGIN`, with the `dockingbird login codex` step). `dockingbird status` shows the move under the agent's kept copy, "claude-1 is moving to Codex after server; nothing here picks it up, so run:" and that command, before that sweep and after it (after it, without the class when the copy's summary names none). Before the sweep, an agent the fleet engine started says "its pickup is running" instead, and under `--json` the kept row carries the ask as `fallback_ask` (its `state`, `class` and `error`); every agent row's `fallback` is the table its agent records, or null. Afterwards the agent keeps the tool it ran last: `dockingbird start --as claude-1` picks it up on Codex, and a `--harness` that names the other tool is refused. `dockingbird status claude-1` says how it got there: "moved from Claude Code to its fallback tool". A start whose fallback tool this home can't sign in runs with its fallback off under `placement = "any"`, the default, and says so once ("claude-1 starts with its fallback off: no Codex sign-in here."), its rules taking the defaults without a tool; under `require-login` it is refused (`FALLBACK_NO_LOGIN`) and nothing starts.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: **Configs.** `--command NAME` starts an agent of a command that a config adds, and so does the command's own name after `dockingbird`: `dockingbird start --command review "Check the login flow"` is `dockingbird review "Check the login flow"`, and its agents are `review-1`, `review-2` and so on.
text:
**Configs.** `--command NAME` starts an agent of a command that a config adds, and so does the command's own name after `dockingbird`: `dockingbird start --command review "Check the login flow"` is `dockingbird review "Check the login flow"`, and its agents are `review-1`, `review-2` and so on. [Your own commands (configs)](#your-own-commands-configs), below, explains configs: what they are, where they come from, a complete example, and how to run, list and remove their commands.

**Connections.** A connection lets the agents of a config that names it fetch and push one GitHub branch, and none of them ever holds the key.

Inside the repo's checkout, on the branch the agents work on, run `dockingbird connect github --github someone/myapp` (`github` is the connection's name; `--branch` names another branch Dockingbird has copied).

When Dockingbird hasn't copied the branch you are on, connect copies it first, as a start does ("Copying myapp (main) for the agents ... done"), then connects; for another branch, switch to it and run connect there.

Dockingbird tries the key files your own ssh would use for GitHub (`ssh -G github.com`), in that order, until GitHub accepts one, or takes the one `--key PATH` names: a file of yours that only you can read, never a link.

When the key has a passphrase, `ssh-keygen` asks you for it once, on your terminal, to make Dockingbird's copy without one; Dockingbird never sees it.

Without `--key`, it asks only when GitHub accepted none of your keys without one, and only for the first.

Dockingbird then checks the copy with GitHub from this Mac, against GitHub's own host keys, and names the account it signed in as: "Connected github: someone/myapp (main) over SSH as somebody, with a copy of ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 (no passphrase) kept in Dockingbird until you disconnect." `dockingbird connect github` copies the SSH key your own git uses for GitHub into Dockingbird's volume, without its passphrase, so agents can fetch and push while you are away; `dockingbird disconnect github` or `dockingbird clean --all` removes the copy.

The key reaches every repository your account can, as it does for you; Dockingbird pushes only the branch you connected.

To limit it to one repository, use a deploy key: `dockingbird connect github --github OWNER/REPO --key PATH`.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: `dockingbird connect github --github OWNER/REPO --agent` uses your Mac's ssh-agent instead of a copy of your key: Docker Desktop forwards the agent into Dockingbird's coordinator, which signs in to GitHub with the keys it holds, as your own git does; no key is copied anywhere.
text:
`dockingbird connect github --github OWNER/REPO --agent` uses your Mac's ssh-agent instead of a copy of your key: Docker Desktop forwards the agent into Dockingbird's coordinator, which signs in to GitHub with the keys it holds, as your own git does; no key is copied anywhere.

It pushes only the branch you connected, but the keys reach every repository your account can; `ssh-add -D` or quitting Docker Desktop ends that at once.

To limit a connection to one repository, use a deploy key with `--key PATH`.

Dockingbird checks your shell's agent with GitHub first, restarts itself to take the forwarded agent when no agent runs ("Restarting Dockingbird to use your Mac's ssh-agent ... done"; while agents run, at its next start, and `status` says so), then asks the agent Docker Desktop reaches whether it has a key: Docker Desktop opened from the Dock or Spotlight has no agent of its own session, so open it from a terminal (`open -a Docker`), and load your key with `ssh-add --apple-use-keychain ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`.

`--agent` needs Docker Desktop; the plain Docker Engine forwards no agent.

If your Mac's agent restarts, its forwarded socket may stop answering: requests then fail "your Mac's ssh-agent isn't reachable", and `dockingbird stop`, then any command, starts Dockingbird with the socket bound anew.

A config names the connection in its `connections` list (`connections = ["github"]`); its agents ask for a fetch or a push with `bus_request`, and Dockingbird's coordinator runs it: a fetch leaves the branch as a bundle file in the agent's log folder, with its SHA-256, and a push sends the head the agents published, never an agent's working copy.

A push needs a fetch of the same connection first, and fails when GitHub's branch has commits the published head lacks: an agent merges its newest fetch into its work and shares it, then pushes again, fetching again first when GitHub's branch moved since that fetch.

`dockingbird connections` lists each connection with what its agents may do with which repo and branch; `dockingbird status` shows each connection after the sign-in line, and `dockingbird status NAME` the agent's last request, and why it failed, in plain words.

A push that stopped midway, after which GitHub's branch moved, has a result Dockingbird can't tell: it holds every other push back and shows under "Needs your attention"; check the branch on GitHub, then run `dockingbird connections --release`.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: Fetch and push over SSH are what connections run today; HTTPS tokens and the cloud accounts' requests are later work.
text:
Fetch and push over SSH are what connections run today; HTTPS tokens and the cloud accounts' requests are later work.

**Folders, databases and services.** A connection is a GitHub repo, a folder of this Mac (read-only unless its config says `write`), a database (read-only, or written through the broker with `--writes`), a service (a program of this Mac you declare), an MCP server or a browser (Google Chrome, Firefox or Safari on this Mac, lent while you run `dockingbird serve chrome`, or the same for the name you gave Firefox or Safari); the forms follow.

- **A database (read-only; PostgreSQL only this round).** `dockingbird connect app-db --database postgres://reader@host.docker.internal:5432/app --password` connects it for the configs that name `app-db`. The URL holds the role, the server's host name in lowercase, the port (5432 when you leave it out) and the database name, and nothing else: a role or database that is not a plain PostgreSQL name (lowercase letters, digits and `_`, not starting with a digit, at most 63 characters), a query, a fragment or a password in the URL is refused before anything is saved, and a password in it is never shown again. `--password` asks for the role's password on your terminal, hidden (without a terminal it is read from what you pipe in), never empty, and keeps it inside Dockingbird, never in a file of yours or on a screen; leave `--password` out for a role the server lets in without one.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: Before it says done, Dockingbird opens the database itself, from its own side and through the same path an agent's query takes, and checks it.
text: Before it says done, Dockingbird opens the database itself, from its own side and through the same path an agent's query takes, and checks it. The role must not be able to write, itself (the role it logs in as, whatever role its sessions start as) or through any role it can switch to: not a superuser, not a role that can create roles or databases, replicate or bypass row security, not a member of any role that can write or that reads or writes the server's files, runs its programs, ends other connections, runs maintenance or forces a checkpoint, owning no table and not the database, with no MAINTAIN right on a table, and with no right to call the function that writes a message into the server's log of changes, nor, in any schema, `dblink`, `dblink_exec` or `dblink_connect` (a second connection, outside the read-only transaction), `lo_export`, `lo_import`, `pg_switch_wal`, `pg_create_restore_point` or `pg_stat_reset`. The server must allow no prepared transactions (their maximum is 0, which is PostgreSQL's default). A database that fails is refused with the fix, the connection is removed again, and nothing is kept; one that passes prints `Connected app-db: host.docker.internal:5432/app as reader, read-only, checked from Dockingbird.` and the line that names it in a config. Dockingbird checks again before every query an agent makes.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: A role made for this is read-only, owns no table, has no MAINTAIN right and is not the database's owner: `CREATE ROLE reader LOGIN;`, `GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE app TO reader;`, `GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO reader;`, `GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO reader;`, and, once for each database, `REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION pg_catalog.pg_logical_emit_message(boolean, text, text, boolean), pg_catalog.pg_logical_emit_message(boolean, text, bytea, boolean) FROM PUBLIC;`.
text:
A role made for this is read-only, owns no table, has no MAINTAIN right and is not the database's owner: `CREATE ROLE reader LOGIN;`, `GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE app TO reader;`, `GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA public TO reader;`, `GRANT SELECT ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO reader;`, and, once for each database, `REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION pg_catalog.pg_logical_emit_message(boolean, text, text, boolean), pg_catalog.pg_logical_emit_message(boolean, text, bytea, boolean) FROM PUBLIC;`. That revoke is the cost of the check: every role may call the function by default, it writes a record to the server's log that a rollback does not undo, and it changes the database for every role, not only this one. On PostgreSQL 16 and earlier the function has no fourth parameter, so name its two forms without it. Where the `dblink` extension is installed, `CREATE EXTENSION` lets every role call `dblink`, `dblink_exec` and `dblink_connect`, so the check refuses every role of that database until, once for it and with `dblink`'s schema on the search path, `REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTION dblink(text), dblink(text, text), dblink(text, boolean), dblink(text, text, boolean), dblink_exec(text), dblink_exec(text, text), dblink_exec(text, boolean), dblink_exec(text, text, boolean), dblink_connect(text), dblink_connect(text, text) FROM PUBLIC;` (every form the extension declares), or `DROP EXTENSION dblink;`. PostgreSQL grants the other functions above to no role by default. If the server asks for a password for the role, give the role one (`ALTER ROLE reader PASSWORD 'a long password';`) and add `--password`; the message that says so names the role.

  An agent of a config that names it asks Dockingbird for one SQL statement that returns rows, and reads the rows as a file of JSON lines in its log folder. It never sees the database, its address or the password; a statement that writes, changes the transaction or runs past its time limit fails and changes nothing, and what the database says in its own words is never shown. The server must accept connections from Docker: on Docker Desktop your Mac is `host.docker.internal`; on a plain Linux Engine name the bridge's address instead, and let the server listen on it (`listen_addresses`) and accept it (`pg_hba.conf`). `--to AGENT --until ISO` gives the database to that running agent too. `dockingbird disconnect app-db` removes the connection and the password it kept.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: - **A database the broker writes to.** `--writes` beside `--database` registers the database for writes through the broker: an agent's `bus_request` with `db.execute` gives one statement as `sql`, the values its `%(name)s` placeholders bind as `arguments` (each a whole number or a text; `{}` for none) and, optionally, the most `rows` it is answered; the broker runs it on its own connection in one read-write transaction, under the statement timeout and the row and byte bounds of a query, commits it when it succeeds and rolls it back on any refusal, and answers its rows (none for an `INSERT` without `RETURNING`).
text:
- **A database the broker writes to.** `--writes` beside `--database` registers the database for writes through the broker: an agent's `bus_request` with `db.execute` gives one statement as `sql`, the values its `%(name)s` placeholders bind as `arguments` (each a whole number or a text; `{}` for none) and, optionally, the most `rows` it is answered; the broker runs it on its own connection in one read-write transaction, under the statement timeout and the row and byte bounds of a query, commits it when it succeeds and rolls it back on any refusal, and answers its rows (none for an `INSERT` without `RETURNING`). `db.query` keeps its proof that the role cannot write, so on a role that writes it is refused `role-can-write`, as today: such a connection's agents read with `db.execute` too.

- **A password vault (gopass).** `dockingbird connect logins --vault gopass --login alice https://site.example alice@site.example --totp alice` connects a gopass store for the configs that name `logins`: an agent of such a config, lent your Chrome (`--browser chrome`, below), can ask Dockingbird to sign in to `https://site.example` as the login `alice`, and Dockingbird types the stored password and, with `--totp`, the current one-time code itself, in a tab of its own, and leaves the agent's tab signed in.

Each `--login` names a login by three words: its name (a slug, the agent's word for it and the store entry's name, never the site's), the site's address (its origin, `https://host` or `https://host:port`, stored as the browser serialises it) and the username; `--totp NAME` marks a login whose entry holds a time-based code.

The store's passphrase is asked on your terminal, hidden (without a terminal it is read from what you pipe in), never empty, and kept inside Dockingbird as a database password is; a password or a code is never asked, read or shown by any Dockingbird command.

The store is yours: a gopass store under `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME/vaults/logins` (the connection's name; `--store NAME` names another folder there), which Dockingbird reads from its own side only, read-only, with the gopass inside its image; Dockingbird runs no gopass on your Mac.

You make the store with gopass 1.17.4, the version Dockingbird's image carries, from gopass's release at https://github.com/gopasspw/gopass/releases/tag/v1.17.4: the archive `gopass-1.17.4-darwin-arm64.tar.gz`, whose sha256 is `b052f36631e619fa9391edeee581d1f3937c4c41d432aa4ba673b53401800c0f` (check it with `shasum -a 256` before you open it), holds a `gopass` program to put on your `PATH`.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: Then, once per store: `GOPASS_HOMEDIR=~/.local/share/dockingbird/vaults/logins GOPASS_AGE_PASSWORD="<the passphrase>" gopass setup --crypto age --storage fs` (the `vaults/logins` folder of your Dockingbird home, which is `~/.local/share/dockingbird` unless you set `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`: use that folder then) makes the store with an age identity under that passphrase (a bare `gopass init` fails: it needs an identity first); and for each login, `GOPASS_HOMEDIR=...
text:
Then, once per store: `GOPASS_HOMEDIR=~/.local/share/dockingbird/vaults/logins GOPASS_AGE_PASSWORD="<the passphrase>" gopass setup --crypto age --storage fs` (the `vaults/logins` folder of your Dockingbird home, which is `~/.local/share/dockingbird` unless you set `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`: use that folder then) makes the store with an age identity under that passphrase (a bare `gopass init` fails: it needs an identity first); and for each login, `GOPASS_HOMEDIR=...

GOPASS_AGE_PASSWORD=... gopass insert alice` with the password on the first line and, for a login with a code, the `otpauth://totp/...` line from the site's two-factor enrolment in the body (a counter-based `otpauth://hotp/...` entry is refused when used).

Keep the whole folder `setup` made, its `.config` and `.cache` included: the reads need them.

Before it says done, Dockingbird checks each word and that the store is a real folder of yours there, and prints `Connected logins: a gopass vault with 1 login.` and the line that names it in a config; `dockingbird connections` lists the vault by its logins' names only, `dockingbird status` by its store and those names, and `dockingbird clean --all` keeps your vaults folder whenever anything is in it.

What an agent can do: ask for one sign-in at a time, by the login's name and the sign-in page's address on that site, naming the password field (and a username or code field) by CSS selector; it is told success or a refusal in words (the page not on the login's site, the field not a password field, the vault unreadable, the site not accepting the sign-in, a counter-based code, a browser without a window), never the password, the code, or how long either is.

What it cannot do: read, list, add or change a login or the store; sign in on your own Chrome profile (sign-ins run only in a temporary profile, so Chrome's save-password offer and your Google account never see the password); ask on Firefox or Safari (refused in words: Chrome only in this release); do anything in the browser while the sign-in is typed (its commands are refused in words until it ends).

The agent keeps the site session the sign-in made: its tab is signed in until the browser session ends with the agent.

`dockingbird disconnect logins` removes the connection and the passphrase it kept; the store stays yours to delete.

heading: Operator guide > Delegated agents
summary: - **Checking an agent's log for a value Dockingbird holds.** The coordinator can tell whether a text, or a running agent's harness log, holds any value it keeps (a vault passphrase, a database password, a sign-in's token, a saved key).
text:
