heading: Operator guide > What lives where
summary: **Docker's own configuration.** Dockingbird runs every docker command with its own `docker-config/` (0700, its `config.json` 0600), never with your `~/.docker` (or `DOCKER_CONFIG`), so your saved registry logins and your credential helper are never used: a helper that hangs, on a keychain prompt or after Docker Desktop crashed, can no longer freeze setup.
text:
**Docker's own configuration.** Dockingbird runs every docker command with its own `docker-config/` (0700, its `config.json` 0600), never with your `~/.docker` (or `DOCKER_CONFIG`), so your saved registry logins and your credential helper are never used: a helper that hangs, on a keychain prompt or after Docker Desktop crashed, can no longer freeze setup. Dockingbird needs no login: its image is built from pinned public base images, pulled without your login, and it pushes nothing. From your configuration it copies only `proxies` and `cliPluginsExtraDirs` (and adds your `cli-plugins` folder, where Docker Desktop links buildx), and it reaches the daemon your `DOCKER_HOST`, `DOCKER_CONTEXT` or current context names. Your `proxies` reach every container Dockingbird creates, as Docker's client applies them, and the harness inside it, a user name and password in the proxy URL included (the harness's subprocesses hold them, and Claude's session settings file in the container's private HOME holds them too). Behind a proxy that every connection must use, start with `--egress full`: the egress proxy of `models` and `allowlist` connects to each host directly. It reads your `config.json` and the context's `meta.json` without following a link and within `DOCKER_CONFIG_MAX_BYTES`; if it can't (a symlink, a file too large or not JSON), or the context uses TLS over TCP, docker runs with your own configuration, as before.

**Tool versions.** Claude Code and Codex run from the program store, a Docker volume (`dockingbird-tools`) that holds one folder per downloaded version of each tool.

The first `dockingbird claude` (or `codex`, `start`, `login`, or `dockingbird claude -- --version`) that finds no version of that tool downloads the latest release into it and waits for it, with or without `--json`, verifies it (Anthropic's signed manifest for Claude Code; OpenAI's Sigstore bundles and published digests for Codex), checks that it starts and prints its version, and only then runs it; the line "Getting Claude Code 2.1.296 ..." shows while it downloads.

A later start runs the version it has; `dockingbird update` fetches the latest of each tool you have used, after its rebuild, and says so ("Claude Code 2.1.296 is the latest." or "Got Claude Code 2.1.296.").

To choose a version yourself, `dockingbird pin claude 2.1.285` (or `codex 0.162.1`) writes `versions.toml` in `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`, one line per tool, which you may also edit by hand; `dockingbird pin --clear claude` follows the latest again.

heading: Operator guide > What lives where
summary: A line is `claude = "2.1.285"` or `codex = "0.162.1"` (a version Dockingbird then downloads if it does not have it; it is never changed by a start or an update, and `dockingbird --version` shows it as pinned: "Claude Code 2.1.285 (pinned)"; `dockingbird status NAME` shows the version that agent runs); `"latest"`, or removing the line, returns the tool to the latest release, and `"stable"` is Claude Code's slower channel.
text:
A line is `claude = "2.1.285"` or `codex = "0.162.1"` (a version Dockingbird then downloads if it does not have it; it is never changed by a start or an update, and `dockingbird --version` shows it as pinned: "Claude Code 2.1.285 (pinned)"; `dockingbird status NAME` shows the version that agent runs); `"latest"`, or removing the line, returns the tool to the latest release, and `"stable"` is Claude Code's slower channel.

A line that is not one of those, an unknown key or a file that is not plain TOML of yours stops the command and names the line ("versions.toml: the claude line isn't a version, latest or stable."), so a pin you wrote is never silently ignored.

A config you added with `config add` can pin its own tool instead, `version = "2.1.285"` at its top level or in one of its commands; a repo's own config can't (`dockingbird -h` and `dockingbird config list` say that `version` works only in a config you add, and a start of its commands says to add the config first).

A download that fails verification is never installed and is said out loud; a version that does not start is set aside until `update` ("Claude Code 2.1.296 didn't start, so Dockingbird keeps 2.1.285."), unless you pinned it, in which case it runs anyway.

Nothing in the store is ever run by the container that downloads it, and every other container mounts the store read-only.

Every start that follows a channel asks it first, with one small conditional request from your Mac (at most `TOOLS_CHECK_TIMEOUT_S`, no credential, no redirect followed; a 304 means nothing new): when it names a newer version, a start waits for the download up to `TOOLS_FOREGROUND_WAIT_S`, at a terminal with a live line ("Getting Claude Code 2.1.296  [########........]  45 MB of 89 MB", then "Getting Claude Code 2.1.296 (89 MB) ... done (12 s)"), and past that runs the version you have ("Still getting Claude Code 2.1.296; this start uses 2.1.285.

The next start uses the new one.") while the download goes on in its own container; when the download it waited for is another command's (an `update`, or a start in another terminal), the line says so and the next start checks again ("Another command is getting Claude Code 2.1.290; this start uses 2.1.285.

heading: Operator guide > What lives where
summary: The next start checks again.", or, before that download has named its version, "Another command is getting the latest Claude Code; this start uses 2.1.285.
text:
The next start checks again.", or, before that download has named its version, "Another command is getting the latest Claude Code; this start uses 2.1.285.

The next start checks again."); an agent your own harness starts over MCP (`dockingbird mcp`), the one start that doesn't wait, runs the version you have at once, or, with none yet, is refused as busy, to be tried again ("Claude Code is being downloaded; try again in a minute.", `PROJECT_BUSY` with cause `TOOL_FETCHING`).

Every start from the command line, at a terminal, on the bus and with or without `--json`, always waits for a first download and for a version you pinned, up to `TOOLS_FETCH_TIMEOUT_S` (15 minutes); a script or agent that gives `dockingbird start` a timeout of its own shorter than that should run `dockingbird claude -- --version` (or `codex`) once first, which waits for the same download with its progress lines, and start after it; an agent started over MCP is refused that same way for both.

When the check gives no answer (offline, a TLS or DNS failure), the version you have runs and only `--verbose` says why; a channel never moves a tool to a version below the one you have.

A download that finished after its start gave up waiting is picked up by the next command that needs that tool, or by the sweep of the next start, `sync`, `stop` or `clean`, and checked before it runs; `dockingbird --version` reads only what Dockingbird recorded and asks Docker nothing, so it names a version once the start that waited for it has finished, and a download another command left going (an agent started over MCP, or a start past its wait) only once one of those commands has picked it up; a download container left running past `TOOLS_FETCH_TIMEOUT_S` is stopped and removed, and `stop` stops one in progress.

Unused versions are removed after a download, by `update` and by `dockingbird clean` (the store keeps every version a container uses, in any state, the current and pinned ones, one previous version for an instant rollback, and the one being started).

heading: Operator guide > What lives where
summary: **Docker volumes**, never on your Mac: `dockingbird-state` (PostgreSQL, the broker's socket, tokens, the agents' protected copies of each linked branch and every agent's own copy), `dockingbird-tools` (the program store: each downloaded version of Claude Code and Codex, see "Tool versions"; mounted read-only into every container that runs a tool and read-write into the short-lived tools container alone), `dockingbird-home-claude` and `dockingbird-home-codex` (each tool's credentials store, its `.dockingbird` with the saved key and your rules' copy; mounted into the coordinator at `/dockingbird/home/<tool>` and into the login, tool-help, put and seed containers, never into an agent, which gets its secrets from the coordinator at its start), and `dockingbird-browser-sock-<name>`, one per agent whose config asks for a browser (the socket folder the agent's browser container and the agent's container share; made before the browser container, removed once the agent's container is gone, and swept with the other leftovers when a start was cut short).

heading: Operator guide > What lives where
summary: - `dockingbird-relay`, while a connection exists, on Docker's default bridge: `dockingbird-relay` carries the agents' fetches and pushes to the hosts you connected; it stays up after Dockingbird's idle stop, until `dockingbird stop` or `dockingbird clean --all`.

heading: Operator guide > What lives where
summary: Every object carries the labels `com.dockingbird.profile=<id>`, `com.dockingbird.kind` and `com.dockingbird.version` (agents also `com.dockingbird.session`, `com.dockingbird.metrics-port` and `com.dockingbird.metrics-path`, the port and path the agent's supervisor serves `GET /metrics` on inside the container), and Dockingbird finds and removes its own objects by those labels, each by exact id.
text:
Every object carries the labels `com.dockingbird.profile=<id>`, `com.dockingbird.kind` and `com.dockingbird.version` (agents also `com.dockingbird.session`, `com.dockingbird.metrics-port` and `com.dockingbird.metrics-path`, the port and path the agent's supervisor serves `GET /metrics` on inside the container), and Dockingbird finds and removes its own objects by those labels, each by exact id.

The image also carries `com.dockingbird.commit`, the commit the installed package was built from when it came from git (`docker image inspect` shows it, and `dockingbird --version` names the same commit): a reinstall of the same bytes keeps the image and its label, so the label names the commit that built that image.

Your checkout gets one line per linked branch in `.git/config`, `branch.<branch>.dockingbird`, which `git branch -m` moves with the branch (status, `stop`, the start's refusals and `clean --all` follow the rename at once, by that line; the next start on it records it) and `clean --all` removes from whichever branch holds it, and, from the first start on a branch, `refs/remotes/dockingbird/<branch>`: the head the agents' copy started from, then their commits as of your last sync, which `clean --all` removes too.

`git branch -d` removes the line with the branch but leaves that ref, so every step for a copy or commits kept on that branch says it is "no longer in your checkout" and makes it again first: "git switch -c feature/x dockingbird/feature/x, then dockingbird claude --as NAME" ("git switch -c feature/x" when the ref is gone too); the start, and `dockingbird sync`, then link it again ("Linked myapp (feature/x) to its agents' copy again.").

A new branch you make under a deleted branch's name is never linked to that branch's agents' copy unasked: when that copy has commits the new branch lacks, the start and `dockingbird sync` ask first ("myapp (feature/x) has the name of a branch you deleted.", those commits, then "Carry on from them here?

[y/N]"; picking up an agent whose work is kept on the branch you deleted, `dockingbird claude --as keep9`, names it first: "keep9's work is on the feature/x you deleted." and "Carry on from them here, and pick keep9 up?

[y/N]", and its no says "Nothing linked; keep9's work stays kept."), and `status`'s heading says so ("has a deleted branch's name, so sync asks first: dockingbird sync"), as does sync's line about it after a sync on another branch.

heading: Operator guide > What lives where
summary: Yes links it and goes on as before (the start's and sync's own merge questions included); no, the default, or Ctrl-C links, starts and syncs nothing, and without a terminal (or with `--json`) nothing is linked either.
text:
Yes links it and goes on as before (the start's and sync's own merge questions included); no, the default, or Ctrl-C links, starts and syncs nothing, and without a terminal (or with `--json`) nothing is linked either.

To keep the new branch apart, rename it (`git branch -m feature/x NEWNAME`, as the no says): no link line names it yet, so the next start gives it its own copy (the start's no says "rename it, then run this again"; sync's says only to rename, since sync on the renamed branch has nothing to take).

A checkout cloned again at the same place, a branch made from the agents' ref as above, and one that already has the agents' commits are linked without a question.

Once linked, `git branch -m` keeps the link.

heading: Operator guide > Egress and what stays open
summary: - **Egress, by mode.** `--egress MODE` on `dockingbird claude`, `codex` and `start`, or `egress` in a config (which a flag can't change), picks how far an agent reaches; with neither, the installation default applies (`dockingbird egress` shows and sets it; Dockingbird's own is `full`, no limit).
text:
- **Egress, by mode.** `--egress MODE` on `dockingbird claude`, `codex` and `start`, or `egress` in a config (which a flag can't change), picks how far an agent reaches; with neither, the installation default applies (`dockingbird egress` shows and sets it; Dockingbird's own is `full`, no limit). `allowlist` reaches its tool's own hosts (the model API and the sign-in), the hosts of its presets (`registries`: the package registries of the ecosystems GitHub's recommended allowlist names, npm and Yarn, PyPI, crates.io, the Go module proxy and checksum database, RubyGems, Maven Central and the Gradle plugin portal, NuGet, Packagist and pub.dev, and Hex; `github`: `github.com`, `api.github.com`, `codeload.github.com` and `*.githubusercontent.com`) and the hosts of its config's `allow`, through a proxy container of its own, and nothing else. `models` reaches its tool's own hosts alone. `none` has no network at all, the model API included. `full` is the agent's own network with NAT out and no proxy, as every agent had before, and, with the connectors off, nothing of your accounts. `full` is the default, so a hijacked agent can send out the repo it works on and its own Docker sign-in or key to any host. `dockingbird egress allowlist` closes that for the agents you start from then on: with the registries and GitHub allowed (its list when you give no `--allow`), installing dependencies and reading GitHub's content still work, while sending something out needs a credential the agent does not hold.

- **Your claude.ai connectors never load in an agent.** Claude Code fetches the connectors of a claude.ai login (Gmail, Drive, Calendar and the rest, which act with your own accounts) at every start; the image's managed settings turn that off (`disableClaudeAiConnectors`), in every mode, `--egress full` included, and a repo's or an agent's own settings cannot turn it back on. An agent gets a document by `send`'s `--file` or an artifact, never through your accounts. That holds from Claude Code 2.1.273 (2.1.290 for a trusted repo's own MCP entries); the default channel is past both, so only a pin you write to an older one can let them load, on a Team or Enterprise login.

heading: Operator guide > Egress and what stays open
summary: - **What a blocked host sees.** A host outside the list gets the proxy's `407` and a message that names Dockingbird and the way out ("Dockingbird's egress proxy refuses with 407 a host that is not in the allow list or whose address is not public, and a request that names an upstream proxy of its own: allow a public host with allow in the config, or start with --egress full.
text:
- **What a blocked host sees.** A host outside the list gets the proxy's `407` and a message that names Dockingbird and the way out ("Dockingbird's egress proxy refuses with 407 a host that is not in the allow list or whose address is not public, and a request that names an upstream proxy of its own: allow a public host with allow in the config, or start with --egress full. A host in the list whose name does not resolve, or that does not answer, gets 502, 504 or 500 instead."), so a tool fails with its own proxy-refused error and not a timeout. A host in the list whose name does not resolve gets the proxy's `502` (`Failed to resolve remote hostname`, the same message appended), as the lookup would fail anywhere. TLS is never opened: the proxy tunnels the connection and sees the host name and the port and nothing inside it, and the tool's own certificate check runs against the real server.

- **In `allowlist` and `models`, a tool that ignores the proxy fails; it does not get around it.** Its network has no route out, no gateway and no IPv6, and its only resolver, Docker's, answers the names of containers on that network and no outside name, so a lookup meant to carry data out gets no answer either. A connection to an IP address or an IPv6 literal, and any other traffic (UDP, QUIC, ping), has no route, or is refused at the proxy.

heading: Operator guide > Egress and what stays open
summary: - **A name whose address is not public is refused whether or not it is allowed.** The proxy refuses every address that is not public: a connection to the Mac, your LAN, `host.docker.internal`, Docker's own ranges or another agent's address gets the same `407` and message, and so does a name in the list that resolves to one of them (`allow = ["host.docker.internal"]` resolves to a private address and is still refused); `--egress full` is the way to reach them.
text:
- **A name whose address is not public is refused whether or not it is allowed.** The proxy refuses every address that is not public: a connection to the Mac, your LAN, `host.docker.internal`, Docker's own ranges or another agent's address gets the same `407` and message, and so does a name in the list that resolves to one of them (`allow = ["host.docker.internal"]` resolves to a private address and is still refused); `--egress full` is the way to reach them. The one exception is an agent started with a local model (`local_model` in a config you added): its own proxy admits `model-runner.docker.internal` on port 80, at the addresses that name resolves to when the proxy starts, and no other agent's proxy does. Under `full` there is no proxy, so an agent's own browser (`browser = "chrome"`) reaches this Mac's loopback services through `host.docker.internal` as any `full` agent can; a browser agent that must not reach them uses `allowlist` or `models`.

- **What the list does not limit.** An entry names a host, not a port: an admitted host is open on every port. A host you allow is a host the agent can post to, so allow only hosts you would let it send the repo to. A `*.` entry (`*.corp.example`) admits every name under that domain: the agent picks the name it asks the proxy for, and the proxy's lookup of it reaches that domain's own nameservers. An internationalized name (an `xn--` label) is not admitted this round; an `allow` entry holding one is refused when the config is read.

heading: Operator guide > Egress and what stays open
summary: - **What widens or narrows it.** Add hosts with `allow` in a config (`allow = ["registries", "github", "docs.python.org"]`) and change one start with `--egress`.
text: - **What widens or narrows it.** Add hosts with `allow` in a config (`allow = ["registries", "github", "docs.python.org"]`) and change one start with `--egress`. A proxy mode needs Docker Engine 28 or later, for the agent's network's isolated gateway (`gateway_mode_ipv4=isolated`), and Dockingbird checks no version: Engine 27 refuses the network's create with Docker's own error (shown as `EGRESS_PROXY_FAILED`), and Engine 26 or older ignores the option, so the agent's internal network keeps an address on the Docker host, where the agent can reach what listens on that host outside the allowed hosts. Update Docker Desktop before using a proxy mode on an older Engine; `full` works on any. About 30 networks fit in Docker's default address pools, shared by every Docker network on the computer (this home's agents, another `DOCKINGBIRD_HOME`'s and other programs'): a start that finds no range left, in any mode, is refused with `START_NETWORK_POOLS_FULL`, which names the steps (`docker network ls` lists the networks; `docker network prune` removes every network no container uses, other programs' included; or give Docker more pools with the Docker Engine setting `default-address-pools`). The start's sweep has already removed this home's unused networks, so Dockingbird has nothing more to free. Behind a proxy that every connection must use, only `--egress full` works (see "Docker's own configuration"). A project config in a checkout you marked untrusted can only narrow (`none`, `models`, or a list the default already covers); anything wider is refused with the step `dockingbird trust`. Set the default for new agents with `dockingbird egress`.

heading: Operator guide > Egress and what stays open
summary: - **The default for new agents, `dockingbird egress`.** `dockingbird egress` shows what the agents you start from now on may reach, and whether `egress.toml` in Dockingbird's folder sets it or it is Dockingbird's own default.
text:
- **The default for new agents, `dockingbird egress`.** `dockingbird egress` shows what the agents you start from now on may reach, and whether `egress.toml` in Dockingbird's folder sets it or it is Dockingbird's own default. `dockingbird egress models` or `dockingbird egress allowlist --allow docs.python.org` sets it for this Mac (an `allowlist` with no `--allow` takes the presets `registries` and `github`, and one with entries is exactly them, besides the tool's own hosts), and `dockingbird egress --reset` removes the file. A config's own `egress`, or the flag on a start, still wins for that agent, and an agent you pick up again keeps the mode its last start ran: the default is for new agents. A file that cannot be read as the command writes it (not TOML, another key, a mode or an entry outside the grammar, or no regular file of yours) refuses every start with the file and the key named, and `dockingbird status` and `dockingbird egress` say so in place of the default; none of them ever falls back to Dockingbird's own default, `full`. `dockingbird egress --reset` removes the damaged file and a new mode writes over it; a folder at that name is the one thing both refuse (they say so), so you remove it yourself and run the command again.

- **An agent can read its own credential**: its tool's sign-in, or the saved key, which it can read but not change. That is inherent to running the tool. It is a Docker-only sign-in, so nothing an agent does touches your Mac's own sign-in. A saved API key (`dockingbird login claude --api-key`, or `codex` for Codex) is checked with its provider before the tool starts, through the agent's own proxy in `allowlist` and `models` and directly in `full` (`none` has no network, so nothing is checked there), so a key the provider refuses is refused in seconds ("its provider refused the saved Claude key"), never after the tool's own timeout; a gateway the proxy's list does not name is refused there, for the check as for the tool.

- **The shared credentials store.** Any agent of a tool can corrupt, replace or delete that tool's store, hold its lock or Claude's lease (a denial of service the next start names), or swap later sessions onto another account. Its harness HOME is private, so planted settings, hooks or plugins never load in another agent.

heading: Operator guide > Egress and what stays open
summary: - **Resume carries the earlier run's files.** A resumed copy gets its `.git/config` and hooks reset, but not its files, so a hostile earlier run under the same name can leave content the next one reads (prompt injection, not code execution on your Mac).
text:
- **Resume carries the earlier run's files.** A resumed copy gets its `.git/config` and hooks reset, but not its files, so a hostile earlier run under the same name can leave content the next one reads (prompt injection, not code execution on your Mac).

- **Filling the disk.** An agent can read its repo's whole history and fill its copy, its `/tmp` volume or Docker's disk. `clean` frees it, and a start offers to when Docker is almost out of space. Dockingbird sets no process limit on its containers, and no CPU or memory limit unless you give one (`--cpus`, `--memory`): Docker's own limits apply beyond that.

- **Compilers and runtimes in the image** add no privilege: they run as your uid on a read-only root, nothing in them is setuid, and an agent could download the same tools itself; what the image adds is that they are pinned and checked at build.

- **Holding a lock, keeping Dockingbird awake.** An agent can flock its read-only protected copy or the socket folder, blocking its repo's shares or a broker restart, and an agent that stays alive keeps Dockingbird from its idle stop. `dockingbird stop claude-1` ends it.

- **Agents cannot reach each other except through Dockingbird.** Each is on a network of its own that no other agent joins. The proxies share one NAT bridge, but a proxy refuses every address that is not public, another proxy's among them, so two agents have no channel through it. Their one channel is the message bus (`bus_send` with `to=<name>`, "Between agents" above), which the coordinator checks and you can read.

- **Trust answers.** An agent can edit the remembered trust answers in its tool's state. That grants nothing: the repo's own layers load only with the coordinator's `trusted` file on the read-only config mount, written from the checkout's mark on this Mac (every checkout is trusted unless you ran `dockingbird trust --off` in it), and only for a tool in `PINNED_HARNESSES` (both today), whatever the agent's tool remembers.

- **Your git after sync.** Sync's protections cover sync's own git calls. Your later git commands in that checkout apply the agents' `.gitattributes` with your configured filters; sync says when that file changed and shows the new lines. Review stays yours, as with any pull request.

heading: Operator guide > Egress and what stays open
summary: - **Same uid everywhere.** Every container runs as your uid.
text:
- **Same uid everywhere.** Every container runs as your uid. The isolation between the coordinator and the agents is what each container mounts, not the uid.

- **Prompt injection** through repo content is not addressed. The rules only make the coordination tools the path of least resistance.

- **The coordinator.** The coordinator has no network but SSH to your connections' hosts, through the relay; an agent can ask it for a fetch or a push of its connection's branch, never for the key, and a hijacked coordinator could reach every repository the copied key reaches.

heading: Dockingbird v0.6.5
summary: Release v0.6.5 is the nineteenth tagged version of Dockingbird.
text: Release v0.6.5 is the nineteenth tagged version of Dockingbird. It adds `dockingbird fleet hosts set`, `rename` and `forget`. The fleet places a swarm in the pool's host order. The Dockingbird GUI 0.1.11 comes with it.

heading: Dockingbird v0.6.5 > Install or update
summary: With a license key, install from Zeusfyi's release index.
text:
```bash
UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_USERNAME=license UV_INDEX_ZEUSFYI_PASSWORD="$(pbpaste)" uv tool install dockingbird --index zeusfyi=https://license.zeus.fyi/simple/
dockingbird update
```

With a license key, install from Zeusfyi's release index. Copy the key from your purchase email, then run the first line. The operator guide's "Install" section gives the Linux form and `dockingbird license activate`.

An installed Dockingbird takes this release with `dockingbird update` alone. The update installs the Dockingbird GUI 0.1.11 in place of 0.1.10. A GUI that is already open keeps its version until its server stops.

An update made while agents run is staged and taken once the last agent ends. `dockingbird --version` prints `0.6.5`. The Dockingbird GUI is not yet available to customers.

heading: Dockingbird v0.6.5 > What v0.6.5 changes > Adding, renaming and forgetting a host
summary: `dockingbird fleet hosts set NAME --ssh DEST` adds another computer.
text:
`dockingbird fleet hosts set NAME --ssh DEST` adds another computer. Use `--gcloud VM --zone ZONE --project PROJECT` for a cloud VM. The command reads the host's Docker and Dockingbird homes. It writes the host into `hosts.toml` only when that worked.

When the command fails, nothing is saved and the message says what to try.

`dockingbird fleet hosts rename OLD NEW` and `dockingbird fleet hosts forget NAME` edit the file too. Your own computer is `local` in every fleet line. `local` cannot be a host's name.

A host has one name across your file, the fleet pool and swarm definitions. A rename of a host the pool holds is refused until it is removed there.

A home that holds only a hand-written `hosts.toml` or `fleet.toml` is now used as Dockingbird's own. Commands no longer refuse it with `HOME_NOT_EMPTY`. A folder with anything else is still refused, and the message lists what it found.

heading: Dockingbird v0.6.5 > What v0.6.5 changes > Placing a swarm
summary: A swarm definition may now leave out its `[placement]`.
text:
A swarm definition may now leave out its `[placement]`. The swarm then goes to every pool host that takes swarms, in the pool's order.

`--rank N` on `dockingbird fleet hosts add` or `dockingbird fleet hosts policy NAME` sets that order, 1 first. Each swarm gets a home the fleet chooses.

The fleet places a swarm on the first host in that order with room and green lines. It passes over a host whose home has no clone of the swarm's repository. The next host takes the swarm in the same pass. `dockingbird fleet why ID` names the home it passed over.

When a home's `[[home]]` in `hosts.toml` names `clones`, a folder, the worker fetches the swarm's branch into a clone of its own there. It makes the clone from the home's clone of the repository, on any branch. Nobody links a branch into a home by hand.

When the worker cannot fetch, `dockingbird fleet why ID` names the home with no clone to fetch from. For a failed fetch it gives git's own last line. Check that the branch is pushed and that the host's git reaches the remote. Then run `dockingbird fleet release ID`.

heading: Dockingbird v0.6.5 > What v0.6.5 changes > Starting agents with their swarm and role
summary: The fleet now starts each agent of a swarm with its swarm, role and workload (`--swarm`, `--role`, `--engine`).
text:
The fleet now starts each agent of a swarm with its swarm, role and workload (`--swarm`, `--role`, `--engine`). A home still at an earlier release refuses each start with `dockingbird start: '--swarm' is not an option.`

The fleet holds the workload with the reason `UNKNOWN_OPTION`, and `dockingbird fleet why ID` says `ID is held: UNKNOWN_OPTION`. Update that home, then run `dockingbird fleet release ID`.

heading: Dockingbird v0.6.5 > What v0.6.5 changes > Retiring and replacing agents
summary: A role of a swarm definition may now name `min = 0` when it neither reviews nor tests.
text:
A role of a swarm definition may now name `min = 0` when it neither reviews nor tests. `dockingbird fleet retire` can then let its last agent go once it is done.

`dockingbird fleet replace` now recovers an agent whose last turn failed or whose process crashed. It does what you would do by hand: stop, then pick up. `fleet retire` of such an agent waits until nothing is open in its inbox.

heading: Dockingbird v0.6.5 > What v0.6.5 changes > Refused starts
summary: Two refusals now name a delete command.
text:
Two refusals now name a delete command. One is a start refused because the name belongs to the other tool's kept copy or ended agent. The other is a `--new` refused because the name's copy is kept.

`dockingbird clean NAME --yes` deletes that agent's copy, results and history and frees the name. It appears beside the pick-up. The pick-up stays the one step `dockingbird ui` offers.

heading: Dockingbird v0.6.5 > What v0.6.5 changes > Sampling and inboxes
summary: The fleet worker now samples its host every 30 seconds whatever its homes' inboxes hold.
text:
The fleet worker now samples its host every 30 seconds whatever its homes' inboxes hold. Before, a home with thousands of open rows made every sample late. The host then read `idle_millicores unread` and the fleet admitted nothing to it.

The homes' inbox and checkout reads now run on a thread of their own.

The engine now marks read the open status rows of its own agents once they are gone. That covers agents that retired or died, and agents whose swarm is done or cancelled. It marks up to a hundred rows per home every 30 seconds, so an engine home's inbox no longer grows with every finished swarm.

A question from such an agent stays open. So does any row from an agent the engine did not start.

heading: Dockingbird v0.6.5 > What v0.6.5 changes > Sending and turn reports
summary: A plain `dockingbird send NAME TEXT` now asks the coordinator for NAME's open questions alone.
text:
A plain `dockingbird send NAME TEXT` now asks the coordinator for NAME's open questions alone. It answers the one question or starts a task however many rows your inbox holds. The refusal that said too many deliveries were pending is gone.

An agent's turn reports no longer pile up in your inbox. Each new `turn N` row from an agent replaces its previous one, and each `turn N failed` row its previous failed one.

Every earlier report stays readable by its id (from `--json inbox` or `wait`) and in its thread.

heading: Dockingbird v0.6.5 > What v0.6.5 changes > The Dockingbird GUI 0.1.11
summary: The GUI adds, renames and forgets a host from its sidebar, with `dockingbird fleet hosts set`, `rename` and `forget`.
text:
The GUI adds, renames and forgets a host from its sidebar, with `dockingbird fleet hosts set`, `rename` and `forget`. The GUI is not yet available to customers.

A right click on the DOCKINGBIRD heading opens its menu, "add a host…". Its questions ask over ssh or a gcloud VM, then the ssh destination, or the VM's name, zone and project.

The next question asks for the host's name in the sidebar. A name from the destination is offered when it is free. Over ssh, the form also asks for PATH for docker there and the docker host URL there, each optional.

A right click on a fleet host's heading opens its menu. "rename…" asks for the new name with the old one offered. "forget…" forgets the host once you type `y`. `local`, this computer, has neither.

The Dockingbird layer's `h` asks the same from the keyboard. While a change runs, the command bar's note says so, then gives the command's answer. A tap on a note the bar cuts short opens it whole.

The DOCKINGBIRD heading now shows as soon as `dockingbird fleet hosts` answers, with this computer alone too. A first host can be added on a fresh install.

While any of the GUI's Dockingbird forms is open, a drag over a pane still selects and copies. The copy view still opens, so a destination or a name can be copied from a pane into the question.

Every right-click menu's items now sit one cell in from its border. A popup drawn over bold text no longer paints its border bold, which a terminal without font fallback showed as missing-glyph boxes.
